en: The Illumination of the Lamp of the Guhyasamāja Tantra: A Commentary on the Six Points, by Vīravajra, a Master of the Two Vedas. Oṃ, homage to the glorious Vajrasattva!
The First Chapter.

Having paid homage to the Lord Śrī Vajrasattva— who is the Sovereign King of Glorious Tantras, who is to be understood through the most clearly revealed Yoga Tantras, who is the Buddha Samāja of the Jinas, whose domain belongs to the Sons of the Conquerors, which is bound by the six parameters, which was obtained from the illustrious Nāgārjuna, which is the abode of the two stages, and which is sealed by all the Buddhas— the powerful Candrakīrti shall now reveal that Lord in due order.
First, there should be the stage of generation (utpattikrama), which accomplishes the form of the mantra;
the second stage is said to be the mere contemplation of the mind (cittanidhyapti).
The third stage is the delightful vision of the truth within the conventional;
the fourth stage is said to be the purification of the conventional through the truth.
The fifth is called "Yuganaddha" (the Union), which is the joining of the two truths;
this sixth branch of the practice is a compendium of the meaning of all tantras.
He who knows the many variations of these sequences through the method of expansion (prastāra),
as well as their synthesis, is indeed a knower of the Tantra.

“Because mantras arise from the mind and because of the purification of this body through the practice of yoga, one should understand the meanings of the five clusters in sequence and enter the six points. Thus it is said.
Up to ya, ra, la, va, ending with ha; those ending with ka, kha, gha; those ending with jha;
and likewise those ending with ḍa, ḍha, pa—each of these is rooted in a single syllable.
This *Śrī-samāja-karaṇḍa* consists of eighty-four thousand sections of Dharma; therefore, it is the crest-jewel of all tantras.
In this short text of great meaning, the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, regarding the difficult-to-master tantra of the *Samāja* of the Great Sage,
people are utterly bewildered by the seven ornaments that are so hard to understand.
Therefore, having understood this with effort through the grace of my guru’s feet,
I shall explain its divisions out of a desire to benefit sentient beings.
The introduction consists of five elements, the logic is fourfold,
the commentary has six aspects, and the narrative is of four kinds.
The fifth has two divisions, the sixth possesses five divisions, and the seventh has two divisions; such, in brief, are the poetic ornaments.
I shall provide a sequential exposition of each one of the seven ornaments, following the method of the explanatory treatises.
What is the name of this treatise, for what purpose was it composed,
who is its author, what is its authority, and what is its purpose?
The name of the tantra shall be its designation; the cause is for passionate people;
Vajrasattva is its author, and its extent is now proclaimed.
Furthermore, it consists of four types: the *pariccheda*, the *kalpa*, the *khaṇḍa*, and the *paṭala*; these exist both according to their textual content and by number.
The purpose, moreover, is mathematics, the ritual procedures for pacification and so forth,
the eight supernatural attainments, and even supreme Buddhahood itself.
The second introductory section (upodghāta) is now stated again:
the continuum (santāna), the cause (nidāna), the etymological explanation (nirukti), and also the reason (hetu).
Birth among human beings is called "continuity" (saṃtāna),
while the departure from the midst of the harem is the "causal basis" (nidāna).
Restraint as taught in the Vinaya is called "etymological definition" (nirukti);
one who practices the Dharma while desiring its fruit is said to be the "cause" (hetu).

This is the fourfold method for the nature of detachment; now I shall explain the arising of the five Buddha families within the framework of the nature of passion, as well as their becoming a single family, which is intended as the principle for the clear realization of the meaning.
This is called the "continuum," and its causal basis has been demonstrated.

The six-fold commentary on the first chapter states: "The grasping of the vajra and so forth, as well as etymological derivation, is declared to be the cause for the practice [of yoga] through the aesthetic sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and others."
Furthermore, the third ornament is the determination of the sixfold points (ṣaṭkoṭipada),
which is taught in the system of Yoga Tantra and serves to awaken the meaning of that which is sealed.

It is explained according to the distinction between intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*), non-intentional language (*asaṃdhyābhāṣā*), provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), and definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
That which is according to the letter and that which is not according to the letter are proclaimed as the six points.
The Jina speaks with indirect meaning (*neyārtha*) for those who are obscured and unfortunate;
he speaks again with direct meaning (*nītārtha*) for the sake of revealing the true reality.
The revelation of the reality of phenomena to beings of superior inclination by means of the employment of contradictory speech— that is called "intentional language" (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*).
In the various rituals of the mandala and so forth, as well as in the conduct [of yoga],
the explicit explanation of the meaning according to its respective context is that which is spoken according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*).
Words such as *koṭākhyaka* and others, which are excluded from both worldly usage and the treatises, are the conventions of the Tathāgatas; that is proclaimed to be "not ordinary speech" (*naruta*).
For the sake of awakening beings with dull faculties, the teaching of reality is very clear and explicit; it is declared not to be of intentional meaning (*saṃdhyā*).
The sixfold division has been stated; now the different modes of exposition are described:
the literal meaning (akṣarārtha), the complete aspect (samastāṅga), the internal (garbha), and the esoteric (kolika).
The first [type] is indeed singular; the [second], comprising all the limbs, is of two kinds. The *garbhin* is known to be threefold, while the *kolika* is considered to be twofold.
Many who are learned in external treatises are devoted solely to the mere words;
therefore, for the sake of illuminating their proficiency therein, the literal meaning is now being declared.

For those who have taken refuge in the sūtras and other scriptures, [this practice] has been revealed with all its constituent parts, in order to eliminate remorse and through the yoga of the generation stage.
It is called "pregnant" because it contains within it the revelation of the dharma of passion;
it is the discernment of the three types of knowledge regarding the realization of the truth of conventional reality.
The luminous light and the awakening to the union (yuganaddha) are declared to be the two kinds of *kolika*; *kola* is a term denoting the ultimate limit.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, the speaker who wishes to cause [the teaching] to be heard does so further through two types of divisions:
that which is designated as the "continuous exposition" (*sattra-vyākhyāna*) and the second, the "exposition for disciples" (*śiṣya-ākhyāna*).
One should not apply the literal meaning, nor the intentional terminology, nor even the interpretable meaning;
rather, the explanation of the entire body of the text according to the literal sense of the syllables is called the "Sattra" exposition.
The non-literal, the definitive meaning, as well as the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā),
the cryptic (garbha), and the esoteric (kolika)— these are held to be the explanations for disciples.
Relying upon the two stages, the Tathāgatas have demonstrated various methods of exposition according to the explanatory tantras for the sake of those to be trained;
these beings in the world are born under the influence of destiny and always seek to hear [the Dharma].
Because they possess various types of mental dispositions, five kinds of persons are recognized:
the jewel, the sandalwood, the lotus, the white lotus, and likewise the blue lotus.
They have been described by the Omniscient One as having distinct characteristics by nature.
One who is skilled in retention but has not heard the subject matter in its entirety will forget it in an instant, like the well-known person Utpala;
having heard much more than can be grasped, he is unable to explain it.
The person known as Puṇḍarīka is like a cotton plant;
being full of faith, compassionate toward his parents, and having a heart that expands through hearing the Dharma, he is like a jointless bamboo.
The person renowned as Padma is a listener who is like a hollow reed.
One who has little learning and is full of conceit cannot be helped when speaking excessively without foundation; such is the person known as "Sandalwood.
One who is well-behaved, pure, skillful, wise, and consistent in his commitments [is worthy of help].
Having heard it, one should proclaim it correctly; these are the renowned jewel-like persons:
Puṇḍarīka, Utpala, Padma, and Candana—these four persons are indeed the persons who explain the discourse on the Dharma.
One who is fit for the yoga of the completion stage, adorned with virtuous conduct,

and known as a "jewel-like person" (ratnapudgala), is a vessel for the explanation [of the teachings] to disciples; having thus examined who is a worthy recipient and who is not, according to the distinctions in the knowledge of persons.
The wise Vajrācārya should provide a twofold explanation:

first, the explanation of the sixfold parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) of the first chapter; and by means of these six ornaments, the determination of the two truths, which is indeed the seventh ornament, the practice of the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
The explanation taught according to the *Vyākhyātantra* is very difficult to obtain;
for it is by this alone that the Yoga Tantras are led [to their meaning], and not otherwise.
Therefore, one should diligently uphold the Yoga Tantras from the Vajra Guru.
"From one skilled in the explanatory tantras,
by means of the sequence of the causes and their application"— this is the logic of the narrative concerning the sevenfold ornaments.
Now, the summary meaning of the seventeen chapters is set forth.
Mahāvajradhara,

consisting therein of both the signifier and the signified, having first bestowed the initiation of knowledge (*vidyābhiṣeka*) upon those capable of hearing it within the emanation mandala (*nirmāṇamaṇḍala*) in the first chapter, taught the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) of the conceptual and perfected stages (*kalpita-niṣpannakrama*) through the distinction between the interpretable and definitive meanings.
Even in the sixteenth chapter of the *Māna*, having reached another point, it describes the yoga of the two types of deities, stating this meaning:
"In the *Samājottara*, the teaching of the Dharma by the Buddhas relies upon two sequences:
the sequence of generation (*utpattikrama*) and the sequence of completion (*niṣpannakrama*)."
In that regard, the second chapter illuminates the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) alone;
the third chapter clarifies the yoga of the completely pure deity;
and the fourth chapter shows the initiation mandala (*abhiṣeka-maṇḍala*).
In the fifth chapter, he teaches the practice of yoga;
in the sixth chapter, he teaches the consecration of body, speech, and mind;
and in the seventh chapter, he elaborates upon the practice taught in the fifth chapter.
In the eighth chapter, he describes the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*);
in the ninth chapter, he describes the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) concerning non-dual reality (*tattvādvaya*);

and in the tenth chapter, he describes the incitement of the heart-mantra of the deity who is of a non-meritorious nature, for the purpose of bringing about the desired accomplishments (*abhimatasiddhi*).
In the eleventh chapter, he demonstrates the accomplishment of the mantra-body and the accomplishment of the gnosis-body;
in the twelfth chapter, he speaks of the transformation of the great mudrā;
and in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters, he speaks of the expansion of ritual activity.

In the fifteenth chapter, it is stated that all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are achieved only by one who has realized the reality (*tattva*); thus, he teaches the illusion-like meditative absorption (*māyopama-samādhi*).
In the sixteenth chapter, as explained in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, he elaborates upon the powder mandala (*rajo-maṇḍala*) described in the fourth chapter.
In the seventeenth chapter, he set forth the commitments and vows (*samaya-saṃvara*).
Now, the division of the sixteen million words (*ṣaṭkoṭipada*) and the division of the fourfold narrative (*caturvidhākhyāyikā*) for the seventeen chapters are being set forth.
From "Thus have I [heard]" up to "dwelt" constitutes the fourfold narrative.
From "inexpressible" onwards, beginning with the assembly and ending with "dwelt in the heart of the garment of bodhicitta," is of interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
The samādhi called Sarvatathāgatābhibhavanavajra, the samādhi called Jñānapradīparajovajra, the samādhi called Kāyavākcittavisaṃvādanavajra, and the fourfold narrative.

The meditative absorption named *Mahārāgavinaya*, the meditative absorption named *Samayodbhavavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Ratnasaṃbhavavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Mahārāgasaṃbhavavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Sarvatathāgatānurāgaṇavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Rāgadharānurāgaṇavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Vairocanavajra*, the meditative absorption named *Sarvatathāgatābhisaṃbodhivajra*, the meditative absorption named *Dharmaratnākara*, the meditative absorption named *Kāyavākcittavajra*, [and] the interpretable and definitive meanings.

"The secret of body, speech, and mind" refers to the words "arising from the vajra-samaya. Thus, the fourfold narrative is the embodiment of the Great Knowledge-Person (*mahāvidyāpuruṣa*). [The mantra: *īrṣyārati*. Aho! Indeed, of Samantabhadra, the Vajra-holder of body, speech, and mind. *First Chapter: Commentary on the Six Points.*
"By means of the practice of non-arising, this arising is proclaimed. This concludes the non-esoteric (nāsandhya) [portion].

From "In the absence [of things], there is no cultivation" and so forth, up to "Homage to you, O Bodhicitta," is the fourfold narrative of Mahāvajradhara’s *bodhicitta* verses. It begins with "One’s own mind is free from all entities, devoid of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and the grasped and the grasper; through the equality of the selflessness of phenomena, it is primordially unarisen and has emptiness as its intrinsic nature," and continues until the end. This is the non-esoteric [portion].

Chapter Two. Now, from the words "Then the Blessed One" (*atha bhagavān*) up to "I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu-vajra*" (*om dharmadhātu-vajra-svabhāvātmako 'ham*), the meaning is both provisional (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*).
From the words "The great jewel of five colors" (*pañcavarṇa-mahāratna*) up to "one should emanate, consisting of emanation" (*sphārayet spharaṇātmakam*), there are four types of narratives.

From the words "One should draw a moon mandala situated in the center of the space-element" (*ākāśadhātumadhyasthaṃ candramaṇḍalamālikhet*) up to "the chapter named Vajravyūha" (*vajjravyaho nāma paṭalam*), the meaning is both provisional and definitive.
The third chapter. From "Then," etc., up to "they requested with the King of Praises," is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
From "All Tathāgatas," etc., up to "O Charioteer of the Sound-Maṇḍala," is without intentional ambiguity (*nāsandhya*).
From "Then, O Vajradhara," etc., up to "the form of the maṇḍala," is according to the literal meaning.
Now, from the words "Then, therefore, I shall fully explain" up to "the mind-maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas," the meaning is to be interpreted (neyārtha).
The Fourth Chapter. From the words "Now" up to "he speaks the characteristics of conduct," the meaning is according to the literal expression (yathāruta).
From the words "arisen from the object free of conceptual construction" up to "the unsurpassed Mahāyāna," the meaning is not esoteric (nāsandhya).
The section beginning with "Caṇḍāla" and ending with "those intent on reviling the teacher do not succeed in the practice" is to be taken literally (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "those who take life" and ending with "they are indeed capable in the practice" is intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
The section beginning with "mother and sister" and ending with "the wise one free from conceptual construction" is of both interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
*Vajū* (omitted in Ms; *vajūmaṇḍala* in M). Chapter on Samādhi. *Maṇḍalamuttamam* (MS: *agrayāne hyanuttare*).

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, from "Then indeed... up to "...this is the stage of the conduct of awakening" is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). From "Then indeed, the ineffable... up to "...they fainted" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Now, from "Then the Blessed Ones... up to "...remained seated upon their respective thrones," this section contains both interpretable (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) meanings; up to the end of the "Chapter on the Supreme Conduct" (Caryāgrapaṭala), it is not in the sandhyā-bhāṣā.
This concludes the fifth chapter. Now, from "Then... up to "...characterized by the definition of mantra," this section contains both interpretable and definitive meanings.

The section ending with "characterized by body, speech, and mind" is intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*); the section ending with "characterized by body, speech, and mind" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). The sixth chapter. Now, beginning with "Then the Blessed One," and so forth; beginning with "Then the glorious Vajradhara," and so forth; and beginning with "Then the Blessed One," and so forth, up to the end of "by serving [the guru], one quickly attains accomplishment," is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "one who eats alms" and ending with "one who enjoys all desires" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The section beginning with "the Buddhas dwell" and ending with "by the service of all desires" consists of four types of narratives.
The section beginning with "through the union of the recollection of the Buddha" and ending with "one shall attain enlightenment" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
The passage beginning with "sixteen years old" and ending with "delightful" is not *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
The passage beginning with "recollection of the Buddha" and ending with "the form of the mandala" is *sandhyābhāṣā*.
The passage beginning with "how is that? and ending with "may it be so for me too" is *yathāruta* (literal).
In this regard, from "How so? up to "one shall attain accomplishment most easily" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language);
from "How so? up to "extremely pure" is *nāsaṃdhyam* (non-intentional language);
and from "How so? up to "the chapter on conduct" (*caryāpaṭala*) is *yathārutam* (literal).
The Seventh Chapter. Now, from "Then the Blessed One... up to "...the Supreme Victor performed the worship of the land" is to be taken literally (*yathāruta*).
From "Passion, hatred, and great delusion... up to "...homage to you, O Vajrayāna" is of both interpretable (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meaning.
From "Now... up to "...O bearer of the Vajra-jewel" is free from intentional terminology (*nāsandhya*).
The section beginning with "pūjām" and ending with "tiryagbhyo 'pi prakalpayet" is *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language);
the section beginning with "śucau" and ending with "meghāṃ sphared budhaḥ" is *yathāruta* (literal);
and the section beginning with "padmam" and ending with "prapūjayet" is of both interpretable (*neya*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meaning.
The passage beginning with "a hundred *yojanas*" and ending with "the secret vajra-knowledge" is to be taken according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).

[The section] marked as "Cintā" [is] "the Buddhas and the secret of the knowledge-vajra holders. This concludes the sixfold commentary on the first chapter. The eighth chapter. The passage beginning with "Then Vajradhara" and ending with "of those possessing Buddha-knowledge" is to be taken according to the literal meaning.
The passage beginning with "situated in the center" and ending with "vajra-array" is of both interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
Now, the section beginning with "atha khalu" and ending with "śuddhatattvārthasamayaḥ" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
This concludes the ninth chapter. Now, the section beginning with "atha bhagavān" and ending with "samatā na kvacit sthitam" is not *saṃdhyābhāṣā*.
Furthermore, the section beginning with "atha bhagavān" and ending with "tasya jīvitam" is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
From "O King" (*rāja*) up to "the ocean of the Victors' bodhicitta" (*jinodadhi*), this is *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).

The tenth chapter. Now, from "Then Vajradhara" (*atha vajradharo*) and "Then the Blessed One" (*atha bhagavān*) up to "the samādhi called Samayavajra" (*samayavajro nāma samādhiḥ*), this is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). From "the Great Vajradhara" (*mahāvajradharam*) up to "the samādhi called Candravajra" (*candravajro nāma samādhiḥ*), this is *sandhyābhāṣā*.
The section beginning with "situated in the center of the element of space" and ending with "the samādhi named Saṃbodhivajra" is of non-implicit meaning (*nāsandhya*).
The section beginning with "on the mountains" and ending with "the compendium of meditative absorptions" (*dhyānasamuccaya*) is of both interpretable and definitive meaning (*neyanītārtha*).
The section beginning with "Akṣobhya" and ending with "knower of the pledge" (*samayābhijña*) is according to the literal expression (*yathāruta*).

The section beginning with "pañcaśūlam" and ending with "vidyāpuruṣapaṭala" is in *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language). The eleventh chapter ends here. Now, the section beginning with "atha vajradhara" and ending with "nāṭako 'yaṃ vibhāvyate" is not in *saṃdhyābhāṣā*.
The section beginning with "mahāṭavī" and ending with "sarvasiddhisamuccaya" contains both interpretable (*neyārtha*) and definitive (*nītārtha*) meanings.
From "body, speech, and mind" up to "possessing a radiance equal to Mañjuvajra" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
From "by one's own mantra" up to "the Vajra-knowledge holders attain accomplishment" is *yathāruta* (literal).
From "by the nectar of service and knowledge" up to "the achiever of the reality-meaning of mantras" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā*.
The passage from "In the great forest," etc., up to "attains accomplishment" (*siddhiṃ samaśnute*) is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The passage from "At the four junctions" (*catuḥ-sandhyā*), etc., up to "by the impelling of the divisions of the day" (*dinabheda-pracodanaiḥ*) is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).

The statement "Accomplishment is said to occur within half a fortnight by those born of the supreme secret" (*pakṣābhyantarataḥ siddhir uktā guhyāgrasaṃbhavaiḥ*) is *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
In that regard, the section beginning with "tattredam" and ending with "sādhanāgranirdeśapaṭala" is to be taken according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
Chapter Twelve. Now, the section beginning with "atha bhagavanta" and ending with "vajraghoṣamudīrayan" is to be taken according to the literal meaning;
the section beginning with "aho buddhanaya" and ending with "mantranayaṃ dṛḍham" is *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
The section beginning with "unproduced" (*anutpanna*) and ending with "the arising of gnosis is cognized" (*jñānotpādaḥ pramīyate*) is not of intentional language (*nāsandhya*).

The section beginning with "Speak, O Blessed One, the delightful compendium of all mantras" and ending with "'recitation' (*jāpa*) is said to be by those who are neuter" is intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
The section beginning with "O Lords of the Vajras" and ending with "by those being served according to their desires" is literal (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "O assembly of delusion" and ending with "the foremost jewel of the practitioner" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The section beginning with "the vajra situated in the center of the heart" and ending with "is spoken for the sake of protecting awakening" is according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The section beginning with "situated in the center of the space-vajra" and ending with "the samādhi called 'illuminator of the mantra of the vajra-jewel'" is intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
From "in all aspects" (*sarvākāra*) up to "one should pierce the wheel upon the water" (*jalasyopari cakramet*), it is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).

From "having emerged from the pledge" (*samayādetya*) up to "the meditative absorption named 'treading upon the feet of the ocean of vajras'" (*vajrodadhipadākrānto nāma samādhiḥ*), it is intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).

From "the maṇḍala of Mahendra" (*māhendramaṇḍala*) up to "the meditative absorption named 'the manifestation of Vajrasumbha'" (*vajrasumbhaprabhāvano nāma samādhiḥ*), it is according to the literal meaning.

The section beginning with "By means of the vajra" and ending with "the vajra-maṇḍalas" is to be interpreted in this manner. Chapter Thirteen. In the fourteenth chapter, the garland-mantras and the applications of ritual activities are presented according to their literal meaning;
however, some among them—occurring within the intervals of the *nirodha-krodhas*—are expressed in the *sandhyā-bhāṣā* (twilight language).

Similarly, in the fifteenth and seventeenth chapters, there are certain vajra-words that are spoken in intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*), some that are not spoken in intentional language, some that are according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*), some that are not according to the literal meaning, and some that are of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) and some that are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Regarding these six categories of words, the Blessed One taught the sūtra and explained it in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*): "There is intentional language, yet no [thing] spoken in intentional language; there is interpretable meaning, yet no [thing] of interpretable meaning."
"In the Yoga Tantra, there is indeed neither 'according to the letter' nor 'not according to the letter' within the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭikāya*).

Thus, by this sequence—beginning from the "abiding place" (*vijahārapada*) through the explanation of the six parameters and the fourfold explanation—the meaning of the *Śrīsamāja* is sealed. Without having realized that, one relies merely on the literal meaning of the words; [this concludes] the explanation of the six parameters for the first chapter.
40–41. Beings attached to sense objects indeed become adversaries; through the cause of the marvelous, they act with negligence and fall under the power of karma.
42. As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇavyākhyātantra*:
43. "O wise ones, having attained this supreme method, the Lord of the Guhyakas..."
44. Having encountered what appears to be the clear meaning, they indeed fall onto a wrong path.
45. Filled with great joy, they say, "We are yogis.
46. Constantly delighting in conceit, they possess a dharma that is merely a fabrication of illusion.
47. They do not understand the assembly, yet they perform the rituals and so forth.
48. They do not protect the secret, but reveal it everywhere.
49. Having attended upon the master, who is like Indra and is truly like a Buddha, [they act thus].
50. In one moment they give rise to hatred, and likewise in a moment they give rise to affection;
51. They go even to those who should not be approached—mother, sister, and son;
52. They commit the murder of mother and father, as well as the killing of other living beings.
53. They indeed speak falsehoods and especially commit theft;
54. they go to the wives of others and perform other despicable acts;
55. they do not know your samādhi, which arises from the knowledge of suchness.
56. Even when there is only a slight fault, they perform malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
57. Lacking the application of yoga, these practitioners of mantras do not achieve success.
58. They are constantly devoted to external treatises and possess skill solely in their practical application.

The father and mother are said to be the support of all, as well as the two syllables. The letter *e* shall be the mother, and the letter *va* is remembered as the father; the *bindu* therein is their union, a union most wonderful.

The *bindu* is the reality (*tattva*) of the Unstruck (*anāhata*), and the syllables born from it are likewise. He who understands these two syllables of the Dharma-seal is a knower of reality;

he shall become a turner of the Wheel of Dharma for all sentient beings. If a person, having understood them, recites these two syllables constantly, they are external to the Buddha-qualities, like an echo, devoid of enjoyment. The Blessed One, possessing the eightfold sovereignty, always abides in the state of bliss. and Dharmadhātuvajra is Samantabhadra.

"By those belonging to the five families, designated as the space-element" means that he dwelt together with the Tathāgatas who pervade the sky;
this refers to the abiding of the Tathāgatas situated within the hollow of the firmament.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, he says "tadyathā" and so forth in order to demonstrate this by means of an analogy:

just as sesame seeds within a sesame pod exist in mutual contact, remaining in a state of mutual compression, so too at the time of teaching, the Blessed Ones—the Tathāgatas of all—remain pervading the sky; such is the intended meaning.
This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
[The phrase] "equal to the atoms of the Buddha-fields" refers to Tathāgatas,
inexpressibly inexpressible Bodhisattvas, and Buddha-fields, all of whom have become the very limbs and members of Mahāvajradhara himself.
