Therefore, that very Blessed One, having expanded his own body into a mandala in the form of the noble mandala-circle, sat in the center of the peaked pavilion for the sake of attracting those beings to be trained.
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Having thus demonstrated the excellence of the teacher, the place, and the assembly, [the author] now says "Then the Blessed One," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the logical method by means of the five strands of sensual pleasure for the sake of those beings dwelling in the desire realm who are attached to sense objects.
Here, "then" (*atha*) signifies immediate succession.
He is called Bhagavān because of his possession of the eightfold sovereign powers.

"He is both great and Vairocana," thus he is Mahāvairocana. Having set aside the form of one free from passion (*vītarāga*), he emanated himself in the form of the Great Vajradhara. For the sake of abandoning passion through passion, he entered that samādhi called "The Great Passion of all Tathāgatas" (*mahārāga*)—wherein "great passion" (*mahārāga*) is attachment to sense objects for the purpose of purifying sentient beings—and having done so, he caused that aforementioned array of all Tathāgatas to enter his own body; the meaning is that he drew them in by means of the hook of light rays from his seed-syllables and caused them to enter his own body as the very nature of the aggregates, elements, and so forth.

Then all those Tathāgatas, for the sake of nourishing the Blessed One and for the sake of gladdening the Blessed One with the bliss of supreme joy, established themselves within the body of the Great Vajradhara; having removed their former appearances and manifested the forms of divine women, they emerged from the body of the Blessed One. Regarding this, he shows it by means of the passage beginning with "some" and so forth: the earth element in the form of Locanā, and the water element in the form of Māmakī.
The fire element is in the form of Paṇḍaravāsinī;
the wind element is situated in the form of Tārā;
furthermore, by way of the intrinsic nature of form, he is Vairocana.
Ratnasambhava by the nature of sound; Amitābha by the nature of fragrance; Amoghasiddhi by the nature of taste.
That Akṣobhya is by way of the intrinsic nature of contact—this is the interpretable meaning (neyārtha).

"Great" and "passion" (rāga) together constitute "great passion" (*mahārāga*); that which has this as its nature is the "one whose nature is great passion. Its "method" (*naya*) is the means for direct realization through purification by way of the sequence of passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion. Having entered into that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he caused that entire array of all Tathāgatas to enter into his own body.

Having removed that attachment to the external array of the Tathāgatas as an object of perception, he empowered himself with the thought, "I am the body composed of all the Tathāgatas. This is because of such statements as: "The self is indeed the state of all Buddhas; it is indeed the state of all Sages," and so forth. (First Chapter: Explanation according to the Six Principles)
Now, "Then all those Tathāgatas," and so forth, is to be understood as before according to the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Having thus demonstrated the mastery over desires through the manifestation of the *dhāraṇī*-maṇḍala of the *sattva*-tantra, [the text] now says "Then," and so forth, showing the activity of Akṣobhya’s manifestation of the gathering maṇḍala (*saṃgraha-maṇḍala*) due to the primacy of his mind;
that is to say, he empowered [it].

"In the wombs (*bhaga*) of all the Tathāgatas' consorts" means, as before, that in the abode of wisdom (*prajñālaya*), he emanates a mandala consisting of a square and other shapes contained therein, because it is free from all impurities. "The stainless Great Samaya" refers to Mahāvajradhara; "he empowered the mandala of the Great Samaya" means that he manifested it.
"Transparent, having that as its intrinsic nature" means it possesses the nature of clarity.
Because one perceives the forms of the deities of the maṇḍala even when standing outside the gabled pavilion, just as one perceives forms within crystal; thus,
"various forms on all sides" refers to the specific distinctions of diverse colors such as sapphire and so forth.
"Completely filled with clouds of Buddhas" means pervaded by the deities belonging to the maṇḍala of the general offering;
"confused by a dense mass of sparks" means...

"Blazing with the rays of the wrathful deities of the ten directions and joined with the maṇḍalas of clarity and so forth" means that it is joined with the maṇḍalas of clarity and so forth, which are the seats such as the moon-maṇḍala; [this is] "the city of all the Tathāgatas."
This city of all the Tathāgatas means the maṇḍala.
Now, with the words beginning "Then," Mahāvajradhara—the sovereign of body, speech, and mind—established himself in the center of the Great Samaya Maṇḍala just described.
Then, with the words beginning "His own," etc.

"He dwelt in the heart of Bodhicittavajra" means that the wheel of deities associated with the five families once again took up residence within the body of Bodhicittavajra; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). Akṣobhya Tathāgata is the essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
All Tathāgatas are the aggregates of form and so forth;
what is that woman who has dwelt in and made her abode within them? It is Prajñāpāramitā.
That very [place] is the *bhaga*, the womb, because it is the cause for the arising of a Buddha;

as was said by the Blessed One in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇatantra*: "The ground upon which all Buddhas dwell is the thirteenth; that is designated as the woman (*yoṣit*), and its nature is called the *bhaga*."
In that [state], he established and stationed himself within the great maṇḍala of the stainless samaya.
To explain what kind it was, he said:

it is clear like crystal, having that as its intrinsic nature; it has the nature of appearance, possessing manifold forms because it is suffused with five-colored rays; it consists of the essence of all Tathāgatas, and it is filled with clouds of Buddhas because it consists of the stainless wrathful deities of light.

The city of all the Tathāgatas, which is the body of Mahāvajradhara, is filled with a dense mass of sparks because it is fashioned from the three appearances beginning with light, and is endowed with the mandalas of the clear and so forth.
Of what kind? It means that he caused [him] to enter the Great Samaya-maṇḍala, which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).

In the *Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana*: "Then, immediately after entering luminosity, the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, the sovereign of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, having emerged from ultimate truth as himself—the essence of all families—established himself in the midst of the Great Samaya-maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas by way of the nature of the single flavor of existence and nirvāṇa. This means that he established him in the state of being the Lord of the Three Worlds.

"Because of the statement in the *Saṃvara*: 'The glorious Vanasattva is established in the space of all space,' the passage beginning with 'Then indeed, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya' and so forth demonstrates the assumption of a nirmāṇakāya by entering into the aggregates and so on for the sake of performing the welfare of sentient beings; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Illuminating that meaning, he says:"
"Then," and so forth:
the unification of the past, future, and present Tathāgatas through the sequence beginning with Candra and Vajra is the "Overpowering of All Tathāgatas.
For that purpose, there is a vajra; the meditative absorption (samādhi) which has that very thing as its name is the one he entered.
"Immediately thereafter," and so forth, means that he became established in the vajra-samaya of all the Tathāgatas;
that is to say, the Great Vajra itself became the members of the maṇḍala (māṇḍaleyas).
To the question, "What was done by that Maṇḍaleya who holds the Great Vajra? he says:
All sentient beings were possessed by the force of Śrī Vajrasattva and attained the state of Vajrasattva;
therefore it is said that they "became possessors of bliss and mental well-being," which constitutes the complete [mantra] limb.

All the Tathāgatas, whose nature consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, are overcome—that is, unified—by means of that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which takes the form of conventional bodhicitta; because it is indestructible like a diamond (*vajra*), the name of that very absorption is "Vajra," and he has entered into that [absorption]. Immediately thereafter, etc.

Regarding the phrase "the entire expanse of space" (*sarvākāśadhātu*): it refers to the hollow core of the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*) of all the Tathāgatas. Here, "Vajra" signifies the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*). The meaning is that [this expanse] became, has become, and is of the nature of—that which consists of—that very essence.
Regarding "all sentient beings" (*sarvasattva*), this refers to stationary objects and so forth.
By the empowerment of Vajrasattva—meaning, through the arising of the wisdom of skillful means—they became recipients of the bliss and mental well-being of all the Tathāgatas.
The meaning is that, through the union of the two organs, they are melted by the fire of great passion (*mahārāga*) and experience the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*).

"Womb-born" (*garbha*) refers to all the Tathāgatas, who are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); their "subjugation" (*abhibhavana*) is their unification within ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). That itself is the "vajra" because of its indestructibility (*abhedyatva*).

Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) bearing that name, immediately upon entering that absorption, he became one with and of the same nature as the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the three voids (*śūnyatraya*), the vajra of all Tathāgatas, and the universal void (*sarvaśūnya*).
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "as many as... (*atha yāvanta...*) also illuminates this very meaning; this is the *kolika* (definitive) explanation.

Having thus brought forth Mahāvajradhara through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), he now says "atha" and so forth, demonstrating the forms of both pure and impure deities; "the vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas" refers to the three syllables, which are called "samaya" because they are not to be transgressed, and their "experience" (*anubhava*) is that very [realization].
Because it has arisen as indivisible, he entered the vajra-samādhi.

"The form of the Mahāvidyā-puruṣa" means that his bodily form was produced by the syllables of the Mahāvidyā-mantras; he is thus called the Mahāvidyā-puruṣa-mūrti. "He empowered the empowerment of the mantras of all the Tathāgatas" means that the mantras of all the Tathāgatas are those beginning with *oṃ*; he is so described because the empowerment—that is, the ritual placement (*nyāsa*)—of these [mantras] was performed upon him.
By this it would be indicated that,

according to the logic stated for the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and following the sequence of the four yogas, having empowered himself as Mahāvajradhara— the embodiment of all mantras— up to the limit of the three *sattvas*, what is the source of his empowerment through truth (*satyādhiṣṭhāna*)?
He has become manifest; thus he says that he has come into the range of vision of those to be trained in the form of three faces.
Therefore he says:
"He was seen by those residing in all world-systems" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The "pledge" (*samaya*) of the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas is *prabhāsvara* (luminosity); that which arises from it, its production, is so called because it is indivisible like a vajra. It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it is supreme, immeasurable, wise, and consists of the activity of vigor and enthusiasm;
and it is designated as "Great" because it is the creator of the most marvelous.
Great Vidyā is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the Person (*puruṣa*) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);
the deity’s form in the shape of a person, produced from those two and endowed with the excellence of all aspects and so forth, is the "form of the Great Vidyā-Person" (*mahāvidyāpuruṣamūrti*).
Mahāvajradhara then empowered this as the empowerment of the mantras of all Tathāgatas.
The intention is that he has brought himself to completion as being composed of the atoms of all the Tathāgatas;
the meaning of "immediately thereafter" and so forth is as explained previously, and the meaning of "then" and so forth is definitive (*nītārtha*).
The Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, their minds drawn forth, emerged from the previously mentioned collection of heart-mantras and uttered this exclamation:
"Aho!
How wonderful!"—the word *aho* being used here in the sense of "for" (*yasmāt*).
"The generation of the thought of awakening" (bodhicittapravartana) means the generation of the forms of the two types of deities within the mental continuums of those to be trained.
This is the secret of all Tathāgatas, belonging to all Tathāgatas; it is to be guarded as a mystery, and because it is free from conceptual construction, it is beyond ratiocination.
Because it has emerged from the three realms, it is "without abode" (*anālaya*); this is not a cryptic teaching (*saṃdhyā*).
Now, in order to establish the relationship between disciple and teacher for future disciples to be trained, he says:
"Now" (*atha*), which signifies immediate succession.

"Having come to the assembly" means having gathered together; having fully worshipped and prostrated with clouds that are masses of the jewels of the reality-seal (*samaya-tattva-ratna*) which consist of the radiation of offerings to all the Tathāgatas, they spoke— this is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The worship performed by all the Tathāgatas’ forms and so forth is "the worship of all the Tathāgatas. Its radiation is its extensive proliferation; that itself is the *samaya* because it is not to be transgressed. The "jewels of reality" are the Three Jewels; their "clouds" are their multitudes. Having worshipped and prostrated with these, he spoke thus—this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
"Speak the *samāja*"—this is the connection [of the words].
"Reality as it truly is" refers to the Tathāgatas, who have the essence of adamant; their "compilation" (*samuccaya*) is characterized by their unification.
"Secret of all Tathāgatas" means the secret that has been handed down through the lineage of all Tathāgatas, which is to be concealed;
"originating from the secret" means it is the very essence of the mystery; "assembly" (*samāja*) means the unification of the two.
Regarding the literal meaning:
"the union of the moon and lotus" refers to the *Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana*; "assembly" (*samāja*) means the assembly of all limbs, that is, the union of wisdom and skillful means.
The "womb" (*garbha*) is the union of the conventional and ultimate truths;
it is an epithet of that very [state] called the "Secret Source" (*guhyasambhava*).
The secret is luminosity; from that, the essence of non-dual gnosis arises, which is to say Mahāvajradhara. This is the *kolika* [meaning].
Then, immediately thereafter, the Vajradhara of the higher mind (*adhicitta*) speaks thus to all the Tathāgatas.

The word *sādhu* (well done) and *sādhvi* (well done, feminine) are used in the sense of acceptance because they illuminate a desired meaning; the word *kiṃ tu* is used in the sense of inquiry or deliberation (*vitarka*).
Since this [teaching] causes doubt even for all the Tathāgatas,
the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas should be regarded as those whose yoga is being practiced;
for there is no doubt among Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have abandoned the latencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*).

Even for those individuals who are like Tathāgatas—jewel-like persons whose roots of merit are fully ripened, who have reached the further shore of learning, who aspire to Buddhahood, and who belong to the fixed lineage—the meaning of the *Samāja* is not within their domain without the oral instruction of a Guru, because it is beyond the reach of intellectual speculation;

how much less so for other Bodhisattvas? For even when it is explained to individuals such as Candana and others, whose roots of merit are ripened but whose inclinations are inferior, they express a lack of enthusiasm because it is difficult to grasp.

Having thus heard the words of the Blessed One, they were struck with wonder, thinking, "This is beyond the scope even of jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) who possess the fixed lineage (*niyatagotra*);
how much more so for those such as Puṇḍarīka who possess the fixed lineage! And being filled with amazement, all the Tathāgatas then spoke thus to the Blessed One:
"Since [the Blessed One] indicates that this is [beyond the reach] of even these very jewel-like persons, despite their being distinguished by such qualities..."

The intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*) of all the Tathāgatas is the secret of body, speech, and mind; it is the transformation of the three families, beginning with the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*);
this is the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*).
The secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the three syllables, comprising all the limbs;
the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the vehicle of the wind that manifests from the nature of the three gnoses;
the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the womb.
Having performed the empowerment of the body consisting of gnosis as the ultimate (kolika) through the words concerning the arising of the vajra-samaya of all Tathāgatas, he established it.
The connection is "may he reveal.

The empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of all Tathāgatas is the entry (*āveśa*) into the body and so forth; having performed that by means of what? By means of the words arising from the vajra-samaya of all Tathāgatas.
The *vajra-samayas* of all the Tathāgatas are the body-vajra and so forth; their "sites of arising" are the seed-syllables from which they originate;
the "entirety of limbs" is the *vajra-samaya*, which is the union of the two organs.
The words for its arising are the drops of bodhicitta; the empowerment is the consecration by means of them, and having performed that, it is the embryo.

The Vajra-samaya is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); its originating states are the Great Emptiness, the Exceeding Emptiness, and the Emptiness. Having performed the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) through these—by manifesting the two types of divine forms within the mental continua of those to be trained—may the Blessed One fully reveal them. This is the *kolika* [explanation]. Thus requested, the Blessed One, having understood the request, emanates the Wisdom Maṇḍala for the sake of their empowerment.
Knowledge itself is the lamp;
thus, "knowledge-lamp" is the literal meaning. [He is] Akṣobhya because he produces the light of knowledge within the mental continua of sentient beings.
Having entered that samādhi which is like a lamp— a lamp because it illuminates the ten directions— wherein knowledge itself, with all its limbs, appears as the threefold consciousness.
The root *garbh* occurs in the sense of "knowing" (*jñā*) and "understanding" (*avabodhana*), as well as in the sense of "prohibition" (*pratiṣedha*).
What is that knowledge in which there is an absence of conceptual cognition? It is the ineffable ultimate truth;
it is itself a lamp because, by outshining all lights without exception, it illuminates infinite world-systems.
Having entered the samādhi named Vajra because of its indestructibility,

and having emerged from the *prabhāsvara* samādhi, he beholds the realm of sentient beings beset by the five afflictions (*pañcakleśa*). Realizing that the very thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the afflictions is awakening (*bodhi*), and thinking "I am of that same nature," he should emit this supreme essence-heart of the Hatred Family from the power of his own body, speech, and mind, in order to purify the affliction of hatred in those to be trained.
"This" refers to that which resides in the intellect;
"great compassion" is the skillful means (*upāya*), and "wrath" is aversion (*dveṣa*). Its "family" is the family of aversion (*dveṣakula*);

because it brings about the desired fruit, it is the supreme essence, the heart-mantra (*hṛdayamantra*). He should emit it from his own body and so forth—that is, he released it through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
According to the literal meaning, "Vajradhr̥k" indicates the fivefold manifest enlightenment;
he who holds the vajra is Vajradhr̥k.
The interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) is that he "holds the vajra-knowledge" which consists of the two truths; thus, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is "Vajradhṛk" (the Vajra-holder).
Now, the connection of the passage beginning with "Then in this" is "he caused [him] to sit";
"he indeed" refers to the aforementioned Mahāvajradhara.
The Vidyāpuruṣa consists of three aspects— body, speech, and mind— and thus has the nature of the two truths;
it is characterized by the bliss drawn forth through the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā) of Akṣobhya and so forth.
Union with her is oneness;
that itself is the supreme state in the form of black, white, and red. As before, he caused [her] to sit upon the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
The meaning is that he sat upon the body, speech, and mind-vajra of Mahāvajradhara;
this is the first chapter, the Emanation from Vajrasattva,
according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).

Immediately following the initial yoga, he indicates the mandala of emission; the connection is: "Then the Blessed One brought forth the heart-mantra. This is the samādhi called "The Garment Arisen from the Samaya."
The meaning of the divisions has been explained.
Delusion (*moha*), which is the flavor of peace (*śāntarasa*), serves to purify those of deluded nature; that very [delusion] is the supreme state (*paramapada*).
Its "family" (*kula*) is the supreme essence (*paramasāra*), and so forth—the meaning of this has already been understood.
*Jinajik*:
those who conquer are the *jinās*, namely the Māras; he conquers them by means of the twelvefold wheel of Dharma, thus he is *jinajik*.
This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The connection is as follows: because he overcomes the four Māras by means of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), he is "Victorious" (*jinajik*) in the definitive sense; that very Blessed One caused [the Buddha] to sit down in front.
Having become one with the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Vairocana, he sat down while gazing directly at the Blessed One in front of him;
the connection [of the passage] beginning with "Then" (*atha*) and so forth is as previously explained in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, according to the literal meaning.
The jewel of all the Tathāgatas is the conventional bodhicitta; because it arises from that, he is Ratnasaṃbhava.
Vajraśrī is that very Mahāmudrā; having brought that forth in this samādhi, [the name] is of interpretable meaning (neyārtha).
The jewel of all the Tathāgatas is the ultimate bodhicitta; because he arises from that, he is Ratnasaṃbhava. Vajraśrī is indestructible glory.
Having entered into the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose name is that very [Vajraśrī], this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Because it fulfills all hopes, it is a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); its family is "the supreme essence," and so forth—the meaning of which has already been explained.
Regarding "Ratnadhṛk":
he is called Ratnadhṛk because he holds the jewel that fulfills all hopes.
The interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) is that he holds the jewel of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭiratna*); thus, he is the "Jewel-Bearer" (*ratnadhṛk*),
which is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The union (*saṃyoga*) is the state of being one with the great seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Ratnasaṃbhava and the pledge (*samaya*);
that itself is the "space-state" (*gaganapada*).
Knowledge of equality, which is like space because it is untainted (*nirlepa*), is called the "space-state."

Having made a Buddha-throne for the sake of giving to those beings who are arrogant with the pride of wealth, and having established them in the state of purification from conceit, they sit upon the right side of the Blessed One.
Just as it is according to the literal meaning,
he says "Then," and so forth, demonstrating the yoga of Amitābha for the purpose of abandoning passion through passion for those beings who delight in passion.
In the same way, the connection of all the Tathāgatas is the Great Passion, the Supreme Bliss;
the Bodhicitta produced from that is Abhitābha, who arises therefrom.
The interpretable meaning is that the great passion of all the Tathāgatas is the Clear Light; from that arises Amitābha,
who takes as his object of focus the very end of the vajra.

The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is as follows: through discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), there is attachment to the primordial wisdoms (*jñāna*); this is *vajrarāga*. His family (*kula*) is the "supreme essence" (*paramasāra*) and so forth; such is the analyzed meaning of *ārolig*.

*Samsāra* is that which goes (*eti*) toward (*ā*) the limit (*ro*) on all sides; therefore, *Ārolik* is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*). *Ro* refers to the three types of gnosis (*jñāna*); [the name signifies] that he has gone (*gata*) from that to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is as follows: the connection with "atha" and so forth is as before; "Sarvatathāgatāmogha" is Amoghasiddhi.

That very commitment (*samaya*)—because it is worthy of being honored through the accomplishment of the welfare of the entire world, characterized by the performance of what is to be done—is itself the *vajra*; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that exists is so called.
This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Amoghasamaya is luminous because it bestows the fruit of signlessness; that very vajra which is its object is thus called the samādhi. This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

For the purpose of purifying the affliction of envy, and for the sake of removing faults such as the violation of commitments (*samaya-bhraṃśa*) by means of summoning, the "family" (*kula*) is the family of summoning the commitment (*samayākarṣaṇakula*).

The conventional truth (*samaya*) is the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*); by means of it, one draws forth the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*), generates supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), and thus the family of purification (*pariśodhanakula*) is the family of drawing forth the conventional truth (*samayākarṣaṇakula*).
This is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The meaning of "paramasāra" and so forth has already been analyzed.
Regarding "prajñādhṛk":
*prajñā* is wisdom characterized by discernment; one who maintains that [wisdom] is "prajñādhṛk."

The provisional meaning (*neyārtha*) is the moon-like appearance of wisdom (*prajñā*); because one sustains that with the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*), it is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), "the bearer of wisdom" (*prajñādhṛk*).
Seated in the north,
[he speaks] according to the literal meaning: "Hatred," and so forth, as explained in the six points of the first chapter.
The desire is the generation of the aspiration for liberation in those to be trained;
liberation is untainted great bliss. This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

"These families are indeed the means for accomplishing both desire and liberation. These families, whose nature consists of the five aggregates (*skandha*), accomplish liberation through the enjoyment of desire; or else, they accomplish both desire and liberation according to the literal meaning.
Therefore, it is said in the *Vyākhyātantra*: "For these aggregates are the 'Vṛddhāsya' [the Old Face], arising from the conditions for the sake of awakening."
"Those Tathāgatas are also known as such through their union with non-dual suchness"—
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Furthermore, for the enjoyment (*upabhoga*) of Vairocana and the others, he emits the four goddesses.
The connection is as follows: "Then," and so forth, ending with "he brought forth.
Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused upon Māmakī—the pledge of passion for the Vajra-holder—he [did so] according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
"Dveṣarati" means attachment (rati) toward Akṣobhya, who is hatred (dveṣa). Thus, it is "attachment to hatred."

"Delight in hatred" (*dveṣarati*) is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), referring to delight in the purification of the affliction of hatred; "delight in hatred" (*dveṣarati*) is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
That very Vajradhara, having assumed the form of Māmakī, should sit in the southwest corner;
as for Sarvatathāgata, he is Vairocana, and his corresponding passion-vajra is Locanā.
According to the literal meaning,
"delusion-delight" (moharati) means that Vairocana is delusion (moha), and there is delight (rati) in him.
"Delight in the purification of delusion" is of interpretable meaning; "delight in delusion" is of definitive meaning.
One should sit in the southeast corner according to the literal meaning of the words beginning with "atha," and so forth.
Amitābha is the bearer of passion;
Pāṇḍaravāsinī is the Vajra of passion for him; and the meditative absorption (samādhi) based upon that is likewise so called.
According to the literal meaning,
"delight in passion" (*rāgarati*) means that passion (*rāga*) is Amitābha, and delight (*rati*) is in him; thus, it is "delight in passion."
Delight in the purification of passion is of interpretable meaning; [delight in the purification of passion itself] is of definitive meaning.
Then, [the words] beginning with "atha" and so forth mean that one should sit in the northwest corner according to the literal meaning of the words beginning with "atha."

The literal meaning is that deceiving others regarding body, speech, and mind is the proclamation to others that "body, speech, and mind are impermanent. The deceptive engagement of body, speech, and mind has as its objective support the realization that "all phenomena are empty."

The "womb" (*garbha*) consists of the deception of body, speech, and mind; having caused the body, speech, and mind— which possess the nature of the three appearances— to enter into the appearance of the subtle element and experience it moment by moment, one then brings about their lack of intrinsic nature.

The making non-manifest of the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, and so forth, by means of the sequential destruction of the grasping at them as a solid mass, is the "deception" of body, speech, and mind; because it is indivisible, it is their "vajra," and the meditative concentration (samādhi) that has that as its object is called the "Vajra Deception of the Body, Speech, and Mind of All Tathāgatas."
Amoghasiddhi, the holder of the wisdom of all Tathāgatas, [became] Kaulika;
Samayatārā, the Vajra of passion for her, became identical in form to him; this means that he established one-pointedness of mind.
According to the literal meaning,
"Vajrarati" means that there is delight (*rati*) in the Vajra, which is Amoghasiddhi.
Vajrarati is of interpretable meaning; it is delight in vajra-wisdom.
The definitive meaning [is explained] in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: "Then," and so forth;
one should sit in the north, that is, the northeast corner.
According to the literal meaning,
these four goddesses are the female companions;
for those who practice union with them, the supreme accomplishment of all the Tathāgatas will be attained.
The sovereignty over desires of the chief queen is expressed by the word "prosperity" (sampat) of the chief queen; this is according to the literal meaning.
The connection is as follows: "Then," and so forth, ending with "he brought forth the wrath.
Vairocana himself, whose nature is consecration (*abhiṣeka*), is the *vajra*; he who possesses that is Vairocanavajra. This refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) focused upon him.
He by whom the maṇḍala of all the Tathāgatas, named Vairocanavajra, is empowered and brought to completion is so designated; [the name] Yamāntakṛt is according to the literal meaning.

*Yamāntakṛt* (the Destroyer of Yama) is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) because he brings an end to and destroys Yama, the hell realm, by means of the Blessed One’s samādhi of great wrath. [In the definitive sense,] *yamāntakṛt* is so called because he brings an end to and destroys Yama— the darkness of delusion, which is ignorance— by means of ultimate truth.
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is as follows:
"Then," and so forth, he sat at the eastern gate according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
"Then," and so forth:
the perfect awakening of all the Tathāgatas is Ratnasaṃbhava;
the one whose vajra is upon his crown is the wrathful Aparājita, and he who has that as his object of focus [is the subject].

The "vajra named the perfect awakening of meditative concentration" is of interpretable meaning; it refers to the perfect awakening of all Tathāgatas, which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), and taking that very [luminosity] as the vajra.
The definitive meaning is that "the one who brings an end to wisdom" (prajñāntakṛt) refers to one who destroys the afflictions through wisdom; thus, he is the one who brings an end to wisdom.
The interpretable meaning is that wisdom consists of conceptualization;
one brings it to an end by entering its luminosity, and thus he is "the one who has brought wisdom to an end" (Prajñāntakṛt).
The definitive meaning is as follows: "Now," and so forth;
the terrifying of the wicked by means of the vajra pledges is "the terrifying of the vajra pledge."
Alternatively, the worldly ḍākinīs of the Vajra-samaya are the "Vajra-samaya-terrifiers"; he sat at the southern gate having terrified them,
according to the literal meaning.
Then, and so forth:
having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after Hayagrīva, whose mine (*ākara*) or lineage (*gotra*) is that very Amitābha, the Jewel of Dharma (*dharmaratna*).

The Jewel of Dharma is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*); it is luminous, and Hayagrīva has that very [Jewel] as his mine—that is, his place of origin—and he has entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which takes that as its object;
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

"Padmāntakṛt" (the destroyer of the lotus) means that, like a lotus unstained by water, he remains unstained by the afflictions (*kleśa*) and then destroys them; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
The lotus is the source;

because he brings about—that is, produces—the bliss of supreme joy therein by means of the union of the two organs, he is the "Maker of the End of the Lotus" (*padmāntakṛt*); this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Then, [the words] beginning with "atha" and so forth,
he sat down in the west according to the literal meaning.

The Blessed One Amoghasiddhi is the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas; he himself is the vajra of the noble wrathful deity Amṛtakuṇḍalika, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that takes him as its object is so called. This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Taking as its object the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*), which is the locus of purification for the vajras of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas—this is the definitive meaning.
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that he is "the ender of obstacles" (*vighnāntakṛt*),
because he brings about the end— that is, the destruction— of obstacles; thus, according to the sixfold commentary on the first chapter, he is Vighnāntakṛt.
The "interpretable meaning" refers to the four elements as obstacles;
they are called obstacles because they afflict the body through their decrease and increase.
He is called Vighnāntakṛt (the Destroyer of Obstacles) because he brings about their destruction through the arising of the knowledge of skillful means; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Then, and so forth, he sat upon the northern [side].
According to the literal meaning,
the maṇḍala of the pledge-beings (*samayasattva*) is for the sake of pleasing those belonging to the maṇḍala;
the pledge-beings are so called because they destroy all obstacles.
One should install them according to the literal meaning; thus, one should install Kalā and the others, beginning from the eastern corner, upon the four gates.
Beginning from the eastern panel, one should place Maitreya and the others;
outside the central maṇḍala, beginning from the eastern corner, one should place Rūpavajrā and the others.
The rules regarding the seats and so forth for all of them have already been established in the *Sādhanopāyikā*.
Lest there be a practice that proceeds without a teacher,
just as the connection with the deities and the mandala have been fully demonstrated by the Blessed One elsewhere,
so too here the body-mandala consists of the arrangement of thirty-two deities, and the utsarga-mandala is likewise.
How is it understood that the body-maṇḍala itself must indeed consist of the arrangement of thirty-two deities?
This has been explained by the Blessed One himself in the *Vyākhyātantra*; it is now introduced here for the sake of removing any doubt among the practitioners of the *Sāmājika* [Guhyasamāja] cycle.
Listen, O Mahāsattva! One should not recollect [this] with a distracted mind.
Within this body of the Vajrācārya, the sequence of the Kāryājinasthiti is established;
first, it is situated by means of the Body-Vajra, which is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The Blessed One abides as the aggregate of sensation through the passion-vajra; he abides as the aggregate of perception through the speech-vajra;
he abides as the aggregate of mental formations through the all-people-vajra.
With the sword of his mind, the Blessed One [perceives] that which is established as the mechanism of consciousness:
the flesh and so forth are the earth element, wherein the Blessed Lady Locanā resides; the blood and so forth are the water element, wherein the Blessed Lady Māmakī resides.

The fire element, which is heat, is the Blessed Lady Pāṇḍaravāsinī; she is situated there, impelled by the wind Marut. The Blessed Lady Tārā is situated in the sense organ of the two eyes, and the Tathāgata Kṣitigarbha is likewise situated there.
The faculty of his two ears is the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi;
the faculty abiding in his nose is the Tathāgata Gaganagañja;
the faculty abiding in his tongue is the Tathāgata Lokeśvara.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated: "The sense faculty abiding in the mind is the Tathāgata Mañjughoṣa;
the body, however, is designated as a mass composed of the four elements."
The Tathāgata Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin resides there; the Tathāgata Samantabhadra resides in the body of all joints,
and the Tathāgata Maitreya resides in the body of all sinews.
At the base of the right arm is the Tathāgata Yamāntaka,
and at the base of the left arm is the Tathāgata Aparājita;
the Tathāgata Hayagrīva resides in the lotus of the mouth.
The Tathāgata Amṛtakuṇḍalin resides in the secret region;
that Tathāgata Acala resides in the right arm;
the Tathāgata Ṭakkirāja resides in the left arm.
The Tathāgata Nīladaṇḍa stands upon the right knee, the Tathāgata Mahābala stands upon the left knee,
and the Tathāgata Cakravartin stands upon the crown of his own head.
The Tathāgata Sumbharāja stands at the feet below, and all the Tathāgatas likewise abide within this entire body;
this is called the Body Maṇḍala of the Vajrācārya.
All these perfectly awakened ones, the entire assembly of the Buddha-body, cause [the teaching] to enter into nirvāṇa; O Vajrī, you teach the conditioned.
Quickly enter nirvāṇa, O Blessed One, and may your virtue become fully matured.
Therefore, all the Victors are established within the body of the Vajra Guru.
O Mahāsattva, listen hereafter: O Amoghadarśaka, this Guru should always be served with diligence by all sentient beings.
Likewise, the great Bodhisattvas of unfailing vision and great renown—
satisfied, joyful, and thrilled— bowed down and prostrated themselves before him,
as it is said in the *Vajramālā*:
By this same principle, the arrangement of the thirty-two deities must also be performed in the written mandala; thus,
even with reference to the underlying cause (nidāna), whatever meaning is demonstrated would be the remaining subject matter of the tantra that has been explained there as a relevant corollary.

Thus ends the first chapter, the commentary on the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*), in the *Guhyasamāja*, the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. Regarding the chapter titled "The Empowerment of the Maṇḍala of All Tathāgatas":

having perceived the secret of body, speech, and mind, this was composed for the *Guhyasamāja*; it is so called because it contains the empowerment of the meditative absorption maṇḍala (*samādhimaṇḍalādhiṣṭhāna*).
The "Chapter on All Tathāgatas" (*sarvatathāgatapaṭala*) is so called because,

just as a cloth (*paṭa*) wards off disturbances such as gadflies and mosquitoes, so too this meaning of the tantra is like a cloth because it wards off disturbances such as afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and birth; it is a "chapter" (*paṭala*) because it is a collection of texts that takes up (*lāti*) or holds (*gṛhṇāti*) that [meaning].
[The text to be translated was not provided.]
The Explanation of the Six Points in the First Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.

Chapter Two. Having thus completed everything by means of the first chapter, he speaks the second chapter on the Awakening Mind (*bodhicitta*) in order to illuminate the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). The connection is as follows:
"Then," and so forth, "having prostrated to the Blessed One, they spoke thus."

The connection [of the text] is as follows: having performed worship to and bowed before Mahāvajradhara— the sovereign of body, speech, and mind— they entreat the Blessed One, saying, "Please speak of the unsurpassed bodhicitta."

It is "essential" because it is liberated from all obscurations; it is "supreme" because it is the undifferentiated nature of the triad of body, speech, and mind; and it is "secret" because, through the metaphorical application of the effect to the cause, it cannot be revealed to those who rely on the systems of ritual action and so forth.
Therefore,
the connection is that the Blessed One then spoke thus to the bodhisattvas:
"By the mind alone," and so forth.

"If the Blessed One would grant us the instruction on the Great Bodhicitta for the sake of accomplishing our own completely pure deity-forms, then it would be for the benefit of great beings"— having thus perceived this reflection of the mind with his own mind, he spoke as follows, according to the literal meaning.
"May you generate [it]," and so forth: "May you generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) by means of the indivisible nature of the three vajras.
To the question "How is that? he says: "The mind in the form of the body" means in the form of the body-vajra;
"the body in the form of the mind" means in the form of the mind-vajra.
"By means of the utterance of speech" (*vākpravyāhāreṇa*) means that the utterance of speech is verbal expression;
the meaning is "by means of that instrument which is speech."
"Pratha," and so forth, means that having joined— i.e., unified— the body, speech, and mind with the form of space, which is the nature of emptiness;
this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
"Let them generate the mind-made body; how shall they accomplish it? To this he says: "The mind in the form of the body.

That which is the accomplishment of the body—namely, the three minds together with the subtle element in the form of the *saṃbhogika* body—is indeed [the accomplishment] of the body in the form of the mind.
For there is nothing other than mind;
mind itself is what is expressed by speech. Therefore, by means of that vocal expression, let them generate mind in its own essential nature.
Regarding "body" and so forth:

having thus joined and unified the perfected body, speech, and mind with that which has the form of space— that is, with the luminosity whose nature is space— one should bring oneself to perfection as Mahāvajradhara.

And it is said in the *Śrīvajramālā-mahāyogatantra*: "There is nothing equal to the three realms; one perceives one's own life as the essence, seeing one's own city as radiant and consisting of ten million realms. This is from the sixth section of the second chapter, the *Yogāntara-vyākhyā*:
"In the three realms, there is nothing superior to one's own life, which constitutes the essence."
One who perceives life as a dream, or the triple world (traidhātuka) as such—
thus bestowing the reality of the triple world’s nature as oneness—
one shall attain the state of empowerment and the accomplishment of its activity.
"Aho hi," and so forth: Samantatabhadra is the Great Vajradhara; the "arousing of his bodhicitta" refers to "aho," meaning wonder, and "hi," meaning because.
"By means of the practice of non-arising" means that non-arising is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
the entry of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) into that is the practice of non-arising.
Therefore, "arising" (utpāda) refers to the luminous characteristic of assuming the form of the perfectly pure deity;
this arising consists of emergence, by which it is celebrated—that is, described—not as being of indeterminate meaning.
Thus, through the respective verses on the *bodhicitta* of the six Tathāgatas, he illuminates this very samādhi.
The perfect awakening (*abhisambodhi*) of all Tathāgatas is characterized by the non-duality of the two truths;
its method (*naya*) is the means for its direct realization. That very [method] is the "vajra" of this samādhi, because it is as indestructible as a vajra.
He is described as such;
there is no "without-secret" (nāsandhya) [teaching],
for in the absence of all stable and powerful entities, there is no efficacy of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), because that which is to be cultivated does not exist.
Cultivation is not indeed cultivation;
even that cultivation which exists for one who is present is not cultivation, because [the object] exists even without cultivation.
Thus, an entity that is joined with both existence and non-existence would not exist.
Therefore, the object of cultivation, the cultivator, and the act of cultivation are not apprehended.
Regarding the literal meaning:

having negated all phenomena through the distinctions of the earth element and so forth, the cultivation that [considers] conditioned and unconditioned phenomena to be empty—of that cultivation there is non-existence, because it is a view characterized by attachment to emptiness.
To eliminate the notion of signs, he says: "cultivation is indeed not cultivation.
Even that cultivation which consists of an adherence to the forms of cause and effect is not at all tenable, because cause and effect are non-dual.
To refute aspiration, he says:
The meaning is as follows: even that fruit of a formal vow (*praṇidhāna*) which has such an external form does not exist, because there is no apprehension of the vow and so forth;
therefore, the cultivation of the form of an external object is not perceived.
Because it consists of mind, no complete limb exists in its absence.

Regarding those things such as dreams and so forth, in their absence, that which is to be cultivated—the mind-only—is not purified because of the non-existence of all [objects]; therefore, in order to refute conventional truth, he says:
"cultivation is indeed no cultivation."

Even that cultivation of the form of a deity, which is like an illusion and consists of the nature of conventional truth, is not tenable because it is purified even by the clear light (*prabhāsvara*);
thus, in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said that the state of conventional truth would not be a [real] entity.
Because that [reality] is non-different from the two truths,
cultivation by means of it is not perceived as a cultivation of the non-dual form of the two truths; the meaning is that it is perceived only with great difficulty.
In the absence of the embryo, there is an absence of cultivation within ultimate truth because of its primordial purity;
even that cultivation which consists of conventional truth is not cultivated.
In this manner, by the statement "because of its being true," the entity consisting of the two truths would not be something to be cultivated,
since liberation occurs merely through the vision of the non-duality of the two truths.

"By that [means], the attachment to the notions of 'the practitioner,' 'the practice,' and 'that which is to be practiced' is not perceived and does not exist for those who have attained the stage of the Union (yuganaddha)—thus spoke Mahāvajradhara. This is the *kolika* [meaning].
Then the Blessed One Vairocanavajra proclaimed this"—such is the connection.

The *samaya* of all the Tathāgatas is the universal form (*abhisamantākāra*), which is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*); that itself is the *vajra*, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is that which has that as its object."
"By all entities," and so forth:

it is free from all entities that serve as the vessel [of the world], and furthermore, it is devoid of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, as well as the grasped and the grasper; it is the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Through that, there is the state of non-dual equality.

By means of that equality of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), the Tathāgata Vairocana declared that one’s own mind is primordially unarisen, possesses a body indivisible from the three vajras, and has emptiness as its intrinsic nature because it is the exclusive domain of the eye alone; this is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
It is the inexhaustible limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of all Tathāgatas, and that itself is the vajra; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which takes that as its object is likewise so called.
The inexhaustible vajra of all Tathāgatas is named as follows: "These phenomena are unarisen.
These external and internal entities are unarisen because they are luminous by nature;
therefore, phenomena do not exist at all.
Nor is there a "dharmatā" for them; since phenomena do not exist, even their dharmatā is not found.
Therefore, this method of awakening—the means to awakening—is firm, essential, and like space.

The Tathāgata Akṣobhya has stated that "the characteristic of selflessness is luminosity"; the connection with the words "not without intentional meaning" (*nāsandhyam*) and so forth is exactly as before.

The selflessness of all Tathāgatas is the ultimate truth; that itself is the vajra, and the meditative absorption (samādhi) focused upon it is the meditative absorption named "the vajra of the selflessness of all Tathāgatas. [They are called] "non-existent" because they are signless (nirnimitta); "all phenomena" refers to those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).
"Devoid of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*)," it is said; since even phenomena themselves are not established, how could there be their characteristics?
If one asks, "In that case, how is the manifestation of a deity [possible]?"—it is like the dark or fair complexion of the son of a barren woman.

"Arising from the selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya-saṃbhūtā*) means that the selflessness of phenomena is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); arising from that by way of the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhānakrama*) is "arising from the selflessness of phenomena. He stated this because of the force of what precedes and follows.
Ratnasaṃbhava is not with hidden meaning (*nāsandhya*).
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: the lamp of the flame of gnosis is the *jñānārci-pradīpa*.
Of what nature is it? It is the luminous world (*prabhāsvaraloka*).
That itself is the *vajra*; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) having that as its object is named "The Wisdom-Flame Like a Lamp" (*jñānārciḥ pradīpavajja*).

Regarding [the phrase] "among phenomena that have arisen": this refers to conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. *Anutpanneṣu-advitīyapaṭala-ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* [End of the] Commentary on the Six Limits of the Second Chapter.
Since there is no "being," there is no state of being cultivated;
and since there is no "cultivation," cultivation itself does not exist.

He says, "by means of the application of the term 'space' (ākāśapadayogena)," in response to the question: "Since there is no object to be cultivated (bhāvya), how can there be union with the deity (devatāyoga)?"

Space is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and the word is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); their union, that is, their becoming one through this conjunction of space and the word—this is the intended meaning. By this principle, "is proclaimed" refers to the state [of] the form of Mahāvajradhara.
"It is sung and spoken"— thus spoke the Tathāgata Amitābha. The connection [of the phrase] "not with intentional ambiguity" (*nāsandhyam*) and so forth is as before.
The vajra-samādhi called "Overpowering All Tathāgatas" has its meaning analyzed as follows:
"all phenomena are luminous by nature."
"Nature and luminosity" means "naturally luminous";
nature is conventional truth,
and luminosity is ultimate truth.
External and internal entities have the nature of the two truths;
therefore, they are primordially pure and equal to space.
Because they are utterly pure, there is no [separate] enlightenment.
The fruit is the direct realization (*nābhisamaya*); the cause is that which brings about its attainment.
This is because there is no identity between cause and fruit.
Amoghasiddhi stated that the thorough knowledge of the non-difference between cause and fruit is itself the firm path to enlightenment;
this is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
Then, moreover, [the text begins with] "atha khalu" and so forth.
The secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas is the mind-made body; its true nature (*dharmatā*) is purity by way of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
and its syllable (*akṣara*) is the verbal formulation that illuminates that excellence.
Having heard that, they were struck with wonder through the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and struck with amazement through the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), exclaiming,
"Aha!"
"Buddha" is a praise by way of the door of conventional truth;
"O, the Dharma! is [a praise] by way of the door of ultimate truth;
and "O, the teaching of the Dharma! praises the cause of the teaching of the Dharma which illuminates the non-differentiated nature of the two truths.
The reality of purity is luminosity;
therefore, the pure object is the perfectly purified body.
Homage to you, O Bodhicitta Mahāvajradhara, distinguished by such qualities!

"Born from the selflessness of phenomena" (dharmanairātmyasaṃbhūta) means that he has arisen from ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). "The perfection stage of the Buddha's awakening" (buddhabodhiniṣpannakrama) refers to him who fulfills the Buddha's awakening by bringing disciples to maturity through that [stage].
Because you have transcended all conceptual construction, you are free from discursive thought (*nirvikalpa*);
for this very reason, because you are without a focal point, you are without support (*nirālamba*). Homage to you!
"Samanta... and so forth.
He is Samantabhadra because he is auspicious in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa; he is Sarvārtha because he is the nature of all perfections;
and he is the initiator of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) through the radiation of the mandala of deities.
Enlightenment is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and that by which it is practiced or attained is the conduct of enlightenment (*bodhicaryā*), which is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*);
O Great Vajra, whose nature consists of these two truths, homage to you!
Regarding "the mind" and so forth:
what is the nature of the mind?
It is *tāthāgata*. One who has gone to *tathatā* (suchness) is a *Tathāgata*; a *Tathāgata* himself is *tāthāgata*.
Therefore, "pure" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), meaning the completely pure mind-made body (*manomayadeha*).

Regarding the phrase "by means of the vajras of body, speech, and mind": because they are perceived by those to be trained (*vineya*) in the form of vajras and so forth, they are the "vajras of body, speech, and mind. Because they bring about the awakening of a Buddha and establish [beings] in the non-abiding realm of nirvana (*apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇadhātu*), they are the "producers of the awakening of a Buddha. Homage to you!
The chapter on the lamp of the awakening mind, which is the explanation according to the literal meaning; the chapter on the awakening mind.
The Explanation of the Six Points of the Second Chapter in the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā* (The Illuminating Commentary).
The Third Chapter.

Introducing the third chapter, which states that practitioners of the two types must perform the cultivation of various subtle yogas, [the text] says "atha" and so forth; the connection is that [he] "uttered.
The Tathāgata of Body, Speech, and Mind Vajra is Mahāvajradhara.

The Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya and the others are those whose emanations pervade the ten directions for the sake of sentient beings; these themselves are the "clouds" because they rain down the water of the Dharma.

This very array (*vyūha*), appearing in various forms due to the diversity of the dispositions of beings with their manifold inclinations, is thus a variegated and indivisible meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Having taken hold of this meditative absorption, which is called "Vajravyūha" because it consists of the "vajras"—that is, the Tathāgatas—and their "array," meaning the assembly or collection within it, he proclaimed that chapter on meditative absorption, the "Vajravyūha Samādhipaṭala," which is established as the object of the cognition "this."
Having thus introduced the chapter, the mantra that serves as a constituent part for the generation of the deity is first indicated:
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
[The phrase] "situated in the middle of the space-element" means situated within the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).

"One should meditate," and so forth: the circle of deities such as Vairocana and others is called "the great array of clouds of light rays. Here, "light rays" refers to the deities connected to their respective families; their "cloud" is a multitude, and that itself is the "array" because they are situated in their proper places.
"Equal in radiance to the flames of the Buddhas" means having a color identical to that of one's own sovereign deity.
"Pervaded by five rays" means endowed with ground portions of five colors;
"perfectly circular on all sides" means auspicious in every respect (*sarvatobhadra*);
and "filled with the five qualities of sensual pleasure" means accompanied by Rūpavajrā and the others.
"Adorned with the five offerings" means accompanied by the five offerings presented by the gods and others; having meditated [upon this] and so forth—
in short, having visualized the circle of deities— one should contemplate the image as oneself, meaning one should establish it as the presiding lord in the center of the wheel.
Now, in order to show that one should meditate on the *mahāmudrā* of Vairocana and the others as the image of Mahāvajradhara in the center, he says "Vairocana," and so forth.

[One should meditate on] the *mahāmudrā* of Vairocana, who is the emanation of Vajradhara and is characterized by body, speech, and mind; for even though he is the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*), Vairocana exists as a subordinate aspect of both speech and mind.

"The yoga of non-duality through withdrawal" (*saṃhārādvayayoga*) means: withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is Mahāvajradhara, because the circle of deities is withdrawn into him; through the yoga of non-duality with him, one should meditate on the *mahāmudrā* of Akṣobhya.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated: "In this way, one should visualize the great mudrā of Ratnaketu and others in the center of the maṇḍala.
This is because of the statement: "He for whom the supreme Vajradhara draws the image in the center—that shall be his place in the maṇḍala."

Showing the distinctions of color and so forth for these, he says "indranīla" and so on: the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, Mahāvajradhara, having entered into Akṣobhya and become the Vajra of Hatred, has arisen with the color of sapphire (indranīla).

Therefore, one should meditate upon Vairocana, who is formidable, fierce, and terrifying, with fangs slightly bared; whose form has the luster of crystal and the moon due to the blending of wrath and great passion; who is adorned with a mass of matted hair and surrounded by a halo of light; whose body is embellished with all the primary marks; and who holds a wheel in his principal hand.
One should meditate upon the nine-pronged [vajra], which has the radiance of Jāmbūnada gold, arises from golden-colored jewels, and is a shimmering array of Tathāgatas;
one should visualize this in the hands of that Dveṣavajra.
With the words beginning with "makarata," he describes the nature of Amoghasiddhi;
with the words beginning with "haste rattaṃ," he explains the emblem of Ratnasaṃbhava;
and with the words beginning with "padmarāga," he states the emblem of Amitābha.

One should meditate on Amoghavajrin, who possesses five rays— meaning he is endowed with white and other colored light— and who holds a sword in his hand, because the entire universe, in its totality, consists of the means for accomplishing the welfare of beings.
In order to show the initial yoga that serves as a limb for the production of these [samādhis], he says "atha" and so forth.

Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the *dharmadhātu* itself, that by which body, speech, and mind are empowered (*adhiṣṭhīyante*)—that is, brought to perfection—is called the empowerment of body, speech, and mind (*kāyavākcittādhiṣṭhāna*). Mahāvajradhara uttered that mantra: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the *dharmadhātu*."

Having empowered oneself with this [mantra] into the form of a lunar disc, and having produced the body of the deity above it by means of the seed-syllable and so forth, one should meditate upon the subtle yoga according to the sequence to be described;
this is the interpretable meaning of the samādhi of the generation stage.

"Then," and so forth: "all Tathāgatas" refers to the five rays; their "emanation" is their proceeding through the upper aperture. From the cloud [comes] the moon; in each individual maṇḍala, there is an array (*vyūha*) as the four maṇḍalas proceed, because they are not differentiated by colors such as white and so on.

Having relied upon that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is the "vajra," which is the imperishable syllable (*tyakṣara*). Its "array" (*vyūha*) is not a mere collection (*vṛnda*), because the vowels and consonants (*ālikālī*), whose nature is neuter and so forth, are established within the imperishable syllable.
"Having concentrated upon that day and night through entering, abiding, and emerging, it is recited"—this is *samādhi*.
That [chapter] in which there is such a form of *samādhi* is thus described; he speaks of that chapter.

By means of the mantra beginning with "Oṃ śūnyatā," it is further stated: "Oṃ" and so forth is the first [syllable]; "śūnyatā" is the second; "jñāna" (knowledge) is the third; and likewise, the fourth is designated as "vajra. This is the sixfold commentary on the third chapter.
The fifth is called "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva), and the sixth is said to be "I" (aham).
Thus has the sixfold [set] of the Tathāgatas been described for the supreme person.
"Oṃ Śūnyatā," beginning with the pair, is the second, the Wisdom-Vajra.
I would consist of that very nature, and here the triad of principles (tritattva) is likewise conceived.
The three principles (tritattva) become one perfectly; this is clearly manifested as that which is designated "the manifest" (vyakta), according to the scripture.
One should meditate upon and visualize the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the midst of the space-element, possessing a body formed by the threefold union.
Of what nature is it?

It is called the "Great Array of Clouds of Rays," which is a mass of light arising from the three appearances; it is "equal in radiance to the flames of a Buddha," adorned with five-colored rays—white and so forth—like a rainbow.
"Pervaded by five rays" means it is composed of subtle elements; "perfectly circular all around" means it is completely round.
"The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is strewn with the five qualities of sensual pleasure" means it is endowed with the five rays, such as marriage and so forth;
"adorned with the five offerings" means that which offers objects is an offering (*upahāra*), namely the five sense faculties, and it is embellished by them because it possesses all the senses.

"One should cause [the practitioner] to enter such a luminous Buddha-maṇḍala" means that having meditated upon oneself in this manner as having entered the state of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), "in brief"— that is, instantaneously— one should visualize, meaning one should understand, the "image" which is the nature of Mahāvajradhara in the "middle," that is, between *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*, as an self devoid of the positions of existence and non-existence.
In this very sequence, having manifested oneself as Vairocana and so forth according to the distinctions of one's inclination, one should accomplish one's own welfare; therefore, he says:
"The great mudrā of Vairocana, characterized by body, speech, and mind," and so on.
He speaks thus in order to strengthen this very yoga of the Great Vajradhara.

Then the Blessed One, whose nature is the luminosity of the *dharmadhātu*, having relied upon that samādhi, spoke his own mantra— the Great Vajra Holder— which effects the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and brings about the perfection of body, speech, and mind.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the essence of the dharmadhātu.
The meaning of this is stated according to the *Vyākhyātantra*: "Oṃ" is to be known as the first; the second is designated as *dharma*;
the third is declared to be *dhātu*; and the fourth is called *svabhāva*.

The fifth is to be known as consisting of the self (ātman), and the sixth arises through conjunction with "I" (ahaṃ). Having uttered this mantra, one who is of the nature of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) should then perform that cultivation.
Thus [it is said].
This is the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
Now, for the purpose of strengthening one's own mind, he teaches the cultivation of the three types of subtle yoga,
beginning with "the five colors," and so forth.

One should meditate on the great jewel born of the five families, marked with the signs such as the vajra, which—due to its great value—is like a precious gem; it should be visualized at the tip of the nose, the size of a mustard seed, through the yoga of one's own deity, always, day and night.
"Steadfast," and so forth:

when the sign of vision has been manifested and arises, then, having recognized that the vajra and so forth are immovable through meditation, one should expand them in order to produce mastery over meditation;
one should not expand them at all if they are unsteady.
One should not expand that which is being meditated upon.
By the words "one should expand" and so forth, he states that once [the deity] has been stabilized through the radiation of the vajra and so on, one should also expand the form of the Mahāmudrā.
This is expressed by the passage beginning with "one should expand with the most excellent [emanations]" and so on.
With excellent clouds that are multitudes of Buddhas, possessing a radiance equal to the flames of a Buddha, and endowed with colors such as white and others.
"By the great clouds of wheel-vajras" means characterized by clouds of wheels, vajras, and jewels. "With the excellent weapons of the lotus-bud" means bearing lotuses and swords.
"By the great clouds of Bodhisattvas" is used as an illustration;

thus, the practitioner, whose nature is that of emanation, should also cause the cavities of space to be pervaded—that is, covered—by the deities associated with the five families. This constitutes the complete practice.

Having visualized the Great Jewel—the conventional *bodhicitta*—the size of a mustard seed, five-colored, and consisting of the essence of the five Tathāgatas at the tip of one's nose, that is, within the opening of one's own *vajra*, one should meditate upon it constantly.
"But one should expand the stable jewel" means that,

having first performed the consecration of the vajra and lotus according to the prescribed method and having stabilized the jewel of one's own mind, one should expand it— that is, emit it— through yoga, which is to say, through meditative union.
One should expand it.
With the words "By means of excellent clouds," and so forth, he explains the mandala of the relinquishing of sons, grandsons, and others who have issued from the *bodhicitta*.
This is the "pregnant" (*garbhī*) [mantra].
The "supreme state" (*parapada*) consists of the nature of all the Tathāgatas.
The great jewel called Anāhata is the size of a mustard seed because it gives rise to the jewel of the Buddha;
it is the measure of a mustard seed because it has the form of a drop (*bindu*).
"At the tip of the nose" means:
One should constantly, day and night, meditate with effort and focused intent upon the pericarp of the heart-lotus by means of the yoga of entry, abiding, emergence, and withdrawal.
What is that which is stable and eternal?
The Unstruck (anāhata).
Therefore, one should emanate a mass of five-colored jewel-rays and set it in motion through the stages of entry, abiding, and emergence.
By the words "unstable" and so forth, he shows that one should perform this yoga only upon attaining the reality of the Unstruck.
Now, he says "The flame of the Buddha," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the procedure for expansion (*sphāraṇa*):
the "flame of the Buddha" refers to the five rays of light.

One should emanate four mandalas with light equal to that [of the central deity], according to the divisions starting from the south, and thus fill the hollow of space with clouds of Tathāgatas. This is the *kolika* (ultimate) sense.
To show the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) of Vairocana and the others, he says: "One should draw the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*)."
And so forth.

Having meditated on a moon disc preceded by taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the object, and having visualized a wheel above it, one should, through its transformation according to the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* of the third chapter, properly contemplate Vairocana.
Likewise, through the transformation of the lotus, the yogi should contemplate Amitābha—who resembles a lotus mandala and has the luster of a ruby—within the Lotus Family.

One devoted to the Jewel, a practitioner of the Jewel family, should meditate on Ratnasaṃbhava, who resembles a jewel maṇḍala and is yellow in color. One should meditate on Amoghasiddhi, who arises from the yoga-maṇḍala, the universal vajra.
[This occurs] "in the vicinity of space."
"Proximity with space" means similarity to space; "situated in that similarity to space" means being as dark as the sky.
"These," and so forth.
What is that body-maṇḍala characterized by the means of accomplishing body, speech, and mind?
It is Akṣobhya, born from all vajras;
these indeed are the most excellent Buddhas.
The application is "those who have obtained the aspect of omniscience.
Those whose nature (*śīla*) it is to cause sentient beings to obtain and grasp omniscience (*sarvajñatva*).
Regarding "Vajravyūha":
the *vajras* are the Tathāgatas; their *vyūha* is their assembly or configuration where [this occurs], hence "the chapter on the Vajravyūha. This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
One should draw and recognize the unstruck (*anāhata*) lunar disc, which is luminous like the element of space and situated therein.

One should meditate upon and recognize the water-mandala, which is white in color, has the nature of Akṣobhya, is produced from the unstruck [sound], is located in the center of the clear mandala, and is motionless due to its slow movement as it proceeds.
One should recognize the fire-mandala, which resembles a lotus mandala, is red in color, has the nature of Amitābha through the meditations on the lotus, and proceeds toward the right.

One who is devoted to jewels and a reciter of the mantra of Ratnasambhava should recognize the Mahendra-maṇḍala as resembling a jewel-maṇḍala, yellow in color, and currently proceeding. One should recognize the Yoga-maṇḍala, which is the Vāyavya-maṇḍala, as black in color, having Amoghasiddhi as its intrinsic nature, and moving to the left.
This has been clearly shown in the Vyākhyā-tantra.
Therefore, it is introduced here:
one should conceive of Yoga as being without beginning or end, extremely subtle,
the union of the unmanifest and the manifest, and born from the nature of that which is devoid of intrinsic self-nature.
The primordial, singular perfection of nature, devoid of both unity and multiplicity,
is the sole source of all phenomena arising within the reality known as dependent origination.
Having made oneself such as this, one should draw the Dharma-maṇḍala;
it is, in brief, red, black, yellow, and white.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, one should draw Pāṇḍarā and the others through the union of the four moments (*turya*);
in their midst is the deity of one's own [lineage], the supreme excellence of the yoga of the fourth moment.
Above, across, and below, the pale [deities] and others are situated as appropriate within their respective circular mandalas of fire, wind, Indra, and Varuṇa.
"Thus spoke the Blessed One"— this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

The Explanation of the Six Points in the Third Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.

The Fourth Chapter.

He describes the procedure for requesting the guru to perform the consecration of the *rajo-maṇḍala* for disciples who have attained specific qualities through the cultivation of subtle yoga preceded by the visualization of the deity—from the words "Now" (*atha*) onwards, up to "they requested.
This is according to the literal meaning.
Having praised the "Tathāgata of All" by way of Akṣobhya, he propitiates him.
"Peaceful" means by way of the intrinsic nature of Vairocana.
"The abode of all Tathāgatas" means...
By the nature of Ratnaketu; all phenomena by the nature of Amitābha; supreme selflessness by the nature of Amoghasiddhi.
Furthermore, he praises [the mandala] by way of the nature of the three families with the words "endowed with all characteristics," and so forth.
The connection is: "Proclaim the mandala that is endowed with all characteristics and devoid of all non-characteristics.

The meaning is: "Reveal this supreme and excellent mandala, which is the foremost body of Samantabhadra, as described above—possessed of the defining characteristics and free from the defects of deficiency or excess."

He is the purifier of the conduct of gnosis (*jñānacaryāviśodhaka*), for he purifies those natures—passion and so forth—which are the threefold appearances of gnosis born from the supreme reality of the peaceful dharmas and produced from ultimate truth; this is because he has attained all sovereignty.

He is Samantabhadra because he has attained mastery over speech, and thus is the foremost in speech. You are the great mind of all sentient beings because you are the vajra-mind of all sentient beings.
It is pure because of the removal of stains such as passion;
it is naturally immaculate because, when investigated, passion and the like are not perceived.
Therefore, Samantabhadra is so called because he has transcended his own mind;
he is the pinnacle of mind because he leads all sentient beings to the city of nirvāṇa.
Speak the Vajra! Reveal the ritual procedure for the mandala.
It is not without a hidden meaning (*nāsandhyam*).
To introduce the words of the Vajradhara, the compiler says "Now," and so forth.
"Vajra" is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*).
He is Vajradhara because he delivers [beings];
he is the Teacher because his instruction conforms to those to be trained;
he is "the three worlds" (triloka) because his nature is the triple world of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ, as he abides by way of the nature of the desire realm and so forth.
The "Vajras supreme in the three worlds" refers to the Pratyekabuddhas and others; he is their foremost lord. The "supreme in the three worlds" refers to Brahmā and others whom he instructs.
Such is Mahāvajradhara.
It is beautiful and pleasing, the abode of all Tathāgatas, having become their very residence.
Because it is the arrival of all Tathāgatas, it is called the "mind-maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas"; this distinguishes it from the maṇḍalas of body and speech.
*Maṇḍa* means Māra; that which takes (*lāti*) or seizes (*gṛhṇāti*) him is a *maṇḍala*. That which possesses the form of such a [seizing] is the "maṇḍala-shape."
He speaks of the mandala of the mind as being thus:
according to the literal meaning.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, while demonstrating the mandala by means of the words of Mahāvajradhara, he says:
Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha ata" and so forth: the word "atha" (now) serves to introduce the discourse, while the word "ataḥ" (therefore) indicates a reason.
Having accepted the student’s request, the intended meaning is: "Since this [student] is endowed with qualities such as faith and the like, therefore I shall fully explain the maṇḍala for him."
The mandala in which the mind is primary is the *cittamaṇḍala*; because of the preeminence of the Vajra family, it is supreme.
For this very reason, it is mentioned first.
*Cittavajra* is Akṣobhya.

Similarly, because it is unshakable by Māra and others, it resembles a vajra-mind; it is the essence (*maṇḍa*) of body, speech, and mind, and it is secret (*guhya*). That which "attains" (*talati*) this is the *kāyavākcittamaṇḍala*. "I shall correctly proclaim that"—this is the yoga.
With the words beginning with "with a new," he demonstrates the procedure by means of that thread:
"with a new" means not used for anything else; "well-applied" means properly wound; "of correct measure" means double the size of the maṇḍala; and "beautiful" means five-colored.
A wise and skilled master, having delineated the mandala, should thus thread and divide it with such a cord;
for it is called a "cord" (sūtra) because it indicates the mandala.
How so? By means of the cultivation of body, speech, and mind, and the concentration of body, speech, and mind,
he demonstrates the measurement of the mandala as being twelve cubits.
