"Square" means having four corners;
"with four gates" means the outer maṇḍala, by implication, is endowed with four gates in the east and other directions.
Regarding the phrase "of that" and so forth:
within that outer maṇḍala endowed with qualities such as being square and so on, one should draw a wheel—the inner maṇḍala—in a circular form.
The procedure [vidhi] consists of the placement of mudrās and so forth; the preparation of the ground, the offering of wealth and so on, constitutes the ritual method.

In that regard, having seen what is prescribed by the rules, one should first complete the foundation mandala by means of that ritual action; immediately thereafter, the preceptor should perform the placement of the vajra and other mudrās.
There are three types of mudrās: the Dharma-mudrā, the Cihna-mudrā, and the Mahāmudrā; the Dharma-mudrās consist of the syllables *hūṃ* and so forth.

One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of these three types of mudrās: the *cihnamudrā*, such as the vajra and so forth; the *devatācakra* of Akṣobhya and the other deities, which is the *mahāmudrā*; and [the *samayamudrā*], with regard to the mental continuums (*santāna*) of all sentient beings and so forth.
In that context, in order to show the symbolic seal (*cihnamudrā*) for the sake of illustration, he says "in its center" and so forth.
"The producer of fear even for fear" means that which generates fear even for fear; this is the *vajra*, because its essential nature (*tattva*) is aversion (*dveṣa*).
The Vajras are the Tathāgatas; their flames are the five-colored rays. Adorned by these, the wheel is dense with a profusion of sparks and strewn with clusters of light-rays.

One should depict the lotus as being made of jewels, possessing a brilliance like that of a ruby because it is of the nature of the discerning wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇajñāna*) of Amitābha, in the western direction, and so forth in the north.
To explain this,
he says "and having entered into meditative absorption" (*samādhiṣya ca*), and so forth; the skillful mantra-practitioner [should act] toward that aforementioned woman.

"Guṇamekhalām" means she whose girdle is a garland made of virtues; having thus directly invested her with that [garland], as if with my own, and having removed her ordinary state and made her a peahen of the five families (pañcakula), he shall delight her.
Then one should emit the gentle semen;
how could those following the path of the thunderbolt cast it outside— the state of the Buddha, which originates from the Buddha?

It is said that one should create and meditate upon an array of Tathāgatas that adorns the realm of space, serving as an ornament for the expanse of the sky—an array pervading the hollow of the firmament, constructed from the atoms of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
This shows that the performance of worship is not by the thought of awakening alone, but also through the outflows of the body; thus he says:
One should offer the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), beginning with feces and urine, to the deities; one should present them as sacrificial porridge (caru) to the maṇḍala circle.
"One should satisfy oneself by that very [means]"—
to the question "What benefit is there when this is done?",
he says "In this way," and so forth.
The Buddhas are the aggregate of form and so forth; the Bodhisattvas are the sense bases such as the eye and so forth.
These Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are pleased; they attain satisfaction.
Those of great renown and swift activity, who bring joy to the eyes of the world, are of interpretable meaning;
this is called the explanation of the Sage.
Now, therefore, I shall describe the supreme mandala of the mind,
which resembles vajra-wisdom, the mandala of body, speech, and mind;
this excellent ninefold [mandala] is well-arranged and thus proclaimed.
That which possesses the two-fold convention of scripture is called the well-measured conventional truth; that which is non-dual and excellent is held to be the ultimate truth.
Therefore, this *Prajñāsūtra* is described as the means for attaining that [ultimate].
By means of the single thread of wisdom and skillful means, this supreme *saṃbhoga*-kāya dharma is delineated as the maṇḍala; depending upon the twelve links [of dependent origination],
it is the Noble Truth, square in shape, with the sublime abodes (*brahmavihāra*) as its corners.
The inner maṇḍala of the wheel, which consists of the fourfold collection of gates known as the "compendium of bases," is the conventional symbol for the reality of the nature of phenomena;
it is the seal of the sapphire (*vajrendranīla*), the sign of indivisible gnosis.
The trident called the "Fivefold Division" is the destroyer of saṃsāra;
the wheel, which was previously situated as a mere mirror, is adorned with flames; and the jewel, known by the name of the southern [direction], possesses flames that are equal on all sides.
The one called the Lotus of Discernment, and the final one, the Ruby;
that which is the ever-ascending mind, which shatters the conceptual constructions of the world.
In the southeast should be Kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-khaḍga, with a radiance equal to the flames of a ray; in the south, Nendra; and in the southwest, Maitrī, with a radiance like a blue cloud;
and in the northwest, that which is called Karuṇā, the Vajra of the Māmakī family.
In the northwest is Padmasaṃjñā, who is Muditā with a well-set face; in the northeast, Utpalā shines forth as Upekṣā, known by her blue color.
Likewise, at the eastern gate is Mudgara, radiant and of beautiful luster, preceded by the gesture of generosity.
Likewise, the staff called *priyavādya*, radiant with the brilliance of a vajra-flame,
belongs to Hayagrīva in the west; the lotus called *arthacaryā* is for the sake of equal conduct (*samānacaryā*) for the wielder of the vajra, Vajrakuṇḍalin.
Thus has the characteristic arrangement of the mudrās been correctly explained,
so that worship may be performed according to their formal positions through the three types of meditative cultivation;
for this is called the Great Mudrā-maṇḍala.

Through the divisions of time such as moments (*kṣaṇa*) and so forth, she is designated as "sixteen-year-old," "dwelling in non-arising," and "dwelling in peace. She is determined to be named "one who has not departed from the peaceful dharmas," possessing beauty and arising with sublime radiance.
Dependent conditioning is the fragrance; the flower is the blossoming of gnosis.
Within the family of the absence of intrinsic nature, one should know the inexhaustible gnosis of the Omniscient One.
A wise man should desire such a woman as the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Neither internal nor external, nor at the end, nor established elsewhere in both;
because it is a yoga of abiding without a location, it is therefore considered "mine" (māmakī).
However, its establishment is said to be the yoga of being of one essence with that very nature.
The state of a Buddha is gentle, dwelling in the unity of space;
these are merely conceptual constructs.

Therefore, one should know from this withdrawal that the objects are the Sūtra, the cognitive faculties are the Prajñā, semen is the praised Dharmatā of purity, and blood is the omniscient gnosis (*sarvajñatājñāna*). Those phenomena which are conceptually constructed are declared to be the deities; their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is the offering.
Thus those Buddhas, the sons of the Conquerors, are especially pleased with those for whom there is mundane conceptualization, exactly as has been stated.

The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the passage beginning with "all Tathāgatas" and so forth is that, through the designation of the mandalas to be drawn and so on, it is precisely the form of the utterly pure deity that is being presented; this is the commentary on the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) of the fourth chapter.

The mandala of the Lord of the Mind-Vajra is the mind-mandala; "mandala" means that which takes or grasps the *maṇḍa*, which is the essence, namely conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). Thus it is called a mandala.
*Ne-yārtha* means the essence (*maṇḍa*), the core, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); that which takes or grasps (*lāti*) that is called *maṇḍala*.
As it was said by the Blessed One in the *Vyākhyātantra*:
"Transcending all limbs of meditative cultivation, free from conceptual construction and its products, and transcending the measures and the bindu— this is the supreme maṇḍala."
Thus [it is said].
The Explanation of the Six Points in the Fourth Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
This is the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
The Fifth Chapter.
Showing that even one who has realized the two stages and received empowerment will not attain accomplishment without the conduct (*caryā*), he says "Then," and so forth.

He is the King consisting of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas; the Sovereign of the Three Worlds; the Foremost, because he surpasses worldly deities such as Hari and Hara, as well as supramundane ones such as the Śrāvakas, by means of his miraculous powers and other qualities; and the Lord of the World (*bhuvaneśvara*), because he governs the realms of *bhuḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*.
The conduct of those belonging to one's own and other schools is "all conduct" (*sarvacaryā*);
the meaning is that it is sought after (*arthyate*).
It is both the supreme dharma (*agradharma*) and the object (*artha*), hence "the object of the supreme dharma" (*agradharmārtha*).
Mahāvajradhara has indeed attained the goal of the supreme dharma through all modes of conduct;
he is thus addressed by all those seeking liberation.

Because omniscience is paramount, there are three kinds of conduct (*caryā*): elaboration (*prapañcatā*), non-elaboration (*niṣprapañcatā*), and absolute non-elaboration (*atyantaniṣprapañcatā*). It is called "conduct" because one conducts oneself by means of it.
He explains its characteristic, its essential nature,
according to the literal meaning,
beginning with "non-conceptual," and so forth.
The non-conceptual is the ultimate truth, characterized by profundity;
the object is the conventional truth, characterized by vastness.
Those who correctly cultivate these two in a non-dual manner have become established in the non-conceptual reality; they are the yogins.
Even those agitated by passion and other afflictions accomplish—that is, bring to completion—the most excellent and supreme siddhi, the siddhi of Mahāmudrā.
This is because the Vajrayāna is the foremost vehicle, as it surpasses all other vehicles;
"relying upon that which is unsurpassed and most excellent" is the implied conclusion of the sentence.
It is not without a hidden meaning (*nāsandhyam*).
Showing that the thorough knowledge of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) alone is the cause of Buddhahood, and not [factors] such as birth (*jāti*), he says:
"Caṇḍāla," and so forth.
This shows the contemptibility of their birth.
"Bamboo-worker" is a name [indicating] their occupation; by the word "etcetera," other occupations are also included, such as traps, mechanical devices, weapons, and snares intended for killing.
Those who contemplate the purpose—the practical aim—of these are "those who contemplate the means of killing."
They are accomplished in this supreme vehicle, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna. The "supreme persons" (agrapudgalas) are those who possess the highest jewels;
they go by means of this, therefore it is called the "supreme vehicle" (agrayāna).
The unsurpassed Mahāyāna is the Vajrayāna;
in that [vehicle], they attain accomplishment.
"The immediate [sins]," and so forth.

The five actions known as killing one’s mother, father, or a monk; destroying a Buddha-image; and rejecting the true Dharma are the "immediate" (*ānantarya*) hells that bring torment immediately after death. Here, the term *ānantarya* is used figuratively to refer to those who commit such acts. By the word "and so forth" (*prabhṛti*), the "near-immediate" (*upānantarya*) offenses are included. These are: violating a mother who is an Arhatī, and killing one who is established in the certainty [of liberation].
For a Bodhisattva in training, there is immediate expulsion from the gate [of the community].

The commentary on the six parameters of the fifth chapter states: "The five acts similar to the immediate [offenses] are the fifth: the destruction of a stūpa. These are the near-immediate offenses for one who has committed great evil."

Those who have fallen from the Buddha's teaching due to the four root downfalls—like a palm tree cut at its base—and are destined for hell, they too, by obtaining the stage of the perfected process (*niṣpannakrama*) here through the grace of the Guru, attain accomplishment;
they reach Buddhahood.
How much more so, then, outcasts and others? Thus he diminishes their faults.
Thus, by acting for the sake of others regardless of whether they are worthy or unworthy recipients, the greatness of the vehicle has been revealed.
One might, however, harbor the suspicion that someone who betrays their guru might sometimes succeed in accomplishing the Vajrayāna, which purifies even the most wicked of people;
therefore, he speaks in order to dispel that doubt.
"Those intent on reviling the teacher," and so forth.

Having previously attended upon the teacher and realized the reality through the sequence of hearing and reflection, he who now disregards the guru, thinking "What is the use of this?", is a reviler of the teacher (*ācāryanindakah*).

Those others who, along with him, engage in social enjoyment such as sharing food and the like, or take pleasure in him, or fill their own bellies and so forth with him—they do not attain success, being utterly excluded.
How much more so, then, one who reviles the Teacher?
By saying "not at all," he emphasizes that such a person never succeeds under any circumstances;
for by accomplishing even the most wicked sinner, he accomplishes the impossible.
The assembly itself is the means; in that means, [the results] are not accomplished. How much less so elsewhere?
As it is said in the venerable *Māyājālatantra*: "Indeed, one will have a vision even in a dream of censuring the teacher."
Those who revile their teacher are seized by obstacles and impediments.
Those of cruel deeds and evil nature should always be avoided on this earth.
Thus;
according to the literal meaning.
Lest this *Tantrarāja* be considered devoid of the status of a teacher (*anācāryaka*), [the author], demonstrating a specific mode of conduct that avoids what is contrary to worldly norms, says:
"Those who take life," and so forth.

The meaning of this is introduced from the explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*): "Those who, through the arising of calm abiding (*śamatha*), bring about the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so on..."
Those who take life would be established in the foremost vehicle.
Those who regard the internal and the external as arising from conditions and place,
being devoted to false speech, are practitioners whose yoga is established in what is not the true locus.
The wisdom of the perfectly enlightened one is designated as "substance" (dravya);
those who delight in the substance of others are considered to be of a nature that seizes that [wisdom].

Those beings who possess the single nature of suchness and are ever-united with the permanence of suchness— they, though delighting in sensual pleasures, shall be the most excellent in the supreme practice.
Due to delusion regarding emptiness, one is terrified; the faculty is called "urine.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, these two are renowned as the "objects," while the enjoyers of those two are the "pacifiers.
Indeed, they are fit for the practice in this supreme Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
This is intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā).
Regarding the passage beginning with "mother-sister" and so forth:
"mother" means one who is as favorable as a mother;
likewise for "sister" and "daughter."

Taking any one of these women of his own family and making her a "five-family peacock" (*pañcakulakalāpinī*) according to the procedure taught for the practice, whatever [woman] the practitioner desires, he shall attain vast and supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*).
Those for whom there is the supreme dharma called the Mahāyāna are the "Mahāyāna supreme dharma" practitioners;
among them, he shall attain vast accomplishment.
From union with an unsuitable mudrā, mental distraction necessarily arises.
Furthermore, suitability occurs through affection even in another lifetime.
If a mudrā who is trained in mantra and tantra and conducive to the practice cannot be found, he says what should then be done:
"Of the Buddha," and so forth.
One should emanate the Mother of the Buddha, Prajñāpāramitā, who resides in one's own heart, and enter into meditative union with her.
The Great Goddess residing in the heart is the bearer of yoga for the yogin.
She is known as the Mother of all Buddhas, the Sovereign Lady of the Vajra Realm.
Because of this statement:
"desiring [them]" means with those who, like mothers, sisters, or daughters, desire his welfare and understand the conventions.
Experiencing the bliss of supreme joy through the *jñānamudrā*, one is "not smeared," meaning one is not touched at all by the afflictions such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
Not only is one unsmeared by defects such as passion, but one also attains all prosperity; thus he says, "is perfected," and so on.

The wisdom of that practitioner—the wise one who possesses the well-trained mudrā, who is free from conceptual construction, and who knows the intrinsic nature—attains Buddhahood; that is, the state of Mahāvajradhara is accomplished spontaneously. This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Furthermore, the explanation according to the Āryas is stated:
One should desire the perfection of wisdom— wisdom which is the sole mother of the Dharmakāya and is called "without intrinsic nature"—
by means of the yoga of non-dual suchness.
One who possesses the yoga of his own presiding deity should desire that very sister, who has become equal to the Sambhogakāya, by means of the mantra-form; the practitioner should,
however, contemplate her as a daughter in the form of the Nirmāṇakāya.
A yogi who desires such a sister, mother,
or daughter shall attain vast accomplishment in the supreme dharmas of the Mahāyāna.
This is the definitive meaning.

With the words beginning with "Then" (*atha*), [the text describes] those who have attained wonder (*āścarya*) upon hearing that even outcasts (*caṇḍāla*) and others can achieve Buddhahood, and those who have attained amazement (*adbhuta*) upon hearing that even those who commit the sins of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) can attain the state of Great Bliss (*mahāsukha*). Thus, Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin and the others—endowed with such wonder and amazement, possessing dull faculties like Puṇḍarīka, and being killers of living beings and so forth—clinging to the literal meaning of the vajra-words spoken in intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*), such as "What is this that the Blessed One... and so on, raise this objection.
The construction is: "What does he say? (*kiṃ bhāṣate iti yogaḥ*).
The Blessed One is endowed with the two accumulations, the Tathāgata of all, the Noble One.
By these two phrases, the impossibility of speaking ill [of him] is shown.
All Tathāgatas are both perfected and unperfected.
Their assembly is a gathering; in the midst of that, even there, it is not at all proper to speak ill-spoken words. "Durbhāṣitavacanam" means the speaking of ill-spoken words.
"Those who take life," and so forth, refers to the characteristic of engaging in ignoble actions.
"Utterance" (*udāhāra*) means that which is spoken; it is ill-spoken speech, and that is the "utterance of ill-spoken words.
For what purpose do you perform that?
"Then," and so forth.
Immediately after the words of the bodhisattvas, all the Tathāgatas—Akṣobhya and the others—spoke to them as follows: "Enough," and so forth. "Alam" means "sufficient."
Your intention is known;
the meaning is "what is the use of saying more?
Thinking that the words of the Blessed One spoken at twilight were taken literally and thus poorly expressed, you will speak in this manner.

Why [is it said] "of those who take life," and so forth? Regarding the *dharmatā* (the nature of reality) expressed by the *vajrapada*: for the Buddhas, who are the ultimate awakeners; for the jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) who possess the knowledge of the essence (*sāra*); those whose knowledge (*jñāna*)—that is, their realization (*avabodha*)—is directed toward that essence, namely non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*), are so described.
The "essential dharma" (*sāradharma*) is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*);
the "object" (*artha*) is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

Produced and attained through a form non-different from those two, it is produced from the essence of the Dharma and its meaning. Such is the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), which is to be given only to jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) and not to others.

Therefore, it is the intention of the Tathāgatas that this was taught in intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*). "This is the state of the conduct of awakening" means that this very conduct of awakening (*bodhicaryā*) is the state of the conduct of awakening, which is the state of Vajradhara.
It is called the "state of conduct" because by means of this [conduct], the state of Vajradhara is certainly and inevitably attained.
This is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).

Now, as for the passage beginning with "indeed, inexpressible," the meaning has been previously analyzed. [They were] terrified—having fallen into fear—because of the bitter ripening of [actions such as] killing living beings and so forth;
and they were agitated by being bewildered as to what should be done, due to the fear arising from both the non-performance [of those acts] and the transgression of the Blessed One’s command.

Thereafter, having heard from the presence of the Tathāgata the vajra-word beginning with "of the one who takes life," they became faint with the intensity of their joy due to the realization of a reality (dharmatā) never realized before; the intention is that because their minds were one-pointed, the activities of the remaining sense-faculties were suspended— this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Furthermore, the explanation according to the Ṛṣis is stated:
This secret, which is without foundation, is the singular peace, the supreme bliss;
it has been spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhyāya*) and leads to the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Due to the union with the infinity of space, form and the other [sensory objects] are infinite;
they are indeed declared to be Tathāgatas and likewise Bodhisattvas.
This very Maṇḍala of the *Tattvasaṃgraha* arises from one's own body.
Conceiving of a self-identity here, these bodhisattvas are indeed deluded;
they do not know it to be thus, and driven by the madness of pleasure, they will say of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas that they are deluded.
The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the passage beginning with "Then," and ending with "these great bodhisattvas," is easy to understand according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
The sameness of space and its equality are neither dual nor non-dual;
the sameness of space is non-dual.

Having entered that very samādhi named Vajra, immediately upon his entering it— meaning, as soon as the Blessed One had entered it— the meaning of which has already been analyzed— by the mere touch, by the mere contact, of the mass of light rays from the splendor of the Great Vajradhara who has become thus, they remained seated each upon their own respective seats.
The statement "they have regained mindfulness" is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);
it refers to space, the three emptinesses, equality, and luminosity— the non-duality of these two, which is their union (*yuganaddhatā*).

Because it is indivisible, it is called "Vajra"; having entered that meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he caused [the assembly] to attain it while they were established in the "Absorption of No-Abiding" (*asthānaka-samādhi*)—that is, while their own selves were abiding in the form of Bodhisattvas. "Immediately upon entering [that state]" means: as soon as the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) had been performed in this manner, by the mere touch of the mass of light—the specific quality of the radiance belonging to Mahāvajradhara—with that radiance whose measure is like the wind that is touched, the meaning is that they emerged from the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*) through the spreading rays of gnosis that have entered the subtle element (*sūkṣmadhātu*).
"On their respective seats" means they were situated in their own world-systems as appropriate; thus,
they became capable of accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings.
The definitive meaning:
"Then," and so forth,
refers to those who attained wonder at the Blessed One’s skill in teaching the profound Dharma.
"Never before occurred" yet "it has occurred"—thus it is marvelous (*adbhuta*).

Through that which is exceedingly marvelous (*atyadbhuta*), there is agitation (*audvilya*); this is "exceeding marvel and agitation" (*atyadbhutaudvilya*), which is a state of bewilderment (*saṃbhrama*) arising from seeing the mass of beings brought to perfection by means of the specific meditative absorption (*samādhi-viśeṣa*) attained through the teaching.

Attaining a state of extreme wonder and agitation, they uttered such a sound of Dharma, a resonance associated with the Dharma, saying, "Such are the dharmas, such is their nature. Having become clear-minded through the teaching of the Dharma, they praised the Tathāgatas—who are themselves the teachers of that Dharma—by means of verses beginning with "Aho! in order to extol the Dharma itself.

I am filled with wonder at the Dharma; by the first word "Dharma," that which is characterized as the teaching is intended, while by the second word "Dharma," the meaning to be established by that teaching is intended.
Regarding the phrase "the source of Dharma and Artha":

*Dharma* is characterized by expression (*abhidhāna*), while *Artha* is characterized by the object to be expressed (*abhidheya*). The "source of Dharma and Artha" (*dharmārthasaṃbhava*) is that from which these two arise.
What is it? It is the selflessness of objects (*artha-nairātmya*) through the purity of Dharma.

Dharma consists of that which arises from hearing (śrutamaya), which has pure meaning, and that which arises from reflection (cintāmaya); selflessness (nairātmya) is brought face-to-face by these two.
What is that? It is the Vajrarāja consisting of cultivation (bhāvanāmaya).
The Vajras are the Tathāgatas; their king and sovereign is Mahāvajradhara.
Homage, homage to you of such a nature!
The word is repeated because the Blessed One consists of the two truths.

Purified by body, speech, and mind, he is not other than the body because they are mutually non-different; his *ālaya* is luminous (*prabhāsvara*), like the equality of space. Because it is free from arising and ceasing, and because it is a pure appearance devoid of transformation, it is "without appearance" (*nirābhāsa*)—the Vajra Body—like a rainbow.
"O Vajra-body, whose imperishable body is fashioned from five rays of light and endowed with the excellence of all aspects—homage, homage to you! This is repeated as before.
Because it is accumulated with all the qualities of a Buddha, the mind (*citta*) is the primordial ground of the Tathāgatas; thus it is "supreme" (*śreṣṭha*), meaning preeminent.
Those whose nature it is to abide upon the path of the three times are "those who abide upon the path of the three times" (*vyadhvapathavartinaḥ*).
You are the entities existing in past and other times, because you are the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena;

you alone are the luminosity of the great space (*mahākāśaprabhāsvara*); you alone have become the element (*dhātubhūta*), for the state of the three realms (*traidhātukatva*) is the state of space due to your attainment of supernatural powers and sovereignty.
"Salutation, salutation to you"—this is repeated because he consists of the two truths.
"Born from the body of space":
his body is like space; thus, he is Vairocana, who is born from that "body-of-space knowledge," which is the mirror-like knowledge (*ādarśajñāna*), because he is identical with it.
The path of space is the gnosis of equality; that from which it proceeds and is accomplished, by virtue of being its source, is Ratnasambhava, the one who moves upon the path of space.
Akṣobhya is "one whose mind is like space" because his nature is the perfectly pure *dharmadhātu*.
Amitābha is the foremost among those phenomena (dharmas) that are absorbed in the lotus, consisting of the gnosis of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Having established the station and foundation for those who are wonders for the sake of the entire world, Amoghasiddhi—whose nature consists of practice and knowledge—praises the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara as being composed of the five families by means of this verse. Conduct that accomplishes the welfare of oneself and others is "universal conduct" (*samantacaryā*); that which is supreme and distinguished is "the pinnacle of universal conduct" (*samantacaryāgra*). The chapter that explains its meaning is titled "The Pinnacle of Universal Conduct."

Not [to be] without the *saṃdhi*. This concludes the commentary on the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) in the fifth chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*. The sixth chapter. The sequence of the empowerment of the body and so forth is now demonstrated, [showing that] the conduct (*caryā*) must be performed preceded by the pride (*ahaṅkāra*) of the stage of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth:
Akṣobhya is the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas.

His secret is the mantra that presides over it; having entered into and brought face-to-face the meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—which is one-pointedness of mind—named after that [mantra], this mind which is about to be described is empowered by it. Because it protects the mind, it is called a "mantra. He uttered it, he spoke it: *oṃ sarvatathāgatacittavajrasvabhāvātmako 'ham* (Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas).
Thus,
"atha" and so forth:
Virajavajra is Vairocana, whose nature is mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
Having taken recourse to that state and the mantra which presides over it—
namely, the one bearing that name— he recited the mantra for the empowerment of the body while relying upon that meditative absorption.
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas.
Thus begins the passage starting with "atha" and so forth.
Because immeasurable and infinite life (*amita-āyuḥ*) is obtained from it, he is Amitāyus. Amitābha consists of the wisdom that discerns the equality of the two [truths];
his "vajra" is the mantra whose nature is indivisible and which presides over him.
Having brought to manifestation the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that, he uttered the mantra for the empowerment of speech.
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
Having thus indicated the mantra for the consecration of the body and so forth, he speaks again, providing a further explanation:
"Trivajra," and so forth:
that in which there are the three vajras of body, speech, and mind is the "trivajra.
What is that? It is the *pada*, the body, because it is the support for the wheel of deities (*devatācakra*).
The "Tathāgata" refers to the intrinsic nature of Akṣobhya and the others;
it is "secret" because it is not fully known by the Śrāvakas and others; and it is the "cultivation of the stages."

"Padam" refers to the triad of arrays beginning with Locanā; it is that [deity] in whom there is the manifestation— that is, the radiation— for the purpose of the empowerment of the Vajra-body and so forth, because it is the basis for the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others.
The mantras are Akṣobhya and the others;
those by which they are indicated are the "mantra-indicators," namely the three syllables.
Having placed these upon the regions of the head, throat, and heart, one is marked by them.

This very [empowerment] should be accomplished—that is, one should empower—by means of these aforementioned excellent and supreme mantras for the empowerment of body and so forth; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Now, the empowerment of body, speech, and mind for practitioners of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is introduced from the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*).
Then the great hero Akṣobhya, having entered the meditative absorption known as the "Empowerment of Mind" (cittādhiṣṭhāna), which pertains to the secrets of body, speech, and mind,
proclaimed the mantra beginning with "Oṃ," as it is celebrated in the sixth chapter of the sixfold commentary.
"O Sarvatathāgata," which is conceived as having a twofold designation; "in the mind," which is joined with two by twos; the fifth, whose nature is the self;
may I be [designated] as the sixth in the enumeration, known as the triad of the six bodies.
Then the glorious Vairocana, having entered the samādhi known as Virajavajra, spoke regarding the empowerment of the body:
"Oṃ" is declared by Brahmā, the source of all the Tathāgatas.
For this Vajra-Veda is proclaimed as being situated within the passion for the body;
it is desire whose nature is the self, and that I am called Kārttikeya.
One should properly analyze the twilight state and then pierce it through the differentiation of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Then, perceiving himself as Amitābha, having entered the vajra-like samādhi of non-dual equality, he should utter the empowerment of speech.
"Oṃ" and so forth is declared to be the non-duality of all Tathāgatas; "vāc" (speech) should be known as the triple quality, which constitutes the pair known as the Vajra.
That which is known as desire, consisting of intrinsic nature, is remembered as "I" (Aham). These three are fully described, each being declared to consist of six parts.
And the transgression of the sequence has been taught regarding mind, body, and speech; those known as the three vajras have arisen from the single nature of sovereignty.
Thus, "the secret of the Tathāgatas, the three vajras" refers to the three vajras as the three gnoses; what are they like?

The secret of the Tathāgata, which has come from the Tathāgata, is not within the sphere of experience for those practicing the generation stage (*utpattikrama*); "pada" refers to the manifestation of the state, and that *pada* is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
Because it serves as the basis for the three consciousnesses, the "ground" (pada) is conventional truth; that which is analyzed and produced from it is the "analysis of the ground" (padavibhāvana),
which is a qualification of ultimate truth itself.
By means of these four supreme voids just mentioned,
there are the mantras which are the Tathāgatas;
their characteristics are the five rays of light.

The definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that one should bring about—that is, accomplish—the *vajradeha* (diamond body), which has become the object of experience characterized by those five characteristics.

Having thus performed the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of one's own body and so forth, and having made one's own consort a "peacock" (*kalāpinī*) of the five families, [the text] says "Then the Blessed One," and so forth, for the purpose of introducing the mantra of the mutual passion of the two wheels; the meaning of these words is already explained.
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra that impassions all Tathāgatas. Thus.

One should recognize this by the fact that immediately following the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), there is the offering to all Tathāgatas and the introduction of the mantra; thus he says, "Then the Blessed One," and so forth,
the meaning of which has already been explained.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the worship of all Tathāgatas. Thus.
In order to produce firm conviction regarding the fact that the practitioner should always conduct himself according to the very procedure just described, he says:
"One should always worship the Buddhas with the five qualities of sensual pleasure according to the prescribed rite."
Furthermore, teaching another method of worship for those practicing the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*),
he says "the five offerings" (*pañcopahāra*) and so forth; they are called "offerings" (*upahāra*) because they are presented (*upahriyante*) or dissolved (*līyante*).
That which possesses five offerings is "pañcopahāra," the sixth Tathāgata; [the word] refers to his worship.
Through the five wisdoms, beginning with the mirror-like wisdom, which have the nature of the five Tathāgatas and serve as the causes, there is the realization of the clear light;
by means of those offerings,
it is "swift," that is, rapid.
"In this very life, one shall attain Buddhahood— the state of the Sugata consisting of the three bodies.
Thus did the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, the sovereign of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas, describe the two types of worship.

Demonstrating this very procedure for worship, he says in the *Vyākhyātantra*: "Having rendered form, sound, smell, taste, the tangible, and the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) devoid of intrinsic nature, that becomes the supreme worship of the Buddha,
[accomplished] by means of those arising from the cognitions of the eye and so forth, and adorned with the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*)."
By means of these five offerings, one may swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Thus is the twilight language (sandhyābhāṣā).

Having thus explained the external and internal worship, he says "Now," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that enlightenment is not swiftly attained without the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*):
Mahāvajradhara [spoke] this mantra of all the Tathāgatas, which is about to be described, as well as the speech, body, and mind of all the Tathāgatas.
By way of illustration, he proclaimed the secret, the state of purity, of those mantras— the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas—
beginning with "The realization of mantra," and so forth.

Mantras are born from the *āli* and *kāli* [vowels and consonants] and have the nature of serpents and so forth; because they are subsumed within the three syllables by way of being female, male, and neuter, those mantras are the three syllables.
The thorough knowledge of them by way of their nature as entry (*praveśa*), abiding (*sthiti*), and emergence (*vyutthāna*) is the "contemplation of mantras" (*mantranidhyapti*).
In that regard, the former [practice] is characterized by the body as the *vajrajāpa* which serves as the means of accomplishment, or by speech through *vajrajāpa*,
while Vajrasattva, who resides in the mind at the heart, is impelled and made an object of experience through the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are.
"One should cultivate" means that one should bring about the four stages of the yogin's continuum which are about to be described;
as to what these are, he says:

He says "excellent" (*pravarām*); it is excellent because it is superior to the *vajrajāpa*, characterized by the discernment of the mind. It is "attainment" (*siddhim*) because the *mahāmudrā*, characterized by self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna*), satisfies the mind; thus it is "mind-satisfying" (*manaḥsantoṣaṇa*) because it brings about the purification of the *mahāmudrā*.
One should bring to manifestation the beloved, desired form of Mahāvajradhara, which is identical in character to existence;
by this, the benefits of vajra-recitation are described.
This concludes the explanation of the six points regarding the sixth chapter, beginning with "the mental realization" (*cittanidhyapti*).
Explaining the four thematic headings of the mind, he says:

through the second stage of profound reflection, there is a thorough knowledge of things as they truly are; that which is produced by this is the selflessness of the mind, which is what is meant by "the selflessness of the mind."
"Speech and body," and so forth;
this refers to the cultivation of the selflessness of both speech and body.
"One should accomplish the penetration of the mind" means that one should perform it;
by this, the triad of body, speech, and mind characterized as wisdom and means is shown.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"Trisamyogam," and so forth:
that in which there is the conjunction—that is, the unification—of the three gnoses is "trisamyoga"; it is the form of the deity consisting of mind, the equality with space, the ultimate truth.
One should bring to completion that Vajradhara whose abode is the place of origin;
for, through the contemplation of body, speech, and mind, no intrinsic nature is perceived.

This means that the intrinsic nature attained by the examination and contemplation of body, speech, and mind—which is conventional truth—is not perceived, because all things have entered into ultimate truth.
By this, the sequence of perfect awakening has been revealed.

One might suspect that even for one who does not find a firm footing in the body consisting of gnosis (*jñānamaya*), a state of abiding in the form of the deity might sometimes be attained through imagined yoga;
to refute this, he says:
Regarding the phrase "by means of the application of the mantra-form" and so forth:
"mantras" refers to the *praṇava* and others;
the "form" (*mūrti*) is that which is fashioned by them.
The mantra-form is its application, which consists of the four vajras; by means of that, there is neither awakening nor Buddhahood,
because the syllables of the mantra and so forth are produced by a collection of causes and conditions, and thus are subject to arising and perishing.
Since [the deity] is identical to space, how could a form be produced by those [elements]?
Furthermore, it cannot be said that there is "cultivation" (bhāvanā), because the form of the deity being cultivated is absent; thus, the cultivation itself is also non-existent.
Thus, because even the *dharmakāya*, the *saṃbhogakāya*, and so forth are to be abandoned,
[the author], demonstrating the state of the Great Vajradhara characterized by the establishment of the self within the assembly (*samāja*),
says "having investigated," and so on.

Having examined and fully understood this aforementioned characteristic of body, speech, and mind through the sequence beginning with the contemplation of mantra (*mantranidhyapti*), one should meditate upon the "union with awakening" (*bodhisaṃyoga*)—the samādhi fashioned by mantra—which is the characteristic of the three voids (*śūnyatraya*) that define body, speech, and mind. This is achieved by means of a concise unification of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) with ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Here, "awakening" (*bodhi*) is ultimate truth; "union" (*saṃyoga*) is that which is joined with it; thus, "union with awakening" is the samādhi, the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*).
The "mantras" are the five rays of light.
One should contemplate— that is, practice— that which has been conceptualized and fashioned by them;
by this, the sequence of the simultaneous flow (yuganaddhavāhikrama) is demonstrated, [which is] the intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā).
Now, he speaks the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth, which again explains the subtle yoga as taught in the third chapter, together with the wind and consciousness:
the word "atha" (now) indicates immediately after the demonstration of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
"Vajradhara" means one who holds the vajra; this is the literal meaning.
He is Vajradhara because he maintains the fivefold knowledge, such as the mirror-like wisdom, by means of being identical with them;
he is Vajradhara because he maintains a mental body (manomayadeha) consisting of all its limbs.
One who is pregnant.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, Vajra is non-dual gnosis; because he maintains that [gnosis] by being identical with it, he is called Vajradhara.

He is "Kolikam" because he is endowed with both accumulations; he is "Śrīmān" (the Glorious One) because he is adorned by Locanā and the other [consorts] of all the Tathāgatas, and thus he is "adorned by all the Tathāgatas."

Among all the Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, the foremost is the Omniscient One, Cittavajra; he speaks this supreme meditation to be described below: one should meditate on a mass of light, a lunar disc of clear radiance, situated in the center of the space-element;
thus, one should first bring forth the Saṃbhogakāya.

Having manifested the form of the Buddha, one should subsequently enter into the five aggregates and so forth, and having produced oneself as the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) composed of the atoms of all Tathāgatas, one should commence the subtle yoga through the process of emanation.

One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose; within that mustard seed, one should meditate upon the entire world of moving and non-moving beings—this delightful secret, fashioned by wisdom, which bestows knowledge.

By this vajra-word "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*), [the author] indicates, by means of the thread [of the teaching], the birth of ordinary beings (*prākṛtasattva*), the object of the imagined deity, the reality of wind (*vāyutattva*), the reality of mantra (*mantratattva*), the reality of gnosis (*jñānatattva*), and the reality of the utterly pure deity.
First, the cause of the birth of beings is indicated:

when the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) situated above unite with the non-dual sense faculties through the internal meditative union of wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*), impelled by joy, the entire body melts by the fire of great passion (*mahārāga*) and falls in the form of drops of bodhicitta upon the tip of the lotus-nose.
For those who practice the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*) of this existence, the Tathāgatas have established a convention using the term "mustard seed.

Regarding this, the *Samājottara* states: "One should emit the breath, which consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements, and then imagine it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the five nostrils."

"The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*. Thus, regarding the mustard seed (*sarṣapa*)—in the mustard seed, within the drop of semen (*śukravindu*), one should contemplate the world of moving and non-moving beings; one should recognize it as arising.

Based on the statement, "The nectar is said to be the semen; from it the three worlds are produced," one should contemplate Vajrasattva together with the moving and non-moving universe within this very mustard seed, having practiced the application of yoga upon it.
One should meditate upon its very qualification: "the delightful state of gnosis, the secret fashioned by gnosis.
This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*);
and he speaks [further] regarding the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).
"One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose," and so forth.

The five rays, whose nature is the five gnoses, residing in the heart, the secret place, the throat, the navel, and throughout the entire body, become the *prāṇāyāma* and emerge from the nostrils at the tip of the nose— the upper opening of the nose— in succession through the rotation of the four mandalas, as stated in the *Vajramālā*:

The sixth chapter, the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*: "At the tip of the nose is that which is called 'mustard seed' (*sarṣapa*); through the visualization of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), the five rays abide within breath control by virtue of the state of Buddhahood."
Emerging above the *prāṇa* through the left, the right, the pair,
and as motionless— thus the internal *velā* is said to be fourfold.
By means of the yoga based on one's own mantra, one should wander everywhere day and night, for a period of half a watch, in regular succession according to the proper order.
"One should contemplate a mustard seed at the tip of the nose"— this is the meaning of this vajra-word;
by this, the wind-element and the mantra-element are explained, as it says,
"the moving and non-moving within the mustard seed."

One should contemplate the threefold consciousness— the moving and the unmoving— which exists as the support and the supported within the subtle element of mustard seed, as being of the nature of awakening; one should understand this as the reality of gnosis (*jñāna-tattva*),
and cultivate the delightful state of gnosis, which is the secret fashioned by gnosis.
This very point is also taught in a Mahāyāna sūtra by means of intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*):

"Just as there is but one hair-tip [of a Buddha], so too are the Buddhas like the sands of the river Gaṅgā; yet this single atom is not a Buddha, nor do the sons of the Buddha sit in its midst. Thus it is said.
The reality of the deity is stated as the definitive meaning (nītārtha).

Now, in order to demonstrate the sequence of reciting the limbs that are undivided according to the distinction of the families during the arising of the four mandalas through the union of mantra and wind, he says "situated in the middle of the space-element," and so forth.

One should meditate upon—that is, one should understand—the sun-maṇḍala originating from that, which is situated in the middle of the space-element (ākāśadhātu), the jewel (ratna), and the unstruck sound (anāhata); and the fire-maṇḍala, which has the nature of red rays and emerges as a mass of light-rays from the right.
Having meditated upon the state that is the Buddha-image: "Buddha" refers to Vairocana, and "image" refers to Amitābha.

One should place— that is, mentally visualize— the syllable *HŪṂ*, which constitutes the emergence [from meditative absorption], above those two syllables *OṂ* that are characterized by their entry, stability, and meditation;
this is the recitation of Amitābha.

The lunar disk is the water mandala, which has a stable nature; it is the form of Locanā. That [vajra] which possesses union with that [water mandala] should be perceived as white and of indistinct movement.
Then, one should meditate upon the vajra-lotus.

Now, "then" (*atha*) means immediately after the transformation of the syllable *Oṃ*. When the lotus has transformed into the syllable *Āḥ*, one should initiate the emergence of the *Hūṃ* of the vajra.
This is the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*).
One should diligently visualize the *ādiyoga* above that maṇḍala—the jewel-maṇḍala of Ratnasaṃbhava, which is the Maheśvara-maṇḍala characterized by the movement of the couple and is yellow in color.

Above that maṇḍala, one should with effort meditate upon the *ādiyoga* as the syllable *kṣya*, whose nature consists of the non-abiding of emanation and reabsorption, through one-pointed concentration.
One should observe this jewel-recitation:
one should visualize a circle of light rays situated in the center of the space-element,
[beginning with] the syllable *aḥ*.

From the unstruck [sound], a black-colored wind-maṇḍala emerges from the left, bearing a circle of rays; above that, one should emit and radiate the gentle, short *huṃ* syllable, the "Buddha-foot. Following the stages of entering and abiding, this is the recitation of Amoghasiddhi, specifically for his retinue.
Of these four maṇḍalas, through the activity of each individual maṇḍala, one should emanate the triad of maṇḍalas as its retinue by including them within it.
Regarding this vajra-recitation, the number of recitations for a day and night is brought down from the Explanatory Tantra (Vyākhyātantra):
"The recitation of Pāṇḍaravāsī and the others is said to be two hundred and twenty-five."
Four times four correctly makes sixteen; [added to] nine, it is one hundred and five.
But that which was seen as nine hundred [breaths] through twenty-four circumambulations—
"From its production, there would be one hundred and sixteen joined with two. Thus,
he states another subtle yoga for those who practice both [methods],
beginning with "The blue lotus," and so forth.
One should visualize a blue lotus-colored *vajra* the size of a barley grain within the aperture of one’s own *vajra*;

and one should visualize a lotus the size of a chickpea seed, adorned with rows of filaments, situated within the *dharmodayā*, which is dedicated to awakening and brings about the attainment of awakening.

Therein, at the tip of the woman’s nose, one should perform the visualization of the wheel, jewel, and *vajra*, each the size of a chickpea seed, according to the distinction of their respective families.
To the question "What then?", he says "it is accomplished," and so forth.
The term *bodhipada* refers to the state of awakening (*bodhi*), which is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*); its *pada* is the cause.
What is that?
It is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), delightful and captivating because it purifies the afflictions (kleśa).
All accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth,

and all qualities (*guṇa*) such as the eightfold sovereignty of desire (*kāmaiśvarya*) and so forth— the state of enlightenment (*bodhipada*), which is the abode or locus of all these accomplishments and qualities, is perfected.
How does that yogin perceive the ultimate truth? To explain how he brings the ultimate truth to direct perception,
the text says "he should create," and so forth.

Having briefly established the Buddhas— the aggregates and so forth— residing in enlightenment and abiding in the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) through the conjunction of the three gnoses, one should create them there, that is, project them into ultimate truth.
Thus, immediately after entering the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), he says "one should emit," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the emergence (*vyutthāna*).

One should bring oneself to completion as the Great Vajradhara, who is characterized by body, speech, and mind, consists of the three bodies (*trikāya*), and for whom that state—the Dharma-Prabhāsvara—is the cause; this is the "Dharma-state" (*dharmapada*).
Now, illustrating the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) by means of the five qualities of sensual pleasure through the language of intentional terminology (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*), he says:
"Then Vajradhara... and so forth, [referring to] the sixfold commentary on the sixth chapter.
Now, following the subtle yoga, there is the welfare of all sentient beings, which is non-dual gnosis; its teacher is the "Teacher of the Welfare of All Sentient Beings.

The practices of all activities consist of the non-conceptual, the utterly non-conceptual, and the supreme non-conceptual practice—namely, the *bhusuku* practice. Purified by that, he speaks of the supreme secret to be described hereafter, beginning with "for six months," in order to attain the state of Vajradhara.
Having realized that one's own nature is indestructible like a vajra, endowed with form, sound, and taste, one should meditate continuously for six months;
and one who desires the fruit of accomplishment should consume feces and urine for the purpose of sustaining the body and for the sake of the activity of taking such food.
Thus it is said.
Regarding "flesh" and so forth:
if one prepares meat for the purpose of providing food, for an offering, or as a sacrificial gift (*nivedya*) for the wrathful deities, then one should prepare the "great flesh" (*mahāmāsa*).
"Secret" (*rahasya*) refers to rites such as killing; that which pertains to or has that as its object is the secret.
What is that?
It shows that body, speech, and mind are accomplished— that is, they enter into a state of conformity— not only in [acts such as] killing and so forth.
"In all accomplishments" means that for the practitioner who has attained [the state of] pills and so forth, stability of body, speech, and mind arises.
Having thus explained the offerings for the wrathful deities of the Vajra family, he speaks as follows, demonstrating those of the Tathāgata and other families:
"Elephant meat," and so forth;
"the best" refers to the statement that one should eat cow meat.
One should offer these four types of meat for the purpose of food and as an offering, and then consume them with the assemblies of wrathful deities of the Tathāgata family and so forth.
To the question of what one should do in the absence of these, he says:
"One should give whatever other meat there may be; one should give whatever other meat there may be."
Furthermore, one should neither eat nor consume boiled rice;
because food has not been offered, he demonstrates the fruit [of such action] as the fierce deeds of those possessed by anger.

By performing worship to the Buddhas such as Akṣobhya and others belonging to one’s own family, one becomes dear to the wise ones who are accompanied by their own mudrās, as well as to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas connected to that family; furthermore, he demonstrates the very benefits [of this] with the words "by this," and so forth.

By this yoga of offering the *vali*, one shall quickly and swiftly attain Buddhahood and the state of enlightenment. Not only does he become a possessor of knowledge, but he becomes the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in the world, performing his activities through the feet [of women].
The "desire realm" refers to all women; he becomes the lord who sports with the universe among them.
As many as there are atoms in thirty-six Mount Merus, so many women shall belong to him.

Since it has already been stated in this very context that he is "the abode of virtues," [the term] *padakarmakṛt* means: in the world, which is the field of action (*karmabhūmi*), his station is irreversible; his activity (*karman*) consists of purification and liberation, and because he performs that, he is called the "performer of the work of the station."

That splendor which overcomes all suffering and mental distress belongs to him; he is radiant because of that splendor in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*. He is powerful because he cannot be overcome by the eight worldly dharmas; he is supreme because he is superior to the imagined yogins; and he is beautiful because Vajrasattva is endowed with youth at all times.
Because he is joyful,

he is pleasant to behold; the great yogin, through his union with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), perceives this world— the people distinguished by categories such as friends and so forth— upon seeing them, as a direct realization.
That [object] is of three kinds— [perceived] by the eye, by hearing, or by the mind—
and one should bring it under control as soon as that mere perception has arisen;
thus, where "he brings" (*ānayati*) was expected, there is a reversal [of the sense].

It is not impelled by external means such as yantras or mudrās; it is not impelled or prompted by a cause, for it is stated in the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi Tantra* that "for one established in signless samādhi, the fruit is signless," and thus all bliss is accomplished entirely without effort.
This which has just been described belongs to "all the Buddhas";

that is, all the imagined yogins, and the Buddhas who are superior to them— those who abide in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the yoga of the perfected stage (*niṣpannakrama*)— their secret, their mystery, is the supreme *bodhicitta*.
Supreme enlightenment is [attained] through the metaphorical designation of its attainment.

This very secret mantra, the Tathāgata-secret just mentioned, transcends the ordinary body, speech, and mind; that by which one transcends them is the reality (*tattva*) known as "the transcendence of body, speech, and mind.
This is what is meant.

"That very reality by which the ordinary body is cast off and a vajra-like body is attained is precisely this; and thus it has been said: 'In this way, by the practitioner endowed with samādhi and free from conceptual construction, the unsurpassed state is attained, transcending all limits of time.'"
The interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) of these very vajra-words is now introduced through its detailed analysis according to the explanatory tantra (*vyākhyātantra*):
"Then the Tathāgata also spoke that supreme secret."
The purifier of the supreme conduct of all, who speaks for the benefit of all sentient beings,
designates the moment, the instant, the brief interval, as well as the periods of fortnights, months, and years—
known as the three numbers and the single time— as a single *kṣaṇa*.
That very [state] which lasts for six months is the *saṃbhoga* [kāya], because it is devoid of intrinsic nature;
it arises in a single moment and is praised as being, by its very essence, beyond the three times.
The skillful practitioner should meditate for six months on that which is endowed with form, sound, and taste.
Having performed that great worship, one should contemplate the secret reality;

free from the existence of sense objects and faculties, performing the functions of eating excrement, urine, and food, they achieve the great, non-conceptual accomplishment which is identical with that [reality].

This very *Tattvānuttara*, the commentary on the six million [verses] of the sixth chapter, is accomplished as the single source of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*), for the sake of non-conceptual reality—unblemished and unconditioned. "Mā" is said to be Māmakī; it is designated as perfect awakening (*samabhisaṃbodhi*).
That which has the food of the joy of meditating on reality as its flesh is called the "Great Flesh of the Horse" through its union with the infinity of space;
this supreme secret state, the triple-vajra, is swiftly accomplished.
The elephant, horse, and so forth of the great pledge, as well as the flesh of dogs and other animals,

which have been described according to the equal number of divisions of the families such as the aggregates (skandha) and so on— this food, through non-dual exertion, belongs to those who possess the single perception of meditative joy.
The nature of the *kavēlika* would be both supramundane and mundane;
those who are most supramundane and proficient in non-conceptualization have the single nature of suchness (*tathatā*), being devoid of both saṃsāra and its opposite.
By this yoga, those of firm vows become dear to the Buddhas and to the wise Bodhisattvas;
they shall swiftly attain enlightenment and become lords of the desire realm in the world through the yoga of the feet.
Radiant, powerful, beautiful, and pleasing to behold,
those who possess this water bring the world under their control by mere sight;
this is the supreme secret of the Buddhas regarding their unsurpassed enlightenment.
"This secret mantra is the reality that transcends the three vajras;
it is the supreme commitment of all Tathāgatas, the most excellent, the highest of commitments"— this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

The term *kāyavākcittādhiṣṭhāna* refers to a chapter (*paṭala*) consisting of a collection of texts that explains how [the three doors] are empowered and accomplished through the reality of the eternal body, speech, and mind, which possesses an indestructible nature. This concludes the explanation of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) in the sixth chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
The Seventh Chapter.
Having thus generally demonstrated the conduct of the supreme yogins, he speaks again in order to elaborate upon that very same [conduct], beginning with "Then," and so forth.

"Great Samaya" refers to Mahāvajradhara; his "reality" (*tattva*) consists of the six-limbed mantra-conduct (*mantracaryā*) and the common means of accomplishment (*sāmānyasādhana*). The perfect awakening attained through these two is the state of Vajradhara; this is the "perfect awakening to the reality of the Great Samaya and mantra-conduct."
The Blessed One uttered that chapter— that collection of texts which explains its meaning— beginning with "Yoga for all desires," and so forth.
All desires are objects such as forms and so forth; their enjoyment is "experience" (*anubhāva*). Regarding how they are enjoyed by those [beings], he says:
"According to their desire" (*yathēcchataḥ*):
"desire" (*icchā*) is "inclination" (*cchandaḥ*);
whatever the desire may be, that is "according to their desire."
The manner of grasping according to desire:

the eye and so forth, as well as visible forms and so forth— whether inferior, middling, or superior— are made objects of perception by the yogins in a single mode, and they must be experienced in accordance with the desire of the sense faculties.
Regarding the phrase "being served according to one's desire," the completion of the sentence is "one should practice the elaborate conduct" (*prapañcacaryā*).
To the question "What follows from that?", he says "by this," and so forth.

By means of this yoga just described— that is, by the union of the sense objects and the senses— one indeed, certainly, attains here and now, swiftly and quickly, the state of Buddhahood, which is the state of Vajradhara.

Having thus explained the practice involving conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), he speaks with reference to the practice free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*) beginning with "all," etc.,
[and] "according to one's wish" (*yathechataḥ*), meaning in accordance with one's own desire.
One should honor and satisfy oneself and others with the five strands of sensual pleasure as they are experienced at will;
how so? Through the yoga of one's own presiding deity and through the illusion-like samādhi.
Therefore, he says:
"By means of difficult practices," and so forth: abstaining from dwellings and the like through the application of physical exhaustion constitutes the "difficult practices" (duṣkara),
as do the twelve ascetic virtues (vrata-guṇa) such as dwelling at the foot of a tree and so on.
The observances (*niyama*) consist of such intense extremes as throwing oneself from mountains or entering fire; one who practices or subjects himself to these does not succeed—
that is, he does not attain awakening (*bodhi*).
To the question "How then? he replies:

"By enjoying all objects of desire, one attains accomplishment quickly. Those things which are desired and sought after are called "all objects of desire" (*sarvakāma*). By enjoying them—that is, by serving and propitiating Mahāvajradhara—one becomes an obtainer of the *mahāmudrā* siddhi in this very life.
Just as the practice free from conceptual proliferation is not [attained] through literal words,

so too, having avoided the attainment of Mahāmudrā-siddhi by means of bodily affliction, the author says "one who eats alms-food" and so forth in order to prohibit even mental affliction for the practitioner.
One who has the habit of eating alms-food should neither mutter nor chatter.
The mention of "eating alms-food" is for the sake of illustration;
therefore, one should not mutter even when engaged in other modes of wretched livelihood, such as wandering for alms or other forms of seeking.
"One should not be devoted to alms" means that "alms" is an illustration for material food;
one should not be addicted to food, being intent upon it.

To the extent that the maintenance of the body is sustained by the commentary on the six million verses of the seventh chapter, one should practice the utterly non-conceptual conduct (atyantaniṣprapañcacaryā) with contentment in that much alone.
To the question of what one who is established in such conduct should do, he says:
"one should recite," and so forth.
"The practitioner of mantra should recite the three-syllable mantra whose limbs are undivided and whose deity-yoga is undivided, which effects the enjoyment of all desires.
To the question, "What is the benefit when this is done? he says:
"Body, speech, and mind," and so forth.
The well-being of body, speech, and mind is the state of meditative equipoise;
having attained that, one attains enlightenment, which is to say, one fully and correctly attains the state of a Great Vajradhara.
By the words "otherwise" and so forth, [the text] illuminates the fault in the practice of austerities and the benefit in the practice of bliss.
Having avoided an untimely death and met his end through natural causes, one who has passed away from that state is cooked in the Avīci hell and other such realms;
this is the provisional meaning (*neyārtha*),
which is now stated as the explanation of the Sage (*ārṣa*).
The field of the divided forms is alms; the utterance of that is eating.
Those whose vows are beneficial do not join these eaters of alms with their desired goal.
The yogi, solely intent on the fourfold yoga, [perceives] inhalation and exhalation.
Established in the state of wisdom and means, the lord of yogis should recite the mantra with its limbs unseparated—
twenty thousand, one thousand, and likewise six hundred times within a single day and night.
To demonstrate that even the Buddhas of the past attained the state of Mahāvajradhara through this very conduct, he says "the Buddhas," and so forth; this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The Buddhas are the jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*); the Bodhisattvas are the white lotuses (*puṇḍarīka*).

The practices taught therein are the mantra-practice, the action-practice (*kriyācaryā*), and both; these practices taken together constitute the yoga-practice. Those whose nature it is to engage in that practice are such [practitioners].

The phenomena (*dharma*) consist of conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) and the syllable (*akṣara*), which is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). That syllable conjoined with the phenomena is the state of the Great Vajra-holder, characterized by the union of the two (*yuganaddha*), because it is the station of all sovereignty.
"Having attained," meaning having directly realized, "the most excellent," meaning the supreme state,

"by means of the enjoyment of all desires"— this [statement] once again negates such things as difficult ascetic practices (*duṣkara*) and so forth, because they lack meditative concentration (*asamādhāna*).

Because they are the instruments [of experience], he prepares this introductory framework (pīṭhikā) in order to demonstrate the threefold nature of those objects that serve as the basis for enjoyment, which are not [to be understood] without the intermediate state (nāsandhyam).
Regarding the passage beginning with "all," etc.:
they are called *kāma* because they are desired and sought after by all sentient beings;
and they are called *guṇa* because Buddhahood possesses the quality of generosity.

These desires and these qualities are "objects of sensual desire" (*kāmaguṇa*). One who possesses passion— meaning one who is attached to objects when they have been attained— should serve and practice them with a non-dual sequence in all modes of conduct, provided they consist of the fivefold objects of the five sense-faculties.
To the question "What is accomplished by doing this?",
he says "toṣayet" and so forth; one should satisfy the Bodhisattvas, such as Kṣitigarbha and others, who have the nature of the eye and the other sense faculties.
The word *tu* is used for emphasis.
To the question, "What do Kṣitigarbha and the others do when they are pleased? he says, "He should arouse passion," and so forth.
Enlightenment has the nature of the earth element and so forth, while Locanā and the others are [the goddesses].

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, those who are joined with them, whose afflictions have been incinerated by the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), and who are radiant, are the "Bodhisauris," namely Vairocana and the other Tathāgatas. One should cause those Tathāgatas—Vairocana and the rest—who are joined with Locanā and the others and who have the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and so forth, to be impassioned, that is, to be satisfied and gladdened; this is because of the archaic usage of the verb *rāgayet*.
The verse beginning with "rūpam" demonstrates the various types of the genitive case used in the sense of the object (*karmaṇi*).

Having discerned and understood form— the object of the eye— which is threefold and of three types as inferior, middling, and superior, the mantra practitioner, established in the practice of conceptual elaboration (*prapañcacaryā*), should worship and satisfy the circle of deities with that which is superior, consisting of various forms of worship for the deities of his own lineage;
for he himself is the Blessed One.
Regarding what was stated as "form is threefold," therein, that other one— the Lord Vairocana himself, who is the universe and the essence of all— likewise,
having known sound in its threefold aspect as the object of the ear, should offer and present that which is excellent therein to the deities of his own family;
he alone is that.
The Blessed One Ratnaketu is none other than that sound which is of three kinds;
likewise, having recognized the threefold fragrance, one should offer and present it to the distinguished Buddhas and others belonging to the family of Amitābha,
for he is indeed that very [fragrance].
That which is called "fragrance" is indeed the Dharma-holder Amitābha himself;
having understood the three kinds of "taste" and so forth, one should offer that which is excellent therein to the deities belonging to the Karmakula.
That threefold taste is the Blessed One Amoghasiddhi himself;
likewise, having understood the threefold touch and so forth, one should offer and satisfy one's own family— the Vajra family— with that which is excellent.
"Sa eva" (that very one) refers to that threefold contact which is indeed Akṣobhya.
By means of the words "rūpa" and so forth, he explains the meaning just mentioned in summary form;
thus, because form and the other [objects] have Vairocana and the others as their essential nature.
One should constantly, day and night, apply the mind and mental attention toward them and generate that which was just described as "this is that," and so forth;
this generation of the mind is the secret and hidden essence of all Buddhas existing throughout the three times, because it brings about the fruit of Buddhahood and is a compendium of the essential.

Having thus established form and the other [sensory objects] as being of the nature of skillful means (*upāya*), he says "form," etc., in order to further demonstrate their transformation into the nature of Locanā and the other [goddesses] who are wisdom (*prajñā*).
Alternatively, the particle "atha vā" (or) indicates another alternative position.
One should always cultivate the goddess Prajñā by means of the objects such as form and so forth;
furthermore, he says [the following] to demonstrate the transformation of those very same [objects], such as Rūpavajrā and the others, according to their respective family divisions.
Alternatively,
"kulabheda" means the division of families; it refers to those by whom that division is discerned or known.

The five families, such as Vajra and the others, consist of the cultivation of the distinctions between the families; through these cultivations of the distinctions between the families, one should cultivate Mahāvajradhara—that is, one should take him as the object of focus—because of the statement in the *Saṃvara*: "Indeed, the Blessed One Vajrasattva is all yoga," and so forth.

The entire limb [of practice], consisting of the elaborate conduct (*prapañcacaryā*) and so on, as explained in the sevenfold commentary on the seventh chapter, is threefold according to the divisions of inhalation, exhalation, and the unmanifested (*avyākṛta*), by means of the natures of passion, dispassion, and equanimity arising from the three appearances.

When an object is perceived and experienced by the eye, that which consists of worship—since it serves as an illustration for the non-apprehension of [separate] worship—is this very nature of the worshipped and the worshipper; thus, one should worship the Self itself.
Therefore, the universe, consisting of the stable and the moving, comprising all families (*sarvakula*), is the Buddha, the abode of Vairocana.

That in which Vairocana is dissolved is the "abode of Vairocana. The Blessed One who accomplishes Vairocana—the Buddha, the Great Vajradhara, who possesses the two accumulations—is himself such a yogi.
Having likewise experienced sound in its three modes, he should offer it to the deities obtained through wisdom and means.

Because the mine of jewels (*ratnākara*) originates from him, the Lord (*prabhu*) is the "mine of jewels. He who is the Great Vajradhara, the self of the universe, is the yogi whose nature consists of the three consciousnesses.
Having obtained and made the object of his senses the scent that is of three kinds, he should offer it to the Buddhas and others, such as Āloka and so forth.
Amitābha, the bearer of the dharma of passion, is the Great Vajradhara; he himself is the taste (*rasa*), and so on.

Amoghavajra is Amoghasiddhi; because he holds him by way of the nature of the progenitor, he is Amoghavajradhṛk, the Great Vajra-holder. He himself should offer himself as his own family, beginning with the words "the untouchable," and so forth.
He whose nature is to attain and produce the form of Akṣobhya and the appearance of Akṣobhya is the "attainer of the form of Akṣobhya," namely the Vajrin, the Great Vajradhara; he is that very one.
Although "attainer" (*lābhī*) would have been the expected form, the archaic reading *lābhinaḥ* is used.
With the words beginning with "form" (*rūpa*), he elucidates the meaning just described.

The intention is that, just as [the notion] "existent" regarding form and so forth is non-different in the past and future moments, one should apply the mind— the threefold consciousness— to the present moment; thus,
one should understand that this very mind is form and so forth.

This very [teaching] just mentioned—that thorough knowledge which is the object to be given by all Buddhas and jewel-like persons—is the "Secret Compendium of the Essence" (*guhya-sārasamuccaya*). Because it cannot be revealed even to those such as [those made of] sandalwood and so forth, it is "secret. It is called a "compendium" (*samuccaya*) because, having been correctly extracted, it is gathered and heaped together.
The "essence" (*sāra*) consists of the Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times.
The method just described is their synthesis;

the mantra-practitioner, reciting the mantra whose limbs are non-different from the deity, should meditate upon the deity— the threefold consciousness— by means of the three aspects beginning with form.
One should know [this];
in order to demonstrate the distinction between the natures of the three types of knowledge,
he says "Alternatively," and so forth.
In that regard, among those [objects] such as form and so forth, "families" refers to passion, dispassion, intermediate passion, and so on;
their "divisions" are the specific varieties. Through the "cultivations" and "experiences" of these, one should "cultivate," meaning one should come to know them.
This is what is meant.

One should know [the nature of reality] by abandoning attachment to external objects such as form and by experiencing the intrinsic nature of the one hundred and sixty types of afflictions, such as desire, which abide in their subtle and other states;
