thus, having understood the threefold forms— beginning with "the womb" (*garbha*) as the nature of non-conceptual conduct (*niṣprapañcacaryā*) and so forth, and ending with the threefold forms beginning with "excellent" (*praṇīta*).

Having fully understood [the three worlds] as being the three appearances, one who knows the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) should perform worship; through the intrinsic nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he should dedicate [the merit].
This alone is the unsurpassed worship.
That which is called "luminosity" is itself Mahāvajradhara.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, because it is the cause of its arising,
the luminous nature (*prabhāsvarasvabhāva*) of sound and the other [objects] should likewise be understood,
as stated in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*).
"Since both the internal and the external are non-apprehendable, that form and so forth should be of three kinds; one should offer them to the deities"—
this is the practice of absolute non-proliferation (*atyantaniṣprapañcacaryā*), which is the *kolika* [ultimate] level.
Now, the six recollections (ṣaḍanusmṛti) state "recollection of the Buddha" and so forth,
[meaning] while meditating upon body, speech, and mind.
Regarding the phrase "cultivate":
when one attains this and cultivates the body by effecting physical seclusion through the differentiation of the hundred families, the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) arises;
likewise, by differentiating speech up to the limit of vajra-recitation, the recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*) arises.
For one who discerns the mind through the sequence of the manifestation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), there is the recollection of the Vajra and the recollection of the Family (*kulānusmṛti*).

Here, "Family" refers to body, speech, and mind; their "recollection" is the distinct thorough knowledge of them by way of the three wisdoms (*jñāna*), followed by their unification. From that "threefold union," there arises the wrathful deity as the method-wisdom; the "recollection" of that is its cultivation, which is the continuous production [of that state].

Through that cultivation of the recollection of wrath, there is the recollection of the deity’s form as the *mahāmudrā*; its thorough cognition by way of forms such as the moon in water; and through that, union—meaning unification with ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). By means of that union, while cultivating and taking as his object the aspect of the two truths, he shall attain enlightenment, which has the single characteristic of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), namely the state of Vajradhara. Illuminating this very meaning, it is said in the *Vyākhyātantra*: "In the delightful bhaga praised by all Buddhas, designated as the singular peace, one should join the vajra born from one's own non-dual reality right there."

The union with the recollection of the Buddha is proclaimed as the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*; through its insertion, there is the yoga of non-duality, which is the visualization of the Buddha’s form. Then the wise one should expand [that form] abiding at the tips of the pores of his skin.
"One should radiate clouds of Buddhas there, especially by means of mandalas"— this is indeed *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).

Having thus produced the form of the deity purified through the gateway of the six recollections (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*), he speaks in order to demonstrate the sequence of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) common to all yogins:

"Having obtained a woman sixteen years of age," and so forth—meaning one who is adorned with fresh youth and the like—one should, having found such a woman as she is, possessing a complete set of limbs, radiant and beautiful, begin the worship of one's own self in secret and agreeable surroundings. This worship consists of the characteristics of sense objects such as form and so on. By what means? "By the three bases" (*adhiṣṭhānapadaiḥ*). That which presides over the sense objects is the "base" (*adhiṣṭhāna*); these are the three natures, beginning with passion (*rāga*), and their "bases" (*padāni*) are the sense objects, beginning with the attractive (*manojña*).
Thus, with these three bases and three types of objects, one should worship oneself.

This concludes the explanation of the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) of the seventh chapter. Having thus described the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of Mahāvajradhara through the three types of touch, he speaks of Vairocana and the others, beginning with the words "The Tathāgata... and so forth.
This is the consort of the Tathāgata;
because she is the preeminent among the mudrās of his family, she is the Great Wife.
The practitioner of Vairocana should visualize—that is, meditate upon—her as previously described.
The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned.
Therefore, it should be supplied that the Jewel-yogi should likewise meditate upon that same Māmakī.
Having meditated in this way, what should he do? And so forth.
"By which faculty" refers to the female and male faculties; their "attainment" is the performance of one's own natural functions, such as embracing and so forth, preceded by mutual passion.
By that, the Buddha Mahāvajradhara is attained; this is his "siddhi."
One shall attain her, whose sole characteristic is supreme bliss. Now, demonstrating another procedure for those devoted to mantra,
he says "HŪM," and so forth.

The meaning of this *vajrapada* is as follows: having meditated upon one’s own *vajra*—fashioned from the syllable *Haṃ* and possessing a jewel-portion empowered by the syllable *Oṃ*; having consecrated the consort’s lotus with the syllable *Āḥ*; possessing the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*) of Ratnasaṃbhava; being intent on the song of the syllables *Noṃ Hūṃ*; and having propitiated one’s own consort, one should cause the *bodhicitta* to descend with the syllable *Phaṭ*.
By the phrase “one should conceptualize,” it is shown that all this, which has the form of the three bodies (*trikāya*), is merely conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) and not reality (*tattva*).
[This applies to] the passage beginning with “five rays” and so forth.
At the time of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), one should visualize the vajra-lotus filled to its hollow interior and completely pervaded by five-colored rays of light, beginning with white.
The word "that" (*tām*) refers to the previously mentioned Locanā, further specifying her as "having moon-like rays" and so forth.
One should visualize and meditate upon a woman who is white like moonlight, blazing with flames, radiant, captivating, and one who seizes the heart of the practitioner.
This is merely an illustration; it is not restricted to this specific case.
Desiring to explain the six recollections (*ṣaḍanusmṛti*) mentioned previously, he composes an introductory summary (*pīṭikā*) beginning with "the recollection of the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*).
Although the form *bodhikāṅkṣī* would be expected, the archaic form *bodhikāṅkṣiṇaḥ* is used.
Therein, by means of the words "How [is it]? and so forth, the Teacher himself raises an objection and then resolves that very question.
Buddha is Vairocana.
The recollection of him is *anusmṛti*. That very recollection, because it arises again and again, is *bhāvanā* (cultivation).
*Bhaga* is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); that into which [something] dissolves is the *liṅga*.
What is that?
Having established conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), one should meditate upon the image of the Buddha, Mahāvajradhara, who enters into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
The meaning is that one should cause [the mind] to emerge from ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

"Through the apertures at the tips of the pores" means: from the pore (*romakūpa*), from the tip of the hair (*romāgra*), and from the space between two hairs (*romavivara*); from that cloud of Buddhas, the cloud of Vairocana, one should emanate—that is, cause to issue forth—the wise one (*budhaḥ*), who knows the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Having thus expanded [the light], one should meditate on the purification of the elements of those beings whose conduct is characterized by delusion, who reside within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges situated in the ten directions; then, having returned, one should visualize them entering into one's own body.
Dharma is Amitābha.
Vajradharma here is Mahāvajradhara, because his nature is indestructible.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, one should emanate the clouds of Dharma—the multitudes of Amitābhas—according to the previously mentioned sequence and then reabsorb them.

Vajra is Akṣobhya; Vajrasattva is the Great Vajra-holder (Mahāvajradhara). The vajra-clouds are the clouds of Akṣobhya. *Ku* means earth; he who takes (*lāti*) and makes his own those beings established therein by means of the gift of jewels is the *kula* (family), namely Ratnaketu—the Buddha, the Great Vajra-holder.
The *kula*-cloud is the delusion of Ratnaketu.
He is called Krodha (Wrath) because he is wrathful toward those who violate the samaya; he is Amoghasiddhi. His recollection is "Krodheśam" (the Lord of Wrath).

Krodha is Akṣobhya; his [emanation] is this Mahāvajradhara. The clouds of wrath are the multitudes of Amoghasiddhi; the commitment (samaya) is Mahāvajradhara, whose body consists of gnosis (jñānamayadeha).

That which is subsequently remembered and contemplated is the *anusmṛti-nirmāṇakāya* (the emanation body of recollection). The cultivation for the sake of nourishing that is the cultivation of the recollection of the pledge (*samayānusmṛtibhāvanā*).
What is that?

Having joined one's own *vajra* with the *vajra* of the tongue—that is, the lotus of the palate—one asks: how, through the application of the two organs, are its drops, which are the *kalās* flowing from the impelling [force], produced? With these, one should worship and satisfy the Buddhas and so forth—the aggregates of form and so on—as well as the Vajrasattvas, who are the mind and mental factors.
Through this drinking of nectar, stability of body, speech, and mind arises.
To demonstrate the purpose of creating nectar through union with an external woman for that very practitioner established in the supreme stage, he says:
The *maṇḍala* is the emission-maṇḍala; it rules over (*indati*) or is desired (*iṣṭe*) as one's own body, thus it is called an "organ" (*indriya*).
The male-female organ is its act of union; one who is skilled in that—that is, proficient in the practice of embracing and so forth—should cause his own essence, his own semen, to flow forth.
Having stimulated the seventy-two thousand channels, the great yogin should cause [the seminal essence] to fall from the path of the *vajra* once it has reached the heart.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:
"The mandala—the circle consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth—is produced. What kind of mandala?
"Maṇḍana" means an ornament.
What is that?
It is Buddhahood; the intention is that one should produce such a maṇḍala of emanation (utsargamaṇḍala) which has the form—that is, the causal basis—of that [Buddhahood].
Sandhyābhāṣā (Intentional Language)
Having applied himself to the practice and investigation of yoga, he says "therein," etc., to show what is to be done:
the body is Vairocana;
its recollection is *anusmṛti*.

That very cultivation belongs to all Buddhas—namely, the emanated body (*nirmita-kāya*) filled with the five aggregates belonging to the Vairocanas residing throughout the ten directions of the three times. It is the aspiration that "even for me who am striving, may this body of such a nature come to be through the cause of the Buddha-body-nature.

Speech is Amitābha because it has that as its nature. Regarding the recollection of that, how is it [related] to Vajradharma? When the words *yad* and *yā* are encountered, [the former refers to the object and the latter to the means].

Regarding "speech" (*vāc*): what kind of speech is it? It is the definitive expression and etymological analysis (*nirukti*). Those [speeches] which are correct are "endowed with etymological analysis" (*niruktisampad*).
The mention of "etymological analysis" (*nirukti*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, the grasping of the eloquence regarding the Dharma and its meaning—such speech as mine, such speech as that of one who is like a bearer of the Dharma—should come to be. The mind is unshakeable;
the recollection of that is itself the cultivation.

Regarding the phrase "of the wise Guhyakendra Samantabhadra": "guhya" refers to non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*); they are called *guhyaka* because they "proclaim" (*kānti*) or speak of that. The verbal root is *kai*, meaning "to sound. One who rules (*indati*) is an *indra*. This concludes the sixth section of the seventh chapter of the *Samantabhadra*.
"Lord of the Guhyakas" means he is the foremost among those who teach reality (*tattva*).

"Of the wise" (*dhīmataḥ*): *dhī* is the Vajra of Touch; he who possesses that is "the wise. For such an Akṣobhya, [the prayer is: "May my mind also become like his mind"—that is, "may mine become like that of me who am comparable to the Vajradhara. This is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
Now, he explains the three empowerments by means of the mere thorough knowledge of the nature of the supreme practice.
In that regard, [he asks] "How is the cultivation of the recollection of sentient beings? and so forth.
Sentient beings are those born from eggs, from a womb, from moisture, and those of miraculous birth.
The cultivation of their recollection:
How is it that the body, speech, and mind of all those sentient beings just mentioned are characterized?
That single mind which serves as the basis for the conceptualization "this is the body," "this is the speech," and "this is the mind"—just as it is for them, so too is it mine.
He asks "Why? and says:
"Because [it belongs] to those who know reality and whose solar energy is equal to space."
Because that mind, through the production of a fragrance of equal flavor like space and the description of omnipresent sovereignty, would constitute the empowerment of the mind therein;
as to how this occurs,
he introduces the empowerment of speech and body.
They are called *mantras* because they are recited and cultivated;
their "form" (*mūrti*) consists of their collections.

That which is called a "collection of speech" (*vāk-saṃghāta*)—the mind that has been transformed into the nature of body—that is the body, speech, and mind (*kāya-vāk-citta*), the mantra-form of all, of all sentient beings.
The recollection of those two by means of body, speech, and mind is itself the cultivation. What is that?
Regarding the phrase "of Mantravajra": *mantra* is speech, and that itself is a *vajra* because it is indivisible. Its *kārya* is its body.

The "manifestation" (*vibhāvana*) refers to the collection of sounds belonging to beings such as those born from eggs, which is perceived and conceptualized; it is the manifestation of the body by means of speech, that is, by verbal expression.
Through the designation of speech, that which is conventionally termed "body" is the manifestation of the body by speech—such is the body.

As for that which was just mentioned, the mantra-body of all sentient beings and their very great vajra-body, it is said: "Just as my own body is, so too is theirs; it is eternal throughout the three times, always present, and its nature is insurmountable. Thus it is taught.
Regarding the phrase "like a mantra-holder": *mantras* are the Tathāgatas;
he who holds them is a "mantra-holder," namely Mahāvajradhara. In the expression "of me, who am like a mantra-holder," the nominative case is used in place of the genitive.
The intentional language (sandhyābhāṣā).
Now, demonstrating the entry into the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) by means of the sequence of the ultimate maṇḍala common to all yogins, he says "Therein," and so forth.

*Samaya* is the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) described as not to be transgressed. *Anusmṛti* (recollection) is the recollection of that [luminosity] which follows (*anu*)—that is, occurs after—the attainment of the Buddha-body; it is the proceeding toward the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

The realization of that is itself the cultivation (*bhāvanā*). "From the pledge (*samaya*), the semen flows" means that from the pledge—the union of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*)—the semen, which is the vital essence (*śukra*), flows; it issues forth.

Then, it develops through the sequence beginning with the *kalala* and so forth, just like a seed and its sprout; having reached the stages of childhood, youth, and middle age, the deities of the maṇḍala, such as Vairocana and the others, remain complete and unimpaired.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said that they experience the five qualities of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
Then, what should one do? To this he says: "And even by means of the ritual, if there is a longing for the fruit."

"Having entered the aggregate of form," and so forth; according to the procedure for entering the ultimate maṇḍala as taught in the *Vajramālā*, one should gradually drink the aggregates and so on, beginning from fifty [breaths], and cause them to enter ultimate truth.
For what purpose?
"By the desire for the fruit":
the fruit is the form of Vajrasattva, who is luminously pure; the desire for that is the aspiration, and by means of that [desire].
"One should slay the Tathāgata array."
Just as they have gone and dissolved by way of the sequence of the ultimate maṇḍala, so too have they returned; thus they are the Tathāgatas.
Vairocana and the others are the conventional designations for the aggregate of form and the rest.
One should "slay" their array.

Established in breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should cause that [consciousness] to enter the ultimate truth by means of its cessation. To the question "What happens then?", he says: "One shall attain success most excellently."
One shall attain the most distinguished and supreme accomplishment of Mahāmudrā.
This is what is meant:
even if one has realized the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), if one’s vigor (*vīrya*) is not heated [through practice], then [one remains as if] merely within the continuum of the world.
Having passed away, one realizes the *utkāya-māyopama-samādhi* (the illusion-like meditative absorption of the risen body).
Illuminating the meaning of this very *vajrapada*, it is said in the *Sandhyāvyākaraṇavyākhyā-tantra*: "Therefore, through the recollections of the *samaya*, the *brahman* (semen) flows profusely."
Through the singular union with the natureless, the wise one should drink according to the ritual;
this great Tathāgata array known as "natureless" is the slaying [of the ego].
By means of this, the intelligent one should perform the slaying and will most certainly attain accomplishment.
Thus it is also said in the *Vajroṣṇīṣa Tantra*: "By means of the non-conceptualization of the name 'death,' through the method of the Perfection of Wisdom,
the Perfection of Wisdom is birth, and the Perfection of Wisdom is mindfulness."
The perfection of wisdom is awakening; the perfection of wisdom is the abode;
the perfection of wisdom is liberation; it is the fulfiller of all hopes.
By the passage beginning with "How is it there in the twilight language? and so forth, he confirms this very point:
wisdom is the light.
In this context, the elision of the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood;
therefore, the perfections of wisdom and skillful means are intended by the term "wisdom" (prajñā). That which has gone to, or reached the end—the limit—of these is the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

What is that ultimate truth? It is itself the *samaya*, because it is not to be transgressed by any sentient beings; its sequential recollection (*anusmṛti*) occurs through the process of grasping the whole as a single unit.
Because that very [consciousness] is practiced continuously, it is "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*);
and because it is "naturally luminous," it is "all"— that is, all three appearances, beginning with light.
Along with the eighty innate natures within passion and the other afflictions, [the luminous ones] are stainless because they depend upon universal emptiness;

they are unarisen because of the non-apprehension of a body that is like an illusion; they are untainted because they are without appearance; this is enlightenment, the fruit, the realization described in the seventh chapter according to the sixfold interpretation.
The cause is of that specific kind;
these two conceptualizations do not exist therein.
Because it sustains, the element (dhātu) is the support (ādhāra).
"Arising" (*saṃbhava*) refers to that which is to be supported;
yet, in that [state], neither the support nor the supported is perceived, nor is there the "non-meeting" (*nāsandhya*).
Now, in order to prepare the foundation for emergence by means of the process of union (*yuganaddha*), he says "In that regard, how... and so forth;
therein, non-arising (*anutpāda*) is the branch of retention (*dhāraṇā*).
Therefore, following that, there is the emergence of mindfulness, which is called "mindfulness"; its cultivation is the samādhi of the Great Vajradhara, whose nature consists of the two truths.
To explain how that is so, he says:
Regarding the passage beginning with *prakṛti* and so forth:
the word *atha* is displaced [in its logical order];
it should be construed as "then, after the limb of concentration (*dhāraṇā*), [one realizes] the natural luminosity (*prakṛtiprabhāsvara*)."
Nature is conventional truth;
luminosity is ultimate truth;
luminosity is conjoined with nature.
What is that? It is the body of Mahāvajradhara, whose nature is non-dual gnosis.
Of what kind is it? "Space," and so forth;
by the word "space," the rainbow situated therein is intended, because of its similarity to space, it is called "space."
Because cause and fruit are non-dual, it is signless (*nirnimitta*); it flows and perishes, thus it is "the perishable" (*kṣara*).
That which is other than that is "the imperishable" (*akṣara*); it is free from that [perishable], thus it is "beyond the syllables" (*nirakṣara*), meaning it is devoid of arising and cessation.

It is neither dual nor non-dual because the two truths have a single flavor; it is not dual because its nature is that of the union [of the two truths], and it is not non-dual because it is characterized by the pacification of all suffering;
it is quiescent because it is not an object of tactile sensation, and it is like space.
"Because it is free from outflows, it is stainless"— this is indeed intentional language (*saṃdhyābhāṣā*).
Having thus ascertained that the Dharma Body and Enjoyment Body possess the characteristic of non-duality, the introduction to the Emanation Body is now presented.
In that regard, as for "how" and so forth:
hatred is Akṣobhya, the Mind-Vajra;
his family (kula) is the wheel of deities manifested from one's own self.

Because it is stated right here that, having manifested the image of a woman, they emerged from the body of the Blessed One Vairocana; by means of that, the worship with offerings such as the *sottara* and so forth is the family worship (*kulapūjā*).
The recollections (*anusmṛti*) are the experience of passion and so forth; that itself is the meditation (*bhāvanā*).
How is that? It is described by the words "twelve-year-old" and so forth.
Having obtained— that is, having found— a maiden of twelve years of age who is steady-minded and of stable nature, there occurs a union with her;
by means of the action characterized by the distinctions arising from that [union], "one's own" (sva) refers to one's own self through the semen (*śukra*).
"Śuk" means sorrow; that which splits it like a saw is "śukra," which is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).
With that *śukra* of supreme bliss, one should worship oneself—by this very statement, he reveals the sovereignty over desires.
To demonstrate the fruit of *anusmṛti*, he says:
"By this," and so forth:
by means of the thorough knowledge of the sixteen recollections (anusmṛti) just mentioned, one attains that which is Tathāgata— the nature of Vairocana and the others— and by this,
there is the acquisition of the presence of Vajrasattva’s longevity, youth, health, and favorable countenance.
The mind of Vajradhara— that is,

the mind associated with Akṣobhya— attains mastery over the mind; the meaning is that one established in the stage of completion (niṣpannakrama) accomplishes whatever he desires by means of the mind, effortlessly.
Amitābha is the bearer of the Dharma;
through his speech, the sovereignty of passion related to that [Dharma] is attained.

How so? One who knows the nature of sound to be like an echo—whatever he utters in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, all that is accomplished. This is the sovereignty of speech belonging to him, the one in his final existence, whose nature is the union of the two (yuganaddha).
By saying "in this very life," he negates the arising of birth through the power of karma,
based on such scriptural statements as "and nirvana in the present life.
He speaks next in order to show the specific excellence of the fruit of this very meditative concentration.
"Body, speech, and mind," and so forth:

the perfect accomplishment of body, speech, and mind is the perfect accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. Likewise, those who are inferior, being devoted to mantras, as well as other worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) arising from them and connected to them, are accomplished for him who abides in the samādhi of the "yoked pair" (*yuganaddha*).
"By recitation" means by recitation with unbroken limbs; "by one who has seen the truth" refers to those whose meditation is indivisible from the three vajras.
"The three garments" refers to the triple world (*tridhātu*);
it is "unbroken" by that.
They are accomplished by means of the cultivation of non-differentiated aspects, which serves as the cause;
for if there were cultivation of differentiated aspects, then even mundane accomplishments would not be achieved, let alone supramundane ones—
this is what is stated by implication.

For the Blessed One, Vajrasattva, is indeed the union with all; according to the statement, "all the enjoyments of the Tathāgata are indeed the entire three realms without exception," this is the "Chapter on Mantra Practice.
They are called *mantras* because they recite and mutter; their practice (*caryā*) is the nature of the cultivation of non-proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
This very collection of words, which is foremost, supreme, and illuminating, is the seventh chapter named *Mantracaryā*,
according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
This concludes the explanation of the six points (*ṣatkoṭivyākhyā*) in the seventh chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
The Eighth Chapter.

To demonstrate that a yogin established in such conduct must perform unsurpassed worship for the sake of fulfilling the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*), he introduces the eighth chapter, saying "Then the Blessed One," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "Then" means immediately after hearing about the conduct, Ratnaketu requested the Blessed One.

The jewel is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*); he whose banner or standard is that very [jewel] is Ratnaketu. Because he seeks the consecration of the thought of awakening and because he is established within the *bhaga*, he is the Blessed One (*Bhagavān*), "the Lord of All," and so forth.

"The Supreme Lord who is the essence of all families"—this refers to Paramālocanā and the others; they praise the Lord, the Master, Mahāvajradhara, by means of this, which is the hymn (*stotra*) to be described hereafter.
By that "King of Hymns," he "supplicated" (adhyeṣayāmāsa), meaning he propitiated him.
He demonstrates this with the words "Vajrarāja" and so forth:

he is called Vajrarāja because he shines (*rājate*) by means of a nature that is indivisible like a vajra. "Mahāyāna" means that great vehicle (*mahāyāna*) by which many (*mahāntaḥ*) beings (*sattvāḥ*) proceed to Buddhahood.
You are the purifier of the practice of space (*ākāśacaryā*).
Space is the ultimate truth;
conduct that is purified by that is "space-conduct" (*ākāśacaryā*).
Because it purifies the continuum of the yogin through that [conduct], it is called the "purifier of space-conduct."
The practice that is free from all conceptual proliferation is the Samantabhadra practice;
you are the foremost, the most excellent, and the supreme among the Victors—the Pratyekabuddhas and others—who have triumphed through it. Therefore, teach and reveal the worship.

The Vajrayāna that purifies passion, hatred, and great delusion according to the literal meaning is the Passion-Hatred-Great-Delusion-Vajrayāna; one who teaches it through its essential extraction is a teacher of the Vajrayāna.
O Jinas, you who abide as Tathāgatas, proclaim the supreme worship, for it is equal to the realm of space! O Ghoṣa, speak!
Their abode is liberation (mokṣa), which is knowledge free from all latent predispositions (vāsanā) that does not proceed toward further saṃsāra because it is generative;
the cause for attaining that is the path (mārga).
Its "proponents" (praṇetāraḥ) refers to those who teach; although the form *praṇetā* would be expected, *praṇetāraḥ* is used as an archaic Vedic form (*ārṣam*).
That by which they go is the "vehicle" (*yāna*), namely the three vehicles beginning with that of the Śrāvakas.
That alone is the path; because it proceeds by way of that very nature,
the Blessed One is the one who traverses the paths of the three vehicles,
the Buddha whose essence is pure through auspiciousness.

The Buddhas are Vairocana and the others; "in them" means within them. "Fortune" (*saubhāgya*) refers to lordship (*adhipatitva*). By that [fortune], O Pure-Souled One, speak the offering, O Best of Men!
"O Wide-Eyed One of Bodhicitta":
he whose mind has the nature of awakening (*bodhi*) is one who possesses *bodhicitta*.

He whose eyes are large is Viśālākṣa; because he sets in motion the twelvefold Wheel of Dharma throughout the three worlds, he is Dharmacakrapravartaka; because he is characterized by the indivisibility of the three vajras, he is Kāyavākcittasaṃśuddha; O Vajrayāna, homage to you—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
Having addressed the Blessed One by means of the three types of knowledge— namely, passion, hatred, and great delusion— he praises him;
passion is the nature of skillful means (*upāya*).
Hatred has wisdom as its nature,
great delusion has ignorance as its nature; it is the indicator of the Vajrayāna.
The Vajra is that very luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) just mentioned; it is a vehicle (*yāna*) because it purifies the natural radiance (*prakṛtyābhāsa*).
It is the Vajrayāna because it reveals that [luminosity]. The Blessed One is its revealer, for he is perceivable solely by the primary sense faculty.
Equal to the element of space, it is supreme because it is the primordial ground of all; thus, O Sound, you are the abode of the Victors worthy of worship.
O Jinas, Vairocana and the others, proclaim the worship whose nature is non-dual gnosis; that in which they abide is the "Jinālaya" (the Abode of the Jinas).

They are the "proponents of the path to liberation" because, by virtue of possessing a vajra-body through union with immeasurable goddesses, they transcend gods and humans throughout the duration of *saṃsāra* by means of the characteristic of supreme bliss. Liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in the experience of the bliss of qualities and sovereignty, and in bringing about the exhaustion of even a trace of the bondage of all sentient beings. Because he teaches the means for attaining that [liberation], the Blessed One is the proponent of the path to liberation.
Wisdom and method are the realization of the three; this very triad is the path, the way to the city of ultimate truth.
He is the initiator of that [path], the one who sets forth the way of the three vehicles;
he is the pure self because he is the Buddha’s good fortune, consisting of the realization of all happiness for oneself and the nature of the two truths.
O Supreme among Men, speak thus of this distinguished offering of worship.
Awakening is ultimate truth;
the mind is conventional truth.
The mind conjoined with awakening is the mind of awakening (bodhicitta), which is none other than Mahāvajradhara himself.

He whose five eyes are vast and wide is Viśālākṣa. Which are they? They are called the flesh-eye, the divine eye, the wisdom-eye, the Dharma-eye, and the Buddha-eye. [He is] the "Turner of the Wheel of Dharma."
Phenomena are both conditioned and unconditioned, consisting of the two truths.

Their "wheel" is their collection; he is the "turner of the wheel of Dharma" because he sets it in motion within the world of sentient beings, as his body, speech, and mind consist of the purity of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, the Blessed One is completely purified in body, speech, and mind.
Because its nature is not subject to decline, homage be to you, the Vajrayāna, which is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
"The great imperishable that is all-space":
all-space is the universal void (*sarvaśūnya*); through its purification, the Blessed One is also all-space.
It is "Mahākṣara" (the Great Imperishable) because it is both great and imperishable.

It is "Sarvābhiṣeka" (the Consecration of All) because it constitutes the consecration for all. It is "Sarvārtha" (the Purpose of All) because it fulfills the heart's desires of all sentient beings through the Gaganagañja samādhi.
It is "Sarveśa" (the Lord of All) because of its sovereignty over the three worlds.
The *vajra* is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) because it fulfills all aspirations;
conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is like a jewel, and because he holds that [ultimate truth] by means of its own nature, he is "Vajraratnadhṛk" (Holder of the Vajra-Jewel).
This is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
"The supreme worship of the Tathāgatas" means:

the Tathāgatas are the Victors (Jinas) existing throughout the three times. Worship related to them is "Tathāgata-worship. It is the most excellent because it is the most distinguished, being uncommon for those who have ascended to the stage of generation.
He asks, "Why? and says:
[It is] because worship, which exists by its very nature as indivisible from the three vajras—that is the subject.

According to the commentary on the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*) of the eighth chapter, it is called "the auspiciousness of body, speech, and mind" because the three realms are brought together (*samājīkaraṇa*) with one's own body, speech, and mind.
"Jinasaṃbhavā" means that from this [earth] the Jinas arise; thus the world spoke of that worship.
This is an intentional terminology (*saṃdhyā-bhāṣā*).
To demonstrate that very point, he says:
"Having attained," and so forth.
She is a maiden (*kanyā*) because her form is desirable.
She is the "large-eyed one" (*viśālākṣīm*), that Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) whose two eyes consist of the two truths which are vast.
Its specific qualification is "adorned with beauty and youth.

Regarding the phrase "taking the twenty-five-fold [consort]," having obtained that Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which consists of the nature of the twenty-five deities and is characterized by self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna), and having received her from the mouth of the Guru, one should perform— that is, offer— that very same as the unsurpassed worship.

The phrase "one should also take from the animals and fashion [the forms]" is to be applied again. This is because the word *tiryak* (animal/transverse) carries the sense of being on the side (*pārśva*).
Therefore, other than the form of the presiding deity, the forms of the maṇḍala deities are taken up, just like Mahāvajradhara, because they are manifestations of Mahāvajradhara’s miraculous power.
This is the *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
Having indicated the worship of the most supramundane yogins, he now speaks in order to demonstrate the worship of the yogins of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*),
beginning with the words "In a pure [place]," and so forth.
The word "or" (*vā*) should be understood as displaced [in the sentence order] for the purpose of indicating an alternative position.
On a spot of earth, a region of the ground, that is purified by the process of purifying all levels (*bhūmi*), secluded, and free from the gathering of people—
the Son of the Jina, the practitioner of mantra (*mantrin*).

In such places as the houses of peaceful virtuous people, in temples of Śiva, or in shrines of deities—on such a site—one should perform the smearing and the drawing of the maṇḍala using cow dung (*viṭ*), cow excrement (*go-viṣṭhā*), cow urine (*gomūtra*), and pure water (*toya*); by the word "etc. (*ādi*), substances such as fragrant pastes are included.
With these substances, beginning with cow dung, one should create the smearing and the maṇḍala on the aforementioned site.
The word "vā" has the sense of including what has not been explicitly mentioned; by it, flowers and so forth are included. Why [should this be done] constantly, that is, every day?
For the sake of worshiping the Victors and for the purpose of propitiating one’s own deity,

having thus prepared the requisites for worship, he speaks— showing the process of transforming oneself and one’s consort (*svamudrā*) into the five families (*pañcakulīkaraṇa*) according to the sequence described in the *Sādhana*—
beginning with the words "between the breasts," and so forth.
Regarding "between the breasts," it refers to the location of the heart.
Regarding "as far as":
one should place the family of Akṣobhya, born from the syllable *hūṃ*, here as far as [that point].
"Up to the crest" (*śikhāntam*): by the word "crest," the hair is indicated, meaning as far as the hairline.
One should place Vairocana, born from the syllable *Oṃ*, upon the region of the hair.
"In the middle": between the heart and the crest; what is that? It is the region of the throat, the mandala of the face; there, one should place Amitābha, the "Arising," born from the syllable *Āḥ*.
"Between the feet" means as far as that point;
"between the foot and the root of the thigh" is what is meant by "between the feet. In that space between the feet.

The word "vā" (or) in the two lines has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Therein, one should place Amoghasiddhi, who is born from the syllable *hā*. "One who knows the ritual" means one who knows the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
In the expression "nābhi-kaṭī-guhya," there is an elision of the locative case ending.
One should place the Ratnasambhava family, born from the syllable *svā*, in these locations.
The "Jinas" are Vairocana and the others.

"Jinātmajas" refers to those born of the lineage of the Victors (*jinakulīna*), as well as the Victors themselves and their own sons (*svajinātmaja*); thus they are called "Jinātmajas. In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, this means that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of Vairocana and the others, along with those of their respective lineages who consist of the five families, according to the procedure taught in the *sādhana*. Having explained this, he speaks the words beginning with "the space-element" (*ākāśadhātu*) in order to demonstrate the process of arising from meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
The space element is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) which is one’s own mudrā.

In its center, the wise one should meditate upon himself as the ocean of gnosis (*jñānasāgara*), the bodhicitta, situated in the middle of the moon, which stands within the aforementioned conventional bodhicitta. Immediately thereafter, having emanated the Tathāgatas, he wears peaceful garments.
One should perform the withdrawal into the heart, that is, into the self.
As for the word "yadi" (if):
the sense is that if there should be a desire for emission and withdrawal, then one should perform them.
The peaceful concentration of the mind is itself the *vajra*; because he wears that, he is "the wearer of the peaceful garment.
Having thus accomplished oneself, one should again fashion a stūpa composed of the five elements, jewels, and so forth.
The four jewels are the nature of the [four] elements; because they consist of those, they are the four goddesses, Locanā and the rest.
It consists of the four jewels; it is adorned and beautified by garlands of rays, such as white and other colored rays.
Regarding "ocean of gnosis" (*jñānodadhi*):

the substantive form of "those existing in the three times" (*vyadhvebhyaḥ*) is "the Tathāgatas, oceans of gnosis. "Existing in the three times" means abiding in the three periods of time. One should contemplate the abode of the Tathāgatas as being present in the three times, as their field (*kṣetra*).
And one should meditate upon a shrine (*caitya*) within one's own body.

As before, from the openings of the pores of one's own body, clouds of worship—which worship and benefit the realms of sentient beings by accomplishing their desired aims—are emitted; these are the "Tathāgatas" (the clouds of worship). One should emanate, that is, cause to issue forth, those clouds.
A Buddha is one who is skilled in the non-arising sequence (*anutpattikrama*) of the Buddhas.
[This is] according to the literal meaning.
Now, demonstrating the component of worship that maintains the union of both, he says:
"The lotus," and so forth.
Because it possesses five colors, such as white and the rest, the wise one—the one who knows the divisions—is one who understands the fivefold variety according to the distinction of the *kulas*.
Likewise, one should offer an *utpala* lotus of five colors;
having prepared three types of *jāti* flowers of three colors, one should present them to the deities.

Similarly, the mantra practitioner, having visualized and produced *kaṇikāra*, *mallikā*, *yūthikā*, and *karavīra* flowers through the power of meditation, should in every way unite them with the Tathāgatas.
This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
He states the explanation according to the *ṛṣis*:
"Those who are called the ten winds are designated as the lotus and the water-lily."
The reality of the three vajras has been explained; the oneness of caste is considered to be the third method.
One should apply the Kaṇikāra, Mallikā, Yūthikā, and Karavīraka flowers to the Maheśvara and other deities, corresponding respectively to the eyes and so forth.
Through the placement of steps that are devoid of intrinsic nature and through union with the form of the deity,
that becomes the great worship which alone satisfies all the Buddhas.
Other people will not accept this *puṣpasandhyā*;
because of their lack of understanding, their attainment remains far off.
Saying, "We are incapable," they thus disparage themselves;
for by disparaging themselves, they indeed disparage all the Buddhas.
Having indeed cast all the Buddhas who have gone to the further shore of nirvāṇa [into the fire].
Thus is the definitive meaning.
Now, in order to show the secret initiation mandala common to both types of yogins, he says "yojana," and so forth.
Because it measures twenty-five *yojanas* on each side, its extent is one hundred *yojanas*; and by the term "wheel" (*cakra*), it is metaphorically designated as such.
Vairocana alone is intended [here].
One should meditate upon— that is, bring to completion— his mandala, the wheel-mandala,
either mentally or by means of drawing.
The phrase "quadrangular" and so forth should also be applied to the lotus that will be described later.

One who is always discerning— that is, never heedless at any time— should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the families (*kula*), such as Akṣobhya and the others, in the directions starting from the east.
Just as the term "wheel-maṇḍala" includes the maṇḍala of Vairocana, so too the lotus [includes] the maṇḍala of Amitābha;
the moon-maṇḍala [includes] the maṇḍala of Akṣobhya;
and the sword-maṇḍala [includes] the maṇḍala of Amoghasiddhi.
"Utpala" refers to the jewel *upalaratna*; the letter "ta" is for the sake of conforming to the meter. Regarding the phrase "in the ten directions":

the wise one—the enlightened one—should visualize the mandala of Ratnasambhava as an *utpala* lotus, starting from a size of one hundred *yojanas* up to a measure of ten million (*koṭi*) *yojanas*, according to the desire and preference of those with great aspirations. Because it is endowed with four colors, the mandala consists of the four jewels; it is transparent like crystal.
By this, the adoption of the white color is indicated.
It is called a *caitya* because it is like a shrine (*caitya*), namely the mandala which is naturally pure;
this is because its essence consists of the reality (*tattva*) of the mandala.

The "abode of the five families" means the foundation or support for the five families; the wise yogin, who knows the secret initiation, should meditate upon it for the sake of worship—that is, for the purpose of the secret initiation.

Thus, having described the activity of the guru, he speaks the words beginning with "with the five qualities of desire" in order to show what must be performed by the disciple who desires the secret initiation immediately following the guru's procedure.

The five objects of the senses are form and so forth, consisting of the five qualities of desire (*pañcakāmaguṇa*). "Of them" refers to the deities who constitute the contents of the mandala; one should "commence," that is, begin, to perform the "ocean of worship," which is a vast sea of various offerings.
To elaborate upon those very five qualities of desire, he says:
"Jewels," and so forth.

Having described jewels such as rubies and so forth, and garments such as silk and the like, which are the objects of the visual faculty, [the author] establishes the objects of the auditory and other faculties by means of the word "etcetera.
One should worship and propitiate [them] daily, until the completion of the consecration.

For what purpose? Because awakening (*bodhi*) is an empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) that serves as the cause for the arising of knowledge through the washing away of all the impurities of the ages; one should worship with longing (*chanda*) for that [awakening]. Worship with the five offerings refers to worship performed with flowers and the other [four] of the five offerings.

Having thus described the worship common to both the deity and the guru by stating that one should always satisfy the deity and the guru with the most excellent of those [offerings], the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana* demonstrates the special worship of the guru through the passage beginning with "a maiden" (*kanyām*).

A maiden whose youth has not faded, a supreme, untainted great bliss that abides throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), because she is the field for its arising; a most excellent "jewel-producer" (*ratnakarī*) lotus-woman (*padminī*), because she is endowed with all feminine virtues;

adorned with various kinds of jewels, garments, perfumes, ointments, and so forth—such a maiden of lovely form belongs to "all the Buddhas. Since the Guru consists of all the Buddhas, even though the Guru is a single person, he is intended here by the term "all the Buddhas."

To him one should give, one should bestow. Why? He says: "Because it is accomplished through the supreme means. That which is accomplished or produced is the "means" (sādhana), namely the general fruit.

What is the supreme means, the distinguished means? It is Buddhahood. To demonstrate the absence of limitation in the practice of giving away all that is to be given for the sake of the Guru—the cause for attaining success (*siddhi*)—he says: [the following].
Regarding the phrase "seven jewels" and so forth:
the seven jewels are ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, emerald, diamond, pearl, and coral;
one should give this field, filled with these, every day.
Or, being discerning through the jewels of women, men, gems, wheels, swords, elephants, and horses; skilled in the accumulation of merit and wisdom;

wise and possessing superior knowledge day by day; seeking knowledge and desiring to establish the negation of duality through the instruction of a guru out of a longing for the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā—such a person should offer [the gift].
"A wise person accomplishes everything even through meditative concentration.
Having thus prepared the requisites for worship, what should the guru do toward the disciple? To this he says, "The Lord," and so forth.

Having taken up and grasped the Mahāmudrā of the sovereign of his own maṇḍala, the Maṇḍalācārya, from the center of the Buddha-maṇḍala— that is, from the midst of the Tathāgata-circle— should bestow upon those Buddhas, the Tathāgatas who possess the cognition of passion (*rāgabuddhi*), the union of touch, which is the bliss produced by the vajra of touch.
To explain how that is so,
he says "the space element" and so forth:
one should contemplate— that is, meditate upon— the array, which is the maṇḍala, situated in the midst of the space element, the sky.

Having meditated, one should cause [the consciousness] to enter the body composed of the gnosis of Vairocana and the others, in the form of the aggregates such as form (*rūpaskandha*), for the purpose of assuming the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Then, having made one's own reflection—the body of oneself as the Great Vajradhara—consisting of the Tathāgatas and constructed from the atoms of all the Tathāgatas such as Vairocana and the rest, one should worship and please the Guru, who is venerable, by means of the "feces" which are the sense objects and the "urine" which is the sense faculty, together with the objects such as form and so forth.
He shows that very same worship with the words beginning with "the woman" (*yoṣit*).

Having meditated upon the woman presented by the disciple—she who has a beautiful face, whose consciousness is clear with joy, and who is delightful (*manoramā*) because she brings delight to the mind—one should perform the *tattvapūjā* characterized by *samāpatti*. Having meditated upon and placed the "seats" (*adhiṣṭhānapada*)—namely, the seed-syllables such as *praṇava* belonging to Vairocana and the other [Buddhas]—in their respective locations on the body of the mudrā, one should then perform the *tattvapūjā*, which consists of the union (*samāpatti*), having made her the embodiment of the five families (*pañcakulakalāpinī*). One should thus consecrate her.

In comparison with external worship, this worship of the deity and reality (*devatātattva-pūjā*)—by means of realizing the state of purification from the afflictions through the sequence of passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion—involves the "semen in the secret wide-eyed one" (*śukre guhyaviśālākṣyām*).

Following the worship of meditative union (*samāpatti-pūjā*), one takes the semen of Viśālākṣī; because of the superior resolve that moves toward awakening, the *bodhicitta* resides within the lotus of the woman, who is the *mudrā*.

The firm-minded Vajra-disciple, having been given this by the Guru, should consume it— thinking, "This is the innermost essence of all the Tathāgatas residing within my own body"— and partake of it. And the Guru, with that very *bodhicitta*, should consecrate the disciple while [the disciple] is positioned according to the prescribed number and so forth, preceded by perfumed water and the *Amogha-maṅgala-gāthā* verses,
as stated by the Blessed One in the *Guhyendutilaka*:

Having emerged from the midst of a lotus blazing with jewels, his form concealed, he consecrates the heads of all the Victors with showers of pure, supreme jewels— the waters of wisdom arising from the pure vajra.
Thus.

"This" refers to that which was just mentioned under the designation of "worship," namely the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*); it belongs to all mantras and all Tathāgatas. It is the "accomplisher of mantra-siddhi" for those who possess the vajra of that knowledge—the yogins engaged in practice—for it effects the accomplishment of mantras, such as those generated from *āli* and *kāli*, including serpents and so forth, which bestow both mundane and supramundane mantra-accomplishments. Because it is hidden from those following the systems of *Kriyātantra* and the like, it is "secret. It is the "accomplisher of mantra-siddhi" because it brings about the complete attainment of perfection therein.
"Because it turns back [the notion of] imperishable body, speech, and mind, there is the worship of body, speech, and mind"—
this is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*). This concludes the explanation of the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) in the eighth chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana* commentary.
The Ninth Chapter.
He speaks of the means for achieving enlightenment even through the performance of the wondrous consecration that causes [the world] to turn back.
"Then," and so forth;
"then" means immediately after the secret consecration (*guhyābhiṣeka*), the Blessed One is the entirety of space by virtue of having the nature of the four voids (*caturvyoma*).
Therefore, he is the Great Imperishable (*mahākṣara*).

Because he stands above all the consecrations and practices (*abhiṣeka-caryā*) of those who have entered the *Kriyātantra* and other systems—all such consecrations and practices—he is the foremost of all consecrations and practices (*sarvābhiṣeka-caryāgra*).

He is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), the sixth Tathāgata, of all "all-purpose" (*sarvārtha*) deities such as Vairocana and others, who are so called because they are sought after and entreated by all those desiring spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The connection is that the Blessed One, being of such a nature, proclaims the mandala of the indivisibility of the three vajras.

"The enjoyment of body, speech, and mind" refers to that mandala in which there is the enjoyment—that is, the utilization—of one's own body, speech, and mind; thus it is the "enjoyment of body, speech, and mind. The "indivisibility of the three vajras" refers to Vairocana and the others; their mandala is an exceedingly marvelous mandala, most excellent and distinguished, because it is the domain of jewel-like individuals (*ratnapudgala*) alone, and it is a secret, not to be disclosed.
Of whom? Of those who possess the wisdom of a Buddha—the Śrāvakas and others—because it acts as a means to destroy their [wrong] views.
Since it was said that he spoke the means for attaining enlightenment by way of such speech contrary to worldly conventions, [the literal meaning] would be:

"Having manifested the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the center of the space-element as the form of the Great Vajradhara, namely Akṣobhyavajra, and having accomplished Akṣobhya through its transformation, one should visualize the vajra in his hand"—this is the description of the primary emblem.
There is no prohibition against other signs;
one should meditate upon the vajra as being intensely dense and solidified, and therefore blazing, flooded with white and other rays of light, along with sparks and droplets.
Having thus visualized the Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times, one should pulverize it.
One should meditate upon the enjoyment—the collection—of their body, speech, and mind as pulverized by the vajra, destroyed, and set to rest.
This aforementioned supreme meditation brings about the accomplishment of the mind and bestows mastery over the mind.
By means of this very secret vajra, one should strike down—that is, destroy—all sentient beings.
By means of this specific meditation, those who have perished are born as Bodhisattvas, the sons of the Victors, in the Buddha-field of Akṣobhyavajra;
this is the reality-commitment (*tattvasamaya*) of the Hatred Family.
Here it is asked: if one [person] has attained nirvāṇa, are there many who have attained nirvāṇa?

"Otherwise, it would be a great heap of merit; [but] otherwise, it is supreme evil"—this concludes the six-fold commentary on the ninth chapter. With the words "Now," and so forth, he explains the commitment (*samaya*) of the family of delusion (*moha*).

He is indeed Mahāvajradhara; ignorance, delusion, and nescience—by means of these, he is the achiever of liberation, the attainer of the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the achiever of knowledge and liberation, pure by nature, and pure by essence. Because he is unstained by merit or demerit, he is untainted (nirlepa).

The practice consisting of the removal of the affliction of stinginess from the mental continuum of sentient beings is the "practice of awakening" (*bodhicaryā*); he teaches this practice extensively, and thus he is the "Proclaimer of the Practice of Awakening.
He speaks the unerring reality that accomplishes the awakening of a Buddha, the commitment (*samaya*) for the summoning of substances.
The passage beginning with "In space," etc., has already been explained.

Having meditated upon oneself as Vairocana through the transformation of the vajra-maṇḍala— the great mudrā of Mahāvajradhara— one should visualize and emanate all the Buddhas who are the deities of the maṇḍala.
To the question "How? he says:
"by means of the application of all jewels" (*sarvaratnaprayogena*).
"All jewels" refers to the various kinds of gems endowed with colors such as white and so forth; the "application" for that purpose is the "application of all jewels."

By means of that, one should visualize—that is, impel—the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya and the others from the vajra-image; for the purpose of extracting whichever jewel corresponds in color to whichever Tathāgata, one should impel that specific Tathāgata. Having thus impelled the Tathāgatas, [the text] shows what is to be performed by the practitioner.
"Seizing," and so forth:

"seizing" refers to the drawing in of substances by the Tathāgatas; one should visualize this by means of the "three vajras"—that is, through body, speech, and mind—as follows: having bound and rendered motionless the desired collection of jewels by means of the conjunction of white and other rays of light emerging from the pores of the skin, one then draws them in with the hook consisting of the syllable *hrīḥ* emerging from the petals of one's own tongue-lotus and establishes them within one's own home.
By the words "one should meditate with the mind," O Blessed One, and so forth,
he describes the purification of those whose mental continuums are defiled by the fault of envy;
[the Blessed One] is a *cintāmaṇi*, a specific kind of gem that bestows desired objects.
Equal to that is the ocean of wealth, an inexhaustible sea;
those who are lords of wealth, being filled by it, become joyful—
not only do they become endowed with worldly prosperity, but [they attain more].
Regarding the passage beginning with "aurasā" and so forth:
those born from the breast (*uras*) are the *aurasā*; they become the principal sons of all Buddhas and subsequently become Tathāgatas themselves.

In the *Sarvakulārṇava*, within the ocean of families beginning with Akṣobhya, the reality (*tattva*) and secret (*rahasya*) of the family of delusion (*moha-kula*), which pertains to the deity-circle associated with Vairocana, is precisely this; because it is not to be transgressed, it is the *samaya*.

Therefore, the Blessed One said in the *Śrīvairocanābhisaṃbodhicaryātantra*: "In this regard, a bodhisattva is completely and in every way abstained from taking what is not given, except in the case of one who is miserly.
Then, [the passage] beginning with "atha" and so forth...

The entry into the commitment (*samaya*) of the Passion Family (*rāgakula*) is that very Blessed One; by offering his own body, he colors consciousness with passion. Thus, through the passions such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, he accomplishes the liberation of those seeking release, characterized by the pacification of all suffering; hence he is the "Accomplisher of Passion and Liberation. Pure in secret, consisting of the two truths, and without support because he abides in non-abiding nirvāṇa, Amitābha proclaims—that is, speaks—the wheel of commitment (*samayacakra*).
"Space," and so forth:
the lotus mandala is the image of Mahāvajradhara; because it gives rise to Amitābha, it is metaphorically [designated as such] as before in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*.
Having meditated on Amitābha through the transformation of Mahāvajradhara, one should fill the interior of all the gabled palaces with the Buddhas and the deities of the maṇḍala,
and radiate them according to their respective places.
Within that maṇḍala, one should visualize and meditate upon the union of the female forms of all the male and female deities belonging to the maṇḍala.
The form of a woman is the form of *styā* (femininity);
conjunction with that is "bondage" (*saṃyojana*), which is the transformation [of the mind] into the form of a female.
To the question "How so? he says:

Regarding the phrase "by means of the yoga of the four commitments" (*catuḥsamayayogena*): the four commitments are the four yogas; the yoga by means of them is the accomplishment of the form of the deity, which is the "yoga of the four commitments.
It should be construed as follows: "one should meditate on the form of the woman by means of the yoga of the four commitments."
This meditation just described is "supreme" within the Vajra Way—that is, the Mahāyāna—because it primarily bestows mastery over desires. Having meditated thus, what should one do? He says:

by means of the application of the two organs, preceded by acts of passion and so forth, through the union of the vajra and the lotus, one should enjoy—that is, desire—all of them simultaneously through the act of universal pleasure, which is the act of one's own pleasure, in a single instant. This meditation just described is the "inseparable accomplishment of the three bodies for all mantras and all practitioners"; it is the meditation that brings about the accomplishment of the inseparability of the three bodies—the forms of the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation.

This commitment (samaya) must be performed within the family of passion (rāgakula); it is to be accomplished and practiced by the practitioner who has ascended to the ritual of generation. The syllable *oṃ* is used for emphasis.
"It must indeed be accomplished"—thus begins the passage starting with "atha" (now) and so forth.
Amoghasiddhi is the entry into the *samaya*; he himself is the Blessed One, the Vajra-mantra, which is the vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) characterized by entering [the mantra] and so forth.

He is the "Accomplisher of the Meaning of Vajra Mantras" because he accomplishes the intended purpose of those to be trained through his instruction. He is "Arisen from Knowledge" because he has emerged from that knowledge which is the Dharmakāya; yet, because his body is like an illusion, he is "Selfless," meaning one from whom the self (*ātman*) has departed (*nirgata*). Thus, he is *nirātmā*.
"Nairātmya," meaning devoid of self, Mahāvajradhara spoke these words that are about to be described; this is the statement of the compiler [of the tantra]. "Ākāśa," and so forth:
one should meditate upon the Buddha-maṇḍala, which is Mahāvajradhara.
Having meditated on Vajrāmoghasiddhi through the transformation of that [state], one should immediately thereafter meditate on all the Buddhas who are the mandala-deities.

Abiding in the meaning of this "vajra-word of falsehood"— namely, that all phenomena are false because they are like an illusion— one should visualize and understand all forms and all sentient beings as being situated right there.
To the question "What should one do after that?", he says:
"One should deceive all the Jinas," and so forth.
"Jinālaya" means those beings who are the abodes of the Victors (*jinālaya*), because they possess the *tathāgatagarbha*. All of them are "abodes of all the Victors" (*sarvajinālaya*).

To deceive them—that is, to deceive all the Tathāgatas and all sentient beings—one should meditate while uttering the words: "All phenomena are non-deceptive, for their intrinsic nature is like an illusion. This is the intended meaning.
And so it has been said in the *Navama-paṭala-ṣaṭkoṭi-vyākhyā*: "O Devaputra, all phenomena are false and illusory;
in that very way I proclaim them, and therefore I am a speaker of falsehood."
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said: "Having properly pulverized that [relic], how can one bring about the accomplishment of the mind?
The past instructors, the present teachers, and the future Buddhas who are to be propitiated are the bestowers of perfect enlightenment."
O Lord, how indeed will they be slain by you with the thunderbolt in the form of Akṣobhya?
How will they comprehend your words according to the reality of their various meanings?
O Blessed One, speak the truth concerning those who are yet to be born.
"Having known which, the sons of the Jina become free from conceptual construction regarding the meaning of the *sandhyā*.
Then, having heard the speech spoken by Vajradhara for the benefit of the world,
the Lord replied once more to the sovereign Vajradhara:
"Excellent, child! Very excellent! Excellent, O Samantabhadra!

This which has just been spoken is dependent upon all Buddhas and all Tathāgatas; because it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it is like the space of speech (*vāgākāśa*). This space of speech is utterly stainless; it is declared to be the secret that brings about the accomplishment of mantra for those of 'knowledge-intellect' (*jñānabuddhi*). For those who possess non-dual knowledge and intellect—that is, those with resolute conviction—and who are striving, it brings about the accomplishment of mantra."

The summoning of all sentient beings by means of the *samaya* is the *samaya*-summoning family, which is the family of Amoghasiddhi; its reality-*samaya* (*tattvasamaya*), the *samaya* as it truly is,
should be impelled and practiced again and again according to the actual state of things, as it is said here:
And for the sake of the happiness of others, by means of the cause of happiness,
and for the benefit of the Three Jewels, one may speak a falsehood;
thus begins the passage starting with "atha" and so forth.

The entry into the commitment (*samaya*) of Ratnasambhava is that very Blessed One, the synthesis of the three vajras of the bodies and so forth. "To be divided" (*bhedyam*) means to be split or made separate; "not to be divided" (*abhedya*) means not being split. He whose form is the indivisibility of the three vajras and is non-distinct is "indivisible by the three vajras" (*trivajrābhedyah*). The "Victors" (*jināḥ*) are the Buddhas existing throughout the three times; he is their "abode" (*ālayaḥ*) because he is the place of their arising.

It is the "indestructible triple-vajra abode of the Jinas" (*trivajrābhedya-jinālaya*); "attainment" (*siddhi*) refers to the state of Vajradhara. Because that very state is indestructible, it is a "vajra," and because it brings about its excellence, he is the "proclaimer of the vajra of attainment" (*siddhivajrapraṇetā*). Thus, according to the sacred tradition (*ārṣa*), he uttered this statement which is about to be described.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "ākāśa" has already been analyzed.

The *samayamaṇḍala* is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of Mahāvajradhara; by means of its transformation, one should meditate upon oneself as Ratnaketu and emanate this [mandala] through all forms—that is, through all the forms of the retinue.
"This should pervade and fill the interior of the gabled chamber with harsh words and the like.
Here, "harsh" (*paruṣa*) means cruel or rough; "harshness" (*pāruṣya*) is simply that which is harsh, and "harsh speech" (*pāruṣyavacana*) is speech that is such harshness.

"By serving Mahāvajradhara and propitiating him through those initial words—which have appeared for the sake of gathering all sentient beings by means of that [method]—one shall attain non-dual gnosis. With these words beginning with "The Blessed One," the compiler concludes the *samaya*. In this manner, Mahāvajradhara, the array of the vajras of all Tathāgatas, spoke; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
He states the explanation according to the Ṛṣis:
"Then, having meditated upon the Lord who is the sole Dharma, the omniscient, the all-knowing master,
Vajrapāṇi spoke to the Protector the discourse on the reality of the *samaya*."

And how could the Buddhas, who arise throughout the three times, whose sole nature is suchness (*tathatā*), and who are uniquely produced from the *dharmakāya*, be pulverized by a vajra? Having properly pulverized them, how could one bring about the accomplishment of the mind (*cittasiddhi*)?
The Buddhas of the past who were instructors, those of the present who are teachers, and those of the future who are to be honored— the givers of perfect enlightenment—
how could you, O Protector, slay them in the form of the Vajra-Akṣobhya?
Since you have entreated me, I shall respond to that which was spoken in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language) according to its intended meaning as it truly is:
"Akṣobhya" is an emanation (*nirmāṇa*), and because of its indivisibility, it is the *vajra*.
His hand should hold the vidyā; therein is the radiant vajra.
From that arises the body consisting of gnosis (*jñānamaya*), blazing with five-colored rays.
The aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are declared to be the Buddhas; their state of being free from the vajras of the three times is *vivajratā*.

The pulverization by the body-vajra is the destruction of the ordinary aggregates; this delightful family of Hatred, born from the Wisdom-Vajra, is Akṣobhya. They attain the great siddhi, and in that field, there is the supreme birth.
Then the glorious Mahāsukha, the accomplisher of wisdom and liberation,
naturally pure and untainted, the accomplisher of the conduct of awakening,
addressed the Lord of all Secrets, Vajrapāṇi of great splendor:
He speaks the commitment, the reality, and the means for accomplishing perfect enlightenment.
By entering into the jewel of the Dharma, one should manifest Vajrasattva;
by means of that body, there is the total removal of all karmic maturations.
The seizure of all wealth accomplishes the enlightenment of the Buddhas;
it is like a wish-fulfilling gem that completely fills the ocean of all riches.
This is proclaimed as the reality and the observance (samaya) of the family of Delusion (moha):
there, the body of illusion shall have immeasurable life, and therein the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth are fully perfected.
In the commentary on the six million [verse] Ninth Chapter, one should cause the aggregates and so forth to be conjoined with the Perfection of Wisdom therein;
through the union of the four voids, one should perform the supreme method of awakening.
The conventional and the ultimate are here [distinguished] by the piercing of the two organs;
that which is called "yoked in union" is their application, which is non-dual.
Through the yoga of meditative absorption in that, one should enjoy them all;
this is the supreme essence of the great passion of all the Buddhas.
Then the Blessed One, Viśva, whose nature is the Victor inseparable from the three vajras and who is the guide to vajra-accomplishment, spoke these words:
The yogi should practice that which is harsh, unpleasant to hear, and expressive of the non-existence of the aggregates and so forth; for that purpose, he shall swiftly attain awakening.
Thus is the definitive meaning.

The great bodhisattvas, situated in the midst of the assembly of the Great Vajradhara, appearing as if they did not understand the definitive meaning of the vajra-words that illuminate the specific samādhi just described, inquire in order to benefit future sentient beings of dull faculties, such as Padma and others. To demonstrate how they thus question him, the compiler says, "Then indeed" (*atha khalu*).
Immediately after the revelation of the fifth section, he attains the equality of all Tathāgatas; therefore, he is the "Samaya of All Tathāgatas."

Who is this Vajraketu? Because he has the vajra as his emblem, he is Vajrapāṇi. With him as their leader and at their head, those bodhisattvas—having attained a state of wonder and marvel by manifesting a particular kind of meditative absorption through a mode of expression that appears contrary to worldly conventions—produced (*akārṣuḥ*), that is, uttered, this vajra-sound (*vajraghoṣam*) which is an unimpeded resonance, in the form that will be described hereafter.

In order to show how they questioned the Blessed One himself under the pretext of the Tathāgata’s inquiry directed toward the assembly, beginning with the words "What is its own characteristic? (*svalakṣaṇa-kim ityādi*), he says: "What? (*kim iti*), [the word] *kim* being used for the purpose of questioning.
The connection is as follows: this Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, speaks the Vajra-word which transcends the three realms (*traidhātuka*).
Because it sustains, it is a realm (*dhātu*);
it is wisdom (*prajñā*) characterized by discernment (*pravicaya*).

It is threefold, distinguished by the divisions of weak, medium, and intense; it specifically transcends, overcomes, and does not follow after the triple world (*traidhātuka*), and is thus "transcending the triple world.
For this very reason, it is "transcending all world-systems" (*sarvalokadhātuvyativṛtta*), because all world-systems exist according to the distinctions of weak and so forth;
and it is marvelous and unprecedented, like coldness in fire, in the midst of the assemblies of all Tathāgatas and all Bodhisattvas.
"Unprecedented" means that which has not arisen; "unprecedented speech" is the word that illuminates that [state],
and that itself is the "path" because it sets [the goal] in motion.
Because it is indestructible and worthy of being accepted, it is "Vajra";
because it is the foundation for all through following the words of the Tathāgatas, it is "Pada" (the Footing); thus, it is the "Vajrapada," the path of speech that is beyond the miraculous.
"What is it that causes remorse in the midst of the two assemblies? It is that which should not be spoken.

Having heard what was just said by the Bodhisattva, the Blessed Ones—the Tathāgatas assembled in the Blessed One’s retinue—perceiving his intention as described in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, respond to the question; in order to demonstrate how they do so, the compiler [of the tantra] composes this introductory section, beginning with "Then," and so forth.
The connection is that "the Blessed Ones have spoken thus.
The meaning of the previously mentioned words beginning with "ineffable" has already been analyzed.
The passage beginning with "O son of good family" is the refutation.
"O son of noble family" (*kulaputra*) is an address used in prohibition. "Noble family" (*kula*) refers to the Vajra-family and so forth; those born therein are "sons of noble family.

*Kulaputtraivaṃ* is an archaic (ārṣa) form. The perception that what was just mentioned—by way of doubt regarding the *samaya*—is inferior or base is called the "perception of inferiority" (*hīnasaṃjñā*).

The term *jugupsitasaṃjñā* refers to the perception that something is loathsome or censured by the world; do not produce either of these two kinds of perception. To explain why one should not produce such perceptions as the notion of inferiority—which would lead to the manifestation of faults—he says, "For what reason? and then states, "Because it is the foremost practice," and so forth.
That is to say, that which is the conduct of a bodhisattva is the supreme conduct when compared with the conduct of śrāvakas and others;

what is the conduct of a bodhisattva? It is the engagement of practitioners (mantrins) according to their capacity, in whatever manner—whether contrary to worldly norms or not—by which the welfare of sentient beings is accomplished. This is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
That is to say: that which is the practice of mantra (mantracaryā) is the practice of the Tathāgata.
Those from whom they proclaim the reality of mantra are the gurus; those mantras are jewel-like persons (ratnapudgala).
Having realized the stage of completion (niṣpannakrama), their practice—that which is the proceeding by means of non-meditative yoga—is this very practice of the Tathāgata.

Having thus established the exposition of the two modes of conduct through the transformation of one's own nature in this very life, he states their accomplishment by means of the distinction between the two truths,
beginning with "tad yathā" (it is as follows).
The phrase "tad yathāpināma" is a collection of particles used in the sense of "just as";
space is ultimate truth,
which is pervasive and permeates all dependently originated phenomena.
All phenomena—the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—follow after space because there is no distinction between phenomena (*dharma*) and the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
thus, they do not abide in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and so forth. This very point is elucidated as follows:
"desires" (*kāma*) refers to those things which one desires or seeks, such as the gods of the Four Great Kings' assembly and others.
Because of their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), there is a dwelling or abode; those [abodes] are the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth,
yet even they do not abide therein, because even the desire realm has entered into ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

That state of existence (*bhava*) in which there is merely attachment to form (*rūpa-rāga*) is the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*); that state of existence in which, through detachment from form, there is mere representation (*vijñapti-mātra*) is the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).

Furthermore, these two do not abide [in the four great elements], nor do they abide in the four great elements. Even that which is established through the sequence of the wind-mandala and so forth—the fourfold mandala that serves as the support for all moving and stationary things—is the "four great elements" (*catur-mahābhūta*); yet even there, they do not abide.
Because all things consist of luminosity,
in this very manner all phenomena, such as the aggregates and so forth, are to be understood;
this is the significance of the point.

Having understood and realized this aforementioned meaning—that ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is dependent upon those things that are dependently originated (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and that it is characterized by dependence on others and is not established by itself—the Tathāgatas, having discerned and determined the dispositions (*āśaya*) and inclinations (*adhimukti*) of sentient beings who abide in various grades such as dull-witted and so forth, teach and reveal the Dharma characterized by vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) to those beings. Like a wish-fulfilling jewel or a magical vase, the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma occurs effortlessly in accordance with the dispositions of sentient beings; this is "teaching" (*deśanā*).

Just as this teaching is, so too is the etymological explanation (*nirukti*) and the synthesis (*pratyāhāra*) of these words; the etymological explanation of the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is equal to the etymological explanation of all words.
