In the same way, through the etymological explanation of the word "space," all the commitments (*samaya*) of all the Tathāgatas just mentioned should be understood as being equal.

Having thus taught the purity of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of all phenomena, he speaks in order to demonstrate the specific skillful means (*upāya-viśeṣa*) that produces the vajra-body, which is not shared with other vehicles:

"Namely, for example," and so forth: the *kāṇḍa* is the fire-drill; the *araṇi* is the wood that serves as the base for churning fire, because by means of this [wood] fire is churned and produced; the *mathani* is the upper piece of wood; and "churning" (*mathana*) is the exertion of the person's hands, which is the rubbing together (*ghaṭana*). Depending upon and relying upon these three, immediately after heat, smoke appears; then, immediately after smoke, fire appears—a mass of elements (*bhūtasaṃghāta*) with a blazing and radiant form—which arises and comes into being.

Heat, smoke, and fire—these three do not reside in the fire-drill (*kāṇḍa*). Thus it is established that they do not reside in the drill, nor do they reside in the friction, nor do they reside in the activity of the person's hands. Just as heat and the others are not perceived separately from the fire-drill and so forth, yet arise through their conjunction in varying degrees, in this very same way all the *vajrasamayas* of all the Tathāgatas are to be understood. Because they are the abode of all the Tathāgatas, all the Tathāgatas are to be understood as emptiness; the *vajra* is great emptiness, and the *samaya* is supreme emptiness. One should understand them as emptiness.
Because these three are followed— that is, understood—
by means of coming, going, and so forth, all the Tathāgatas and others are thus known.
"Gamana" (going) refers to the proceeding toward ultimate truth by means of the sequence of the three voids;
therefore, "coming" is the attainment of the great void, the supreme void, and emptiness.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), there is the inclusion of the absence of both going and coming, because for that which is perfected, there is no entering or arising.
The word *iti* marks the conclusion.
Having thus heard and comprehended the reality of the Dharma, which is supremely profound, those with distressed minds utter an udāna; showing this, he says "atha" and so forth.

At the moment of their arrival, they were struck with wonder by the arising of light; then, having realized the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), their eyes blossomed with amazement, and through the arising of the knowledge of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*), they uttered these words—which are about to be described—whose nature is to illuminate the reality of their own self-realization, beginning with "In the great elements" (*mahābhūteṣu*).
Here, "the great element" (*mahābhūta*) refers to the phenomenon (*dharma*) that is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
The plural number is used for the sake of the genus because it is all-pervasive; that very [reality] is like space,
as it cannot be conceptualized by logicians.
It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*). It is pure (*śuddha*) because it is purified by conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
Within that ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it conceals or covers the path of vision by means of its absence as an object (*viṣayatā*).
The conventional reality is the form of Vajradhara.

The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "again. That which is sung—that having become empty through the realization of ultimate truth, it again attains visibility—is what constitutes this marvel.

The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). Being pure by virtue of that, he is the "Pure Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-śuddha*); and he is also the "Reality-meaning" (*tattvārtha*), namely Mahāvajradhara.
He alone is the "pledge" (*samaya*) because he is not to be transgressed.
And the textual composition that expounds this is the "Ultimate Pure Reality-Meaning" (Paramārtha-śuddhatattvārtha).
This is the intentional terminology (sandhyābhāṣā).
The Explanation of the Six Points in the Ninth Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
The Tenth Chapter.

When practitioners who rely on the common and supreme means (*sāmānyottamasādhana*) and have mastered their efforts through various practices such as the *prapañca* [rites] do not attain accomplishment (*siddhi*), then an exhortation to the heart of one's own deity must be performed.
With the words beginning "Now" (*atha*), he introduces the tenth chapter;
the connection is with the phrase "Then they said" (*athāhuḥ*).

"Having again assembled in the gathering" means that, according to the sequence described in the first chapter, Mahāsamayavajra— Mahāvajradhara— having paid homage to that very [state] characterized by the non-duality of the two truths of the perfect awakening to reality (tattvābhisaṃbodhi), which is the secret of body, speech, and mind because it is the secret of body, speech, and mind, and having become a Tathāgata because he has attained [the state] in accordance with the various inclinations of those to be trained, spoke as follows.

"Reality" (*tattva*) is that which is non-deceptive. "Mantras" are those produced from the *mālā* and *ali* [vowels and consonants], such as the *sarpa* and *kabandha* [types of mantras]. Their "essences" (*sāra*) are the three primary ones beginning with *Oṃ*. The "collection" (*samuccaya*) of these is their "kindling" (*uddīpana*). The "Tathāgatas" are body, speech, and mind. Their "secret" (*guhya*), known as the "esoteric" (*rahasya*), consists of the systems for great accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi-naya*), meaning the means for great accomplishment. "Please speak"—that is, reveal—that which is the most excellent and distinguished among them; this is the request.
Following the request, Vajradhara is the "King" (*rāja*) because he shines forth by virtue of having attained wisdom (*prajñā*) and method (*upāya*), whose nature is the knowledge of skillful means.

All afflictions (*kleśa*), such as passion (*rāga*) and the rest, are like the ocean because they are divided into primary and secondary categories; thus, they are the "oceans of all afflictions. He is the "Lord" (*prabhu*) because, having overcome the nature of suffering, mental distress, and so forth within those oceans, he manifests and sports in the form of supreme bliss.
He is "blazing" (*dīpta*) because he burns the fuel of all suffering, and for that very reason, he is "fierce" (*caṇḍa*) due to his nature of wrath.
Upon his appearance, because he caused even ordinary people to have their eyes wide open with joy, he was called Viśālākṣa;
for the proclamation [of his name] depended entirely upon him.
"Body," and so forth.

The cultivation of the body and so on means the cultivation—that is, the thorough knowledge—of the body, speech, and mind in their true nature as the vajras of body, speech, and mind; that must be performed.
How?
"Non-conceptual" (*nirvikalpa*) and "without support" (*nirālamba*) are adjectives modifying the action.

It is non-conceptual because, in reality, there is no differentiation such as "this is the body," "this is speech," or "this is the mind. It is without support because there is no mutual dependence between them. Their single flavor (*ekarasa*) is their equality; by means of that, it does not abide anywhere.
Regarding the term *samatayā*, although one might expect *samate*, the form *samatayā* is used according to the archaic style (*ārṣa*); it is not a hiatus.

Thus, having demonstrated through the words of the Blessed One that the body and so forth are ultimately non-different, the compiler, composing a brief prologue suitable for stimulating the heart, says "Then," and so forth.

According to the sequence just described, the Tathāgata is pure by nature; the Pāramitās such as Locanā and others are the mantras; and Vairocana and others are the upāyas. Their mutual propitiation is precisely that which is the vajra, because it is indestructible.

Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that [state]—the one-pointedness of mind—the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara spoke thus to those requesting [teachings], all the Tathāgatas: "It exists," and so forth. This refers to the meaning that is about to be explained. "O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas" is an address.

"All the Tathāgatas, headed by Akṣobhya" refers to the application of the act of demonstration. All the Tathāgatas are seated upon the forms of women, who are the Vidyā-devis; they are manifold through their various attendants and so forth. Together with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of them—of whom these are indicative signs because they are immeasurable—the beings desire liberation through the enjoyment of sense objects. The performance of purposeful activity for them consists in leading them to enlightenment according to their inclinations. This is like a drama being enacted by a stage-manager who has entered the arena of selflessness; they demonstrate that drama.

How so? He says: in world-systems extending to the limits of the world-systems of the ten directions, they play, perform miracles, and take delight with the five qualities of sensual pleasure—forms and so forth—which provide constant joy; they sport with goddesses through universal delight, and being honored by the hosts of vidyās, they in turn honor them. This is "service. Furthermore, they do not even look upon one who is devoted to the practice of mantra.

Those Tathāgatas, experiencing the bliss of supreme joy by way of play, [teach] the fourfold mantra-discourse, namely: the designation of mantra, the meaning of mantra, the interweaving of mantra, and the adamantine speech devoid of vocal tones.

Through these means, there is engagement in rites such as pacification; this is the practice of mantra. Those who are devoted to it and whose minds are fixed upon it do not look [at others], nor do they hold them in high regard.
He shows the reason for not looking [elsewhere] with the words, "He has indeed attained perfection," and so forth.

"This one" refers to the one devoted to mantra. A *mantra* is that which is spoken by the Tathāgatas of the three times; it is that which is whispered by the gurus. The practice concerning that is *mantracaryā*. It is called a *naya* (method) because it leads to or brings about that practice; it is sevenfold. Namely:
the mandala, the gaṇacakra, the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), the ritual offering (*bali*), and the sequence of the assembly (*melāpakakrama*).
Reality, explained in seven ways, is called the Way of Mantra.
Thus,
it is the nature of things that this very *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage) is obstructed by those established in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
One who has emerged from or departed from such dharmas of the mantra-practice system transmitted through the succession of Tathāgatas is "external" (*bāhya*).
Since "from dharma" (dharmāt) was expected, "dharma" is used as an archaic Vedic form (*ārṣa*).
The word "vata" expresses disregard.
The word "iti" is indicated by elision.

Thus, having observed the turning away from the Tathāgatas among those devoted to mantras, the compiler [of the scripture] spoke the following— beginning with "That" (*tat*) and so forth— in order to show the means by which the Blessed One grants them a vision of the Tathāgata for the sake of their accomplishment and favor.

Since the Tathāgatas do not attend to the practitioner while they experience the bliss of supreme joy through the gateways of play and the like, he uttered what is about to be described in order to cause those great beings, the Tathāgatas, to look upon him, and to generate faith by turning them toward the practitioner.

"Of all," and so forth. This is the commentary on the six points of the tenth chapter. It is the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. "All mantras" refers to the mantra-deities such as the snake-gods (*sarpa*); that by which their heart—their very life—is impelled and awakened is called "the Impeller of the Heart of All Mantras. It is the supreme secret, to be strictly concealed from those who are unworthy vessels. The "pledge" (*samaya*) consists of the body, speech, and mind of those belonging to the deluded family (*mohakula*) of all Tathāgatas; it is so called because they proceed correctly toward it. That which is taken up by practitioners through mental attention is the "object" (*ālambana*). Thus, the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) is the "perfect object" (*samālambana*).

Thus, from his own body, speech, and mind, he uttered—that is, emitted—the syllable *oṃ* from the body of himself as Mahāvajradhara, the syllable *āḥ* from his speech, and the syllable *hūṃ* from his mind, in that order. These serve as the objects of focus for the bodies and so forth of all Vajradharas, namely Meghanāda, and as the objects of focus for the supreme bodies and so forth of all phenomena, namely the syllable *āḥ*.
How so? By means of "the definition of the path of speech": the path of speech is speech itself; by that, "definition" (*nirukti*) means the act of explaining.

By means of that etymological explanation, he uttered [it] with both mind and body, as well as with vocal speech— how much more so with speech alone! Those phonemes (varṇa), which possess the nature of female, male, and neuter, are combined and gathered together in that which is called the "Collection of Mantras" (mantrasamuccaya).
He uttered those three syllables.
"Then," and so forth.

"Then," meaning immediately after the example of the collection of mantras, at the very moment this three-syllable [mantra] was spoken—that is, upon its utterance—all the Buddhas, beginning with Akṣobhya, together with their own offspring and the assembly of Bodhisattvas, were shaken by the gaze of Mahāvajradhara for the sake of bestowing grace upon these beings and fell into a swoon.

Recalling Vajrasattva, the sovereign of all families, and remembering his nature as the benefactor of all beings, they fell into a swoon; that is, they attained an overflowing of joy. They reached it. They obtained it.

Then, immediately after the recollection, Vajrapāṇi, the Great Vajra-holder, uttered this form of the deity’s commitment (*samaya*) which is about to be described, beginning with "Space" and so forth.

Space is suchness (*tathatā*); that in which one is held or established is the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), the commitment-being (*samayasattva*). Its center is the heart; one should meditate upon—that is, visualize—the arrayed mandala of the wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*) situated therein.

Therein, one should visualize—that is, bring to completion—this pair by means of their own forms (*svabimba*): the *jñānasattva* situated in the center, located in the heart, which is the syllable *HŪṂ*, known as the *samādhisattva*. Among these, one should contemplate the *samādhisattva* as blazing intensely with vajra-rays and radiating forth.

One should visualize [the deity] as intensely blazing—that is, exceedingly radiant—and as flashing and flaming with the rays of the five Vajras, which are the Tathāgatas; these rays are white and so forth.

One should meditate and contemplate that the body, speech, and mind—the power of the body, speech, and mind—of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas both manifest and unmanifest such as Vairocana and others who reside in the world-systems of the ten directions, is drawn into the heart by means of the limbs of the white and other rays issued from the Samādhisattva. One should thus meditate.

The connection [of the meaning] is as follows: practicing in this way, the practitioner, at that very moment, having drawn [the deity] forth and merely upon its entry into the *samādhi-sattva*, shall overcome all [obstacles] and become Vajrasattva.
Of what nature is he? Because his own nature consists of the indivisible body and so forth.

The Tathāgatas are "great" because they uphold the vajras of body, speech, and mind; he is the "Great King" (*mahārāja*) because he delights them. He is the "Supreme Lord of All" (*sarvāgraḥ parameśvaraḥ*) because he exercises both restraint and grace over all things, both stationary and moving, including the foremost among them such as Hari, Hara, and others.
One should meditate on oneself as Mahāvajradhara of such a form—this is the meaning.

One’s own maṇḍala is one’s own body-maṇḍala; the method for its accomplishment by means of one’s own vajra, which is one’s own mind, is this which has just been described. It is the essence of all Buddhas existing in the three times, which has become stable; "vajras" refers to the minds of the Tathāgatas, and their "samuccaya" is their extraction.
It is so called because that by which [the essence] is gathered—that is, extracted—is thus designated.
Having thus produced oneself as consisting of the mind of all the Tathāgatas, one produces the circle of the retinue accordingly. To demonstrate that,
he says "sva" and so forth.

One should meditate upon and practice [the visualization] by contemplating one's own self in four locations—the eastern and other directions—in terms of form, that is, in the nature of the colors, arms, and so forth as previously described. Regarding the phrase "by means of the union with the three-faced forms" (*trimukhākārayogena*): "forms" (*ākāra*) are those things which are fashioned, manifested, or grasped, namely passion (*rāga*) and the rest; the "union with the three-faced forms" (*trimukhākārayoga*) is the connection with them. Having characterized oneself by that, one should meditate upon and cultivate the Mantra-beings (*mantrapuruṣa*), such as Vairocana and the others, by means of the three syllables, having visualized them in those respective locations.
By this method, one should emanate the arrays of Tathāgatas according to their respective deities associated with those families,
since the four Tathāgatas are intended as an illustration.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Vajradhara, the Pledge of Space-Vajra.
Having thus manifested the mandala of the gathering, he states what one should do next with the words beginning "Then" (*tatra*).

Therein, in the context of the exhortation of the Tathāgatas' hearts, one should perform the subtle visualization of this supreme, most excellent vajra-secret—the secret of the Tathāgatas—which resides within the heart of each of the mandalas; for since the mandalas and those who dwell within them (*māṇḍaleya*) are non-different, [the secret] is situated in the center of the heart of those mandalas, resting upon the moon of the heart.
It is called *vibhāvana* because it is specifically manifested; that is to say, one should cultivate the subtle *jñānasattva*, which consists of gnosis.

Situated in the center of that *jñānasattva*, namely within the moon at the heart, is likewise each individual syllable, whose nature is indestructible, supreme, and most excellent because it arises from the *anāhata*. Through yoga, it joins the practitioner with the highest good (*śreyaḥ*) as the word *hūṃ*; thus, yoga is the *samādhisattva*. Therefore, one should cultivate—that is, meditate upon—the five-pronged great vajra, which is formidable.
In this manner, one should contemplate those three—known as the Samaya-jñāna and the Samādhi-sattva—as vajras because they are indivisible.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the application of the vajra-hook":
the Tathāgatas are the vajras; their hook is like a hook for an elephant.
Its application is the application of the vajra-hook; therefore, one should contemplate three vajras within that application of the vajra-hook. To demonstrate that very application, he says:
"The heart," and so forth.
With those three vajras, one should strike—that is, move—the heart, which is the heart of the deity to be accomplished (*sādhya-devatā*).

By means of a mass of light rays that have become unified, taking the form of a hook and consisting of the Maṇḍala deities headed by the Lord (*adhipati*) and the nature of the three beings (*tri-sattva*), one should cause the heart of the deity to be accomplished—known as the "three beings"—to tremble, or else impel the deity.
The word "or" (*vā*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

Regarding the *Vajrāṅkuśabheda*, the commentary on the ten million points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) of the tenth chapter: immediately after the emanation and generation [of the deity], the practitioner should visualize the deity as King Niśumbha standing before him, seeking an order; he should then cause that [deity] to grant the accomplishment of the pledge (*samayasiddhi*) through the Tathāgatas.
He should urge and command him.
This procedure which has just been described is the means for accomplishing the awakening of the Buddhas for all Vajras and all practitioners.
The Buddhas are the Tathāgatas; for them, there is the accomplishment and summoning of the bodhicitta.
Regarding "Vajra" and so forth: the visualization of the vajra-hook consisting of the three beings just mentioned is performed by those belonging to the Vajra and Padma families and others.
This should be practiced by practitioners belonging to the Tathāgata, Ratna, and Karma families.
This "incitement in the heart" (hṛdaye codana) just mentioned—the incitement of the Tathāgata’s heart—is called "born of drama" (*nāṭakasaṃbhava*) because it arises like a drama.

Just as in a drama a single stage director is imagined through costumes and the like to take on the forms of Indra and other deities, so too here, the single *cittavajra* (mind-vajra) is imagined in the form of the goal, the practitioner, and the means of accomplishment; such is the meaning.
To demonstrate the duration of time for this ritual procedure for stimulating the heart, he says:
"For seven days," and so forth.
One should perform it for seven days, starting from the day of commencement.
"This is the supreme Vajra-method.

The Tathāgatas are the *vajras*; those ritual procedures by which they are led—that is, drawn forth—are the *vajranayas*. Among these, the "supreme" means the most excellent; thus, it is the "supreme Vajra-method.
One should practice that ritual procedure.
With the words "it is accomplished" and so forth, he states the praise of the ritual procedure:

the body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas—which are to be accomplished through [the practitioner's] body, speech, and mind—are accomplished as a secret for the practitioners who possess the wisdom-vajra, because it is obtainable through the guru’s oral instruction.
"Terrified" means they have been overcome by fear; even though the Tathāgatas are in such a state, with minds full of alarm, they—
having come under the sway of compassion and possessing unimpeded minds— look upon the practitioner as givers of boons and favor them by bestowing the desired boon.
Having shown favor, what do they do? He says: "They give," and so forth.
By means of satisfying the mind, they give—that is, they present—the vast and great, beloved, and desired accomplishment characterized as both mundane and supramundane.
He asks, "Who gives? and answers, "The Buddhas," and so forth.

The Buddhas are Akṣobhya and the others; the Bodhisattvas are Maitreya and the others; and the practitioners who uphold the supreme mantra-conduct are the perfected beings striving for the sake of enlightenment. He then asks: what would happen to the practitioner who does not practice in this way? He says:
"Should one transgress," and so forth.
If, moreover, one whose nature is delusion (*moha*) thinks, "These Tathāgatas are [ordinary beings]," or entertains the conceptualization that "I am ordinary"—that is delusion.
One whose self-nature (*ātman*), or intrinsic being (*svabhāva*), is such delusion is "one whose nature is delusion."
The life of that practitioner ends with that very rite by which he desires success;
by that same rite he exhausts his life and does not attain success, provided he is devoid of the arousal of the heart— this is the intended meaning.
As it is literally stated:

having thus explained the application for stimulating the heart (*hṛdayasaṃcodanaprayoga*) for those engaged in the common means of accomplishment (*sāmānyasādhana*), he now states the stage of the supreme means of accomplishment (*uttamasādhana*).
The meaning of "Now," and so forth, has already been analyzed.
He made this sound, he uttered these words; he spoke.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated: "As many as there may be persons engaged in the secret of mantra—those 'mantra-persons' who are Tathāgatas possessing the three vajra-knowledges—it is when they are filled and completely full that the conceptualization of all phenomena (*sarvabhāvavikalpana*) occurs through the application of the two organs, and not otherwise.

All phenomena refers to those already mentioned and those yet to be described, such as the applications of the means and the goal (*sādhyasādhanādiprayoga*); their conceptualization is their accomplishment—that is what is meant by 'the conceptualization of all phenomena.'"

"By the application of the two organs" (*dvayendriya-prayogena*) means: the two organs are the two truths; their application is their union. Whatever mundane or supramundane accomplishment (*siddhi*) there may be, it is accomplished through the application of the two organs. The intention is that the conceptualization of all phenomena cannot be perfected without that. The practice (*sādhana*) produced by the aforementioned application is the means of accomplishment for those who do not transgress the mantra-samaya related to all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas; they are the "mantra-samayas," and this is their *sādhana*, the method of accomplishment.
With the words "Vidyeśvarī," and so forth, he explains the means for accomplishing the application of the two organs.
Vidyeśvarī is Prajñāpāramitā.

When the aggregates (*skandhas*) and other phenomena have been entered into by her and rendered free from appearance (*nirābhāsīkṛta*), one should perform the meditation on the "vajra"—that is, their union or unification.
Then, he states what one who has attained accomplishment (*siddha*) should do:
"The red one," and so forth.

Immediately after entering ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), one should manifest one's own Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which consists of the two truths; that [seal] is "red" (*raktā*), meaning attached (*saktā*), through its union with the non-abandonment of the triple world (*traidhātuka*).

Having generated the thought, "This mass of sentient beings dwelling in the three realms, with their blood-red eyes, is our father," and so forth, one should look upon them with passion and great respect, and thus understand.
This which was just mentioned is the *samayamaṇḍala*.
*Samaya* is Mahāvajradhara; his *maṇḍa* is the essential method (*vidhi*); that which takes up or grasps this is the *samayamaṇḍala*.
What is that procedure?
Having thus demonstrated the exhortation of the heart along with its methods and its fruits, he says "Now," etc., in order to show the activity of the yogin who has achieved that [exhortation].

"All Tathāgatas" refers to the aggregates of form and so forth, which are conceptualized as having Vairocana and the others as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Their "self" (*ātman*) is their intrinsic nature, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); born from that is the "Son of All Tathāgatas," Mahāvajradhara.
Because he is the state of consecration for all Buddhas, he is "All Consecrations.
For this very reason, he is the "Foremost of All Buddhas."
He spoke these words that are about to be stated:

"In all the infinite and boundless world-systems, however many women are known—whether classified as inferior, middling, or superior—such as Rūpavajrā and others, who are conceptualized as the two kinds of Mahāmudrās, namely, the mantra-body (*mantramūrti*) and the gnosis-body (*jñānamūrti*); their *ādiyoga* is the focal point of the Tathāgatas. By means of that, one should enjoy those objects such as form and the rest."

There, one should emanate the state of Buddhahood by means of the innumerable millions of vajras; there, in the yoga of Mahāmudrā and so forth, the Lord, the Bodhisattva-samaya, the Great Vajradhara, said: "The Vajrin, by means of the Vajra, should emanate the state of Buddhahood—the emanation of Buddhas—which is innumerable in measure, immeasurable.
This is the commentary on the six-fold [meaning] of the tenth chapter: by this yoga, one shall attain enlightenment (*bodhi*).
It is called *bodhi* because it awakens sentient beings to the nature of the self.
Of what nature is it? It is like the diamond-like space;
its intrinsic nature is that of the body-vajra and the others.
Because it is intangible, it is like space;
one attains that awakening.
This shows the benefit even during the stage of striving.
"He shall become," and so forth.
Striving together with the Bodhisattvas, he is presented with health and other benefits directly by Vajrasattva himself.

He whose life-span is long is "Vajrasattvāyuḥ" (one with the life-span of Vajrasattva). By metaphorical usage, the "Jinas" are the Conquerors of Qualities; he shall become an ocean, a locus for them, just as the ocean is the locus for all jewels.
The Sandhyābhāṣā: The Chapter on the Exhortation of the Tathāgata’s Heart for the Sake of Attaining Both Mundane and Supramundane Siddhis.

The Explanation of the Six Points in the Tenth Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
[The text provided consists solely of two vertical bars (||), which in this context serve as a punctuation mark indicating the end of a section or verse. [End of Section]
The eleventh chapter.

Having thus explained the twofold heart-excitation for practitioners of both types [the conceptual and the non-conceptual], he now introduces the eleventh chapter, intending to illuminate the two kinds of deity forms mentioned in the first chapter for the sake of the conceptual and perfected practitioners.
He says, "Then," and so forth.

Having entered—that is, having brought face-to-face—the meditative absorption (samādhi) of one-pointedness of mind named after the "Vajra of all Tathāgatas," which consists of the three syllables beginning with *praṇava* (*oṃ*), and in which the supreme persons, the deities, are generated, he uttered this.
What is that?
It is the mantra of all the Tathāgatas.

The secret Vajra-vidyā is the Vajra-vidyā of the mantras of all the Tathāgatas; it is precisely the triad beginning with the syllable Oṃ which is produced by them as the male deity in this chapter—thus says the compiler. Demonstrating this very meaning through the words of the Blessed One, he says:

The "three vajras" are the vajras of body, speech, and mind; the "syllables of the three vajras" are the syllables such as *oṃ* and so forth that produce them. These are the "foremost of mantras" because they possess the power of all mantras.
By means of these, one should perform the visualization of the Mahāmudrā.

It is called "Mahāmudrā" because it proceeds toward—meaning it attains—the great joy (*muda*) or rapture, being worthy of worship in the realms of *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*. Thus, it is the "Great Seal."

Its manifestation must be performed and practiced by the practitioner with the wisdom-vajra; by the passage beginning with "the syllable Oṃ which brings about all enlightenment," he shows that the three syllables effect the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*).

The syllable *Oṃ* is the heart of the Tathāgata; because it brings about for the yogin an indestructible body, it brings forth the vajra-body. Awakening (*bodhi*) is suchness (*tathatā*); he whose self (*ātmā*) is emanated and perfected from that is the "selfless awakening" (*bodhirnirātmā*), namely Amitābha.
His state is selflessness (*nairātmya*).
The syllable *ĀḤ* is selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is its intrinsic nature; because it is indivisible and irreversible for the practitioner, it brings about the "Vajra of Speech.
Mind is the support of body and speech, thus [it is called] "body-speech-mind," having the nature of Akṣobhya.

That mind in which the three vajras are indivisible—that is, their non-differentiation—is "the indivisibility of the three vajras. Because it brings this to perfection within the continuum of the yogin, the Great Vajradhara, the Mantra-Person of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, spoke thus regarding the syllable *HŪṂ*: "It brings about the indivisibility of the three vajras."
Demonstrating the sequence for the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā just described, he says "khavajra," and so forth.
One should contemplate the space-vajra as the center; situated therein, one should meditate upon the entire vajra mandala.
"All vajras" refers to the four goddesses beginning with Locanā; one should visualize the mandala produced by them in due order.

There, upon the ground, is the syllable *bhrūṃ*, which is the cause for the manifestation of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Through the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) regarding those multitudes of Tathāgatas who are like clouds of vajras, it brings about and sustains the radiation [of light] according to their respective places; thus, it is called "the bringer of the radiation of vajra-clouds. By the words beginning with "there," the syllable *bhrūṃ* is shown. One should visualize the vajra-maṇḍala, the sun-maṇḍala, and the syllable *hūṃ* situated in its center.
The intended meaning is that one should meditate upon a solar mandala produced from the syllable *hūṃ*;
likewise, one should meditate upon a lunar and lotus mandala produced from the syllables *oṃ* and *āḥ*.
Having thus brought forth these three mandalas, the traditional instruction (*āmnāya*) is that one should place those very same seed-syllables upon the pericarp of the lotus.
With the passage beginning "The garland of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*," he concludes the meaning previously stated:
having meditated thus upon the foundation mandala, one should visualize the three symbols;
it is not otherwise.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the heart" (*hṛdaya*),
since it refers to the Tathāgatas of the three times— that is, the Buddhas of the three times—
it follows that there is a moon disc in the heart because the mind is conventionally designated as such.

Body, speech, and mind are the three syllables; therefore, that in which one is attached and remains is the "delighting of body, speech, and mind. One should meditate on the lunar disc as the object to be crushed by means of these three signs.
To the question "What then? he says: *Oṃ*, etc.
And upon that lunar mandala, one should place the syllable *Oṃ*, which is designated as the Buddha-body, and likewise the syllable *Āḥ*, which is the path of the Buddha's speech.

That in which there is a flood—that is, a collection—of the natures of the various cognitions is the "flood of cognition" (*jñānaugha*), which is the mind; the syllable *HŪṂ* has that as its intrinsic nature.
This triad of syllables is called "the supreme method of awakening.
Here, "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the state of great bliss (*mahāsukha*).
That by which one is led—that is, attained—is the *bodhanaya*.

What is that? It is the *vajra* produced through the transformation of the three syllables, which indicates the fivefold manifest enlightenment (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*). That very [vajra] is supreme because it is distinguished above all families.
"This" refers to the *vajra* just mentioned; it is that which accomplishes the awakening of all Buddhas, the practitioners of the Great Vajradhara yoga.
"Created by means of the generation stage as the producer of Mahāmudrā"—
this form of Mahāmudrā was created and revealed by Jñānavajra, the Great Vajradhara.
For what purpose? Because the Buddhas are jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*); conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*) is their cause and ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) is their fruit.
Since it arises—that is, is produced—by means of both cause and fruit, it is called "the arising from cause and fruit" (*hetuphalodaya*).
The forms of the completely pure deities were emanated for that purpose by Mahāvajradhara;
these mantras and vidyās, beginning with "eta," were proclaimed at the beginning of the ritual manual (kalpa) through the samayas of accomplishment and so forth.
It has already been stated that the accomplishment [of the mandala] is together with the pledges (samaya) of protection, consumption, and so forth;
he asks: "Why are the Buddhas, such as Akṣobhya and the others, [the ones who accomplish it], and not anyone else?"

By means of the meditations on the indivisibility of the three vajras, the Tathāgatas [realize] the syllable *tya*, which is the commitment (*samaya*) of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. From that arises the triad of mandalas, beginning with the sun; within that is the reality, the syllable *tya* upon a lotus, which is "knowledge" (*jñāna*). Thus, the moon mandala—which is perfected through the transformation of all things—is established. Upon the moon mandala is the great five-pronged vajra, produced from the three syllables arranged thereon. By this, one is consecrated (*adhiṣṭhīyate*), meaning it is brought to completion. In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, "consecration" refers to the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), and its cause is the instrumental reason for it.

Concentration (*samādhi*) is one-pointedness of mind that accomplishes that [meditative object]; it is described as such by the passage beginning with "in seclusion," which demonstrates the practitioner's application.

Having stayed in secluded places— delightful locations devoid of the crowds of people, adorned with various beautiful trees endowed with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, and graced by pleasing reservoirs of water— the practitioner who undertakes and practices this yoga just described will,
within a single fortnight, accomplish and attain the state of Mahāvajradhara through body, speech, and mind.
The "wing" (*pakṣa*) refers to conviction regarding the Guru and the deity;

by means of that single, certain, and devoted [conviction], there is no doubt that body, speech, and mind are necessarily perfected through this sequence. The intention is that the mantra-practitioner, by training in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and attaining the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), will certainly attain the state of a Great Vajradhara in this very life.

Having thus demonstrated the generation stage practice (*utpattikrama-sādhana*) for the yogins of Mahāvajradhara, he speaks in order to show the meditative concentration of single-minded recollection (*ekasmṛti-samādhi*) for the yogins of Vairocana and the others: "One should contemplate the supreme, clear mandala situated in the center of the space-vajra."

Following the sequence of verses beginning with "abhāva," one enters through meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) up to the arrangement of the thirty-two deities within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). Then, having rendered everything free of appearance by means of the mantra beginning with "na śūnyatā," one generates the moon, sun, and lotus by means of the three syllables beginning with *oṃ*. Having visualized the three syllables upon the pericarp of the lotus, one should contemplate the clear mandala—the moon mandala—through the transformation of all [phenomena] into its own nature; this is called "one's own mantra-samaya."
Having placed the three syllables upon the lunar disc and meditated on the maṇḍala through their transformation, one should visualize the Vairocana Samayasattva born from that.

Having visualized the Jñānasattva in his heart, one should place the syllable Oṃ—known as the Samādhisattva, which constitutes the very heart—in the heart of that [Jñānasattva] as well; it is five-rayed and endowed with five rays.
Through the supreme meditations of Vairocana, that is, by the yogins of Vairocana, one should meditate while emanating great clouds—that is, multitudes of Vairocanas—from that syllable Oṃ.

By means of this samādhi, for the practitioner whose body is accomplished within a mere fortnight through the mere application of samādhi and without dependence on the elaborations of ritual action— because he is the source of those belonging to his own family, like an ocean for Vajravairocana who knows the generation stage of the Buddha—
the intended meaning is that the Buddha-body, the vajra-body endowed with all the marks, is attained.

Possessing a radiance equal to that and an accomplishment equal to that, one succeeds for three *kalpas* of the Vajra; having become a manifestation of the Great Vajradhara, while serving those who possess the five wisdoms, one may abide.

One should abide in the five wisdoms—the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth. Those objects, such as form and so on, for which these [consciousnesses] have the nature of subjects are the "possessors of the five wisdoms."

The Blessed One, the Secret of the Body-Vajra, Mahāvajradhara, said that one should remain experiencing those [blisses] until the end of saṃsāra. Therein, the "moon-maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas" refers to the vajra, whose nature is indivisible; the "wheel" (*cakra*) is its array of rays (*raśmivyūha*), which takes the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*). The eleventh chapter’s commentary on the six million verses states that the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which accomplishes that is named "the Array of Vajra-Rays of All Tathāgatas. Regarding the passage beginning with "Khavajra," etc.: *Khavajra* (Space-Vajra) and so forth refer to the space-vajra, which is the nature of the mind (*cittasvabhāva*). *Khadhātu* (Space-Element) is the expanse of space. *Vajradhātu* (Vajra-Element) is the vajra-realm. *Vajrasattva* is the essence of the vajra. *Vajradharma* is the dharma of the vajra. *Vajrakarma* is the activity of the vajra. *Vajraratna* is the jewel of the vajra. *Vajrateja* is the splendor of the vajra. *Vajratīkṣṇa* is the sharpness of the vajra. *Vajraketu* is the banner of the vajra. *Vajrahāsa* is the laughter of the vajra. *Vajrarakṣa* is the protection of the vajra. *Vajrayakṣa* is the yakṣa of the vajra. *Vajrasādhu* is the "well done" of the vajra. *Vajravidyottama* is the supreme vidyā of the vajra. *Vajracakra* is the wheel of the vajra. *Vajratuṣṭi* is the satisfaction of the vajra. *Vajralāsyā* is the dance of the vajra. *Vajramālā* is the garland of the vajra. *Vajragītā* is the song of the Having likewise accomplished everything and meditated upon the supreme lotus mandala of Dharma—red and eight-petaled—one should, through its transformation, manifest the Mantra-Person (mantrapuruṣa) Amitābha. Having meditated on the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) at his heart, one should place the five-colored Great Vajra—the Samādhi-Being (samādhisattva) consisting of the syllable ĀḤ—within the Knowledge-Being on the path of speech. This is to be done by means of the foremost meditations on Lokeśvara and the mental activities directed toward the state of Amitābha. Having thus produced it, one establishes the "elaboration of the commitment-knowledge-speech-commitment" (*samaya-jñāna-vāk-samayaprapañcakam*). Here, *samaya* refers to the Commitment-Being (*samayasattva*), and *jñāna* refers to the Knowledge-Being (*jñānasattva*).
Having accomplished these three beings— the Speech-samaya and the Samādhi-sattva— and having unified them, one should meditate;
by this same method, one should likewise meditate on the pentad of the five Tathāgatas through the encapsulation within the three beings.

The path of speech of the Dharma is the meditative absorption of Amitābha; having ascended to it, one attains the Dharma, which is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and the Vajra, which is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

The Vajra conjoined with the Dharma is the "Dharma-Vajra," which brings about and causes one to attain the state of the Great Vajradhara for three vajra-aeons (*trivajrakalpa*); such is the meaning of the passage beginning with these words, as explained.

The *sarvatathāgata-jñānasattva* (the wisdom-being of all Tathāgatas) is the *samayasattva* (pledge-being) who is the commitment of the speech-vajra-samādhisattva. That samādhi in which there is the manifestation of the speech-vajra-commitments of all Tathāgatas is described as such. Having accomplished everything—beginning with "space-vajra" and so forth, like the samādhi of Mahāvajradhara—and having produced one's own reflected-form person as the *samayasattva*, one should contemplate the mind as the *jñānasattva*. One should contemplate the syllable *HŪṂ*, situated within that *jñānasattva*, located in the heart, which is called the *samādhisattva*.
Sarvavajra-jina is Akṣobhya; his abode is thus the body of the three beings, the Great Samaya-being Akṣobhya, endowed with a halo of light from rays of five colors.
He says this to demonstrate that one attains the accomplishment of the Mahāmudrā through the Wisdom-Vajra, the practitioner of Akṣobhya.
"Vajracitta," and so forth:

*vajra* is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) and *citta* is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*); that which is fashioned from these two is "consisting of vajra-mind. Because he instructs gods and humans, he is the Teacher (*śāstṛ*).
The qualities of gnosis (*jñānaguṇa*) are the eight [masteries], such as mastery over desire (*kāmaiśvarya*) and so on; because he is the source (*ākara*) of these, he is their "ocean" (*udadhi*).
The passage beginning with "trivajrakalpam" has its meaning already explained.
Here, *vajra* refers to the *samayasattva*, *citta* refers to the *jñānasattva*, and *guhya* refers to the *samādhisattva*.
Thus, because he consists of these three *sattvas*, he is called Mahāvajradhara, the secret of the vajra-mind. So it is said.
With the words beginning "All Tathāgatas," he concludes the meaning of the chapter:

"All Tathāgatas" refers to Mahāvajradhara; "body, speech, and mind" refers to the triad beginning with Vairocana; "pledge" (samaya) is Amoghasiddhi; and "vajra" is Ratnasaṃbhava. Because they are non-differentiated through metaphorical designation, this is called the "Vajra of the Pledge of the Body, Speech, and Mind of All Tathāgatas."

Having thus indicated the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) as the fruit of the imagined yoga (*kalpitayoga*) according to the literal meaning, [the author] says "Mahāvajradhara," etc., in order to demonstrate that very same [completion stage] directly in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*.

"Jñāna" (knowledge) is that which is known; its "maṇḍala" is its stable assembly or collection, namely the three worlds (*trailokya*). Having established within that [maṇḍala] the Great Vajra as one's own form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) by means of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and having placed it as the presiding lord, one should—through the sequence of non-penetration (*anubhedakrama*) consisting of the syllable *khaṃ* which renders all things into space—render everything within all bodies, both stationary and moving, free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*). Having performed that [process], one becomes equal to the space-vajra knowledge (*khavajrajñāna*); one becomes the single essence of the three beings (*trisattva*).
"Kham" is the clear light;

and that [clear light] is repeatedly honored at every moment— according to the sequence beginning with "having entered the aggregate of form"— by the Buddhas whose intrinsic nature is Vairocana and the others, and by the Bodhisattvas whose intrinsic nature is Kṣitigarbha and the others, [the latter] being the eyes and so forth, which are the aggregates of form and so on.

Being introduced into oneself, which consists of the three knowledges (*jñāna*), one is conceptualized as having a nature perceived through wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*); thus, it is the "three conceptualizations" (*trikalpa*). That in which those three knowledges are pacified—that is, undergo dissolution—is the "pacification of the three conceptualizations" (*trikalpasamaya*), the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). One should abide in that; while abiding there, one is not seen even by the Buddhas—meaning the Buddhas [are themselves] the three knowledges.
The Blessed One said, "One should abide in the *khavajrasamaya*," so that even by them it is not seen, and just as it is not seen, there is no appearance.

Here, *khavajra* is the *prabhāsvara*; from that, one comes together (*sameti*) or arises, thus it is the *khavajrasamaya*, the Mahāvajradhara. Indicating the meditative absorption of emergence (*vyutthānasamādhi*) which is to be described, he says "body," and so forth.

The *kāyavākcittavajra* is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); its disappearance is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). That from which [all things] arise is "origination" (*saṃbhava*). The "array" (*vyūha*) is the Gnosis Body (*jñānakāya*), which consists of all phenomena, both stable and moving. Its "garland" (*mālā*) is the manifestation in the forms of Vairocana and so forth, according to the inclinations [of beings]. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that occurs at a single moment of mind is thus described.
To demonstrate that very same universal meditative absorption, he says "having meditated" (*dhyātvā*), and so forth.

Having meditated upon the form of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which is the manifestation of one’s own mantra-person and is utterly pure, arising from the midst of the luminosity within the center of the vajra-maṇḍala; and immediately thereafter, having assumed the emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) that becomes an object for ordinary beings, and having placed within the heart the unstruck (anāhata) syllable *HŪṂ*—known as the vajra—which constitutes the limb of breath control (prāṇāyāma); one should subsequently perform the visualization of rays. Ten rays abide in the breath control;
their visualization is their activity proceeding through the sequence of entry and so forth, according to the divisions of the right [nostril] and so on.
"Hūṃ" is the indicator of the ineffable and the inexpressible;

Mañjuravinaśvara is the glorious Prabhāśvara. Because he arises from that, it is the "Mañjuśrī-samaya. He is experienced and made the object of the irreversible [state]; thus, that itself is the *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment), the *jñāna-samaya-kāya*. Having attained that, one possesses the body, speech, and mind-vajras, which are the emanated (*nirmita*) body, speech, and mind; such a one is "the Vajra-holder of Body, Speech, and Mind" (*kāyavākcittavajrin*). This is how the term *vajrī* is obtained.

Enlightenment is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya) and sentient beings are the conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya); he whose self and body are these two is "one whose self is a bodhisattva" (bodhisattvātmā).
He is established upon the ten stages (daśabhūmi), which are like ten rays of light.

The practitioner who follows the sequence just described may thus come to be; with the words "the Bodhisattva," and so forth, he concludes the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) by means of the two truths, [stating that] form is embraced by the two truths, which is the Bodhisattva.
And that gnosis is itself the *samaya*;
it is the moon because it covers the triple world (*traidhātuka*), and it is the vajra because it accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings;
the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces it is likewise so called.
Regarding the *sandhyābhāṣā* (intentional language),

in order to demonstrate the fruit by means of the purification of the sense-bases such as the eyes while abiding in the *nirmāṇakāya* according to the sequence just described, he says "the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so forth.
First, the emptiness obtained by emptying the eyeball is the space-element.

In the center of that is the syllable *thlīṃ*, possessing the brilliant luster of a flame and blazing with the rays of the sun and moon. It is called an *astra* because it is hurled or cast forth; since it is for the sake of [subduing] the supreme hosts of obstacles such as Śakra and others, it is the *paramāstra*. Because all obstacles are destroyed by the whirling of the eyes produced from that [syllable], the syllable *thlīṃ* is the *paramāstra*. Having meditated upon that *thlīṃ* as having the nature of Kṣitigarbha with a vajra-body, one becomes equal to the vajra-body of space.

Like Mahāvajradhara, abiding in infinite world-systems, one should perceive all phenomena as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. *Thlīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) indicating the aforementioned meaning. *Khavajrasamaya* is Mahāvajradhara;
his manifestation (*vyūha*) is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is the *ālaya*—the locus or abode—of that Kṣitigarbha. Thus, he is called *khavajrasamayavyūhālaya*.
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that indicates this is also described in that way;

thus, the yogi who cultivates the divine eye, ear, and so forth, according to the sequence just mentioned and that which is yet to be explained, becomes equal to one possessing the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and equal to the Great Vajradhara.
How so?

By means of the supreme commitments (*samaya*) of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of the Buddhas—the Victors (*jina*) existing throughout the three times—and by those supreme commitments of their superknowledges, such as the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and so forth, one becomes equal to the Great Vajradhara.
"This" refers to that which was just mentioned: the divine eye of all the Siddhis.

All those belonging to one's own or other schools realize their own minds as they truly are through those accomplishments; thus, these are the superknowledges of the Buddhas, the great yogins. The supreme means for them, the foremost means even among all accomplishments, is the Buddha-maṇḍala, the supreme commitment (*samaya*) of all Tathāgatas.
Vajrasattva is the being whose nature is indivisible like a vajra;

having meditated upon—that is, having brought to completion—that [being], one should meditate on the syllable OṂ as the wisdom-OṂ, which produces Vajrapāṇi, the wisdom residing in the midst of the space-element (khadhātu) and situated within the luminosity (prabhāsvara) meditated upon at the location of the ears.
Vajrapāṇi is the triple-vajra commitment (trivajrasamaya).

By means of its accomplishment—that is, by becoming identical with it—the yogin becomes equal to the Immovable One of the Three Vajras, the Great Vajradhara. Because he grasps all the various sounds existing in infinite world-systems as if they were a single sound fallen upon the ear, he is equal to that; thus he is "equal to the Immovable One of the Three Vajras. So said the Blessed One, Akṣobhyavajra, the Great Vajradhara, [with the words] "by means of a body equal to Akṣobhya."

Possessing a body equal to that of Mahāvajradhara, and likewise because he maintains extraordinary speech and mind, he is the eternal holder of the supreme speech and mind; at all times and in all world-systems, he is worshipped as Akṣobhyavajrin by Vajrapāṇi, who resides in his ear—he is served and honored. Because he arises from the "unshakeable commitment" (akṣobhyasamaya), which is Akṣobhya himself, Vajrapāṇi is called the "Manifest Arising from the Unshakeable Commitment" (akṣobhyasamayābhisaṃbhava); the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces him is also designated by that same name.
With the words "In the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so forth, he describes the *ākāśagarbha* samādhi:
one should contemplate the Buddha-maṇḍala situated in the middle of the space-element— that is, situated in the midst of the clear light— as the body-maṇḍala of Mahāvajradhara,
having manifested the space-vajra.

Even for the form of Mahāmudrā, one should meditate on the space-vajra (ākāśavajra) as luminosity in the region of the olfactory faculty; the Jewel is Ākāśagarbha, and its producer is the syllable Oṃ—the Jewel Oṃ—one should visualize that through the meditation on the three-vajra samaya. "Three-vajra" refers to the threefold fragrance.
"He who meets and goes toward that is the Trivajrasamaya, Ākāśagarbha.

Through meditation upon him—that is, by taking his own nature as the object of focus—the Mahāvajradhara Trivajraketu becomes equal to him by perceiving the fragrances residing in manifold world-systems. Thus spoke the Blessed One, Ratnaketuvajra, the Mahāvajradhara.
"Body," and so forth:
thus the practitioner, by means of a body, speech, and mind that are not ordinary, becomes equal in radiance to Ratnaketu;
through the *gaganagañja* samādhi, he becomes possessed of the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of Ratnaketu.
The selflessness of enlightenment (*bodhinairātmya*) is the clear light; therein, the gnosis consisting of the four voids has the form of Mahāvajradhara.
Because that very [gnosis] is not the object of the Śrāvakas and others, it is secret (*guhya*).
He whose body (*samālaya*) is equal to that is the practitioner who possesses the secret treasury of the gnosis of the selflessness of enlightenment, the *ratnasamaya*.
The threefold scent is that by which it is enjoyed and experienced; he is Ratnasamayasaṃbhogavajra, Ākāśagarbha.
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that brings about that [scent] is likewise "the sphere of space" (*khadhātu*), and so forth.

Having produced the form of Mahāmudrā as before, one should meditate upon it: in that region of the tongue is Lokanātha, who is the *bhūtakoṭi*; because he manifests that, Dharma is Lokanātha; the syllable Oṃ is the Dharma that brings about that [state], thus it is the "Dharma-Oṃ. One should contemplate that with the words "trivajre" and so forth.
"Trivajra" refers to the threefold essence (*rasa*); because he goes to or unites with that, he is the "Trivajrasamaya," namely Lokanātha.

Through that meditation, by means of that gateway, because of the experience of the three kinds of flavors, one becomes equal to Mahāvajradhara, who is immeasurable in the three vajras; by experiencing the nine flavors throughout the succession of world-systems in the ten directions, one becomes his equal—thus spoke the Blessed One Amitavajra.
Whoever meditates in this way shall possess an immeasurable lifespan and equal splendor for the body and so forth;
he is the path of the Mahāyāna, the path of the Buddha, for all sentient beings, including those with the three or two faculties.

He for whose sake there is this means— the arising of the Mahāyāna path— is the one of immeasurable qualities, Mahāvajradhara. In him, because he possesses the splendor and glory (*śrī*) that shines forth by grasping all the flavors residing in the three realms with his tongue-sense organ, as if they were held in his hand, he is Amitaguṇaprabhāśrī, the Lord of the World (*Lokeśvara*).
The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that indicates this is also named after it.
Regarding the passage beginning with "in the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so forth:

having performed the initial yoga as before, one should manifest the *samaya* syllable Oṃ; this is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*). The *samaya* is Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin; the seed-syllable (*bīja*) that produces him is the *samaya* syllable Oṃ. In the location of the tactile faculty (*sparśendriya*), having first purified it through luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), one should manifest that *samaya* syllable Oṃ. A vajra that is an utpala is a "vajrotpala" because of its bud-like shape; one should manifest that.
The "Three-Vajra Samaya" refers to that which meets or attains the three kinds of vajras and the three kinds of touch;

it is Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin. Through meditation upon him, one becomes equal to the Three-Vajra Amoghasiddhi by experiencing the many touches residing in infinite world-systems as being identical to the single touch-vajra located within the lotus of the mudrā.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Amoghavajra, the Great Vajradhara.
Regarding the demonstration of its benefits, the passage beginning with "body" (*kāya*) and so forth means:
he who meditates in this way becomes Amoghavajra—Amoghasiddhi—by means of his body and other factors; one whose splendor is equal to that [of Amoghasiddhi] is described as such.
It is known that Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin has the ocean as his abode and Amoghasiddhi [is his nature].
He possesses *śrī*, which is the bliss of supreme joy; thus he is "the Glorious One" (*śrīmān*). He is the welfare of all sentient beings (*sarvasattvārtha*);

because he arises from that which has the characteristic of generating the welfare of all sentient beings, he is "the Source of All Sentient Beings" (*sarvasattvasaṃbhava*). He is the Unfailing Commitment (*amoghasamaya*) and the Unfailing Accomplishment (*amoghasiddhi*).
Therefore, he from whom [the rays] originate is Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin.
His rays are the drops of bodhicitta issued forth from him.
That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which their origin—that is, their production—occurs is described as such.

Having thus explained the placement [of mantras] upon the eye-faculty and so forth of the Bodhisattvas, he says "the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so on, showing that one should also accomplish it through the placement of the Tathāgatas:

"The space-element is suchness (*tathatā*); from the midst of that comes 'situated in the center of the space-element,' meaning accomplished through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). One should contemplate oneself as the radiant Buddha-maṇḍala, the form of Mahāvajradhara, and meditate upon it."

Having manifested the Vairocana-vajra in the place of his eye, and having manifested the *oṃ* syllable of the three bodies (*trikāya*), one should manifest the Vairocana-vajra from that *oṃ* syllable of the three bodies; such is the sequence of yoga. Vairocana is the three bodies, and the *oṃ* syllable is that which produces them; thus it is the *oṃ* syllable of the three bodies.
Having meditated upon that within the eyeball, through its transformation, Vairocana himself [appears] in the very form of the eye-faculty.
The "Threefold Vajra Samaya" is Vairocana, who, having united with the threefold form—the three vajras—through the nature of the eye faculty, takes them as his object.
By means of meditative concentration on the state of his eye, one becomes equal to that Mahāvajradhara, the Threefold-Vajra Vairocana, as described previously.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Vajra Vairocana.

With the words beginning with "kāya," he states the benefits: the practitioner who meditates in this way becomes equal in radiance to Vairocana through the vajra of body and so forth; equal in majesty to Vairocana, he awakens by means of the nature of gnosis—that is, as the embodiment of gnosis. In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said that "gnosis-awakening" (*jñānasaṃbodhi*) means that which is known. He accomplishes the state of the Great Vajradhara, which is indivisible from the three bodies; thus, he becomes a practitioner who accomplishes the indivisibility of the three bodies.

That which is perceived and grasped through the reality (*tattva*) of body, speech, and mind is the "object of focus for body, speech, and mind" (*kāyavākcittālambana*), namely the form of Mahāvajradhara. Because he abides in the locus of the eye faculty and perfectly awakens to—that is, knows—the three kinds of forms, he is "perfect awakening" (*saṃbodhi*).

Since that very [awakening] spreads unhindered, it is a "vajra"; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that accomplishes this is also called the "Vajra of Perfect Awakening as the Object of Focus for Body, Speech, and Mind.
This is not of intentional meaning (*nāsandhya*).
With the words "on mountains," and so forth, he describes the place for the practice.

On mountains—on mountain peaks adorned with fruits, flowers, and the like; in secluded places devoid of the movement of people; at river sources and springs; in areas near gardens and such; and in cremation grounds and the like.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [places] such as solitary trees, empty houses, temples, and other locations agreeable to the mind are included. This aforementioned collection of meditations—the multitude of samādhis beginning with Kṣitigarbha—should be performed; it is to be practiced.
This is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

It is not so; rather, the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is that this collection of meditations (*dhyānasamuccaya*) should be practiced upon mountains, among women endowed with full breasts and hips, in secluded places, among maidens, at rivers and springs, among women common to all people such as courtesans, and in cremation grounds—meaning among the women of outcastes, washermen, and the like who are despised by the world.

Having thus attained the perfection of place and described the means for achieving the divine eye through the placement (*nyāsa*) of Vairocana, he likewise describes the means for achieving the divine ear and so forth through the placement of the presiding deities (*adhipati*) and others, beginning with the words "Akṣobhya... and so on.

The wisdom that produces Akṣobhya has the seed-syllable *oṃ* as its source; through its transformation (*parāvṛtti*), the Vajra Akṣobhya arises. [Likewise arise] the Vajras of Akṣobhya-wisdom and so forth—Akṣobhya, Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, and Amoghasiddhi.

As before, having meditated upon the sense-bases such as the ear with the luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) as the preliminary object, and by means of the application of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) and the yoga of Mahāvajradhara, one should perform the meditation on those "foremost Buddhas"—Vairocana and the others—in their respective places, such as the place of Kṣitigarbha and the rest.

Thus spoke the Blessed One. "The Great Vajras" refers to the practitioners; their "Vajra of Samaya" is the indestructible commitment (*abhedyasamaya*). He who knows how to instruct them is the "Great Vajra-Samaya," the Vajra-Abhijña, the Mahāvajradhara—this is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).

Having taught the accomplishment of the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) through the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), preceded by the placement of seed-syllables (*bījanyāsa*), he speaks while introducing [the topic] by means of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*):
"Five-pronged," and so forth.

The five prongs are the five sense faculties, so called because they plunge into their objects like spikes; that very thing is the Great Vajra because its radiance is unimpeded. The "five flames" are the five rays of light, such as the upward-moving [flame] and others; it is adorned and embellished by them through the performance of emanation and reabsorption.

The five bases, such as form, sound, and so forth, are [the objects] in that application; by means of their expansion, the one possessing vajra-superknowledge, the Mahāvajradhara, becomes equal to them.

This is the commentary on the eleven chapters according to the six-fold method (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*): one’s own mantra, whose intrinsic nature is the entry [of consciousness] and so forth, consists of the three syllables. Because it proceeds incessantly like a waterwheel (*ghaṭīyantra*), it functions day and night.

A wheel dense and agitated by sparks, consisting of five rays and the nature of the five vajras—by means of the application of these, in their impelling, one becomes equal to the vajra-supernormal knowledges.

The space-vajra is the form of one’s own *mahāmudrā*. Situated within that is the wheel, which is the collection of the sense faculties. The Buddhas are Vairocana and the others; their characteristic flames are the white and other colored rays. Having meditated upon—that is, having realized—that [the practitioner] possesses a radiance equal to them, meaning a color identical to theirs, the "Buddhas" are the objects such as form and so forth. Through entering into union with them, the "Buddhas" here are the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Their support is Mahāvajradhara, whose body is gnosis (*jñānamūrti*); [the practitioner] should become equal to him.
Introducing another samādhi by means of the very process of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), he says: "The Buddha-maṇḍala," and so forth.
That which is awakened is called "the Awakened" (*buddha*); what is that?
It is the sphere of the knowable, one's own body.
Having resolved that the body of the triple world is Vairocana, one should place Vairocana—that is, one should visualize Vairocana.
"Having meditated on the syllable Oṃ in the heart" means:

having meditated on the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva) as the syllable Oṃ within the heart of the Body-Vajra, whose nature is the threefold world, one should perform the meditation on consciousness within the mantra-Knowledge Being—that is, the meditation on the Samādhi Being whose essence is the drop (bindu).

When the mind of the yogi practicing in this way enters into cessation and, having even abandoned the meditation on the drop, becomes established in the Clear Light (prabhāsvara), then that yogi, like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi), fulfills all desired aims because he is endowed with the two accumulations.
The glorious one, the foremost of all Buddhas, Mahāvajradhara, accomplishes him; thus he becomes the "Accomplisher of the Foremost of All Buddhas.

In this way, one should visualize one's own mind as the nature of the mind of the triple world, causing it to be stirred. Then, having meditated upon the syllable *HŪṂ* as the Jñānasattva within the heart of the Samayasattva of the triple world, one should place the mind, which has entered the bindu. Thus, one should place the mind—which is called the Jñānasattva residing in the heart of the Samayasattva—into the form of the Samādhisattva, having entered the bindu.
Having meditated on one's own speech-vajra as before, having the nature of the speech of the triple world, one should visualize it as Amitābha.
Having meditated on the syllable ĀḤ in the heart of the Samayasattva in the form of the Jñānasattva, one should place—that is, establish—the vajra, which is one's own mind, within the Samādhisattva.

With the words "This is the supreme commitment" (*samayāgram idam*) and so forth, he concludes the praise of the three aforementioned meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). The cultivation of the generation stage (*utpattikrama-bhāvanā*) is its "supreme," which is the Three Vajras—the body, speech, and mind of all sentient beings. Cultivation by means of that [Three Vajras] through the indivisibility of one's own body, speech, and mind-vajras is "cultivation as the indivisibility of the Three Vajras. The "commitment of cessation" (*nirodha-samaya*) is retention; the knowledge by which that is known is the "knowledge of the commitment of cessation" (*nirodha-samayajñāna*). The "Buddhas" are the aggregates (*skandha*) such as form and so forth. Their "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is the departure from the ordinary body and the assumption of a body of gnosis (*jñānadeha*) characterized by magnificence and profundity.
It brings about, that is, it causes one to attain, the accomplishment of Buddhahood; thus, it is "that which brings about the accomplishment of a Buddha.
Illuminating this very same meaning by way of another method, he says:
"By the mouth of space," and so forth.

The "space-vajra" (*khavajra*) is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*) as explained in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*; that which is maintained therein is the "space-vajra-realm" (*khavajradhātu*). One should meditate upon the triple world (*traidhātuka*) as being situated there. The transparent mandala is the body-vajra (*kāyavajra*); one should contemplate the syllable *Grom*, the gnosis-being (*jñānasattva*), within the body, speech, and mind of the triple world. This means that by means of the crushing of body, speech, and mind, one should meditate upon the gnosis-body (*jñānakāya*) within the triple world.
To the question "In what way? he says:
"He remains for an eon" (*kalpaṃ saṃtiṣṭhati*). An eon (*kalpa*) is the conceptualization and fulfillment of the desires of all sentient beings.

He remains in that [state]—meaning, having become the embodiment of the three bodies (*trikāya*), he remains until the end of cyclic existence (*āsaṃsāram*) as one capable of accomplishing all the intended aims of the entire world.

Both types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) should also be understood through this very explanation. Regarding the phrase "having meditated upon the commitment (*samaya*) of the three vajra-epochs":
he who fashions—that is, accomplishes—the welfare of the world by means of the vajras of body and so forth is the Commitment of the Three Vajra-Epochs, namely, Mahāvajradhara.
The benefits begin with the words "from which time onwards" and so forth.

Having attained this twofold yoga and being authorized by the gurus, from whatever time one begins—whether one who recites it, meaning one who teaches it to others; or contemplates it, meaning one who practices it oneself—that person shall become a Vajradhara.
The intention is that he is not merely the practitioner;
rather, the mantras of all the Tathāgatas, beginning with the syllable *oṃ*,
constitute the *samaya* perfected by them, namely Mahāvajradhara.
That very reality for those devoted to mantra is the *vidyā*, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*); the person arisen from that is the *vidyāpuruṣa*.

Because he is the pledge of gnosis (*jñānasamaya*), he is supreme; he is both the reality of the pledge of the mantras of all Tathāgatas and the supreme *vidyāpuruṣa*. This is the chapter on the reality of the pledge of the mantras of all Tathāgatas and the supreme *vidyāpuruṣa*, spoken in intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*).
Having thus established the purification of the paths of action, the author introduces the twelfth chapter to demonstrate the transformation into Mahāmudrā through both stages,
saying "atha" and so forth;
[he is] the Teacher because he teaches the worlds of Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, and Svaḥ.

Because he alone is the progenitor, the "Creator" is the Great Vajradhara, the Trivajrasamaya who accomplishes the "Supreme Knowledge" by establishing those jewel-like individuals (*ratnapudgala*) in the Vajropama-samādhi; thus he is the "Accomplisher of Supreme Knowledge. His "Reality" is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); regarding that, one should "utter" his speech-vajra, which will have the characteristics to be described. Although the reading *udājahāra* (he uttered) would be expected, it says *khatulye*, etc.: "space" (*kha*) is the sky; that which is equal to it is the ultimate truth, and being identical with that is the "Space-like Samaya" (*khatulyasamaya*), because all things are established in the ultimate truth.
When all beings have attained equality equal to space, those whose intrinsic nature is non-conceptual are "those of non-conceptual nature.
In them— those of non-conceptual nature,
and therefore in phenomena that are pure by nature— this aforementioned proliferation is manifested, displayed like a drama.
"Without a secret convention" (*nāsandhyam*) refers to [the teaching] in the regions of great forests (*mahāṭavī*);
that is, in excellent locations within great forests because of their enchanting features such as bodies of water and so forth.

On a mountain adorned with fruits, flowers, and so forth, or in another secluded and solitary place, that which is the "Collection of All Siddhis"—Buddhahood itself, in which all mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) are gathered and subsumed—is the goal to be accomplished; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

Regarding the explanation by the Sage (*ārṣa*), it says: "Through the application of the conceptualization of space, the great forest of the aggregates (*skandha*) is considered [the dwelling place]."

By way of abiding in the non-abiding, in this region of the great abode, within this manifold wish-fulfilling tree of enjoyment nourished by various accomplishments and resplendent with the fruit of emanation, upon the mountain of perfect and complete enlightenment—
"In the solitary and delightful state devoid of intrinsic nature, that which is to be accomplished is designated as 'Vajra'";
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The syllable *paṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) indicating the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) to be described hereafter.
"Body," and so forth;
it is called *mañju* because it is joined with and cultivated by the nature of the mind,
and that very [mind] is a *vajra* because of its indivisibility.

The manifestation of that [light] is the manifestation of Mañjuvajra; it should be performed not only within one's own body, speech, and mind, but also by pervading the body, speech, and mind of the three realms. Consequently, one becomes equal to Mañjuvajra.

According to the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, the construction is as follows: "A hundred yojanas, a hundred yojanas"—that is, with a blazing vajra whose extent is immeasurable, she who acts for her own purpose is "Blazing Vajra" (*Dīptavajrā*); by means of that radiance, she illuminates and brings light to infinite world-systems.
Pure in essence because his body is like an illusion,

and adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, he is embellished by every ornament. Even the gods, such as Brahmā and others, never at any time behold one who has attained such a body of gnosis (jñānakāya), let alone others, for he is within the exclusive domain of those who are non-retrogressive (avaivartika).
The *Mañjuśrīvajrāgrasamaya* is the form of Mañjuśrī’s great mudrā; this is the samādhi called "the maker of invisibility" because it renders him invisible and intangible to ordinary beings.
To accomplish this very illusory body through the purification of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he says "feces and urine," and so forth.

Excrement and urine are the objects of the sense faculties; through their mutual union with the five pledges (*pañcasamaya*), one should form and accomplish a body endowed with the three metals and joined with the three appearances, which is a mind indivisible from the three vajras produced therefrom. Having caused it to enter the mouth of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) by means of seizing the mass and subsequent dissolution, one should meditate upon it.
Therein, within that luminosity, one should manifest the mind of all Buddhas and all logicians—which is indivisible and beyond their scope—as the activity of primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

The yogin who meditates in this way becomes, at that very moment—precisely from the moment of emergence [from meditation]—equal in radiance to Mañjuvajra; this is indeed *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
Having thus taught the samādhi of the Mañjuśrī-samaya, he speaks, introducing the accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as those of the Cakravidyādhara and others:
"By one's own mantra," and so forth:

first, having brought to manifestation the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Vairocana, one should visualize before oneself—by means of one's own mantra, the *praṇava* which produces Vairocana—an eight-spoked wheel, white in color, with the brilliant luster of sparks, adorned with rays of light in the form of sparks. Having visualized it as the abode, that is, the locus, of all Buddhas belonging to the Tathāgata family, one should practice until it smokes, emits heat, or blazes up; whoever, having grasped [this state], remains [therein], that yogi becomes equal to a Buddha, resembling the Great Vajradhara.
