Thus, he describes the majesty of the accomplished *vidyādhara* with the words beginning "thirty-six," and so forth: the attendants and retinue of that [accomplished one] are as numerous as the atoms contained within thirty-six Mount Sumerus;
what is their nature? They possess an indestructible essence, just like all the Vajradharas.
The *samādhi* by which one attains or reaches the wheel is the *samādhi* named "Wheel-Samaya.
This should be understood as being like the yoga of Vairocana, beginning with "by means of one's own mantra" and so forth.

One's own mantra is the syllable *hūṃ*. Regarding the statement that the mandala will be the space-mandala and women, this demonstrates mastery over desires (*kāmaiśvarya*). Because he is the Great Vajradhara, he becomes the Great Vajradhara.
By the additional statement "honored by Rudra," he indicates that [the Buddha] is honored by the three realms (*traidhātuka*), because Rudra himself is honored by the three realms.

Regarding the *Vajra* in the *Twelfth Chapter’s Sixty-Million-Verse Commentary*: "The Vajra is the Great Vajradhara. *Samatā* refers to the *ḍākinīs*, for they are called *samatā* because they move together (*samam saha atanti gacchanti*) with equality.
"Vajra" and "Samatā" are the beloved consorts who accompany him; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which he and they are united is thus described.
Such phenomena (*dharma*) belong to the family of Amitābha; their abode, or place of origin, is Vajradharma, that is, Lokeśvara. One should become equal to him.
As many as there are atoms produced from thirty-six Mount Sumerus, so many are the pure-souled Buddhas of the Lotus family who are the supreme forms of skillful means (*upāya*).
Their mandala is their assembly;
therein all the hosts of mantras and mudrās establish [the practitioner] and consecrate the adept (*sādhaka*) as their own sovereign—this is the meaning.
"Padmas" refers to those belonging to the Lotus family; that samādhi in which there is equality with them due to non-differentiation is so called.
"One should remain," and so forth, has its meaning already explained;
[the phrase] "one should attend upon the three secrets" [is as follows].
He attends upon, attains, and becomes identical with the secret body, speech, and mind associated with all Buddhas—this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "his own mantra from his own mantra," five rays of light emerge in equal measure, neither less nor more; that radiance in which these exist is "the radiance equal to five rays. Having grasped with his hand that sword (*khaḍga*) possessing such radiance equal to five rays, the wide-eyed practitioner, who maintains as his very self the *vidyās*—that is, the great mudrās (*mahāmudrās*)—perfected by the three vajras, is called a "Holder of the Vidyā of the Three Vajras" (*trivajravidyādhara*).

He should be honored by those who are great and preeminent within the three realms—the lords of the Daityas and the foremost among the Asuras—as well as by those headed by Brahmā and Indra; indeed, he would be saluted even by them.

In the triple-thousandfold world system, he is the sole hero because of his sovereignty therein. Among those who hold the secrets and abide in common accomplishments, he is the most excellent and preeminent. He is the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind; as the practitioner of the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, whatever he desires and whatever he prays for—be it mundane or supramundane—he bestows and grants that very accomplishment (siddhi) of such a nature, manifested by the Mind-Vajra and conceived by the mind. Being the essence of all Tathāgatas, he is the sword; since he is indivisible from all swords, the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is also named "All-Sword."

Having thus explained the attainments (*siddhi*) of the vajra-wheel and so forth, he now says "Oṃkāram" and so on, in order to demonstrate the attainment of the pill (*gulikā-siddhi*) by means of mantra alone, setting aside the attainment of the pill produced from external substances.

One should meditate on the syllable *oṃ* itself as a pill the size of a jujube seed (*caṇaka*). Having meditated on the form of one's own deity within the center of that pill, one should cause it to enter through the opening at the crown of the head and contemplate it as being in its true form; one should visualize it and practice this again and again.
He who practices in this way, from that very moment onward, becomes one whose radiance is equal to that of a Bodhisattva.

Here, "Bodhi" (enlightenment) is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and "Sattva" (being) is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*). He who abides in the non-dual nature of these two is a Bodhisattva, namely Mahāvajradhara.
The practitioner becomes one whose radiance—meaning his miraculous power (*ṛddhi*)—is equal to his, such that he is difficult to behold due to his splendor.

Resembling the rising sun and possessing a radiance equal to refined gold—such are the qualities. One should meditate on this form, which is red in color and characterized by stability, in the mouth at the location of the throat.

Furthermore, one should meditate on the pride of Mahāvajradhara within the knowledge of awakening, in the form of a pill (*gulikā*), upon the white lotus of the heart, characterized by the nature of emergence (*vyutthāna*).
Now, introducing accomplishment even by way of the form of Mahāmudrā,
he says "the space-element" and so forth;
the space-element is suchness (*tathatā*).
There, having visualized a clear moon disc and oneself as Vairocana situated in its center, and having meditated on an eight-spoked wheel in his hand, one becomes a *vidyādhara*.
If one asks how this should be done: "The great wheel family," and so forth.

Having visualized that great wheel family—the family of Vairocana—as before, by means of the wisdom-vajra of the supreme wisdom of Vairocana, the practitioner, through the yoga of the supreme body, becomes a possessor of the yoga of Vairocana.

"Khadhātāv ityādi": Having meditated upon a vajra, that is, a solar mandala, within the space-element (*khadhātu*), one should visualize oneself as Akṣobhya, whose nature is non-dual gnosis, situated in its center.
"Haste vajram ityādi": As before, having visualized a jewel within the space-element, one should visualize oneself as Ratnasaṃbhava, the Jewel-Vajra, situated in its center.
The passage beginning with "A jewel in the hand" is explained as follows:

having visualized an eight-petaled lotus of phenomena (*dharmāṣṭadalapadma*) in the space-element (*khadhātu*), and having meditated upon oneself as Amitāyus situated in its center, one should accomplish everything as before.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In the space-element, situated in the midst of the pledge (*samaya*), standing upon a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*), the supreme Amogha," the meaning has already been explained.

Having thus explained the means of accomplishment consisting of the marks such as the wheel, it is stated that other marks of the Wrathful Kings must also be accomplished; therefore, the tridents and so forth are taken up "by means of the application of the vajra. This means they are to be accomplished through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Akṣobhya;
by means of the meditation on that Akṣobhya, these tridents and so forth are perfected—that is, they are accomplished.
"By what means of accomplishing body, speech, and mind?

refers to those who are capable of removing the ordinary state of body, speech, and mind and establishing them in a distinguished state; they are the "means of accomplishing body, speech, and mind. It is by these that [the goal] is accomplished, and not by others. Thus, the "Great Pledge" (*mahāsamaya*) is the Mahāyāna; the "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) therein is that which was just mentioned. The "Vajra" is that which reveals it. The conclusion of the section is expressed as "Mahāsamayasiddhivajra said.
He now states the method for accomplishing the accomplishment, beginning with "at the crossroads," and so forth.

The fourfold mudrās born of families such as the Brāhmaṇas, or else, being alone under a single tree, at a single *liṅga*, or in a temple of Śiva with women of the Caṇḍāla caste and so forth— by assuming an attire identical to their own— in these places as they may be found, one draws forth the "Vajra," which is the threefold gnosis (*jñāna*), and experiences it directly. One should accomplish that "vajra-drawing," characterized by meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), especially and with excellence, because [this practice] proceeds more slowly in other objects.

Having thus taught the attainment of one’s own purpose through the specific meaning of the intentional language (*sandhyābhāṣā*), [the author], in order to win over the minds of those to be trained, says "the threefold yoga" and so forth.

Having meditated upon oneself as the mantra-person of the threefold yoga— the mantra-person consisting of the three vajras— the Vajrin of the threefold yoga, that is, as having the nature of the three beings, and having thus perfected oneself, one should meditate upon one's own body, speech, and mind as being of the nature of the hook (*aṅkuśa*).
For what purpose? It is for the sake of attracting the Buddhas—the jewel-like persons whose intellects consist of gnosis and who seek non-dual knowledge.

Demonstrating the application for that very purpose, he says "vāyavya" and so forth: having meditated upon a wind-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *yaṃ*, which is mobile in form, and having placed the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) therein, one should attach oneself to his body, speech, and mind as a limb of the rays of one’s own body, speech, and mind. Then, having gradually returned to one's own presence, descended from the wind-maṇḍala, and stood upon a great earth-maṇḍala arising from the syllable *laṃ*, one should meditate upon him bowing down.
Regarding "the summoning of the Buddhas": the ritual procedure just described is the supreme method for summoning the minds of worthy beings, a practice not shared by others.
By this very application, one should summon and enjoy the women established in the commitments (*samaya*) of the ten directions, and enjoin them to one's own command.
These goddesses are the deities of the commitment of the space-element (*khadhātu-samayā*); their "vajra-summoning" is an indivisible summoning.
"Vairocana," and so forth:

one should meditate upon the great wheel of Vairocana—the wheel bearing the insignia of Vairocana—because it is the cause of the arising of those belonging to the family of Vairocana; this is the abode of the Victors (*jinālaya*). Having visualized it in the form of a hook and having attached it to the heart of the object of practice (*sādhya*), one should summon [them] as before.
He says "Vajra," etc., [meaning] that one should perform the summoning with the remaining various [mantras] in this very same sequence.
The "pledge-beings of the three realms" (*traidhātuka-samayā*) are the *yakṣiṇīs* and so forth; the summoning of them is the "summoning of the pledge-beings of the three realms."
"One endowed with the excellence of all aspects" means that one should visualize oneself as the Buddha-form of Mahāvajradhara, constructed from the forms of Vairocana and the other [Tathāgatas];
in his hand— that is, in his palm— one should visualize the body, speech, and mind of the object of practice (sādhya) as the hook and so forth.
The phrase "with the goad and so forth" is to be understood as follows:
having drawn [the deity] with the goad, bound with the noose, mounted upon the wind-mandala, and brought [there], one should seize [him] with the hand and seal him—this is the intended meaning.

By means of this application of sealing, the practitioner becomes a "performer of the action of the state," that is, he performs the activity (*karma*) of that state, which is the state of Vajrasattva (*vajrasattvapada*). Thus, he becomes a performer of the action of the state.
With the words beginning "in all aspects" (*sarvākāra*), he explains the very meaning just mentioned:
one should meditate upon the body-vajra, which is one's own body endowed with the characteristics as described; this is the process of becoming Vairocana.

The tongue itself is the *vajra*; thus, "tongue-vajra" (*jihvāvajra*). Its application is the recitation of mantras. Through that, one becomes equal to Vāg-Amitābha; this is the "making [oneself] Amitābha.

Possessing the ego-identity (*ahaṅkāra*) of one's own deity, and having meditated upon the object to be accomplished held in the hand and the meaning of the syllables of the mantra to be recited, one becomes equal to the *Vajra* [Akṣobhya]; this is the "making [oneself] equal to that," which is the "making [oneself] Akṣobhya."

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated: "In this manner, the three secrets are body, speech, and mind; they proceed toward that samaya which has the nature of the three bodies and so forth—thus [are] Vairocana and the others, the Samayas of the Three Secrets. Having performed the supreme worship of them—the worship characterized by the thorough knowledge of their own nature—one should accomplish [it]; one should bring to completion this practice just described."

The ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) just described is that by which the essence belonging to all Buddhas and all Tathāgatas—the distinguished, secret, and hidden—is gathered and drawn forth; thus, it is the "Secret Compendium" (*Guhyasamuccaya*). It is the great secret (*mahāguhya*) that attracts gods and others, and it is the commitment (*samaya*) that must not be transgressed. He who possesses this is the "One of the Great Secret Commitment" (*Mahāguhyasamaya*), namely Mahāvajradhara himself. Thus says the compiler (*saṃgītikāra*). Regarding the non-differentiation of activities, he says "Great Flesh" (*mahāmāṃsa*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate the consumption of meat.

Great men—because their flesh arises from the dead—it is the *samaya*; having offered a bali-oblation with that, one should swiftly accomplish one's own body as the supreme triple-vajra. Having offered a bali-oblation to all spirits for the sake of pacifying obstacles using blameless human flesh obtained [in this way], one should accomplish the state of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*). Regarding "by the supreme *samaya*": human flesh and so forth, combined with feces and urine, is the "supreme *samaya*"; one who desires to accomplish the state of a knowledge-holder (*vidyādhara*) should offer a bali-oblation with that.
An elephant itself is the *samaya* because it is dead;
one who desires the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*) should offer an oblation (*bali*) with its flesh.
Likewise, one should accomplish the siddhi of invisibility (*antardhāna*) with horse meat.
Regarding the different types of ritual action (*karmabheda*), he states the procedure for obtaining meat, beginning with the words "with dog," and so forth.
It should be understood that one should accomplish the specified *siddhi* by means of dog meat.
Likewise, by offering faultless beef, even those difficult to subdue, such as kings and others, are brought under control.
Regarding the procedure for when faultless meat is unavailable, it is said: even if the aforementioned meat cannot be obtained, one should accomplish the rite by visualizing the flesh;

or else, having fashioned a corpse of a human or other being from flour and so forth, and having visualized the life-force as having emerged in its true form, one should perform the accomplishment with a portion of that.
By means of this vajra-yoga, which is the method of the indivisible offering just described, one is empowered by all the Buddhas.
The practitioner attains the accomplishment of the desired goal;
he now describes the procedure for nourishment for the sake of bodily strength,
beginning with the words "in all forms," and so forth.

Having meditated upon oneself as Mahāvajradhara, the possessor of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, one should next meditate upon the Jñānasattva—the pledge of gnosis—within the moon mandala situated at the heart-lotus; then, within his heart as well, one should meditate upon the Samādhisattva.

Upon his crown, in the place of the *uṣṇīṣa*, one should meditate upon Mahāvajradhara, the bearer of the supreme vajra, resembling a mass of moonbeams, dripping with nectar, who is the delighter and the proclaimer of the pledge-gnosis-sattvas of all the Buddhas.

In this aforementioned system of all the pledges (*samaya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*) must perform—that is, it is indeed to be done—the supreme, distinguished meditation which, by means of the foremost pledge, brings about all supreme accomplishments.

All the pledges are practitioners; their "wisdom-vajra" (*jñānavajra*) is the food, the *bodhicitta*, which is the means of gratification in this meditative absorption (*samādhi*) explained according to the twelve chapters and six parameters.
He speaks thus according to the divisions of the families: "at the tip of the tongue-pledge-vajra."
The Samayavajras are the practitioners of the five families; among them, Akṣobhya’s family is supreme, and he abides therein.

One should meditate on the tongue as the Vajra-holder of the syllable *huṃ*, and visualize the *vajra* as the transformation of that *huṃ*. While consuming a small amount of food and so forth, one should employ it through the application of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the process of transforming [the food] into the five nectars; thus, one shall attain the tranquility of the three *vajras*: body, speech, and mind.
This aforementioned characteristic of the practice of eating is the supreme method of the Vajra Way.

This should also be performed by the Amitābha-yogin from the *āḥ* and *auṃ* syllables of the samaya. Having meditated on the tongue as a lotus characterized by the transformation of the enclosure (*prākāra-parāvṛtti*), and having meditated on a wheel produced from the *praṇava* (oṃ) by the Vairocana-yogin—it should be performed in this manner.
By means of this yoga of the act of eating, one attains the pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) of the body and so forth, and becomes equal to the Great Vajradhara.

The *samayavajra* is a specific type of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) characterized by the transformation of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛtīkaraṇa*). That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the *amṛtamālā* (garland of nectar) is produced by means of the *amṛtapuñja-samayavajra* is so designated.

Having thus indicated the mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*) through the gateway of yogic activity, [the author] now introduces the means for achieving the *mudrā*siddhis for those established in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) with the words beginning "trivajra."

That in which the three vajras—body, speech, and mind—meet and dissolve is the *trivajrasamaya*, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). That itself is the supreme accomplishment (*siddhyagra*). Within that, there is the triple body (*trikāya*) characterized as the Dharma, Enjoyment, and Emanation bodies; because he possesses that vajra, he becomes the Trikāyavajrin, the Great Vajradhara. Although the form *vajrī* would have been expected, the reading *vajriṇaḥ* follows the archaic style (*ārṣa*).

Thus, for one who has attained perfection, there is the display of miracles in the ten directions and so forth. The "ocean of wish-fulfilling jewels" (*cintāmaṇyodadhi*) refers to the ocean of wish-fulfilling jewels belonging to all perfected sentient beings situated in the ten directions; he becomes one who has reached that. Being of the nature of vajra (*vajrātmā*), meaning possessing a vajra-body, he illuminates the world-systems in every direction with the radiance of his own body—that is, he lights up the world-systems of the ten directions. The description of its pervasiveness begins with "the commitment of the wheel" (*cakrasamaya*) and so forth: the "commitment of the wheel" is Vairocana; the accomplishment bound to him is the "accomplishment of the commitment of the wheel. That very [accomplishment] is the foremost (*agrayā*) within it.

"He would become equal to the body of Vuddhaka" means he would become like him; this refers to the signs of accomplishment connected with Akṣobhya and the others, for since they serve as its indicators,
it is "accomplished on all sides."

Through the nature of all things just described, accomplishment is attained everywhere; one may traverse world-systems in the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, and so forth—all these commitments (*samaya*), such as the commitments of the *ḍākas* and *ḍākinīs*, are supreme among them. The "knowledge" (*vidyā*) therein is the mantra for its realization; one who holds that is a "knowledge-holder" (*vidyādhara*). One shall become even their lord.

"Of all," and so forth: when the aforementioned accomplishments of the *ḍāka*s and others are present before one, the cultivation of the *kāyavajra*— that is, the cultivation of the *mahāmudrā*— while remaining within all forms of invisibility, meaning within the invisibility of speech, actions, and the members of the body, makes one illuminate the entire triple-thousandfold world system.
Even while illuminating the three-thousandfold world system with a single radiance, he removes— that is, seizes— the transformative power associated with all the Buddhas and all the siddhis;
he draws in and enjoys— that is, experiences— the daughters of the foremost gods, such as Śakra and others.

"Gaṅgā," and so forth: [the practitioner] sees—meaning beholds—with the eye-vajra, which is the subtle, pure divine eye, the Jinas equal in number to the sands of the Gaṅgā; "of him" refers to the Great Vajradhara of the Three Vajras; his "abode" is the world-system that is infinite and boundless; [the practitioner] sees those residing therein, situated within it.

Like an *āmalaka* fruit held in the palm of his hand, he hears all the sounds—whether produced by the great elements that are appropriated, unappropriated, or both—within those fields, which are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; he hears them all as if they were a sound clinging to his ear.
He is the one who possesses the supernormal power (*abhijñā*) therein, the bull-like leader, the lord, the preeminent one; thus he is the "one with the bull-like supernormal power" (*abhijñārṣabha*).

By means of the characteristics of body, speech, and mind—that is, through the intrinsic natures of the body and so forth—he knows that which is called "mind," which causes the hundred and sixty innate dispositions (*prakṛti*) to arise; he knows how it vibrates in manifold ways like a drama among all sentient beings within world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, characterized by body, speech, and mind.

He remembers its arising within cyclic existence—the wandering through the five realms of rebirth throughout beginningless *saṃsāra* under the power of virtuous and non-virtuous karma—as well as its occurrence in former abodes, meaning in previous births, for a specific duration (*samaya*), just as one remembers three days past, as if they were three days ago.

With as many bodies as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, adorned with clouds of Buddhas and the like, and adorned with the mandalas of the deities of the five families such as Vairocana, he remains for eons equal to the sands of the Ganges and emanates them; by means of his miraculous power, he possesses the supreme vajra, the luminosity of a Buddha—he is the possessor of the supreme vajra of miraculous power. Having attained the state of a Vajrin, the Great Vajradhara, who knows the *samaya*, spoke thus.
"Vajra-eye," and so forth:
the "vajra" is the Great Vajradhara; his "eye" is the vision purified by luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); this is the "vajra-eye.
The same applies to the others.
Regarding this, he asks "What for the sake of others? and says "Buddha," and so forth.

The superknowledges (*abhijñā*) of a Buddha are the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) and the rest; by means of these, there is the accomplishment of the goal, which is the perfect fulfillment of the welfare of others.
"One should become equal to the Buddha-body"— since the Buddha-bodies, their ultimate meanings, and their activities are infinite, that [attainment] is likewise infinite. Thus,
he explains how one dwells in the accomplishment endowed with the fulfillment of the welfare of others:

"Surrounded by an entourage as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," and so forth: surrounded and preceded by attendants such as the Abhedya-cetas, who are accompanied by a vast array of offerings; the Great Vajradhara, whose body, speech, and mind pervade the world-systems situated throughout the ten directions, "wanders"—that is, he dwells. This is a portion of the fruit. Having taught the general and supreme means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) as appropriate, starting from the term "he dwelt" (*vijahāra*), he now speaks again to clarify the constituent parts of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) practice: [The text continues: "He dwelt in the palace of the great celestial mansion, which is like the center of the sky, adorned with all manner of jewels, filled with various precious ornaments, and resplendent with the light of the sun and moon. There, he dwelt together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Ākāśagarbha, Avalokiteśvara, Vajrapāṇi, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Samantabhadra, and others, as well as Śakra, Brahmā, the Lokapālas, and other gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans. This describes the place where he dwelt. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" refers to those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) and perfections (*pāramitā*). "Mañjuśrī" is the embodiment of wisdom (*prajñā*). "Maitreya" is the embodiment of compassion (*karuṇā*). "Ākāśagarbha" is the embodiment of the bodhicitta. "Avalokiteśvara" is the embodiment of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*). "Vajrapāṇi" is the embodiment of the power of the vajra. "Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin" is the embodiment of the purification of obscurations. "Samantabhadra" is the embodiment of the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*). "And others" refers to the remaining Bodhisattvas. "Śakra" is the lord of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. "Brahmā" is the lord of the Sahā world-system. "Lokapālas" refers to the four guardians of the world. "Other gods" refers to the deities of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and form realm (*rūpadhātu*). "Nāgas" refers to the lords of the water element. "Yakṣas" refers to the lords of the earth element. "Gandharvas" refers to the lords of fragrance. "Asuras" refers to the lords of pride. "Garuḍas" refers to the lords of the air element. "Kiṃnaras" refers to the lords of song. "Mahoragas" refers to the lords of the fire element. "Humans" refers to the lords of the human race. "Non-humans" refers to the lords of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Together with these, he dwelt in the palace of the great celestial mansion. "Palace" (*vimāna*) means a residence. "Great" (*mahā*) means vast. "Celestial mansion" (*vimāna*) means a divine abode. "Like the center of the sky" means it is situated in the center of the firmament. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" means it is embellished with every kind of gem. "Filled with various precious ornaments" means it is replete with diverse types of jewels. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" means it shines with the radiance of the sun and moon. "There" means in that place. "Together with" means in company with. "Retinue of Bodhisattvas" refers to the aforementioned assembly. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth are their names. "And others" refers to the remaining Bodhisattvas. "Śakra" and so forth are their names. "And others" refers to the remaining gods, nāgas, and so on. "Dwelt" means he remained there. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" describes the location where he dwelt. "Which is like the center of the sky" describes its position. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" describes its ornamentation. "Filled with various precious ornaments" describes its abundance. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" describes its brilliance. "There" indicates the specific location. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his companions. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their identities. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their identities. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Dwelt" indicates his activity. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the location of his dwelling. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its spatial orientation. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its decorative features. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its richness. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its luminosity. "There" indicates the site. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his associates. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the rest. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the rest. "Dwelt" indicates his state of abiding. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the specific abode. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its placement. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its adornments. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its plenitude. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its splendor. "There" indicates the locus. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his circle. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their designations. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their designations. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Dwelt" indicates his presence. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the dwelling place. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its location. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its decorations. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its wealth. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its radiance. "There" indicates the spot. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his followers. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their titles. "And others" indicates the rest. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their titles. "And others" indicates the rest. "Dwelt" indicates his abiding. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the residence. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its position. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its embellishments. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its opulence. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its brilliance. "There" indicates the location. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his company. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Dwelt" indicates his staying. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the site of his residence. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its placement. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its ornaments. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its abundance. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its luster. "There" indicates the place. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his entourage. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their identities. "And others" indicates the rest. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their identities. "And others" indicates the rest. "Dwelt" indicates his remaining. "In the palace of the great celestial mansion" indicates the dwelling. "Which is like the center of the sky" indicates its location. "Adorned with all manner of jewels" indicates its decoration. "Filled with various precious ornaments" indicates its richness. "Resplendent with the light of the sun and moon" indicates its brightness. "There" indicates the spot. "Together with a retinue of Bodhisattvas" indicates his companions. "Mañjuśrī" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Śakra" and so forth indicate their names. "And others" indicates the remainder. "Dwelt" indicates his abiding. "In the

"Sevā," and so forth: it is that which is served or taken as an object; thus, according to the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* on the twelfth chapter, *sevā* (service) is suchness (*tathatā*), and that itself is the *samaya* (commitment). The conjunction and accomplishment of the site and other elements is the "conjunction of service and commitment" (*sevā-samaya-saṃyoga*), which is the first limb: the taking of emptiness as the object. The taking of the sun and other [elements] as the object is the *upasādhana* (near-attainment).

That very process, extending up to the arrangement of mantras (*mantravinyāsa*), is possible; thus, the second is the "subsidiary practice" (*upasādhana*). And the "pledge" (*samaya*) for the purpose of the "practice" (*sādhana*) is the meaning for the presentation of the practice; the request for the sake of the practice is the pledge (*samaya*). It goes toward me, thus it is a *samaya*; both the *samādhisattva* and the *jñānasattva* are the pledge and the purpose of the practice—the third. The great accomplishment (*mahāsādhana*) is the accomplishment of the remaining great benefit for others, extending from the *maṇḍalarājāgrī* to the *karmarājāgrī*; that is the fourth.

Having understood these four limbs according to the divisions of the *vajra* and the divisions of the *kula*, one should thereafter accomplish the rites to be described as if they were already taught; this is the summary.

By means of the passage beginning with "service (*sevā*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*)," he indicates the limbs that were previously summarized: "Service is the focal point of the signs of awakening."

That very [state] is concentrated and established in the mind, thus it is *samādhi*. It is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*). What is that? It is the accomplishment through resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) of everything from the site of the earth up to the maṇḍala-circle; this is service (*sevā*) and *samādhi*. Having performed that conjunction of service and *samādhi* (*sevā-samādhi-saṃyoga*), one should meditate upon the supreme secret enlightenment characterized by suchness (*tathatā*), which arises from the accumulation of the meaning of the mantra "Oṃ Śūnyatā."

Having established the sun, moon, and lotus sequentially one above the other, and having placed the *tyakṣara* (the syllable *tya*) upon them, through the crushing of all [elements], there arises the lunar disc (*śaśāṅkamaṇḍala*). Upon that again, the *tyakṣara* is placed; through its transformation (*parāvṛtti*), the *cihna* (symbol) is produced, and through the transformation of the symbol, the form of the *mahāmudrā* is accomplished. Because the goal (*sādhya*) is accomplished in proximity (*upa*) to this, it is called *upasādhana*. *Siddhi* refers to the accomplishment of the *mahāmudrā*. The *agras* (foremost) of that are the mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ). That in which these exist is the *upasādhanasiddhyagra*. The form of the *mahāmudrā* is that in which all the syllables of the mantras are arranged. The *vajras* are those from Vairocana down to the seventh [Akṣobhya]. Their *āyatanas* are the aggregates (*skandhas*) such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth. Having determined them according to the sequence of the third arrangement, the investigation into the thorough knowledge of cause and effect is accomplished. That by which they are worshipped for the sake of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is called the *sādhanacodana*; this is the explanation of the synonyms.
What is that? It is the two verses beginning with "bearing the Buddha-body" (*buddhakāyadhara*).
Regarding the phrase "the visualization of the lords of mantras" (*mantrādhipativibhāvana*):

"mantras" refers to *oṃ* and so forth; "lords" refers to the Lords of Samādhi-sattvas, who are the Jñāna-sattvas. The "visualization of the lords of mantras" is the meditation upon the lords of mantras according to their respective divisions of families as they occur.
"Mahāsādhana," and so forth.

At the times of accomplishing that which was prescribed as the *mahāsādhana*, the mantra-practitioner, possessing the yoga of his own tutelary deity (*svādhidaivata*), performs the meditative union (*samāpatti*) preceded by the consecration of the vajra and the lotus. Having visualized the image (*bimba*) known as the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) of the Tathāgatas produced from his own mantras—such as Vajradhṛk and others—who are the holders of the vajra of those mantras; and having visualized the Lord upon the crown [of that image], he attains accomplishment (*siddhi*). That is to say, having visualized the Lord Mahāvajradhara in the matted-hair crown of the Great Seal-form of the five Tathāgatas, and having visualized Vairocana and the others in the crowns of the remaining members of their respective families, he succeeds and attains accomplishment.

As explained according to the literal meaning in the *Guhyasamājapradīpoddyotana*, the propitiation of Vajrasattva through the sequence of the four yogas has thus been established. Now, he describes the accomplishment of Mahāvajradhara by means of the six-limbed sequence, beginning with the words "In the *Samājottara*," and so forth:
"Service (sevā) is of two kinds, distinguished as common and supreme."

The common and supreme service (*sevā*) is to be performed by means of the four vajras and the six limbs with the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*). It is called *sevā* because it is served—that is, practiced—by those seeking liberation.
What is that? It is the perfectly pure form of the deity.

This must be accomplished and perfected in every way, by all means, always, at all times, and in all modes of conduct, through the nectar of gnosis (*jñānāmṛta*) alone and through the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) alone—the word "alone" (*eva*) being used for emphasis.

For this very six-limbed yoga, called the nectar of gnosis, is the mantra of all mantras and of all Tathāgatas; it is the reality (*tattva*), which is the reality of the deity, and its purpose is the fruit, namely the samādhi of unified union (*yuganaddha*). Because it accomplishes that, it is the mantra that realizes the meaning of reality.
Since this is so—the sense of "hi" being "because"—therefore, service (*sevā*) must be performed by means of that very [six-limbed yoga].
Those six limbs, beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), are specified in the *Samājottara*: "Having performed the supreme practice for all [beings] by means of the six-limbed yoga..."
Otherwise, the supreme accomplishment will certainly not arise.
Withdrawal, as well as meditation, breath control, concentration, recollection, and absorption— this is called the six-limbed yoga.

Thus he provides the detailed explanation for these summary headings: "The withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) of all ten faculties while they remain in their own respective functions is proclaimed as such; with respect to the withdrawal of desires, there are five desires in brief through the application of the five Buddhas."
Meditation is said to be conceptualization; that meditation is fivefold:
applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joy (prīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittaikāgratā)—these five are the constituents of meditation.
The secret is initial mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*); the third is the enjoyment thereof; the fourth is the gathering of bliss;
the fifth is to be known as one's own mind, wherein the arising of knowledge and the object of knowledge is exhausted.
Consisting of all Buddhas, peaceful,
and established in all space.

The commentary on the twelve-chapter [work] consisting of sixty million [verses] states: One should expel the breath, which consists of the five gnoses and has the nature of the five elements, and imagine it in the form of a single mass at the tip of the lotus-nose.
The great jewel of five colors is known as *prāṇāyāma*.
Having meditated upon one’s own mantra in the heart, one should place the vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the *bindu*.
When one's own sensory jewel has ceased, one should maintain that retention; this is known as *dhāraṇā*. When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the apprehension of signs arises.
The sign of the five elements is cultivated by means of the vajra of awakening:
first, the appearance of a mirage; second, the appearance of smoke;
third, the appearance of fireflies; and fourth, like a blazing lamp.
The fifth, however, is the constant light, resembling a cloudless sky;
one should indeed expand that stable [light] through the path of the vajra within one's own elements.
Having meditated upon that which is to be recollected, one should then recollect it in its specific form;
this is to be known as "recollection" (anusmṛti), for therein an appearance arises.
Having condensed all phenomena through the union of wisdom and means,
one should meditate upon them as a mass within the center of the image.
The instantaneous accomplishment of knowledge is designated as "samādhi.
Thus it is said.
"Of the ten," and so forth.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) and the objects of the sense faculties (*indriyārtha*) constitute the "faculties. The "own-functioning" (*svavṛtti*) of these ten faculties—the subjects and their objects—is their activity according to their respective natures as the grasped and the grasper; that is, their own-functioning. That which abides therein is "abiding in its own-functioning" (*svavṛttistha*).

The term *pratyāhāra* refers to the repeated withdrawal (*prati-prati āharaṇa*) by means of the senses from the objects of desire (*kāma*), which are so called because they are desired or longed for— namely, form and the rest— whether they be inferior, middling, or superior in every respect. Having thus defined the first limb, he states the second limb for the purpose of purifying that withdrawal, beginning with the word "five" (*pañca*).

The five objects of desire, such as form and so forth, which are the sense-fields, are in brief the five Buddhas—the eye and so forth—by virtue of their becoming one with the senses. Their conjunction, or application, is through the employment of the five Buddhas. Therefore, that pure conceptualization which consists in the thought that even form and the other objects are the five Buddhas is *dhyāna*.
That becomes fivefold through the divisions of *vitarka* and so forth.
The passage beginning with "vitarka" and so forth is an explanation of its divisions.
Regarding the passage beginning with "guhyatayā" and so forth:
the sense faculties, their objects, and the cognitions of the sense faculties constitute the three secrets.
The five sense faculties, the sensory cognitions, and their objects consist of the nature of the five Tathāgatas;
the conceptualization thereof is *vitarka* (initial inquiry),
and the sustained examination of that very [conceptualization] is *vicāra* (sustained investigation).

For one who reflects in this way, that which is characterized by mental well-being (*saumanasya*) through the orientation toward entering reality is called "joy" (*prīti*) in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*. The bliss (*sukha*) attained through the intense application to reality, characterized by physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) and so forth, is the "gathering of bliss" (*sukhasaṃgraha*).

For one who practices thus, due to reaching the ultimate limit of excellence, there is the "arising of knowledge and the knowable": the arising of the six active consciousnesses, such as the eye-consciousness, with respect to their objects, from form (*rūpa*) up to the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Its destruction is as follows:
the one-pointedness of mind characterized by the thorough knowledge of the mind's emptiness of grasped and grasper is called "one's own mind.
Such is that own mind of the yogin.
"Pervaded by all Buddhas and peaceful" means that through the pacification of conceptual constructions such as the grasped and so forth,
that which is merely a manifestation arises as peace, having its sole foundation in universal emptiness.
This is the second limb, consisting of five subdivisions.
"Five," and so forth.

One should meditate on that very downward breath—which has the nature of the five cognitions beginning with the mirror-like [wisdom] and consists of earth and the other elements—as having emerged from the opening of one's own vajra, in the form of a mass, in the form of a drop of bodhicitta, at the tip of the lotus-nose.

That very upward-moving breath, which is five-colored and consists of the five Tathāgatas, and is therefore a "great jewel" (*mahāratna*) because it extends—that is, lengthens—the life-force (*prāṇa*), is called *prāṇāyāma*.
"Recited" means known;
for that very [mantra] is to be recited day and night by way of its nature as entry and so forth.
Having meditated upon one's own mantra in the heart—that is, in the white lotus of one's own heart—one should place the breath, concentrated within the *bindu*. This is the third limb.
"Ceased," and so forth.

One's own [objects] are form and the rest; the sense organs are the eye and the rest. When that [set of] one's own sense organs has ceased—that is, dissolved—into the jewel which serves as the support for both objects and organs, and when, along with *prāṇāyāma*, the jewel of the mind (*cittaratna*) has also ceased—that is, set—the state one should maintain is "retention" (*dhāraṇā*).
What is that?
The limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
This is the fourth limb, called retention (*dhāraṇā*).
When the mind has entered the vajra of cessation, the apprehension of signs (*nimittodgrāha*) arises.
The vajra of cessation is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). When the mind has become that and arisen from that, the grasping of signs occurs; the appearance of signs is born, it arises.
As for the sign of the five elements, it is cultivated by means of the *bodhivatra*.
Thus, because earth dissolves into water, it appears in the form of a mirage; this is the first sign.
Thus, from the dissolution of water into fire, there is the second [sign], which has the appearance of smoke;
from the dissolution of fire into air, the third, which has the appearance of a firefly;
and from the movement of the three appearances into the subtle element, the fourth, which has the nature of a mass of light like a lamp.
Due to the dissolution of the appearance of the *prakṛti*, there arises the fifth [sign], which is like a cloudless sky, constantly luminous, and consisting of mere radiance (*prabhāsvara*).
These five signs lead to the attainment of *nirvāṇa*,
as it is stated in the *Karmāntavibhāga*.
First the earth goes to the water; the water goes to the fire;
the fire follows after the wind; and the wind enters into consciousness.
Thus, consciousness, having attained a state of retention, should then enter the luminosity.

The commentary on the six corners of the twelfth chapter begins with the words "sthiram" (firm). By means of the vajra-path, which is unassailable, one should cause that which is firm and pure—attained through the sequence of the five signs and entry into the clear light—to emanate and meditate within one's own elements and the world-systems in the form of the Dharmakāya.

Having thus visualized and directly realized oneself as having entered the clear light, one should cause that which was previously brought to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) by means of recollection in the forms of a mirage and so forth, to emanate and be perfected in that very same form and by that same sequence.
This fifth limb, which was just mentioned, should be known—that is, understood—as *anusmṛti*.
The manifestation of consciousness arises therein, within the limb of *anusmṛti*, and not elsewhere.
[Regarding the phrase] "wisdom and means," and so forth:

Having unified all entities—both the stationary and the moving—through the meditative absorption of wisdom and means, by way of the union of the conventional and the ultimate, in the form of a single mass of stability, that is, in the form of Mahāmudrā; one should visualize, or rather know, the image of the Great Vajradhara whose nature is the yoked pair (*yuganaddha*) in the midst of those stationary and moving beings. By this sequence, the instantaneous perfection of gnosis (*jñāna*), the perfection of the body of gnosis, is called the sixth limb, *samādhi*.

In the *Śrī-māyājāla* as well, illuminating this very distinction in the manifestation of the deities, it is said: "Yoga is to be known as threefold: the foundational (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the imagined (*parikalpita*), and the perfected (*niṣpanna*).
This yoga of the mental image (*cittabimba*) has been described by the Buddhas."
The union of the ego with the mere substratum is the purification of the substratum-consciousness (bodhicitta); this is called the arising of the seed-syllable of mantra, which is great.
The image produced through the successive stages is the mudrā fashioned by the assembly;
that which is fashioned is called yoga, and it is said to be "fashioned" (kalpita).
Endowed with the excellence of all aspects, performing emanation and reabsorption,
the yoga that is instantaneously perfected through gnosis is called "perfected."
Thus it is said.
In the *Vairocanābhisambodhi-tantra* as well, he teaches the two-fold yoga of the deity:
"O Lord of Guhyakas, the form of the deity is also twofold: completely pure and impure."
In that regard, the completely pure is the realized form, free from all signs (*nimitta*);
the impure consists of all signs, as well as color and shape.
Therein, through the two kinds of deity forms, the accomplishment of the two kinds of activity occurs.
Accomplishment with signs arises through that which has signs;
accomplishment without signs is always desired by the supreme Victors through that which is signless. Indeed, by abiding in the signless, that which has signs is perfected.
Therefore, in every respect, the signless is established as the negation [of signs].
This is intentional terminology (saṃdhyābhāṣā).

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, having thus indicated the two-fold yoga of the deity, he now states the place for practice, beginning with "in great forest regions," and so forth; this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
In a region of the great forest called Ādarśa, known as Samatā,
within the victory named Pratyavekṣā, in the pure mountain cave.
By practicing according to one's own nature in these very three groves, happiness is thus attained.
This is the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
BHA. Having thus provided the description of the locations for the yogins who possess waves [of bliss], he says "Now," and so forth, in order to describe their practice (*sādhana*) in brief.
This does not refer to those established in the practice of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).
The four vajras have been explained in the *Samājottara*.
"First is emptiness, which is awakening; second is the gathering of the seed-syllable;
third is the perfection of the reflection; and fourth is the placement of the syllable. This is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

For those established in the supreme means, however, there is the fourfold vajra, which is the fourfold emptiness; by means of that, service (sevā) should be performed. One should strive for the attainment of Mahāvajradhara with firm vows and ardent vigor.
The "Great Vajra-holder" is the body of the three vajras;
one makes oneself equal to him.

By means of this—through the cultivation of the fourfold vajra just mentioned and through the thorough knowledge of the nature of phenomena—one attains accomplishment, namely, the accomplishment of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā).
This is the definitive meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with "four junctures" (*catuḥsandhyā*) and so forth: "in the five locations" refers to when the objects of the senses—form and the rest—are present as distinct objects for the bound soul (*paśu*). The "four junctures" are the four goddesses; their "application" (*prayoga*) consists of worshiping them through modes such as embracing. By means of that application of the four junctures, the "wise one" is one who knows sexual union (*surata*).

Having meditated on the syllable *oṃ* at the tip of the vajra, and having delighted with that very *jñānavajra*—one’s own vajra empowered by the syllable *oṃ*—one should indicate, that is, bestow, the *saṃvara*, the true bliss.

Thus, demonstrating the benefit for one who possesses the complete assembly of conditions and who strives for the sake of the *samādhi* of great bliss together with the mudrās of his own mind, he says:
"For days," and so forth.
The time for accomplishment for one of superior faculties is seven days;
for one of middling faculties, a fortnight, which is fifteen days;
and for one of dull faculties, a month.
In one and a half months—
that is, an extra month added to a fortnight is "one and a half months"—
or within that time, one of dull faculties attains success.
The *vajra* is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*); because one attains accomplishment simultaneously with it, at the same time, it is called the *vajrasamaya*, the Great Vajradhara.
Having generated that [deity] and having accomplished oneself through its nature, accomplishment consisting of the *mahāmudrā* is swiftly and quickly attained.

Having explained the distinction of time for one abiding in the conceptualized *samādhi*, he speaks next to show the lack of restriction regarding time for those established in the supreme practice, by way of its opposite:
"Extensively," and so forth.

Previously, for those who are beginners, I have explained the twelve chapters of the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* extensively through detailed elaborations and the various classifications of days, such as the statement beginning with "the seven days.
Now, the intention of the first half [of the verse] is that [the rite] is performed for subjugation by one established in the supreme samādhi.
According to the literal meaning:
"Wing" refers to the conventional and the ultimate; the interior between them is the middle.
What is that?
Abiding through the non-duality of the two truths, the attainment of the state of Mahāvajradhara is then described as being achieved from within the [two] positions.

By whom? By those born from the supreme secret—those Tathāgatas existing throughout the paths whose origin is that which is luminous (prabhāsvara) as the supreme secret. This is in the sandhyābhāṣā (intentional language).

Showing that, according to the sequence just described, the practitioner’s engagement in the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is preceded by the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the body and so forth, he says:
"In that regard," and so on.
The word "in that regard" (*tatra*) serves as a rhetorical ornament.

The *upasādhana* (near-attainment) is the Body-Vajra, so called because it approaches and reaches the body of the practitioner and, having reached him, accomplishes the practitioner—that is, renders him a worthy vessel (*pātrīkaroti*).
That very [Body-Vajra] is concealed (*saṃvriyate*) or sought after (*prārthyate*), thus it is the *saṃvara* (vow/enclosure).
The *upasādhanasaṃvara* is Vairocana.
Its scope is expressed by the verse beginning with "bearing the Buddha-body," which will be explained below.
The Buddhas are the Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times. He is called "bearing the Buddha-body" because he maintains their activity through being of that same nature.
Śrī is she who possesses the eye; he who possesses her is Śrīmān.
Trivajra is the Great Vajra-holder. He has been meditated upon as being of one essence with that [Śrī] through indivisibility.
May Vairocana, the Holder of the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajrin*), establish my body—through its empowerment—as a firm foundation.
Although the term *kāyavajrin* is used here, [it refers to Vairocana].
Having thus entreated the Lord, one entreats that wheel with the words beginning "In the ten directions," and so forth.
With the words "Tattva" and so forth, he introduces the presiding deity of speech.

Because he, by abiding in speech, accomplishes—that is, brings to completion—the practitioner (*sādhaka*), he is the "Accomplisher" (*sādhana*). He is the "Vow of the Accomplisher" (*sādhanasaṃvara*) because he is concealed and prayed to; this refers to Amitābha.
His object is the verse that is about to be spoken.
Dharma is Amitābha; he is the path of speech because his nature is speech. Śrī is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; he who is joined with her is "the Glorious One" (Śrīmān).

“*Trivajra*,” and so forth, is as before. Regarding the passage beginning with “*tatra*”: the empowerment of mind (*cittādhiṣṭhāna*) is the Great Mind; abiding in that, one who attains mastery over the mind of the practitioner is the Great Accomplisher (*mahāsādhana*). He himself is the Vow (*saṃvara*), Akṣobhya; the verse has him as its subject. The mind that is like a vajra is *vajracitta*; because it does not cling to either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, he who maintains such a mind is the Holder of the Vajra Mind (*vajracittadhara*), Akṣobhya. Māmakī is called “Glorious” (*śrīmān*) because she is associated with me (*mama*).
The remainder is as before.
Having thus demonstrated in detail the deity yoga up to the point of the empowerment of body, speech, and mind, he concludes by way of explaining its necessity, saying:
"Or the Buddha," and so forth.

Buddha is the yogin of Vairocana due to non-differentiation; Dharma is the yogin of Amitābha; Vajrasattva is the yogin of Akṣobhya. If, however, one whose nature is deluded—because he has not received the oral instructions—is overcome by delusion and should transgress the empowerment of body, speech, and mind by conceptualizing them as distinct, he becomes clearly distant from the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*). Regarding this, Mahāvajradhara said that no doubt or hesitation should be entertained toward my words. All the Tathāgatas, such as Kāyavajra and the others, possess an indivisible nature; their fourfold yoga is "Vajrayoga. It is called a *samaya* because by means of it, they are equally measured (*samamīyate*) or understood (*gamya*).

That very [reality], because it is the nature of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*); because it brings about the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), it is the foremost; "instruction" (*nirdeśa*) means illumination; "chapter" (*paṭala*) means a composition of the text; and with respect to its distinct subject matter, it is the twelfth.
This is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
The Explanation of the Six Points in the Twelfth Chapter of the *Pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*.
The Thirteenth Chapter.

The practitioner who has engaged in the practice of the two-fold sequence must also perform the expansion of ritual activities (*karmaprasara*) in order to attract those to be trained (*vineyajana*). To demonstrate this, the author introduces the thirteenth chapter, beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*), and so forth. "Now" (*atha*) means immediately after the *vidyā* of service (*āsevā*) and the rest. Because they are endowed with mastery over desires and other qualities, the Blessed Ones (*bhagavantah*)—the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya and the others—are called "holders of the supreme wisdom-vajra" (*jñānavajrāgradhāriṇaḥ*). "Wisdom-vajra" (*jñānavajra*) is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*); it is "supreme" (*agra*) because it is the primary [wisdom], and they are its "holders" (*dhāriṇaḥ*) because they maintain it.
The "benefit" (artha) for all sentient beings refers to purposes such as pacification (śāntika) and so forth; those who have arisen for that purpose are "exerted" (udyata). Who are they?

The wise Bodhisattvas, Kṣitigarbha and the others, remaining in their respective mudrās—such Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—having worshipped with external and internal offerings the Great Teacher Mahāvajradhara, the Great Śāstra because he acts according to the minds of all Tathāgatas; the Sage because his power is unimpeded in both worldly and transcendent traditions; and the Vajra of All Aims because of his thorough knowledge of the two truths, or because he knows the reality of the *samaya*—uttered the sound of the vajra (*vajraghoṣa*). Uttering the sound of the vajra as the speech of requesting the expansion of activity, they spoke according to the literal meaning:
"Aho! What a marvel!"
The Buddha-system is the yoga of the six limbs beginning with withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Having transcended the four vajras, behold the divine yoga of the six limbs!
Praising by means of the union of the two truths, he says again, "Aho!

The yoga of the six limbs of enlightenment is its system; it is the application of the two truths. That alone is supreme and distinguished because it encompasses the meaning of the speech of all the Tathāgatas.
"Again, oh! [he says].
Dharma is the two truths; its *naya* is their unification, which is peaceful and free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
With "Again, oh! and so forth, he concludes the praise.
The mantras are the Tathāgatas; their *naya* is the means for attaining awakening.
It is "firm" (*dṛḍha*) and "indestructible" (*abhedyam*) because it cannot be destroyed by the Śrāvakas and others. This is *saṃdhyābhāṣā*.

While phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*)—which are unarisen, primordially peaceful, distinguished by a superior nature (*svabhāva*) insofar as they bring about awakening, non-conceptual, free from mental construction, and existent because they are delightful when not analyzed—thus exist as real; it is marvelous that the Blessed One proclaims and describes the emergence of gnosis, the arising of Vajrasattva, through the means of the six-limbed yoga (*ṣaḍaṅgayoga*) regarding such phenomena.
This is a marvel.
Not without a secret convention.
Having thus praised and propitiated the Blessed One, he requested him to explain the desired subject, saying:
"Speak!

"Speak of that mandala—the locus for the practice of vajra-recitation (*vajrajāpa*) and its associated recitations—which is the collection and compendium of all mantras resembling vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*). It is the 'Great Knowledge' because it brings about the attainment of unsurpassed knowledge; it is the 'Abode of the Great Vajradhara,' who is inseparable from the three bodies (*trikāya*), and it functions as the very nature of his entering, abiding, and arising."

He further qualifies that very [state]: "Speak" refers to the yoga wherein one abides having attained the Buddha-knowledges—the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and so forth—by means of the practitioners who cultivate the indivisibility of the three vajras.

Its specific qualification is "the vajra-recitation," which is *vajrajāpa*; its "application" is the mental construction of it in the form of entry (*praveśa*) and so forth. By that [application], one is empowered—that is, accepted—by all the Vajras, the Tathāgatas.
Regarding the phrase "of the families" (*kulānām*), and so forth:
The characteristic of the body, speech, and mind of all mantras—the families and hosts of snakes and so forth—is the intrinsic nature of the body and the other [faculties].
Now, O Proclaimer, speak of the mantra-recitation, the vajra-recitation.
For what purpose? So that the oceans of gnosis, the jewel-like persons, may hear and understand.
Having arisen throughout the three times, they have become—that is, been produced and perfected—by way of entry, abiding, and emergence.
Who are they?

They are the Vajra-holders of Body, Speech, and Mind; "all the Buddhas" refers to those who have attained incomparable gnosis, the non-dual gnosis, through the manifestations of vajra-mantras—that is, through the thorough knowledge of vajra-recitation.
Now, immediately following the request:

because he is produced from both—the space-vajra, which is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), and gnosis (*jñāna*), which is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*)—the Great Vajradhara is the "source of space-vajra-gnosis. By the words beginning with "What shall I do? and so forth, he qualifies that very [being] as the "agent" (*kartā*) because he accomplishes pacification and the other rites; as the "creator" (*sraṣṭā*) because he cuts off unauthorised acts such as malevolent sorcery (*abhicāra*); and as the "supreme among the supreme" (*varāgrāgra*) because the Blessed One himself is superior even to the "supreme trees" (*vara-vṛkṣa*) and so forth, namely the Arhats and others. He uttered—that is, spoke—the recitation of his own vajra.

Regarding the passage beginning with "sarvamantra" and so forth: "all mantras" refers to [beings] such as serpents; their "meaning" consists of the three syllables; the "recitation" (*jāpa*) of that [meaning] consists of the three [stages] such as the location (*pradeśa*). When these exist, he proclaimed the "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*), which has the characteristic of being indivisible like the Three Vajras and whose nature is that [same indivisibility]. Thus is the connection. Hearing this, he says "tribhede" and so forth.

The threefold division is the division of body and so forth; its placement, culminating in the Vajra and having the Holder of the Vajra as its sole ultimate, is the thorough knowledge of it in its essential nature as entry and so on. That is called the "Three Vajras.
To show its object, he says "threefold," and so forth.
What is the gathering and appropriation of body, speech, and mind?
It is the assumption of the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). When that exists, the threefold radiation characterized by entering and so forth is the effect to be accomplished.

He states its benefit: by means of this aforementioned "vowelmantle" (*jāpavajra*), that is, by the vajra-recitation, one becomes equal to the Great Vajradhara—the nature of whose body of gnosis is inseparable from the mind of the Three Vajras (body and so forth) through their manifestation as body and so on.
Demonstrating the unsurpassed worship, he says "of the Buddhas" and so forth;

having meditated upon— that is, having brought to completion— the assumption of forms through the emanations of body, speech, and mind, one should perform the conceptualization of the specific worship for the Buddhas residing in the world-systems of the ten directions.
By what?

By means of the wisdom-vajra (*jñānavajra*), having ascended to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*). The benefits beginning with "the three vajras" (*trivajra*) are as before.
To lead [the practitioner] away from attachment to external worship, he says: "Furthermore, of the Buddhas," and so forth.

Having visualized the supreme arrangement of worship—the entire array of offerings throughout all world-realms—and having mentally projected it, one should perform the worship of the body, speech, and mind of the Buddhas.
This array of superior and other forms of worship should be understood as being of the nature of the Tathāgata’s body and so forth.
Through the Vajra of Gnosis, this kind of thorough understanding brings about enlightenment and is the activity that accomplishes the state of a Mahāvajradhara; such is the praise [of its benefits].
Having thus demonstrated the ritual procedure for worship for one of superior faculties, [the author], showing it also for one of dull faculties,
says "Alternatively," and so forth;
"Alternatively" is a particle indicating another method.

Each and every emanation of the deity, through its threefold division, must perform its activity by means of the differentiation of the body— emanating it individually and separately from one's own body-maṇḍala.
To eliminate any perception of [independent] existence within the emanated maṇḍalas, he says "kāya" and so forth.

The selflessness of body, speech, and mind means that one should cause the lack of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvābhāvya*) of the bodies and so forth of those deities to radiate— that is, to manifest— by means of a specific gnosis consisting of the discernment of gnosis-mind (*jñānacitta*). He speaks of the "encasement" (*saṃpuṭīkaraṇa*) with the words beginning "having uttered," and so forth.

Having uttered the vajra—the form of the emanated deity—from its place, having raised it from that location, one should cause it to radiate and establish it within oneself in the nature of the aggregates and so forth;
at the conclusion, during the state of the activity of making [the visualization] manifest, one should indicate and perform the withdrawal, which is the entry of the samādhi-sattva.

This which has just been described—that by which the body-vajra Vairocana is realized and accomplished for all Buddhas and all individuals whose eyes are opened by gnosis (*jñāna*) and whose eyes of wisdom are unveiled—is the syllable *Oṃ*, known as the "awakening of the body-vajra" (*kāyavajrābhisaṃbodhi*). The thorough knowledge of it as existing through its being within the range of the path of hearing, and as non-existing through its lack of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and the investigation into its existence and non-existence—this is declared to be the "Buddha-body" (*buddhakāya*); that is called the "recitation of the body" (*kāyajāpa*).
The "vow of speech" (*vāksamaya*) is Amitābha.

Its mode of manifestation is perfect awakening; it is called "sound" (*śabda*) because it is grasped by the auditory faculty, and its opposite is "non-sound. That which is grasped or not grasped by the ear—namely, the mental engagement (*parāmarśa*) consisting of the investigation of sound and non-sound—is declared to be the "vajra of speech," and that is called the "recitation of speech" (*vāgjāpa*).

The commitment of mind (*cittasamaya*) is Akṣobhya; his awakening is the syllable *HŪṂ*; that which abides in it has the nature of the vajra. The investigation of that is the examination of the mind as being neither mind nor non-mind according to reality; this is called the "mind-vajra" and is termed the "mind-recitation. Having thus explained the vajra-recitation by way of body, speech, and mind, he speaks in order to show the primary vajra-recitation:
"Following the meaning," and so forth:

the meaning of the *oṃ* syllable and the others is "entry" and so on; the recitation (*jāpa*) performed in accordance with—that is, following—that meaning, as explained in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, is "recitation following the meaning. By that means, through the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound which is devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), free from self-nature (*nirgatasvabhāva*), beautiful, and of a continuously vibrating form, there is the non-differentiation due to being of the three times, existing throughout the three periods. For the sake of the realization of all Tathāgatas in the form of the unstruck sound, which is the consciousness for the purpose of warding off [obstacles], that is called the "jewel-recitation" (*ratnajāpa*).
Furthermore, showing the re-emergence [from meditative absorption], he says:
"Radiation," and so forth:

from the Buddha-field, that is, from the heart-lotus, there is a radiation consisting of entering, abiding, and arising—by means of the unstruck body-cloud into the sense-bases such as the eyes and so on—for the sake of the vajra-movement of going and coming; this is called the "unfailing recitation.
Having thus explained the mental recitation, he speaks to demonstrate the verbal recitation:

"Mantras" refers to those such as serpents who hear; their "syllables and words" begin with the syllable *oṃ*. One's own "vajra" is one's own tongue; that by which [the mantra] is rubbed or uttered is the "maṇḍala," meaning the body. Thus, "the maṇḍala rubbed by one's own vajra" is that which hears it, whether oneself or another. The "mantras" of the wrathful deities such as Yamāntaka and others constitute their "samaya," which is the procedure for recitation. Through the thorough knowledge of that, the recitation is called "wrathful recitation."

Desires are the objects such as forms and so forth; for their sake, beings become distraught and intent upon seeking them. Desiring the welfare of all sentient beings, one should establish those beings—who are solely devoted to their own self-interest—within that "state" (*pada*) of Vairocana, which is Delusion (*moha*) as the purification of delusion. The contemplation directed toward that [state] is known as the recitation (*jāpa*) of delusion.

Attachment (*rāga*) is the mutual passion between men and women; because of their union, it is a *vajra*. Having heard the speech—the voice—arising from that or produced by that, which resides in body, speech, and mind, or the speech pertaining to the beauty of the body and so forth, the yogin establishes all those who possess attachment in the state of the ocean of attachment, Amitābha, which is the purity of attachment. Whatever meditation the yogin performs therein is known as the "recitation born of attachment. Hatred (*dveṣa*) is the malice toward sentient beings; that itself is the *vajra*, and the mind contained within it resides in body, speech, and mind. Knowing the objects of the body and so forth, hatred—which seeks out sentient beings—is Akṣobhya. His abode is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*); having established [the mind] therein, whatever thorough knowledge is produced is the "recitation born of hatred. The "Three-Vajra Samaya" is Mahāvajradhara. His reality is the Clear Light, which is the heart-essence situated in the midst of the Tathāgatas who are the Samaya-Vajrins. That very thing is called the "neuter recitation" or the "recitation of the absence of intrinsic nature" for the practitioners who are the Samaya-Vajrins.
"Sandhyābhāṣā" refers to Vajra, the Great Vajradhara; those for whom he is the lord are the "Vajrādhipatis. They are all practitioners of two kinds.
Since neither passion nor dispassion is perceived, the middle is not found—this is the reality of passion (*rāgatattva*).
Its meaning is as follows: those who accomplish the reality of passion know the thorough knowledge of things as they truly are;

and through the recitation born of passion, which arises from the enjoyment of the qualities of sensual pleasure, they bring about and perfect the awakening that benefits all sentient beings—the state of the Great Vajradhara.
It is not only men who thus accomplish the awakening born of passion.
However, he says "even women" and so forth: *locanādyāḥ* refers to Locanā and the others;

*padmetyādayaḥ* refers to Padma and the others; *mahāvidyāsu śikṣitāḥ* refers to the Mudrās such as Kāmarūpā and the rest. Their *artha* is the purification (*viśuddhi*) of those [deities]; *tatparāḥ* means those who are solely intent upon that meditation. By means of the enjoyments of desire—the sense objects—being served and practiced according to one's wish (*yathecchataḥ*) and at ease (*yathāsukham*), they achieve success; they attain the state of Vajradhara.

According to the literal meaning: "Arising from the *moha*-samaya" and so forth. The *moha*-samaya is Vairocana; those arising from that, manifested from that, are the Knowledge-Kings (*vidyārāja*) such as the Uṣṇīṣas, and the Vajrins such as Kṣitigarbha. "Accomplished in the neuter state" (*napuṃsakapade siddhāḥ*): the neuter state is the syllable OṂ; from that they are perfected, and they bestow—that is, grant—the supreme accomplishment, which is awakening (*bodhi*).

The wrathful deities such as Yamāntaka and others arise from the syllable *huṃ*, which is the abode of hatred; born from it and perfected within it, they are intent on slaying and perform the activity of subduing the wicked. Through this fierce activity for the purpose of killing, they accomplish their intended goal for the practitioner who possesses a highly exalted nature—this is the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).

The time of delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*); from that, the Knowledge-Kings (*vidyārāja*), the Vajra-holders, and men, women, and neuters have arisen. Ignorance is the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*). Its locus is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). By realizing it through direct witness within that state, they are perfected and accomplished; they bestow and grant to practitioners the supreme, distinguished accomplishment, the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrāsiddhi*).

The *krodhas* have wrath as their nature; they are abodes of hatred, born from that [wrath], arising from it, and are always—at all times—intent on slaying and characterized by violence. Such natures are "for the sake of slaying" (*māraṇārthāḥ*). "Slaying" (*māraṇa*) means rendering the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Its "purpose" (*artha*) is the arising of the state of a Vajradhara through the non-duality of the two truths. By that purpose of slaying, the "own-nature" (*svadharma*) is the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*). For that person of supreme dharma—the jewel-like individual (*ratnapudgala*)—who possesses this, the natures are accomplished and brought under control.

"This is the pledge of the Great Being, Mahāvajradhara," so he said— this is the words of the compiler (*saṃgītikāra*), and it is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Furthermore, he speaks of another stage of meditation,
beginning with "in the heart" (*hṛdi*), and so forth.

In the heart of the Knowledge-Vajra, that is, the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva), one should meditate upon the wheel located in the center—the center of the heart—which is the symbol of Vairocana. Of what nature is it? One should visualize it as being situated in the midst of a clear mandala, namely, a moon-mandala.
"In the center" means "in the center of the wheel";

"the cultivation of the purpose of the wheel" (*cakrārthabhāvanā*) means that the purpose is accomplished by means of the wheel, thus the "purpose of the wheel" (*cakrārtha*) is the goal to be accomplished; its cultivation must be performed.

This is what is meant: one who possesses the yoga of Vairocana should visualize a wheel upon a moon-maṇḍala in the heart of his own Jñānasattva, draw in the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), cause it to enter therein, establish it, and perform pacification (*śānti*) accordingly.

"One should act" means that one who possesses the yoga of Akṣobhya should visualize, within the heart of the Knowledge-Vajra—the Knowledge-Being—a vajra situated in the center of a maṇḍala-diagram and resting upon a solar disc; therein, the meditation on the meaning of the Vajra-mantra must be performed.

The "Vajra-mantra" is the syllable *HŪṂ*. That which is sought or afflicted by it is the "meaning of the Vajra-mantra," namely the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*); the meditation upon that [object] is to be carried out.

One possessing the yoga of Ratnasaṃbhava should visualize, within the heart of the Knowledge-Being (jñānasattva) who possesses jewel-knowledge, a jewel situated upon a jewel atop a jewel-maṇḍala; therein is the meditation on the meaning of the Jewel-Mantra. The "Jewel-Mantra" refers to its own form; that which is sought and nourished by it is the "meaning of the Jewel-Mantra," namely the object to be accomplished (sādhya). That meditation [upon it] is thus described.
