One who possesses the yoga of Amitābha should visualize a lotus situated in the center of the dharma-maṇḍala within the heart of the Jñānasattva residing in his own heart—the Jñānasattva of Padmajñāna. Upon that lotus, one should perform the meditation on the meaning of the mantra, which is the "lotus-mantra," namely the syllable *ĀḤ*.

The "meaning of the lotus-mantra" refers to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because it is by means of that [syllable] that [the object] is sought or brought under control; one must perform the meditation upon that.

One possessing the yoga of Amoghasiddhi should visualize the sword within the heart of the Knowledge Being (jñānasattva) of the Sword-Knowledge, situated in the center of the pledge-maṇḍala and resting upon a double vajra (viśvavajra). Within that sword, one should perform the meditation on the meaning of the sword-mantra. The sword-mantra is the syllable *HĀ*; it is called the "sword-mantra" because by means of it, the goal is sought and accomplished in every way—this is the meaning of the sword-mantra’s objective. One must perform its meditation. Regarding this very point, he states the remainder of the procedure:
having placed the five Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, in due order upon the four sides of all the maṇḍalas, such as the wheel-maṇḍala and so forth, one should meditate upon them.
One should meditate on [the deity] while emitting [light] through the differentiation of five rays, each with a color corresponding to the specific activity;
to the question "What then?", he says:
"The attainment of enlightenment—the accomplishment of the desired fruit—is achieved."
Now, he describes the emanation according to the distinction of sequence,
beginning with "the emanation" and so forth:
the emanation of all mantras and all practitioners— the manifestation of deities— is proclaimed to be of two kinds, distinguished as perfected and unperfected.
He speaks of the samādhi of the generation stage, beginning with the words "the three bodies" and so forth:
by means of the divisions of the vajras of body and so on, one should place the withdrawal and radiation; that is, one should perform the radiation and withdrawal of the deities.
Clarifying that very point, he says "the nature of the body," and so forth:

having known that one's own mind—which is the nature of the body—is to be worshipped in its form as Vairocana; or that one's own speech—the collection of words—is to be worshipped in its form as Akṣobhya through the nature of that [speech]; and having known that which is to be worshipped, one shall obtain and attain the accomplishment of desired aims.

The "great mandalas" are the mandalas of body, speech, and mind; their "wheel" (*cakra*) is their assembly. By means of that great mandala-wheel, one should perform the visualization of the five-vajra Great Vajradhara. Regarding the phrase "in the center," and so forth:

having meditated upon the sovereign wisdom-being (*jñānasattva*), who is one's own form—the form of the fundamental nature—within the heart, that is, in the center of the previously mentioned Samayasattva of Body-Vajrin; and having meditated upon the form, the embodiment, of the Samādhisattva—one's own mantra-vajra—within the heart of that wisdom-being.

Furthermore, having conceptualized and meditated upon the four maṇḍalas—the four maṇḍalas beginning with that of Varuṇa—using the four colors such as white and so forth, one should perform the contemplation and thorough understanding of the mantras, such as Oṃ and others, within the center of the maṇḍala of Varuṇa and the rest, regarding their entry and so forth. For the yogi who possesses the vajra of meditation, the fourfold vajra—the four maṇḍalas beginning with that of Varuṇa—performs and accomplishes the activities, such as pacification and the rest.
For this is the procedure for all lords of yoga; it is the supreme, eternal secret contained within the tradition of all Tathāgatas, the uncommon reality for beginners.
Teaching this very fourfold vajra according to the divisions of ritual action, he says "in pacification" and so forth:
in pacifying rites characterized by the removal of fevers and the like, one should meditate on the mandala of Varuṇa, which has the form of Locanā, is white in color, and is pure by nature.
In rites for nourishment (*pauṣṭika*), such as the increase of wealth and so forth, there is the "station of Vairocana" according to the yoga;

it shines and blazes like molten gold, thus he is Vairocana, who is Ratnaketu. His station is a yellow radiance, the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, which has emerged from the pair [of nostrils]. Likewise, in the rite of subjugation (*vaśya*), there is the yoga of the "Lotus-Vajra-holder":

in the rite of subjugation characterized by causing those not yet converted to become devoted, one should meditate on the Fire-maṇḍala emerging from the southern gate, which is the nature of red light rays belonging to the Lotus-Vajra-holder.

In the case of *abhicāruka*—the fierce rites of killing and so forth—one should meditate on Vajrakrodha, who has the nature of black rays and has emerged from the left gate, as being the mandala [described by] "this is that," and so forth. This fourfold mandala, which was just mentioned, is the secret and mystery revealed by Mahāvajradhara, arising from the three bodies (*trikāya*) of all Vajras and all practitioners. It is the "dramatic performance of rites" (*kriyānāṭaka*), consisting of the collection of ritual acts such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth; it is "the secret" because it is characterized and marked by that. Such is the yoga.

In order to demonstrate the difficulty of performing *abhicāra* (malevolent rites) among the four types of ritual actions, and with the intention of explaining it, he shows its specific scope by saying "those who speak words of non-devotion. Here, "non-devotion" (*abhakti*) means a lack of veneration; those beings who speak such words regarding the Three Jewels are the nihilists (*anāstika*). "The Vajrin masters" refers to the Vajrācāryas.

And for those who revile them, as well as for others who have committed the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and so forth—whenever they are seen—one must perform the action characterized by incitement, which consists of the command: "Kill such-and-such a person. This is the deed that is to be done.
The Great Vajradhara, who is the Great Wisdom Wheel-Vajra and consists of the nature of the two families, spoke thus:
"In the triple world," and so forth.

The practitioner should visualize—that is, have firm conviction in—the sentient beings residing in the triple world, those included within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness, as well as the egg-born and other classes of beings, as being the Buddha-body, the Buddha-bodies, the *tathāgatagarbhas*. Having meditated upon the enemies as having been struck down by the seven [deities] to be accomplished, he should then commence the ritual activity.
Having accumulated the aforementioned sins according to the sequence just described, one should suppress them by first performing the opening of the casket (*saṃpuṭodghāṭana*).

First, the practitioner should visualize himself as situated in the midst of the space-element (*khadhātu*), having entered into luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); immediately thereafter, he should meditate upon himself transformed into the form of a solar disc.

Above that, having meditated upon a five-pronged, formidable *vajra* produced by a long *hūṃ*, one should visualize Vajrasattva—arisen from its transformation—as four-faced, with a face formidable with fangs, possessing the luster of sapphire, having as many arms as there are excellent forms, embodying all the specific characteristics of the wrathful deities, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, situated in the center of the wheel, and appearing according to the oral instructions. One should visualize the assembly of deities beginning with Vairocana, which is the "Buddha-vajra" born from that Vajradhara—the "Samaya of the Three Times" mentioned immediately above.
This aforementioned great garment of the Buddha-wheel is to be meditated upon in the right hand, on the right side of Vajrasattva, because it serves his purpose;
meanwhile, the wheel of goddesses, consisting of the five families, is to be placed on the left side—this is the traditional teaching.

Having gathered all the Tathāgatas situated in the ten directions by means of the differentiation of the Buddha-bodies according to the divisions of the families starting with Vairocana, and having unified them through the yoga of the mass (*piṇḍayoga*) into their respective forms as Great Seals (*mahāmudrā*), one should cause that array of deities to enter into one's own body in the form of the aggregates of form and so forth, and thus seal them in union.
Immediately after re-entering, the emanation and departure of those possessing the vajra of gnosis (jñānavajrin)—who abide within the body of gnosis—must be performed.
To explain what this is like, he says "the wrathful ones," and so forth; the yoga consists of visualizing them in the form of the wrathful deities and others, and then emanating them.

"Angry" means those whose minds are agitated by wrath; "therefore, with their bodies" he says they are "fierce, violent, and terrifying. Their fierceness (*vikaṭatva*) consists in being endowed with knitted brows, bloodshot eyes, and mouths made formidable by fangs.
His ferocity arises from his massive body; his terrifying nature from being adorned with a girdle of snakes and other ornaments;
and the fact that the tips of his hands hold various weapons arises from his hands being occupied with axes, mallets, and the like.
Māraṇa is Mahāvajradhara; his *āmnāya* is a specific command.

Those who kill or threaten even Vajrasattva himself—those whose minds are fixed on such [deeds] and who destroy those adorned by assistance to the Three Jewels and other [objects of refuge], though they be great evildoers.

If even Vajradhara were thus wicked, he would harm him as well; how much more so another? Thus, the inability [of such a person] is shown by way of its being like an illusion. To dispel remorse, he says "Buddha," and so forth.

The Buddha is the Great Vajradhara; because he bestows the instruction for maintaining the bodies beginning with the Dharma-body, he is the "Bestower of the Three Bodies. Sentient beings are the three vajras; their abode is the maṇḍala, which is the triple world (traidhātuka), because that [maṇḍala] has the nature of those [beings].
Thus, he is the "Abode-Maṇḍala of the Three Vajras."

The "deluded soul" (*mohātmā*) refers to one who, due to being under the sway of negligence, is deluded (*mūḍha*) regarding the commentary on the thirteen million verses in the thirteenth chapter; such a deluded soul bestows accomplishment (*siddhi*)— the intended goal— upon the practitioner,
and no doubt is raised regarding the granting of that accomplishment.
This raudra-rite must be performed for seven days;
otherwise, even for a Buddha, it will not succeed within those seven days.
Herein is the procedure:

Having generated oneself as Mahāvajradhara according to the sequence just described, and having performed the emanation of the wrathful deities as previously stated, one should command the pillar standing in their midst. One should then visualize the *sādhya* before oneself—his neck bound with a noose, being dragged by a hook, standing upon a fire-maṇḍala atop a wind-maṇḍala, with disheveled hair, his body smeared with oil, his mouth wide open, without refuge, and overcome with remorse; and one should contemplate him being pierced by the various weapons of the wrathful deities until his life-force has departed and he has been reborn in a Buddha-field.

The *vajrasamayas* are the wrathful deities (*krodhas*); "let their gnosis (*jñāna*) thus cause affliction" is the application [of the mantra]. This is the *vajrasamaya-jñāna*, which is itself the *cakra*; this is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) so named.

Thus, having first demonstrated the wheel of command (*ājñā-cakra*) for the yogin of Akṣobhya, he speaks the words beginning with "the sphere of space" (*khadhātu*) and so forth, while also demonstrating it for the yogin of Vairocana.

Having generated oneself as Vairocana according to the sequence previously described, one should immediately thereafter visualize the highly renowned Vajrasattva—arisen from the commitment (*samaya*) of the three times and the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of Vairocana—in a state of wrath. One should meditate on a vajra in his hand, blazing with sparks of fire and possessing a formidable vajra-form.

Then, having honored the Tathāgatas situated in the ten directions—who are manifested through the divisions of the vajra-body and the distinctions of male and female—with a mass of light rays emanating from one’s own body, and having withdrawn and drawn them in, one should cause those Tathāgatas to enter into one’s own body.

The practitioner, who is the kinsman of the supreme gnosis (*jñānāgravandhu*), must perform the emanation and dispatching of all vajras— the maṇḍala deities residing within his own body. Thereafter, he demonstrates the sequence for giving them their commands,
beginning with the words "Let them listen," and so forth.
May all those who are the essence of all Buddhas, the sons of all Tathāgatas, the possessors of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, and whose nature is the three vajras, listen!
What does he say? "I," and so forth.
I am the one who brings about the *ājñācakra*.

With this thunderbolt (*vajra*), whose body is ablaze and which devours with its garlands of flames, I shatter—that is, I pulverize—those born from the three bodies, those produced from the unity of the three bodies.
Therefore, if anyone should transgress the pledge (*samaya*) and act in opposition to this command, he shall be shattered and destroyed.
"There is no doubt in this," he said, thereby manifesting his own sovereignty. Vajrasamaya is Vairocana.
Therefore, the one who has become the thunderbolt of gnosis is Vajrasattva; this is the meditative absorption (samādhi) bearing that name.
In the same way, the transformation of Ratnasaṃbhava and the others should also be applied.
He also speaks of their retinues:
"Khavajre," and so forth.

One should visualize oneself as the Vajrin of the Buddha-maṇḍala, situated in the center of the space-vajra (*khavajra*), established in the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Thereupon, one should fashion oneself—known as the Space-Vajra—as Yamāntaka, the Samaya-cakra together with his retinue. One should further fashion the Buddhas, such as Vairocana and others, and the Bodhisattvas, such as Maitreya and others, as having entered into the maṇḍala of the three bodies within body, speech, and mind.
Furthermore, one should again and again emanate Buddhas who abide in a gentle state yet resemble the form of Yamāntaka.
One should then meditate thus upon those Tathāgatas who have been emanated: they have arisen throughout the three times and consist of the three bodies (*trikāya*).
One should meditate upon them as destroyers of enemies—those whose minds are intent on committing evil deeds with malicious intent, who are engaged in harming the Three Jewels and so forth.

The wrathful one is this Vajra; it belongs to those Tathāgatas. It is the command regarding the destruction of the wicked, and because it takes (*lāti*)—that is, grasps and appropriates—the *maṇḍa*, which is the primary essence (*pradhāna*), it is called a *maṇḍala*.
What is that?
It is the Lord of the Maṇḍala himself.

"Universal Samaya" refers to Mahāvajradhara; "born from that" refers to Yamāri. That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the "Vajras of the Three Bodies"—the retinue of wrathful deities who are identical in form to him—is present, is so described.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Body" (*kāya*): he speaks thus to explain that the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) is common to all deities.
The wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) should be employed by means of the five [Buddhas], Vairocana and the others, together with their respective goddesses.

Their own mantras are those bound to their respective families, such as Maitreya and the rest; their "meaning" (*artha*) is the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) accomplished exactly as it is; its "quality" (*guṇa*) is the subduing of the wicked through the forms of the Wrathful Ones (*krodha*) produced from the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of that [meaning]. The "pledge" (*samaya*) refers to the Uṣṇīṣas, the Kings of Wrath who abide in the upper portion; all the Wrathful Ones are "pledges of the Uṣṇīṣas" (*uṣṇīṣasamayāḥ*) because they attain equality (*samatā*) with them. One should employ the wheel of command even with these. Showing the purpose of the wheel of command immediately following its employment, he says:
"Rakṣārtham" and so forth.

For the sake of protection—that is, for the purpose of warding off all mantras [of obstructors] such as Indra and others who cause obstacles, this wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) must be performed by the practitioner, the "Foremost Vajra of Gnosis.
To the question, "For what purpose is this aforementioned removal of obstacles performed?", he says:

This demonstrates the purpose of the command-wheel (*ājñācakra*), namely for the protection of the awakening of all Vajras and all practitioners from those who cause mental distraction, and for their protection;
it is according to the literal meaning (*yathāruta*).
Now, he explains the method for subduing malevolent grahas even for those established in the stage of completion (niṣpannakrama),
beginning with "In the mouth of space" and so forth.
Because he illuminates through the suppression of the malevolent, the one to be accomplished (sādhya) is Vairocana.

Having meditated upon the Dharma—which arises from the supreme body, consists of the three bodies (*trikāya*), is composed of body, speech, and mind, resides within the center of the *khavatra*, and has become empty—one should fashion the seat as the basis for that which is to be accomplished.
One should visualize that very sphere of space as being completely filled and pervaded by the five rays of light of all the Buddhas.

According to the commentary on the six million [verses] of the thirteenth chapter: one should, however, manifest for oneself one's own mantra-syllable as speech, the state, the body, and gnosis (*jñāna*)—the form of the mind, which is like an illusion.

Furthermore, immediately thereafter, one should withdraw—that is, cause to enter—into one’s own Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which is manifested as mind-only, the five rays of light just described for the Buddhas.
Having understood all this as the Mind-Vajra and having realized Vajra-Gnosis, one should cause it to enter one’s own body, speech, and mind as the three bodies (trikāya).
By this, the intended purpose is accomplished.

The vajra is difficult to pierce and is that which is to be accomplished; the mantra-jewel is the specific application that pierces it. The samādhi named "The Illuminator," which makes it manifest and reveals it, is [taught here]. This is in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (twilight language).
He now describes the application for immobilization (*stambhana*).
First, having produced oneself as consisting of illusion, one should place [that self] in the midst of space.
Having established the Buddhas—Akṣobhya and the others—whose natures are those of space, wind, fire, water, and earth, one by one in succession from above downward, one should walk upon the water.
This is according to the literal text.

The application of the water-vow (*samayādaka*) for one established in the meditative absorption of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is as follows: by means of the unification of the two truths, one should perform the practice of walking upon the surface of water with that body consisting of gnosis (*jñānamaya-deha*).
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Sixth, who is pure by nature.
"Vajra" refers to the two types of yogins; that meditative absorption in which they walk, treading with their feet upon the ocean and so forth, is described in that way.
The Sandhyābhāṣā:

Having meditated upon the Maheśvara mandala, which arises from the syllable *laṃ*, is yellow in color, and marked with a vajra and a lotus in the center of the hollow of the mouth, one should place above it the Wrathful One (*krodha*) produced from a long *hūṃ*, bearing a blazing vajra.

Upon the head—that is, the head of the victim—one should visualize the Karma-vajra, which is a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*); that very same [double-vajra] is the foot, and he should contemplate Amṛtakuṇḍalin standing, having trampled upon it.

"All heretics" refers to the Kṣapaṇakas and others who are proponents of opposing doctrines and adversaries; "their machine" is the paralysis of their bodies and so forth, and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the occurrence of that [paralysis] takes place is described as such.
Regarding the passage beginning with "wrath," etc.:

The practitioner himself, as Mahāvajradhara, having transformed into the form of whichever wrathful deity he has assumed, should visualize his own retinue—the foremost of the three vajras—as resembling yellow filaments, tawny like the king of lotuses, and equal in size to Sumeru, the king of mountains; having meditated upon and contemplated them as being above a fourfold army, he should radiate light and behold the entire host as if it were situated in the netherworld (pātāla).
Even the Buddhas, who are skilled in paralyzing, have their armies paralyzed by him.
What more need be said?

"No doubt is to be entertained here," so said the Blessed One, the Sixth, who is the source of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. "The entire army" refers to the army of the Buddhas; that which effects its immobilization is thus described.
Regarding the passage beginning with "terrifying the enemies" (*ripusaṃtrāsana*):
at the time of terrifying—that is, at the time of causing fear in enemies such as those who reject the true Dharma—one should apply and perform this meditation being described.
Even a beginner, if he should transcend and practice this application, it will burst forth and become manifest in the world.
There is no doubt about this.
The word "says" (*āha*) indicates the demonstration of the ritual application.

Having meditated upon the fierce *vajra* produced from the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*, measuring [the body] in size and shape, having five prongs, fashioned with a *vajra-kila* at the top, endowed with parts such as eyes and so forth, and below the navel having a single-pointed tip in the form of a coiled serpent—the practitioner, by means of that *kila*, should perform this breaking and cutting within his own heart and the heart of the object to be subdued; he should bring it to completion.
Those who are not Buddhas and are unskilled in Tantra and Mantra—[the practitioner] should destroy and instruct their army when it is increased, enraged, and acting as an adversary;
of this there is no doubt.
An enemy (*ripu*) is a foe (*śatru*); his delusion (*moha*) consists in engaging in equanimity even toward those with a virtuous intention (*kalyāṇādhyāśaya*).
The samādhi in which there is the removal—that is, the dispelling—of that [harm] is so described.
He now states the ritual application for pacification for those afflicted by noble beings (*ārya*) and others:
"In the city," and so forth.
One should apply this in a city, a capital, a village, a district, or a region. By the words "one should perform the practice" and so forth, he demonstrates the efficacy of the practice.

First of all, the practitioners, having taken up great compassion for sentient beings, should visualize a great vajra, five-colored with rays of light and the size of a palm tree trunk, situated in the sky above the city and other locations.

Having visualized a mass of rays streaming downward from that [vajra], like the conflagration at the end of an eon or the fire at the end of a yuga that burns away all the sins of sentient beings, one should thereafter perform the withdrawal; one should instruct and effect the entry of sentient beings into that vajra.
Furthermore, the emanation—the emergence from that vajra—should be performed as the practice.

How so? One should visualize the multitudes of sentient beings—whose bodies have been purified according to the sequence just described—as being characterized by the light of jewels such as rubies (*padmarāga*) and wish-fulfilling gems (*cintāmaṇi*), and whose bodily complexion is as clear as the radiance of a crystal gem. Having established them in their respective places, one should then bestow the consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

According to this tradition, one should meditate upon the array of Vairocana above the sky, joined with his consort, and consecrate the sentient beings with streams of bodhicitta flowing forth from him.

By means of this very "meditation-vajra" (dhyānavajra) just described for the purpose of pacification, even that which is difficult to fill becomes completely filled; its limbs become full. Thus, through the fruit of meditation, his body is nourished. He is the *Cintāmaṇi* (Wish-fulfilling Gem), namely Ratnasaṃbhava. His "glory" (*śrī*) is prosperity (*sampat*). He who possesses it is "the glorious *Cintāmaṇi*" (*cintāmaṇiśrīmān*). [He is] the "giver of garments" (*dānavastra*), meaning he possesses an excellence of giving; he "brings forth" (*prabhāvayati*) or manifests that. This is the explanation of the sixfold parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*) of the thirteenth chapter:
"The Manifestation of the Giver-Vajra" (*Dānavajraprabhāvaka*).
One should emanate—that is, meditate upon—that earth which serves as the support for sentient beings, [visualizing it] as Vairocana and as the host of Akṣobhya, well-consecrated.
Why is that? It is said:

for a period exceeding three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), that location, beginning with the city, is consecrated and protected by all the Buddhas. This aforementioned secret of the body—the protection of the body—is the unclouded and non-deceptive [teaching] of all the Buddhas.

"All diseases" refers to fevers and so forth; their "removal" is their pacification. Following that, the meditative absorption (samādhi) named after the arising of a body like a vajra is [the *vajrakāyasambhava*].

With the words "by the meditation-vajra" (*dhyānavajreṇa*) and so forth, [the text describes] the protective rite that constitutes a limb of the virtuous practice for beginners. By means of the meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—which consists of the undertaking of the protective rite through a meditated malevolent *kīla* (stake) at the four junctions of the day—at whatever place it may be, in a location favorable to the mind, one should begin the meditation and protective rite as will be explained. The yoga preceded by that is the meditative absorption; abiding by means of that meditative yoga and practicing the yoga of Vajrasattva and the others, one is empowered by one's own deities and attains oneness with them. Showing that meditative *kīla*, he says "vajra" and so forth.

One should visualize the Vajra, the Great King of Nectar, as Amṛtakuṇḍalin; that Vajrakīla has the form of a wrathful deity from the navel upward and the form of a spike below. One should drive and fix the stake—which is like a mass of sparks and flames—into the heads of the guardians of the ten directions, beginning with the east, who are the lords at the forefront of their respective mandalas, as well as into the heads of all other obstructors.

The world-subduers (*jagadvinayāḥ*) are the obstacles (*vighnāḥ*), so called because they lead—that is, cause—the world and its practitioners to undergo transformation through the planting of the tree of the mind and so forth. The "vajra" is the very pacification and eradication of those [obstacles], which, due to its indestructibility, is like a diamond (*vajra*).
One should contemplate—that is, meditate upon—the supreme, peaceful mandala situated in the center of the space-vajra, which is located within the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).

Having meditated correctly upon the form of Vairocana produced from the syllable *Oṃ* therein, one should place—that is, establish—the seeker (*arthin*), the object of accomplishment, within his heart.

Immediately thereafter, one should visualize the expanse of space, the hollow of the sky, as being completely filled and pervaded by the "foremost Locanās"—that is, multitudes of Vairocanas—who have entered into the great bliss with those foremost Locanās.

Having gathered together and unified all those who have entered into meditative absorption, one should cause that mass of light-rays, which is a flood of nectar, to fall upon the head of the afflicted person, thereby destroying all their defilements.

Then, having brought the patient down from the heart of the woman and freed him from defilement, the practitioner (*vratin*) should place him before himself upon a moon-maṇḍala. He should emanate (*spharet*) clouds of Buddhas from the openings at the tips of his own pores through the opening of his own *vajra*, entering [the patient] through the opening at the crown of his head;
how so?

By means of those [clouds], he covers—that is, fills—the hollow of space with the array of Vairocana. Furthermore, in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated that "vratī" is so called because of the etymological derivation: he covers or fills the expanse of the sky.
Then, at that time, while he is seated before him, the Buddha-clouds, having entered into union with their respective mudrās, bestow the consecration as before by means of streams of bodhicitta.

By this particular meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), *sa* signifies bliss (*sukha*); *ayaḥ* signifies that which has transcended the *samaya*, the mass of suffering; and *vajrasamaya* refers to that in which the *samaya*—the mass of suffering that is indestructible and difficult to cross—is [transcended].
The afflicted person, in an instant and without delay, becomes illustrious, with healthy limbs and a well-nourished body; he is so born.

The "clouds" are the assemblies of Vairocana and Locanā; the "array" (*vyūha*) is the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) within which that [absorption] is named. By the words beginning with "space-vajra," he briefly indicates two meditative absorptions:
one should meditate on the Maheśvara-maṇḍala situated within the *dharmodayā*.

Based on the statement, "Having meditated on the image as the Dharma-holder for the sake of the accomplishment of Ratnasaṃbhava," one should meditate on a fire-maṇḍala for the sake of the accomplishment of Amitābha. Within the heart of Ratnasaṃbhava and within the heart of Amitābha, one should place the supplicant and, as appropriate, the two objects to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
"One should fill the delightful realm of the space-element with those called Pāṇḍara"—
this statement is made with reference to the Amitābha-samādhi;
however, in the Ratnasaṃbhava-samādhi, it is stated that [one should fill it] with arrays of Māmakī who are yellow in color.

"Jewel" refers to gold and the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); "ruby" refers to the radiance of those two. One should gather—that is, unify—this [radiance] by means of a circle of rays through the power of the essence of light. This gathered duality of bodhicitta should be caused to descend, as before, into the body—the abode of the body, speech, and mind—of the practitioner who seeks the goal.
The practitioner, a yogin of Amitābha, should emit clouds of Ratnasambhava from the openings at the tips of the pores;
he should contemplate and emit clouds of Dharma, and bestow consecration. Thus, for one who has previously sat down, he should perform the consecration with clouds of jewels and clouds of Dharma.

By means of this aforementioned elaboration of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prapañca*), even that which is difficult to fill becomes completely filled; thus, the statement beginning with "for he" (*sa hi*) is for the purpose of [explaining] nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
Its meaning is as follows:

for he is the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) because he bestows the desired goal upon the practitioner (*sādhaka*), resembling a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*); and he is like a king because he is endowed with sovereignty and other such qualities.

The glorious Dharma Amitābha is called "Dānavajraprabhāsaka" because he illuminates—that is, makes radiant—the uninterrupted giving that is like a thunderbolt (vajra) for the sake of bestowing gifts (dāna). His "cloud" (megha) is a mass [of such gifts], and the "array" (vyūha) is the meditative attainment (samāpatti) of those; the samādhi in which this occurs is thus named.

Extracting [the passage] beginning with "Ratnamegha" and so forth from this context, the phrase "situated in the center of the space-element" has already been explained. Having meditated upon the wind-maṇḍala marked by a vajra and a crescent moon, within that [maṇḍala] one should meditate on the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Amoghasiddhi—[he who is] "Dharmāgra," meaning he before whom are Dharmavajra (Akṣobhya) and Dharma (Amitābha)—and having meditated on that, one should place the seeker, who desires the subjugation of all people, into the heart of that Amoghasiddhi.
One should meditate upon the desire-maṇḍala as being completely filled with Buddhas such as Vairocana and Bodhisattvas such as Maitreya, together with the mudrās of their respective families.
According to the distinct colors of the five Tathāgatas, one should cause the splendor—the stream of the fivefold bodhicitta—to fall upon that object of practice (*sādhya*).
Such a practitioner causes that very object of practice to become, at that very moment and without delay, beloved by all the Tathāgatas.

One who shines forth correctly, equal to and similar to Mañjuśrī, is called *saṃkāśa*; "pada" refers to sovereignty and so forth; one who performs action—that is, performs activity—therein becomes the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
As before, the five families of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, being delighted, bestow a great festival of consecration upon the noble-souled one seated in front;
to the question "What happens then? he says:

"Brings under control" (*vaśamānayati*) means that he, arisen from the entire world, having attained his emergence, brings [all] under his sway by mere sight—that is, by the simple act of seeing. "Jewel-pledge" (*ratnasamaya*) refers to the kings and ministers; their "assemblies" (*mevāḥ*) are their multitudes. The "array" (*vyūha*) formed by them constitutes the "service" (*paryupāsana*) to the path of the goal; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which possesses that name is called *Khavajradharmāgra*. Regarding the Akṣobhya-samādhi established therein, he states its remaining function in the passage beginning with "Space-vajra" (*khavajra*).

One who possesses the yoga of Akṣobhya should visualize the sky-vajra—the hollow expanse of space—as filled with cruel rākṣasas, yakṣas, and the like; with fierce enemies of others, those intent on destruction, the violent, those of unimpeded prowess, those terrible with wrath, those under the sway of anger, jackals, jackal-like beasts, and various flesh-eating beings; and with crows, vultures, and dogs. Then, one should visualize the enemy, the adversary, situated within a fiery maṇḍala, with his mouth wide open.
Having meditated that he is a benefactor to all Buddhas and all sentient beings, one should employ this yoga.
One should visualize that the entrails and other internal organs of the victim are drawn out and seized by all the *rākṣasa*s and others, who then devour them;

furthermore, one should visualize him being overwhelmed by those bearing various weapons and being cut into pieces. Then, if he is visualized and contemplated through this practice—whether he be a Buddha, a follower of the Buddha-vehicle, a Vajradhara, or a beginner—he will die or perish within a fortnight, or before the fortnight, or at the completion of the fortnight.
There is no doubt about this.
Vajramegha is Akṣobhya; his *samayas* are the rākṣasas and others. The *vyūha*, or manifestation, of these within a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is the samādhi bearing that name.

Furthermore, he describes the arrangement of the faces, arms, colors, and weapons of the very deities already mentioned, beginning with the words "three-faced," etc., thereby expressing the state of Vairocana.
One should meditate on that which has the luster of autumnal clouds, like a lotus stalk (*kamuda*) or a *śarada-kāṇḍa* (autumnal stalk).

It possesses three faces—white, black, and deep red. Among them, the white face is the central one; the black face is the right one; and the left face is deep red, the color of the *kusumbha* flower. Adorned with a crown of matted locks (*jaṭāmakuṭa*), such is the rule for the colors of the faces of Vairocana.
Likewise, one should meditate on the Holder of the Vajra, Akṣobhya, whose faces are black, red, and white.
One should meditate upon Amitābha, who is thus passionate, three-faced, adorned with a crown of matted locks, surrounded by a clear maṇḍala-circle amidst the turbulence of the world-system;
by meditating thus on these three deities,
one certainly succeeds in all rites of liberation.
One should visualize Vairocana and the others holding a vajra, a wheel, and a lotus in their right root hands;
one should visualize the vajra in the form of a six-armed mudrā,
bearing various weapons according to the sequence stated in the *sādhana*, and carrying their respective emblems.
Because it accomplishes auspicious and desired aims,
one should likewise visualize the primary seal of Ratnasambhava and the others;
one should contemplate Locanā as having three faces, like Vairocana, with the mudrā of Vairocana.

One should visualize the Great Queen Māmakī, the foremost consort, who desires the welfare of all beings and brings peace to all beings; she is the "Space-Vajra Leader" (khavajranetrī) because she leads Akṣobhya—the Space-Vajra—into her own presence; she has three faces and is to be visualized like Akṣobhya.

Vāgvajra is Amitābha; she who leads him is Vāgvajranetrī, Pāṇḍaravāsinī. One should meditate on her as being like Amitābha. She holds a lotus marked with a vajra, thus she is Vajrotpaladhara. One should meditate on the vidyā Tārā, the mudrā of Amoghasiddhi, as being like Amoghasiddhi in her face and other features.
From the passage beginning with "Yamāntaka" up to "the meditation maṇḍala," the meaning is easy to understand.

The dhyāna-maṇḍala, the ājñā-cakra, the mass of splendor (tejorāśi), the Jayoṣṇīṣa and other wrathful deities (krodhas), and those others who possess the wheel of mantras such as Maitreya and so forth—

these are "enjoyments of the pledge" (samayasambhogas) because they are enjoyed within the family at the time of the pledge. One should meditate upon each of them individually and separately by means of their respective symbols, such as the vajra and so forth.
The meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) of the mantras and deities,

which are immeasurable nectars (*amṛta*), have been fully proclaimed and described; therefore, for each individual wrathful deity (*krodha*) such as Yamāntaka and the rest, there are indeed meditative absorptions according to the various modes of their male servants (*ceṭa*), female servants (*ceṭī*), spirits (*bhūta*), and so forth.
Thereafter, because even the space-element becomes more extensive, the incalculability of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) has been explained.
Now, demonstrating the accomplishment of the perfected deity, he says "the space-element" (*khadhātu*), and so forth.

The space-element is luminosity (*prabhāsvara*); that which has become like it is the pure mandala of the three appearances, which is supreme because it does not depend upon the moon, vajra, and so forth.

Having thus manifested and accomplished the form of the Buddha as the Great Vajradhara, one should then manifest Vairocana and emanate him. How? He is clear like the moon because he is free from defects such as mist; he resembles the lunar orb, being peaceful and endowed with the quality of gentleness; he possesses a radiance equal to various rays, having a halo of light formed by five rays. Like a mirror—that is, a reflecting surface—he is born from that and resides within it; he is the ornament of the mouth of the three realms, for the triple world is like an ornament because he is endowed with the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*).

Having thus meditated upon and known oneself as adorned with all ornaments, one beholds and attains enlightenment—the non-abiding nirvāṇa—by means of this cultivation of the vajra-meditation; this is the yoga.

The majesty of the Buddha, the sovereignty of the Buddha, which brings all worlds under control and does not cause one to fall to the level of the Śrāvakas and others, is attained right here in this very life, remaining within this very body.

The samādhi in which the manifestation of Vairocana occurs through the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) is thus [described]; "the sphere of space" (*khadhātu*) and so forth refers to the threefold appearance of the vajra-maṇḍala, "the image of the Buddha" and so forth as previously explained.
The sixth [deity] has a pure body and is similar to that [deity], because he is slightly endowed with weapons;
he shall quickly attain the state of being fierce, peaceful, adamantine, aged, and light.

All the *samayas* are the deities of the maṇḍala; that in which they all arise is called "the source of all *samayas*" (*sarvasamayasaṃbhava*). Akṣobhya is the beautiful vajra; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which he resides is thus named.
"Space-vajra," and so forth,
refers to the three appearances of the dharma-maṇḍala; "the image of the Buddha," and so forth, is as described previously.

The indivisible triple body is Mahāvajradhara; having attained and obtained the majesty of the Dharma and mastery over speech arising from him— that is, produced from him— one who abides in the consecration of the completion stage becomes adorned by the ocean of gnosis.
Since that Amitābha, the Being of Dharma (*dharmasattva*), arises from the Great Vajradhara who is the source of the Being of the True Dharma (*saddharmasattva*), he is the "Arising of the Samaya.

That very [state] is the perfected stage (*pariniṣpannakrama*), which is the Vajra; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that exists is thus described as "the Sphere of Space" (*khadhātu*), and so forth.
The mandala characterized by the moon, the threefold appearance, the form of the Buddha, and so forth,
as previously described.

In the hand—the right hand, which is the principal one—is the jewel-wheel (*cakraratna*), the jewel that brings mastery over the three realms; the description of its nature is "the wisdom that effects all purification. For the practitioner himself, it has the luster of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and resembles the wish-fulfilling gem.
The *Locanā-samaya* refers to Locanā as the *mahāmudrā*. That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which her hand-tip—the essence of the hand—is the wheel (*cakra*) is so described.
"Space-vajra" and so forth refer to the moon-maṇḍala, which represents the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*).
"Buddhavimva" is as before;
Khavajrāgrī is Māmakī,
Khaṃ is Akṣobhya, and his wife is Samayāgrī.
In her right hand is a blue lotus suffused with red;
"of the three realms," and so forth, is an epithet of that very [lotus],
which is a secret belonging to the practitioners who are the Vajras of Accomplishment.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: "Kha" is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*); that which has "bhā" as its source is "khabhā," namely Akṣobhya.

"Ratnaraśmimegha" is a mass of jewel-rays; he whose vajra-nature is that [mass] is Ratnaraśmimeghavajra, i.e., Ratnaketu. The gladdening of those two is Māmakī; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which this occurs is named accordingly, beginning with "Khavajra," and so forth.

The *dharmamaṇḍala*, the three knowledges, the image of the Buddha, and so forth—as previously described—are characterized by illusion; thus, they are "characterized by illusion" (*māyālakṣya*). That very [state] is the "supreme" (*agra*) because it is the primary [reality], namely the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Therefore, "arisen from that which is characterized by illusion and supreme" means arisen from that which is characterized by illusion and is supreme.
Amitābha wears red garments; his beloved is the consort (iṣṭā);

his reality is the ultimate reality (paramārtha-tattva), which is itself perfect enlightenment (abhisaṃbodhi). Pāṇḍaravāsinī is the vajra of the vision of that [reality]. The meditative absorption (samādhi) in which this occurs is thus [named]; "space-vajra" and so forth.
The mandala of accomplishment, which is attained through wisdom and means, is the form of the Buddha, and so forth, as previously described;
this is the pledge of Amoghasiddhi.
Tārā is his chief wife, endowed with preeminent qualities; the meditative absorption (samādhi) in which she resides is thus named.
Now he describes the wrathful meditative absorption (*krodhasamādhi*) with the words "Space-vajra" and so forth.
That which is characterized by the solar disc, such as the light-radiance (*ālokābhāsa*) and so on, is the "Buddha-image," and so on, as previously explained.

The essence of fear is its core; that which takes hold of these is the *bhayamaṇḍala*. Visualizing Vairocana residing upon the crown of him who holds a sword in his primary right hand, the Vajrins are satisfied and rejoice. The practitioners—those who do no harm to others and so forth—are the wrathful ones (*krodha*). For all those wrathful ones who are Vajra-wisdom practitioners, their commitment (*samaya*) is the path that is beyond characteristics (*alakṣaṇīya*).

Yamāntaka is the radiating one; he is the Great Vajradhara by whom [the mandala] is rested upon—that is, brought to completion. Thus, "the radiance of the radiation of Yamāntaka" refers to Yamāntaka himself. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which there is the mental visualization (*cintā*) of his array (*vyūha*) is so named. "Space-vajra," etc., is as before.
The meditative absorption in which there is the accomplishment (*niṣpatti*) of the invincible vajra-array is likewise so named.
"Khavajña," and so forth, is as explained previously.
"Haya" refers to Hayagrīva;
that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which there is the manifestation or arrangement of his birth is thus described.
"O Khavajña," and so forth, is as before.
"Consisting of nectar" refers to Amṛtakuṇḍalin. He who grasps the "vajra," which is a specific mode of arising, is the "Vajrālaya-maṇḍala.
That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which there are three kinds of "vajra-eyes" is thus described.
"Khavajña," and so forth, is as explained previously.
"Kṛṣṇodadhi" means the ocean of wrath; his weapon is the staff-vajra (*daṇḍavajra*) by nature, thus he is the "Staff-Vajrin.
A staff marked with a vajra is a "staff-vajra" (*daṇḍavajra*); it is the foremost of commitments (*samaya*) because it is not to be transgressed.
That [samādhi] in which there is the supreme commitment (*samaya*) of the Vajra-staff is named after that;
it is the "Space-Vajra," the threefold manifestation, whose element is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*); the samādhi in which that very state (*pada*) is traversed is thus called.
Regarding the phrase "khavajra" and so forth:
*vidyā* refers to mundane accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*);
that which possesses a *cakra*, meaning a collection, of these is the *vidyā-cakra*, which one should cause to manifest.
Surrounded by vajra-flames, with a body embraced by the rays of the wheel,
and possessing uṣṇīṣas that move through the sky— their *cakra* is a collection;
because they are approached and worshipped by that [collection], it is called the *uṣṇīṣacakrasamaya*.
The *vidyādhara-samaya* is that which is joined with it; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that exists is so called.
According to the literal meaning.
"In the element of space," and so forth:
he whose body is cloud-colored is Meghavajrī;
Vajrasumbha is "prabhāvyate" (manifested) in that samādhi, which is thus described.
Having thus indicated the two types of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through the two-fold sequence, he concludes in the same manner, saying "cessation" and so forth:
cessation—such as death and the like—is brought about by the wheel of wrath, that is, by the meditative absorptions such as Yamāntaka;
by what [is it brought about]?
To the question of how that too should be performed by one who frequents the wheel of Buddhas and takes the wheel of deities as his object of focus, he says "samādhi" and so forth.

Preceded by taking *tathatā* as the object, there is the taking of the moon disc as the object; upon that, preceded by the placement of the seed-syllable (*bīja*), there is the taking of the vajra and so forth as the object;

and through the transformation of that, there is the taking of deities such as Mahāvajradhara as the object—these are the concentrations and vajra-knowledges that are accomplished and bear fruit from the vajra-maṇḍala, by means of taking the wheel of command (*ājñācakra*) as the object.
The term *neyārtha* refers to the Buddhas such as Vairocana and others; their "wheel" (*cakra*) is their assembly, and thus the "Buddha-wheel.
Those whose nature is to cultivate the conceptualization of this Buddha-wheel are the aggregates of form and so forth, who are the "cultivators of the Buddha-wheel" (*buddhacakraniṣevinaḥ*).
Their cessation is the entry into ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

"Wrath" (*krodha*) refers to the turning away from the ordinary body; he who possesses that very wheel as his weapon is one established in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*) of the Wrathful Wheel (*krodhacakra*).

Therefore, the vision of the emergence from the body consists of the vajra-knowledges of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). These internal vajra-knowledges of meditative absorption are accomplished for one who has emerged from the vajra-maṇḍala, which is the ultimate maṇḍala;
this is the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

"Vajra" refers to the Tathāgatas, the Samayas, Locanā and the others, the arrays (*vyūha*), and the Wrathful Deities. For the sake of their accomplishment, there is the cultivation of the reality-meaning (*tattvārtha*), which takes ultimate truth as its object. Preceded by that, awakening is the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*).
A collection of texts that expounds that [subject].
The Explanation of the Six Points in the Thirteenth Chapter of the *Pradīpoddyotana-Ṭīkā*.
The Fourteenth Chapter.

Now, the fourteenth chapter is introduced to demonstrate that the expansion of ritual activities, such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, should be performed in accordance with the fourfold systems of mantra-exposition.
Therein, first, the sequence of the expansion of rituals is brought down from the *Tantra* for explanation:
"One should perform the rite of pacification (*śāntika*) and that of nourishment (*paiṣṭika*) during the bright fortnight."
One should commence rites for subjugation, malevolent magic, and so forth during the dark fortnight.
Facing north, one performs rites of pacification and nourishment; facing east, likewise, rites of wrath;
facing south, rites of fierce action; and facing west, rites of subjugation and attraction.
Thus, killing is performed in the southeast, the act of inciting hatred in the northeast,
the displacement from one's position in the northwest, and immobilization occurs in the northeast.
In rites for pacification, the color is white; in rites for enrichment, yellow;
for subjugation and attraction, red; and for killing, black.
Peaceful rites are performed with a mind of loving-kindness; nourishing rites with a joyful mind;
subjugation with a mind of passion; and killing with a mind of wrath.
One should perform rites for pacification (śāntika) at dusk, and likewise rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) at dawn;
rites for subjugation (vaśya) and malevolent magic (abhicāruka) should be performed at midday and at midnight.
However, for one established in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), the distinction is that one should perform rites such as pacification (*śāntika*) by relying on the time of midday.
As stated by the Blessed One in the Explanatory Tantra (*vyākhyātantra*):
Vajrapāṇi said:
“Blessed One, what is meant by ‘the internal time’?
The Blessed One replied:
“Vajrapāṇi, that which is called the ‘internal time’ is the subtle empowerment of the bodhicitta, the most secret of all secrets.”
Knowledge leads to the liberation of sentient beings in the accomplishment of the success of mantras,
as well as in the rites of pacification and enrichment, and likewise in subjugation and malevolent magic.
The Blessed One is ungraspable and peaceful; the realm of the mind is the Tathāgata.
The commentary on the six points of the fourteenth chapter: Just as fragrance exists within a flower, so does [the nature] abide in the heart of sentient beings;
one should dwell for the duration of half a watch, following the sequence in due order.
"In the circles of Agni, Vāyu, Mahendra, and Varuṇa,
[the colors] are, in brief, red, black, yellow, and white respectively."
By this it is meant:
the Varuṇa-maṇḍala resides in the heart-lotus.
At the time of its rising, a white-colored ray of light issues forth and remains for half a watch (ardhayāma).
Then one should perform the Great Peace (mahāśānti).
The Māhendra-maṇḍala resides in the secret lotus.
At its arising, yellow-colored rays of light emerge and remain for half a watch (ardhayāma).
Then one should perform the rite for enrichment (pauṣṭika).
The fire-maṇḍala resides in the throat-lotus;
at its rising, a red ray of light emerges and remains for half a watch (ardhayāma).
Then one should perform the rite of subjugation and attraction (*vaśyākarṣaṇa*).
The wind mandala is situated at the navel lotus.
At its rising, a ray of dark-blue light emerges and remains for half a watch (*ardhayāma*).
At that time, one should perform fierce rites (*raudrakarman*).
Now, the chapter is introduced,
beginning with "Then," and so forth.
"All Tathāgatas" refers to Akṣobhya and the others; "pledges" (samayas) refers to the goddesses;
their sovereign is Mahāvajradhara.
*Śānti* is the pacification of fever and other ailments.
That which attains this is *śāntisamaya*. It is precisely that [which is referred to] as "the supreme" (*ayaḥ*) because of its distinction.

Having entered—that is, having attained—the specific meditative state (*samādhi*) named after that [mantra], all the Tathāgatas, who are the practitioners (*sādhakas*), caused the *dhāraṇī* to be held by the consort to issue forth and manifest from their own body, speech, mind, and garments, which were united as one.
The mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and so forth is known as the "Sarpa" (Snake).
And it is said in the *Vajroṣṇīṣa*: "That which is joined with the syllable Oṃ at the beginning and joined with Svāhā at the end..."
All this should be understood by practitioners of mantra in rites for pacification.
The meaning of mantra, as indicated by its designation, must be explained. For example:
because the letters *ā*, *u*, and the *anusvāra* consist of the three vajras, the syllable *oṃ* is used for the acquisition of merit.
*Ruru*: the abode of the mantra-deity. *Ru* means "shine forth"; *sphura*, "cause to shine.
*Sphura*, "throb" (in the sense of manifesting). *Jvala*, "be exceedingly radiant. Be full of splendor.
"Remain, having fulfilled all hopes.
"Siddhalocanā" refers to her whose eye or vision is perfected and unimpeded;
this is an address.
"O Sarvārthasādhani, svāhā!"—this is the seed-syllable that kindles peace (*śānti*).
Here, for the purpose of kindling peace, the mantra must be interwoven (*vidarbhaṇa*).
How so?
"O Svāhā, perform the pacification for [Name]!
In this regard, the syllables of the mantra, as well as the flowers, perfumes, and so forth, should be visualized as being exclusively white in color.

When this dhāraṇī is merely sung or merely uttered, all beings who possess the wisdom of complete prosperity and who desire health—recalling the Buddha-vajra Vairocana—become satisfied, joyful, and delighted, and they attain, have attained, and continue to attain one-pointedness of mind.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, the Buddhas are considered to be the practitioners (*sādhakas*); she is the mother who generates peace for them. She is not merely the mother who generates peace; rather, through the distinctions of exhortation, caste, and intention, she is the accomplisher of all rites. Because she revives the dead, the power of the mantra is called "the reviver of the dead" (*mṛtasaṃjīvanī*). Vajrasamaya is Vairocana.
"He impels that" refers to the *dhāraṇī* of the Vajra-samaya-impeller; thus says Mahāvajradhara—this being the statement of the compiler (*saṃgītikāra*).
"Now," and so forth, refers to the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara.
The "three bodies" (*trikāya*) are the triple world (*vaidhātuka*).
Because he approaches and follows that [reality], he is the Wrathful One of the Three-Body Vow (trikāyasamaya).
He is the indivisible vajra; the Blessed One is the Wrathful Vajra of the Three-Body Vow.
Phenomena (bhāva) are obstacles; their non-existence is "the absence of phenomena" (bhāvābhāva).

His *samaya* is its non-transgression; that itself is the *vajra*. Having entered and taken as an object the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that, Vajradhara—the destroyer of all the wicked, the holder of all *vajras*—emitted from the *vajras* of his own body, speech, and mind his chief consort, who is like a chief queen and the foremost among all *dhāraṇīs*.
"Oṃ" and so forth: "sarpa" [is the word].
"Oṃ" has the meaning already explained.
"Śaṅkare" means "O bringer of peace.
"Ghuṭṭini" is an address;
"ghuṭṭi" means "strike," which is an exhortation.

*Śama* means "pacification"; she is *Śaṅkarā* because she pacifies the wicked. Immediately after the pacification of the wicked, she is the *Śāntikarā* (Bringer of Peace). *Ghuṭṭa*, destroy the wicked!
*Ghuṭṭi* means "striking down."
*Ghuṭṭini*: [a term] for the destruction of the wicked; the repetition is due to extreme urgency.
*Ghātaya*: destroy! *Nāśaya*: annihilate! [The root] *hana* is used in the sense of harming.
In this context, one should interpose the mantra "Protect, protect [so-and-so]! preceded by *svāhā*.
Then, regarding the passage beginning with "In this...

and so forth: all sentient beings are the three vajras; those practitioners who possess a body that is an indivisible vajra through them are the "possessors of the indivisible vajra of the three vajras. With eyes like blue lotuses blooming with joy, they meditated while recollecting the Vajra-mind, Akṣobhya.
That very [mudrā] is protection against Māris and others because it is indestructible like a vajra;
in its applications, which primarily consist of protection, it constantly and always brings about the accomplishment of the three bodies (trikāya).

Moreover, for those afflicted and oppressed by the fear of the Great Vajra and the fear of obstructors (*vighna*) and leaders of obstacles (*vināyaka*), this *dhāraṇī* is remembered as that which constantly bestows strength and the power to conquer obstacles.
This very *dhāraṇī* belongs also to those of the Jewel Family (*ratnakula*), because Māmakī is common to both families. Thus begins the passage starting with "Then," and so forth.

The Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, Amitābha, who is the pledge (*samaya*) of great passion, entered the meditative absorption called "the observation of the pledge of great passion" (*mahārāgasamayāvalokana*). Having brought this concentration to manifestation, he emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the *dhāraṇī*— which must be specifically upheld as the foremost consort among the goddesses of the Lotus family who constitute the body of the Dharma-pledge (*dharmasamayakāya*)—
beginning with "Oṃ," and so forth.
*Kaṭe* means in a harsh existence; *atitīkṣṇapoṣaṇokaḍha* (?); *kṛcchrajīvane* means in a life of hardship; *vikaṭe* means in a particularly difficult existence;
*nikaṭe* means near to the practitioner; *kaṭaṃkaṭe* means in an extremely harsh existence.
Here, the mantra is to be interlaced (*vidarbhaṇa*) as follows: preceded by the utterance of *svāhā*, [one says] "Perform the nourishment (*puṣṭi*) of so-and-so, *vauṣaṭ*!"
"Then," and so forth.

Those who practice the supreme conduct of Vajradharma—those who have resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in the Lotus family—recalling Vajradharma and focusing upon Abhitābha, entered into meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), that is, they attained one-pointedness of mind.
[This practice] brings about the increase of great wealth and grain.
Dharma consists of generosity and so forth; nourishment is the nourishment of the body; and strength is vigor in action.
All of this is accomplished by mere recitation, by merely chanting it—how much more so when it has been mastered?
Just as the word of Vāgvajra brings about the accomplishment of one's intended aim, so it is for the practitioner.
"Then," and so forth:

the Blessed One Vajradhara, who arises as Samantasamaya (the Universal Pledge), that is, Amoghasiddhi, having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after him, emitted from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind this *dhāraṇī*—the foremost consort among the beings of that pledge, Amoghasiddhi, who belong to the Amogha family, and who is to be specifically maintained.
Oṃ, the meaning is understood. She is Tārā because she carries one across the ocean of suffering; she is Tuttārā because she protects one from distress.
*tud* means "to strike" or "to cause pain";
*trai* means "to protect";
*tvarā* means "acting quickly."
*Tura* means "to hasten.
These three words are used in the vocative.
One should perform the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) of the mantra by placing [the name] preceded by *svāhā*, such as: "Bring so-and-so under control; go forth! (or *nirgaccha*).

“Then,” and so forth. All the Buddhas—Amoghasiddhi and those born of him, who are inseparable from him—being delighted and satisfied in mind, while recollecting and meditating upon the Vajra-body Amoghasiddhi, attained *jñāna*, which is one-pointedness of mind.

These Buddhas, the preeminent persons; these Vajras, whose hearts are firm; these great armies, the kings—they bring the realm of sentient beings, the common light, under their control on all sides and in every way, like servants.

"The Blessed One said that he makes all those not mentioned here— those who are necessarily subject to accomplishment, those who are motionless, and those who are supremely submissive— at that very moment, immediately; thus says the compiler of the collection," beginning with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth.
With the words "The Blessed One," and so forth, he speaks to Mahāvajradhara:
"Vimalaraśmi" means white light; a mass of that is a "cloud of stainless rays" (*vimalaraśmimegha*). That which is as indestructible as a vajra is "Vimalaraśmimeghavajra," namely Vairocana.
Because it brings about that [result], the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is also described in that way.
One should emanate from one’s own body, speech, and mind-vajras this Vajra Wrath named Vajrayamāntaka, having entered into that [absorption].
At the time of reciting the mantra, "Homage to the Vajras of the Body, Speech, and Mind of All" (*namaḥ samantakāyavākcittavajrāṇām*), it should be recited by the practitioners of mantra.

The mantra beginning with *oṃ* and so forth—*kha kha khāhi khāhi*—is the incitement of Yamāntaka toward the devouring of the wicked. It is an address to the subduer of all wicked beings: "O you who hold a sword, mace, axe, and noose in your hands; four-armed, four-faced, and six-legged! Come, come! O destroyer of the lives of all wicked beings, slayer of great obstacles, deformed-faced one, terrifier of all spirits, you who utter the loud *aṭṭāṭṭa* laugh, you who are clothed in a tiger skin! This is found in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*.
Kuru kuru all rites! Chinda chinda all mantras! Bhinda bhinda the supreme mudrā! Ākarṣaya ākarṣaya all spirits! Matha matha, nirmatha nirmatha all the wicked!
Praveśaya praveśaya into the center of the maṇḍala! Thus is the incitement.
"O destroyer of the life of Vaivasvata!
Vaivasvata is Yama;
you are the one who brings about the destruction of his life, thus you are Vaivasvatājīvitāntakara. Perform, perform all my tasks! Accomplish, accomplish! Burn, burn! Reduce all sins to ashes!"
Reduce to ashes!
Cook, cook all evils!
Do not delay, do not delay; do not waste time!
The time has come! Remember the command of Vajrasattva!

HŪṂ HŪṂ—threaten the obstructors! PHAṬ PHAṬ—shatter the obstructors! SPHOṬAYA SPHOṬAYA—rend asunder the obstructors! VIDĀRAYA—tear apart all obstructors! NĀŚAYA—destroy all enemies! KARA KARA—having cut through the obstructors, scatter them in the ten directions! O fulfiller of all hopes! HE HE BHAGAVAN—thus is the invocation.
Why do you delay? For what reason do you linger?
Accomplish and bring to completion all my purposes and all my tasks.
"SVĀHĀ [preceded by] 'ATTRACTION OF SO-AND-SO, HŪṂ'—this is the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) of the mantra.

Then, as soon as this king of mantras was spoken, all the Buddhas, because they were known as the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) and as those to be tamed, and Śakra and the other world-protectors of great renown, became afraid, bewildered, their minds terrified and agitated; recollecting the Vajra-mind, the Great Vajradhara, they went for refuge.

One who possesses the Vairocana-yoga, having taken a flawless skull-cup of beautiful form belonging to a woman—one that is wise and pleasing to the mind—should draw the likeness of the woman upon its back with lac juice and inscribe her name-syllables in the region of the heart.

With his left foot, which is pressed down by Yamāntaka and empowered by a vajra-hook arisen from the syllable *hūṃ* atop a solar disc, he should stand in the *ālīḍha* posture and trample [the figure]. Piercing the heart with that hook, he should visualize the desired woman being drawn forth and recollect this mantra; one should utter it while enraged. Then, what happens? He says:
"Locanā," and so forth:
Locanā is a Brāhmaṇa girl; Māmakī is a Kṣatriya girl; Mahāvajrā refers to queens and ministers; "of their noble lineage" means a woman of their family.
Having recited the nāla-mantra three times at the three junctions of the day according to one's ability, she is certainly summoned within a moment or, at the latest, within seven days.

"One who desires to summon a person should draw the *piṇḍa*; the specific procedure for one desiring to summon a man is as follows: having drawn a likeness of the man upon a human skull according to the method just described, one should step upon it with the *pratyālīḍha* stance and summon him.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Mind-Vajra, the Great Vajradhara.
"Then," and so forth:
Vairocana is the Tathāgata;

Mahāvajradhara is Samaya, who is Amoghasiddhi. His rays are emerald-colored lights; by them, the "going" is pervaded—the form of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), which is also the meditative absorption (samādhi) due to their non-differentiation.

Having thus entered that meditative absorption, Amṛtasamaya Amoghasiddhi should emanate from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind—which consist of the wrathful vajra born from that [absorption]—the [deity] whose nature is the wrathful Vajra;
the meaning of "namaḥ samanta... and so forth has already been explained, while the mantra beginning with "om" and so forth follows.

The invocation beginning with "Amṛtakuṇḍali," followed by "kha kha khāhi khāhi tiṣṭha tiṣṭha bandha bandha hana hana daha daha garja garja visphoṭaya visphoṭaya sarvavighnavināyakān mahāvajrakrodha mahādaṃṣṭrautkaṭa bhairavāya asimusalaparaśupāśahastāya mahāgaṇapatijīvitāntakarāya," is recited; then the insertion (*vidarbhaṇa*) of the mantra is performed with "svāhā" at the beginning, followed by the name of the person [e.g., *amuka*], then "uccāṭaya," and finally "hūṃ.
This is Vajrakāya Amoghasiddhi.

All the mantras presiding over expulsion meditated upon that [Vajrapāṇi]. Even when their applications were employed, they were difficult to accomplish due to the adamantine nature of suffering. When the rite of expulsion was to be performed according to the procedure taught in the ritual manual (*kalpa*), the Buddhas, who are skilled in the expansion of activities, should themselves—while in the yoga of Amoghasiddhi—expel their army, that is, their host, and cause them to fall from their position.

In this sequence, having combined black mustard oil, poison, thorn-apple juice, and blood from the ring finger, one should draw a wind-mandala in the shape of a half-moon marked with vajras on both sides upon a cloth from a cremation ground; then, having inscribed the syllables of the name of the person to be targeted in its center and performed the invocation, one should step upon it and bury it in the cremation ground as before—it will certainly cause [the target] to be driven away.

The Blessed One is the Jewel; he whose crest-banner (ketu) or flag is the jewel of reality is the Tathāgata Ratnaketu, the Great Vajradhara. He is the source from which the jewel-like radiance of the Buddhas arises. Because it is indivisible, that [reality] is a vajra; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces it is also called by that name because it is indivisible. Having entered into that absorption and brought it before him, he should emit from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind the great wrathful deity Vajrāparājita, who is of the nature of mantra. The meaning of "Namaḥ" and so forth is already explained. "Oṃ" and so forth is the wrathful mantra.
This is its meaning: *Oṃ* has the meaning already stated;
*hūṃ* is for threatening; *ajapya* means "O Conqueror"; *riṭiṭa* is for addressing; [the phrase] "crush the obstacles" (*vighnān cūrṇaya*) follows; and *hūṃ phaṭ* has an understood meaning.
"Vimocaya amukam rākṣasādibhyaḥ svāhā hrīḥ"— this is the *vidarbhaṇa*.
The "Buddhas" are so called because they are intended by the practitioner as those to be restrained,
and because they are endowed with heroic power (*vīrya*).

The high-souled ones, terrified and with minds trembling with fear, meditated while recollecting the jewel-born *bodhicitta*. As for the flesh-eating *rākṣasas*, the fierce beasts such as lions, and the cruel adversaries—

amidst these tormentors and in a place filled with great terror and crowded with fears of fire, snakes, and the like— one should perform, or cause to be performed, the rite of protection according to the rule prescribed in the *Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana* as taught in the ritual manual.

The Mind-Vajra is the Great Vajra-Holder; he by whom [Ratnasambhava] is employed or impelled is thus "employed by the Mind-Vajra. Having taken recourse to the meditative absorption (samādhi) of Ratnasambhava, the intention is: "Command Aparājita! Herein is the procedure:

One who possesses the yoga of Ratnasaṃbhava, having meditated on two sun-maṇḍalas through the transformation of two long *hūṃ* syllables in his two palms, and having commanded Aparājita to seize the bodies of those to be converted who have been seized by *rākṣasas* and the like, he should visualize the *rākṣasas* and others being drawn forth and situated between the two suns; then, burning them with the rays of the sun and reducing them to ashes, he should recite the mantra, and [the victim] becomes restored to health.

He who arises within that samādhi is Amitābha; having taken as his objective support that samādhi called the "Vajra of Boundless Arising," Padma Amitābha—Hayagrīva, who arises from him—should emit that great wrathful one, whose essence is mantra, from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind.
The meaning of the components beginning with *namaḥ* has already been analyzed;
the mantra begins with *oṃ*.

Because he threatens the bodies, speech, and minds of wicked beings with *tri-hūṃ*, he is the "Crosser" (*taru*); because he takes up (*lāti*) the crossing over (*taraṇa*) of all calamities, he is *tarula*.
Because he destroys (*ru* = *bhaṅga*) the transformations (*vī* = *vikārāḥ*) by taking them up, he is *virula*.
He is the destroyer of all poisons because he neutralizes the poisons of both stationary and moving beings;

he is accompanied by hands that hold blazing sparks, lamps, and fire; he is accompanied by the sound of loud, boisterous laughter; and he is a lion, the king of beasts, whose "mane" (saṭā) is a magnificent display like that of a lion's mane—those long hairs hanging from its shoulders—and he possesses such a majestic display.

O you who cause the surface of the earth to tremble by the striking of your diamond hooves; O you by whom the surface of the earth is shaken by the blow of your diamond hooves; O you by whom the mountain ranges are tossed upward by the wind of your breath—that is, the wind from your nostrils—by which the mountains are lifted up;
O you of terrifying, loud, boisterous laughter; O you of immeasurable strength and prowess—these are the vocative epithets, which are easy to understand.

The noble host of the terrified spirits: the Tathāgatas are "noble" (ārya), and because they are counted by them, they are the "noble host" (āryagaṇa). The "terrified spirits" (bhītabhūtagaṇa) refers to those hosts of spirits such as the asuras who are frightened and trembling. Through the awakening of both the enlightened and the unenlightened, there is an impelling: "O Hayagrīva! Eat! Devour all the wicked! Cut! Cut!
Bestow success upon me! Command! [Subdue] all fevers and piśācas!"
Be unimpeded among all the seizing spirits, O Vajradaṃṣṭra; why do you delay?
Shake, shake, and cause this evil seizing spirit or evil serpent to tremble!
"Roll it over!
Crush it, crush it! Destroy it! Perform the ritual as authorized by the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha!"—thus he urges [the practitioner].
When [the opponent] does not act, then, having stated his own form, [he recites]: "Phaṭ to Hayagrīva! Phaṭ to Vajra! Phaṭ to Vajramātṛkā!"

*Phaṭ* to Vajranetra, *phaṭ* to Vajradaṃṣṭra, *phaṭ* to Vajrakhura, *phaṭ* to Vajrakhuranirghātana—*phaṭ* to the Terrifier of the Three Worlds, *phaṭ* to the Unobstructed in All Actions, *phaṭ*—churn, churn! To the One who Inspires Terror in the Vajra Family of the Fourteenth Chapter, *phaṭ*! *Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*! Thus the Blessed One threatens Hayagrīva.
Having thus threatened [the obstacle], one consoles [the deity] at the end with the sound "svāhā.

For it is stated in the *Vajrāmṛta*: "The utterance of 'svāhā' belongs to Māmakī and bestows all accomplishments. Thus, one should interweave the mantra: "Remove the poison and so forth of [Name]! HŪṂ!"

Hayagrīva and the others—the obstacles to be subdued by him—attained one-pointedness of mind while recollecting and meditating upon Vajrarāja Amitābha. [They wondered: "How can the space-realm, the hollow of the sky, be filled with poison? Even if it were so, how could the vajra be impenetrable, even by the specific poison Hālāhala?"
It renders all that poisonless through the impelling and incitements of the Wrathful King;
herein lies the instruction.

Having ascertained that the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) consists of the three truths, one should fill the body of the *sādhya* with rays from the Samādhisattva situated upon the moon in his heart and thus incinerate the poison. Then, having visualized a white syllable *haṃ* upon a moon on the palm of the right hand, and having placed the mantra *oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ saḥ* upon the joints and fingers of the hand, one should meditate—beginning from the head—that the poison, appearing blue, descends and becomes void by means of a dense stream of droplets projected by white rays. By the falling of the fingernails accompanied by the recitation of the mantra, one removes the poison.

Amoghasamaya is Amoghasiddhi; his manifestation (*saṃbhava*) is himself the banner (*ketu*), the insignia (*dhvaja*), the indivisible sign. Having entered that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which bears that name, he should cause this King of Wrathful Deities, Nīladaṇḍa, to emerge from his own body and so forth.
The mantra beginning with *om* and so forth is for the purpose of manifesting [him] through the words "Homage" (*namaḥ*) and so on.
"Ehyehi" is the call;
"Bhagavan Nīlavajradaṇḍa" is the address;
"Turu turu hulu hulu" is for the purpose of urging haste.
"Hā hā! is the exclamation; "gulugulu," "torment," "gulāpaya," "gulāpaya," and "with your retinue, cause them to be tormented."
"Krama krama" is an encouragement;
"kramu" means taking a step; "bhagavan" is an address to the Blessed One; and "vāyuvegena" means with the speed of the wind.
Quickly burn, burn the beings! Reduce them to ashes! Tear, tear! Rend them! Carry them away, carry them away! Slay them!
Cook, cook! Make them choke! Churn, churn! Roll them over, roll them over! Cast them down, cast them down! Place them below!

Maṭa maṭa! Destroy! Moṭāpaya moṭāpaya! Destroy the retinues! Chinda chinda! Cut asunder all rites! Destroy, destroy the uprooting spells and other such acts employed by enemies! Nāśaya nāśaya! Destroy, destroy!

Consume, consume the fat of this victim! His blood! O you who delight in fat, marrow, grease, and blood, come, come, O Blessed One! [Destroy] all obstacles, all ignorance and the like, all mantras, all root-rites, artificial poisons and the like, and all seizing spirits! Bind, bind! Strike, strike! Break, break! Crush, crush! Grind, grind! Accomplish this task—this which is desired, this very thing that is spoken of! Sādhaya! (Accomplish it!)
With the syllable *hūṃ* as an imitation-sound, he threatens:
"O Blue One, O Blue Vajra-staff! *Turu turu*, be swift! Destroy, destroy the obstructors and Vināyakas!
*Huru huru*, be ready!"
To the blazing and fierce one, for the sake of exceeding wrath: "Pierce the hearts of all enemies! Cut! Cut! O destroyer of the spells of others! Cut the spells of others!"—up to this point.
*Hūṃ* is the seed-syllable that illuminates that;
O performer of the remainder of the spells, remember the pledge (*samaya*), the word of Vajradhara!

Cut through the vital points! HŪṂ! Impel! Kill! Kill! Burn! Burn! Speed! Speed! Huru! Huru! PHAṬ PHAṬ! HŪṂ HŪṂ! To Kṛtānta, to Yama, the terrifier of divine sages, kill! kill! with the vajra-staff! SVĀHĀ!
The interlacing [of the mantra] is: *svāhā* first, then *amukaṃ māraya phaṭ phaṭ*. Now, beginning with "thus," there arise the sounds of obstacles produced by the foremost of all evil beings.
The rest is easy to understand:
by reciting this king of wrathful mantras eight hundred times according to the ritual prescribed in the *kalpa*, it becomes the slayer of all malevolent beings.

"Krama" refers to the ritual application (*prayoga*), which is the impelling of the deity through the thorough understanding of the mantra's meaning and so forth.
