Herein is the procedure: on a cloth from a cremation ground, one should draw a sixteen-spoked wheel with a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) upon it, and within its hub (*varaṭaka*), a fire-mandala, using these substances—mustard seeds, salt, oil, poison, and the juice of *dhattūra*. Having first performed the invocation, one should insert [the mixture] into the heart of an effigy (*puttalikā*), accompanied by the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).

Having fashioned that [image] from the clay of an anthill on both banks [of a river], mixed with the dust of the tree to be targeted and combined with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), one should place it within a hollowed-out skull-cup.
Then, at midday or at midnight, having stepped upon it with the left foot, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times; [the target] will die.
If it does not perish, then one should grind it into powder with three skull-cups, place the apparatus upon it, and heat it with a fire of funeral-pyre wood;
when it is seized by a burning fever,
one should throw that very apparatus into the fire.
Then, he dies immediately.
"Then," and so forth:
the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, who abides through the transformation of Vajradhara, possesses the glory of clouds raining down from all sides; thus he is "Samantameghaśrī.
That which brings about his great power is likewise called by that name, because the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces it is non-different from him.
Having brought that Mahābala to mind, one should emanate him from one's own body and so forth;
"Namaḥ" has its meaning already explained,
while the mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and so on follows.
He who has a fierce and sharp trident in his hand is thus [described];
he whose roar is like that of a lightning bolt is thus [described].
"Svāhā! Let fall a stream of rain!"—this is the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) with the mantra.
The meaning of "atha" and so forth has already been explained.
Regarding "japa" and so forth:
by means of the practice of reciting [the mantra] one hundred and eight times, one should accomplish the various rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) through those respective applications.
Having pacified drought, rain, and the obstruction of rain, he causes a downpour of rain.
This is the procedure:

having drawn the eight nāgas upon an eight-petaled lotus on a cloth from a cremation ground using substances for sorcery (*abhicāruka*), one should enclose their hearts and heads with the mantra *hūṃ naṃ hūṃ*. Then, in the center of the pericarp, one should place [the mantra]: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ vajradhara ājñāpayati sarvanāgā varṣadhārām utsṛjanti hrīḥ svāhā*.
Again, having similarly drawn a second yantra and forming an enclosure, one should cast it into the heart of the effigy after first performing the invocation;
by this procedure one should have the effigy made.

Indeed, with clay from both riverbanks mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and smeared with substances for malevolent rites (abhicāruka), one should heat it in the cremation-ground fire while reciting the mantra.
The nāgas cause the downpour of rain.
"Then," and so forth:

he whose vajra-thunder is a resonance pervading all directions is Samantanirghoṣavajra, namely Ṭakkirāja; the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces him is also called by that name because it is non-different [from him].
Having brought that [absorption] into manifestation, the "Ṭakki of all Tathāgatas" is so called because he binds those obstructors who are highly precious to all Tathāgatas.
The verbal root *ṭakk* means "to bind";
since he is the primary one, he is the King.
He emitted that Great Wrathful One, whose nature is mantra, from his own body and so forth.
The meaning of the case endings in "nama" and so forth has already been explained.
The mantra "ṭakki hūṃ jaḥ" is known as the "Extraction" (uddhāra). As it has been said: "That which lacks 'svāhā' and the vowel 'au' is called an extraction."
Thus,
"Ṭakki" is an address meaning "O evil binder," and "Hūṃ" is a threat to the wicked.
*Jaḥ*: an impelling for the exit of the wicked;
*Amukam ākarṣaya hrīḥ*: the interlacing (*vidarbhaṇa*) of the mantra; then, etc.
All the Buddhas, having become the obstacles to be accomplished, are the sons of the Great Being; possessing great supernatural powers,
they are terrified and utterly alarmed.
Meditating upon the Vajra-body Mahāvajradhara, they attained the *samaya* known as the King Ṭakki; that is, they reached it through their realization.
Regarding the phrase "the *liṅga*" and so forth:

having drawn the *liṅga*—the image of the victim—upon the ground with chalk (*girikā*), and having inscribed the name in the region of the heart, the yogin, established in the *samādhi* of Vajradhara and preceded by the invocation of consciousness (*vijñāna-āvāhana*), should step upon it with his right foot empowered by the Vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*). This is the mantra-wheel of the three vajras, which is the mantra of the King Ṭakki.
By reciting that [mantra] one hundred and eight times, the summoning of all the kings of mantras and so forth shall be accomplished.
Now, regarding the phrase "and so forth":
the *Jñānamālāmbuvajra* is the immovable [deity], and the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that produces it is likewise so called because of its non-difference from it.
Having brought that [mantra] to mind, the Blessed One emitted from his own body and so forth this *acalavajrasamaya*, which consists of mantra,
beginning with "namaḥ" and so on; the meaning of these words has already been explained, while the mantra beginning with "acala" is as follows.
This mantra is called *kavandha*; it contains "svāhā" but lacks the *praṇava*. It is known as *kavandha* and is taught in all ritual procedures as well as in the *Vajroṣṇīṣa*.
Thus, in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, the meaning of the mantra is explained.

He is "Immovable" (*acala*) because he cannot be shaken by obstacles; he is "One-eyed" (*kāṇa*) because he produces blindness in obstacles; he is "Fierce" (*caṇḍa*), "Wrathful" (*krodhana*), "Dancer" (*naṭṭa*), "Destroyer" (*śātana*), and "Cutter" (*chedana*).
In the case of eating at night, a reversal of the colors is to be observed: *maṭṭaḥ* becomes *mattaḥ*.
The root *madi* means "joy";
here too there is a reversal of the phonemes,
[resulting in] *moṭṭi*, meaning "of large body."
*Saṭṭaḥ* means one who causes despondency or destruction; *ṣaḍḍu* means in the sense of causing despondency;
*taṭṭaḥ* means one who causes ruin.

O Destroyer, slay him, slay him! Burn him, burn him! Delude him, delude him, O Causer of Delusion! Laugh, laugh, perform the vajra-laugh! Be victorious, be victorious, O Mandaraṭ! Roar, roar! Bind him, bind him, with the binding [mantra] *ṇaha*!
Stay, stay! Stay to carry out my commands;
enter, enter the body of the sādhya as a petitioner—this very great mantra is the garland-mantra (mālā-mantra).
Because he accomplishes that purpose, he is the Immovable One (Acala), the protector of the great mantra;
*dhuna dhuna*—shake, shake! *kampaya kampaya*—cause to tremble, cause to tremble!
Three, three, sharp and pungent, he leads; three, eat, eat the obstacles! Kill, kill the wicked! Devour, devour!
Perform, perform! Kuru, kuru!
Kiri, kiri! Scatter the body of the one to be accomplished;
cause a great poison-like vajra-explosion within the bodies of the wicked, shatter it, and bring it forth!

Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ is the word of exhortation; the three folds are the triple world itself, which is the stage for the dance. Upon that, the dancer is Aṃ Āṃ for bringing [the deity] and Hāṃ Hāṃ for addressing [him].
O Acala servant, messenger of Vajradhara! Shatter, shatter! Perform the rending, perform it! Hūṃ hūṃ! Those who are not near, those who are not close—*trāṭ*!
O you of great power, shatter them! Strike down and cut asunder the mantras and spells of others!
Āṃ for commanding; hāṃ for addressing. Having attained [this], may the world be purified, may it become sanctified;
may the Vajrin be pleased, may the Vajrins be pleased; homage to those of unopposed power, to the ten powers.
Blaze up! Inflame! Trāt! Shatter!
O Unbearable One, [destroy] all afflictions!
"Those who cannot be overcome are the Asahas, the Tathāgatas; to them, homage, svāhā!
Regarding "atha" and so forth:
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, together with their servants and their messengers.
The mantra-body is Mahāvajradhara;

they recollect him with this aforementioned garland-mantra. The gods, such as Īśvara and others, being terrified by the fear of violating their commitments (samaya), are drawn in by the *saṃpuṭa*-body, that is, by the *saṃpuṭa*-machine.
In this regard, the application is as follows:

having drawn an image of the person to be acted upon, marked with their name, upon birch bark or similar material using yellow pigment (*gorocanā*) and the like, and having covered it again with another *yantra*, one treads upon it with the left leg in the *pratyālīḍha* posture marked by a vajra-hook; then, by means of recitation (*jāpa*) at the three junctions of the day, one effects the summoning—thus, and so forth.

The *samaya* is the command (*ājñā*) of Vajradhara; its manifestation is its activity. That very [activity] is the *vajra* because of its indivisibility. Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that, he—whose nature is the command of all *samayas* of all Vajradharas, being the destroyer of the wicked—caused the Great Wrathful One, Sumbhana, to emerge from his own body and so forth.
The mantra beginning with "Oṃ" is known as *nirantara*;
it is the *praṇava*, and because it lacks *svāhā*, it is called *nirantara*.
In this context, the meaning is as follows:
"O slayer of Sumbha" is an address; [the command] "O Nisumbha" means "destroy completely."
HŪṂ! O Lamp-seed-syllable, seize, seize the afflictions;
protect, seize them with [your] retinues, cause them to be seized, cause them to be seized!
"HŪṂ!
By means of the vajra-yoga of exhortation, having bound him with the vajra-hook at the heart, he should be brought forth! HOḤ! O Blessed One, King of Knowledge!"—thus she consoles Sumbha.
"Hūṃ phaṭ" is used in the rite of killing;
"atha" and so forth has already been explained.
Vajrasattva is his own gnosis-being (jñānasattva); his "place" (pada) refers to the rays [of light], by which [the victim] is "overpowered," meaning embraced.
Having bound the *sādhya-jñānasattva*—the lord of *ṛddhi* who has come from all directions—with the Vajra-noose, the summoning of the maiden (*kanyākarṣaṇa*) is performed;
"maiden" here is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Now, introducing the sequence for the summoning and so forth even for those devoted to the internal (*adhyātmaparāyaṇa*), he says:

Then, etc.: the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, relying upon the samādhi named "The Vajra" (*vajra*)—which is indivisible (*abhedya*) and in which there is the arising (*utpatti*), that is, the manifestation, of the reality (*tattva*) of practitioners who possess the great vajra-commitments (*mahāvajrasamaya*) through means such as summoning for the sake of sentient beings; [relying on] those who are practitioners of the great commitments (*mahāsamaya*); [he taught] the secret (*guhya*)—so called because it is to be concealed and not revealed—of their three vajra-body, speech, and mind;
the reality (*tattva*) of the verbal commitment (*vāksamaya*), which is its non-alterability (*ananyathātva*); and the state (*pada*) which is its foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*).
One should emanate from the forms of one’s own body, speech, and mind the rites of summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) and so forth.

Even those who are difficult to subdue are the Buddhas and Vajras; within their three bodies—body, speech, and mind—the practitioner, being a Vajrasattva of steady mind, must perform the visualization (*vibhāvanā*), which is a specific form of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). With those holding nooses, vajras, and hooks, one should visualize masses of light rays entering the body and other parts of the object to be subdued (*sādhya*) in due order, taking the forms of nooses and so on. This is the supreme, primary method for the summoning of the Buddhas, known as "summoning by means of the mass" (*piṇḍākarṣaṇa*).

Buddha: The petitioner is his speech and body, the collection of words; he who possesses the great wheel (*mahācakra*) or mandala is the Lord of the Great Wheel Mandala (*mahācakramaṇḍalādhipati*). For the purpose of attracting his mind, through the application—that is, the impelling—of the Vajra Hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*), Vajrasattva, the Great King, is certainly and exclusively attracted to that Mind-Vajra at all times, immediately, by means of the meditations on the indivisibility of the Three Vajras, namely the Wheel, Lotus, and Great Vajra, which are fashioned from delusion, passion, and hatred by the yogins such as Vairocana and the others.

The "vajra-hook" is the hook beginning with the vajra; by means of its specific differentiation, when it is attached to the heart of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), there is the summoning of all mantras and the supreme summoning of all those to be accomplished.
This summoning is also performed by means of one's own emblem (*svacihna*).

The yogin of Mahāvajrasattva, having meditated upon his own mantra-person as his own deity—auspicious, beautiful, and composed entirely of vajras—and having meditated upon an excellent human woman situated therein, draws her in by means of the heart-vajra-hook; being drawn in by the vajra-hook attached to the heart, she is impelled by a whirlwind through the conjunction with the wind-maṇḍala, and thus she is drawn forth. (From the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*).

By that same method, the yogin of Vairocana, having meditated upon the great rite of Vairocana as transformed into the shape of a moon disc, should draw Śacī, the wife of Śakra, away from the abode of Śakra by means of Amṛtakuṇḍalin; having meditated on her being placed there and being brought forth, he should summon her while reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalin mantra fifty times.
Or, having meditated upon Ṭakkirāja of the vajra-maṇḍala holding a vajra-hook, he should summon a celestial maiden mounted upon him, drawn by his heart and impelled by the wind.

Krodhavajra is Akṣobhya; his *samaya* is his command. Having exhorted Sumbharāja, who dwells in the Vajra-netherworld and possesses that *krodhavajrasamaya*, one should—having pierced him in the heart with that trident (*śūla*), drawn him in with the vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*), and bound him with the noose (*pāśa*)—visualize the Asura maiden being dragged along as she rides upon a wind-wheel, and thus attract her.

Using pigments such as red ochre (*gairika*) through the application of the *vajrāṅkuśa* (thunderbolt-hook), one should cast the form of a *vajrāṅkuśa* into the mouth, the *vajra*, or the *dharmodaya* during a lunar eclipse. One should perform the practice with full devotion until the release from the eclipse; then, having removed it and preserved it, one should write the name of any deity such as Brahmā and so forth. That [deity] will certainly come.
This is the unimpeded speech of Vāgvajra, and likewise "in all forms," and so on.

Having visualized oneself as Mañjuśrī, endowed with all forms and possessed of all the [major and minor] marks, and having again emanated Yamāntaka, one should visualize a vajra-hook through his transformation.

Then, having meditated upon a great wheel of the conflagration at the end of the aeon—a circle of fire with blazing sparks—one draws the desired yakṣī into that [wheel] with the hook, mounts her, and, being driven by the wind, brings her near oneself and enjoys her;
thus he concludes.

Through the distinction of *mudrās*—that is, through the two types of distinctions of the *mahāmudrā*—the recitation (*mantraṇa*) or the muttering (*japa*) of the mantras of all deities is twofold: the verbal muttering (*vāgjāpa*) and the adamantine muttering (*vajrajāpa*). If it is said that the practice of summoning (*ākarṣaṇaprayoga*) has been taught and explained in its entirety and without remainder through these two types of distinctions of muttering, then if one does not accomplish it in these two ways, one will meet with destruction—that is, one will fail to attain accomplishment. Regarding "Vajra" and so forth: Vajrasattva is the sixth; he is this Great King because he is the support for the [other] five. He is to be urged again and again, repeatedly, and is to be taken as the object of focus.
Why? Because he is the eternal and perpetual king of all mantras and all Tathāgatas, the illuminator;
therefore, in all rites and in all circumstances, he should be taken as the object of focus.
"Then," and so forth.

The Blessed One Mahāvajradhara is eternal like the sky and space, without beginning or end; he is that in whom the universal vajra—its form quivering and expanding everywhere in all directions—is fully manifested. Because it is non-different from him, the samādhi that produces Amoghasiddhi, who is characterized by that universally manifested vajra, is likewise so called.

Having entered—that is, having attained—the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) known as the "Fourteen-Paṭala-Ṣaṭkoṭi," which is a particular state of being, he brought forth from his own body and so forth this [deity] of the nature of a vajra, Ekajaṭā—she who has a single braid (*ekā veṇī*). She is the Vajra-Ekajaṭā, whose essence is mantra, the Great Samaya Aparājitā, the Speech-Amoghasiddhi; she is the foremost, the principal among those [deities] of the maṇḍala, the Vajras.
[He brought her forth] with the mantra beginning with *Oṃ*, Śūlinī, the wielder of the trident.
"O Wielder of the Trident"—this is the address.
"Then," and so forth:

as soon as this vidyā had issued forth, having emerged from the lotus-face of the Blessed One, the daughters of the nāgas and great ṛṣis, being consumed by the fire of passion, naked and under the sway of another, meditated upon the awakening of the Buddha, Amoghasiddhi.
By this mantra-knowledge, when employed according to the ritual procedure, all serpents come here.
This is the procedure:

having drawn a wind-maṇḍala with red ochre upon a human skull in the manner previously described, and having drawn the image of any one serpent beginning with Vāsuki in its center, one should inscribe their name within it (*vidarbha*), step upon it with the left foot marked by a vajra-hook, and while reciting the mantra together with the *vidarbha*, one draws the nāgas forth.
By this very procedure, having drawn a nāga maiden upon a female skull, one attracts her;
therefore it says:
"Having attracted a large-eyed nāga maiden, one should enjoy her."
Then, with the words beginning with "atha," the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara— [who is] the Gaganasamayasambhava, meaning that from which Amitābha, the Gaganasamaya, arises—
having brought to mind this [samādhi], [uttered] this Great...
Mahādharmāmitābha’s *samaya* consists of those belonging to his family; from among them, he caused the indestructible Vajrabhṛkuṭī—the one possessing a frown—to emerge from his own body and so forth.

The mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and so on destroys all fear caused by thieves and the like, thus it is "fear-destroying" (*bhayanāśanī*). It terrifies enemies, thus it is "terrifying" (*trāsanī*). To the one whose form is like that of a mantra, he issues the command: "Terrify! because her form is as flickering as lightning.
She is *Bhṛkuṭī* because she roars like a mass of clouds;
she is *Vairaṭī* because she has removed all stains of the impurities of the Kali age; she is *Śvetā* because she is pure through the purification of passion (*rāga*);
and she is *Śvetajaṭinī*, she whose matted locks (*jaṭā*) upon her head possess that white Amitābha.
"Bhayanāśanī" and so forth are vocative terms.
Then, "atha" and so forth:

as soon as this vidyā was uttered, all the sons of the Vidyādharas—the Vidyādharīs and the daughters of the Vidyādharas—trembled; agitated by passion, they meditated while recollecting Jñānavajra Amitābha.

He fell into fear and longing when he obtained the great daughter of a Vidyādhara, endowed with beauty and other virtues, wearing swaying golden earrings and trembling ear-ornaments; having drawn her near by means of the previously mentioned mantra-knowledge and through a specific ritual procedure, he brought her forth.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, the procedure here is as follows: on a female skull, one should draw the wind-maṇḍala and in its center a maiden of the Vidyādharas. Having stepped upon her with the *pratyālīḍha* posture empowered by the vajra-hook, one attracts her while reciting the mantra beginning with "nirodha," and so forth. "Ni rodha" refers to all mantras—snakes and the like—which are restrained and gathered according to their distinctions of female, male, and neuter; thus it is "nirodha. "Vajrarāja" is the three-syllable mantra. That which is both "nirodha" and "vajrarāja" is "Nirodhavajrarāja. By means of that, which is accomplished in the form of entry and so forth, proceeding incessantly, which is foremost and beautiful because it accomplishes desired aims, and which is excellent, the mantras of Locanā and others, and Yamāntaka and others, who have arisen from the Three-Vajra Wisdom beings such as Akṣobhya and the rest, are attracted instantly—that is, they are drawn in and attain accomplishment. "From everywhere" means all mantras. This is the "sandhyā-bhāṣā" (twilight language). He speaks of the specific rule for those devoted to mantras, starting with "Alternatively," and so forth. "All wrathful ones" refers to Yamāntaka and others; their mantras, through a hundred thousand recitations, are said to be the servants of the practitioner, the mantra-master, accomplishing all aims. In solitary places such as great forests, or on great mountains, those intent on reviling the Ācārya—those who revile the Guru, revile the Vajrācārya, revile the supreme Mahāyāna, and reject the Vajrayāna—these and other evildoers are to be slain with effort and unflagging vigor. Or else, their displacement from their place (*uccāṭana*) should be performed. By performing this very rite, one shall obtain supreme enlightenment characterized by non-abiding and mantra-accomplishment. Thus spoke Mahāvajradhara; this is the speech of the compiler. Regarding the "opening of the joint" (*sampuṭodghāṭana*) for those to be killed, he says "in the ten directions," and so forth. The destruction of the body, speech, and mind of the multitudes of sentient beings included within the ten directions is what is to be slain; it is to be meditated upon by the practitioner. Of whom? He says: "of enemies, of evil-minded ones"—that is, of those with malicious intent who revile the Ācārya. This is connected with the phrase "is to be meditated upon. Regarding "blood," and so forth: having combined blood, hot water, feces, and urine, and having washed a cloth with them, having covered one's body with it, and having stepped upon the *liṅga* (the effigy), one should make an image of the target using substances for sorcery (*abhicāruka*). Having inscribed the name in the heart, and having stepped upon the image with the right foot marked by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), the practitioner in the yoga of Akṣobhya should recite the mantra of whichever wrathful king, such as Yamāntaka, one hundred and eight times. Even a Buddha, though skilled in the expansion of activities, is destroyed—that is, he dies. "Moistened by water" refers to the cloth; even after washing it with mere hot water, one should perform the previously mentioned rite. Having soaked it even in feces and urine, one should begin the application. Likewise, having dyed the cloth with ash-water, one should begin the slaying. Even one difficult to subdue dies. This is the commentary on the six million verses of the fourteenth chapter. Regarding "naked," and so forth: the practitioner, assuming the pride (*ahaṅkāra*) of the wrathful deities such as Yamāntaka, is "terrible" (*kaṭa*) due to the fierceness of his fangs, "exalted" (*utkaṭa*) due to his extremely tall body, and "agitated" (*saṃbhrānta*) due to his readiness to destroy. Having stepped upon the *liṅga*—the effigy produced as before—with the sole of the right foot marked by a double-vajra, he reveals the greatness of meditation through the hyperbole: "even the *khadhātu*," meaning even the formless space, let alone the formed. By "mother's house," and so forth, he states the location for the rite under discussion. The seven mothers of the world are Brahmāṇī, Vaiṣṇavī, Rudrāṇī, Indrāṇī, Kauverī, Vārāhī, and Cāmuṇḍā. In their houses, in cremation grounds, empty houses, crossroads, solitary *liṅgas*, or solitary trees, one should take a bone from the shank region measuring eight finger-widths made of human bone. On a cloth from a cemetery, having drawn a double-vajra with substances for sorcery, having written the name of the target in its hub, and having inserted that wheel into the hollow of the bone, one should cover it with the dust from the target's feet and bury it at the door of the enemy, having recited the wrathful mantra one hundred and eight times. "Buddhas" are wise beings of the three bodies; they are "givers of boons" (*varada*) because they grant desired aims. "Knowledge" is the thought of returning a favor; "ignorance" is indifference. Though he is devoid of these two, he may be defiled by reviling the Ācārya. Within a fortnight or a full month, he falls from his position or dies. Taking a flawless skull filled with [substances], the wise one should know that on that skull one should write the words of the mantra—the wrathful mantra as intended—along with the name of the target. Reciting it, or "with the vajra-speech"—vajra-speech being the speech of wrath—one should perform the vocal recitation. One should bury that skull at the door of the enemy or in the village; he will certainly be driven away (*uccāṭayet*). On a palm leaf or elsewhere, such as a cloth, having written the wrathful mantra along with the name using substances for sorcery, and having hidden it near the enemy's house or at the door, one should recite that same mantra with the voice of wrath at the four junctions of the day. When this is done, he withers according to the previous sequence and subsequently dies. The "Great Samaya" is the slaying and so forth; its cause is the "Vajra," the compiler, Mahāvajradhara. Thus he spoke. Starting with "Now," the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara, having brought to presence the samādhi named "Vajra"—whose nature is indivisible—in which the binding of the body, speech, and mind of those targets who have become evil-natured is rendered immobile, emitted from his own body and so forth the mantra for the purpose of afflicting the body and so forth of the "Three-Dhātu" beings—the low, middling, and superior, the three types of targets. The mantra beginning with "Oṃ" and so forth is continuous: "Gha gha gha gha ghātaka" is the address; "Kill all the wicked" is the command; "Phaṭ phaṭ" is its seed-syllable; "Kīlaya kīlaya" means "make immobile all sins"—those with sinful intentions; "Phaṭ" is the breaking; "Hūṃ hūṃ" is the impelling of reality; "Vajra-kīla" is the address by way of the function; "Vajradhara commands" is how Vajradhara himself designates himself; "Body, Speech, and Mind Vajra" refers to the wicked. "Hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ" is the further impelling. Starting with "Now," when this "kīlana" mantra has been emitted, the "Vajras"—Indra and others—who are "great" due to their great power, were first stunned by the touch of the mantra and fell into fear. Immediately thereafter, having regained consciousness, terrified, they went for refuge to Mahāvajradhara, whose mind is the Space-Vajra. Regarding "human bones," and so forth, he states the procedure here: having made an image of the target with substances for sorcery, having written the name with poison and so forth on a cloth, and having placed it in the heart of the doll, one should fashion a stake from human bone or the heartwood of *khadira* wood, shaped like a spear in the form of a wrathful deity. Having recited
Vajrasattva, the Great King, shall perform the ritual of *kīlana*; the practitioner [will achieve that] the [target] dies swiftly.
Because he has been consecrated as the Dharma King of the three worlds, he is the Great King;
because of his firm vigor, he is Vajrasattva. If one performs the *kīlana* according to this procedure, then the object of the rite (*sādhya*) will die quickly and swiftly.
He also taught the ritual procedure for piercing through the union of the vajra and the lotus,
beginning with "Then," etc.,
the Blessed One Mahāvajradhara.

The body whose intrinsic nature is Mahāvairocana is the "Mahāvairocana-body," which is the body of the one to be accomplished (*sādhyadeha*). Having entered that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the manifestation of the stake (*kīla*) is displayed, he— [the one whose] commitment is his own body (*svakāyasamaya*), meaning the strength of his body— emitted from his own body and so forth the Vajrakīla mantra, which projects and cuts through that [strength].
The mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *iti*, namely:
*chinda chinda sādhyakāyaṃ hana hana kāyabalaṃ*.
Furthermore, [he visualizes] a blazing vajra and a wheel upon his body; she to whom this belongs is addressed as "O Blazing Vajra-Wheel," with the exhortation "HŪṂ PHAṬ.
With the words beginning "mutually" (*anyonya*), he describes the application of the ritual of staking (*kīlana*).

One who possesses the yoga of Akṣobhya, having placed Māmakī in front of him, performs acts such as embracing in the manner of mutual entwining; then, regarding "the closing of the thumb and the foot":
the thumb is one's own *sādhana*, and the foot is the *mudrā* because it is the secret place of passion (*ratisthāna*); "the opening of the two" refers to their unification.
How is it "trampled by the feet of Vairocana"?
The "foot of Vairocana" is the body of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*); that by which this is trampled—that is, pinned down—is "trampled by the feet of Vairocana.
This is also an epithet for the joining of the thumbs.
While reciting this mantra, one should perform [the rite];

at the mere stroke of the vajra upon the head of the target, even if he be a great being (*mahāsattva*) of great power, born from the vajra of the three bodies (*trikāyavajrasambhava*), and consisting of those [three] natures— if he rises or moves from his place, the state of destruction shall not occur.

Then, with the words beginning with "atha," he entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) known as "the manifestation in the pinning down of the speech of the nature of Lokeśvara"— that is, the speech of Lokeśvara, which is the statement of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

From that, he uttered the mantra, the "indestructible pinning vajra" (*vajrābhedyakīlana*), which is the force (*samaya*) or power of that speech, the object to be accomplished, and which effects its suppression (*stambhana*).
The mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *nirantaḥ*,
the seed-syllable *hrīḥ* for the attraction of the speech of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), and the vocative *bhūr bhuvaḥ* followed by *vikasitaḥ* and so forth.

The "blooming lotus" (*vikasitajñānapadma*) refers to the expanded and extended lotus of gnosis that brings about the arising of the three types of gnosis; by means of that blooming lotus of gnosis, [one acts] with the vulva of a woman. Regarding the phrase "the vajra-finger" (*vajrāṅguli*): the vajra itself is the "finger. Its qualification is "trampled by the foot of Rāgavajra. *Rāgavajra* is the continuous discourse of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*). "Trampled by its foot"—that is, by the tip of the thunderbolt (*kuliśāgra*)—means it is to be trampled in such a way that this "striking down of the vajra-stake" (*vajrakīlanipātana*) occurs.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said: "As soon as [the mantra] is uttered, when the tongue-tip of the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) is visualized within the womb and touched, the Great King Amitābha— the very nature of the proliferation of the object's speech, arising from the abode of the three bodies, manifested from space—
arises and departs from the tongue of the object."

If the one to be accomplished does not die by means of the "peak of the pledge"— that is, by the specific application just described— then, with the words beginning with "atha," he teaches the procedure for pinning down the mind (*cittakīlana*).
Having entered into that [meditative absorption] in which the pinning down of the mind of the one to be accomplished is manifested, it is the "pledge of the mind" (*cittasamaya*).
The exertion of the mind (*cittotsāha*) is its projection; leading [the mind] toward such exertion, he uttered the mantra for the pinning down (*pratikīlana*):

*oṃ vajrarāja oṃ cittavajra hūṃ*. The meaning of the mantra is: "May [the obstructor] flee from here, from the heart of the one to be subdued (*sādhya*). This is done by means of the binding with the five-pronged [vajra].

One should perform the meditation on a vajra filled with sparks, which has the nature of five spikes. How? This striking down of the vajra-stake should be performed in such a way that it overcomes the "mind-vajra"—that is, the mind—its locus being the heart-lotus.

Regarding the passage beginning with "immediately upon being struck" (*hatamātra*): as soon as the target (*sādhya*)—who resides within the fiery mandala contained inside the *dharmodaya* of one’s own mudrā—is struck, that is, merely tapped, by the radiant *vajra* of oneself, the "great garment," which is the mind of the target, [and] the mind whose nature is that [of the target], emerges from the heart by means of the tip of the *vajra-samaya* through a specific application; that is, it exits from the heart.
If the target does not thus undergo the state of the five elements (*pañcatva*), then he rises.
"Then," and so forth.

What kind of beings were those Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas established in the *niṣpannakrama* (the stage of completion)? They were followers of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayānīya*), those who had set out upon the priceless vehicle, beginners (*ādikarmika*), possessed of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the foremost among them, desiring the welfare of the realm of sentient beings, and capable of accomplishing the aims of sentient beings. Being satisfied merely by hearing [this teaching] at first, they subsequently attained an extraordinary joy and intense delight. Then, regarding their own realization, they made this sound—which will be described below—to proclaim their own experience; that is, they uttered it.

"Aho" expresses wonder. "Guhyapada" (the secret word) refers to the mantra-word; that is the most excellent "Sārasamuccaya" (Compendium of Essence), which is the specific application of mantras. "Dharmapada" (the word of Dharma) refers to Śāntīmati, the accomplishment of that very word through meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
"Vajravidāraṇa" is the seizing of the wicked grahas.

The pinning down (*kīlana*) of all the Buddhas, who possess the power of the expansion of karma—that too is a marvel. The pinning down of other Bodhisattvas, ordinary beings, those of great renown, and the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*)—that too is a marvel.

Furthermore, that which is described as the pinning down of the body and so forth individually through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*)—that too is called a marvel by the Jewel-like Persons (*ratnapudgala*).

That which was just described is this *kīlana*— the act of pinning down and rendering immovable— which arises from the reality (*tattva*) useful for practitioners of both types among all mantras, as revealed by Mahāvajradhara; it bestows boons upon practitioners of body, speech, and mind, granting their desired fruits,
and is thus called the *Mantratattvasamuccaya*.

The compiler states that the "mantras" refer to those such as serpents; their thorough knowledge of the reality (*tattva*), meaning (*artha*), and so forth, is called the "extraction and explanation" (*samuccayoddhṛtyakathana*).
Thus, in the fourteenth chapter of the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*, it is said that the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas are themselves the marvelous [mantras].

Even though body, speech, and mind are one, they cut [everything] by taking as their object the distinction between self and other. Thus, the entry of the three genders of the mantras produced from *āli* and *kāli* into the three syllables of their own nature—that is their attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*). By that, there is a blossoming (*vijṛmbhita*) or play, which is the accomplishment of the expansion of activities such as pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth; it "shines" or "blazes" by means of that very [process]. This is the meaning. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named "The King Blossomed in the Attraction of the Wondrous Mantras of Body, Speech, and Mind" is expressed by that collection of words which illuminates it.
Esoteric terminology.
The Explanation of the Six Points in the Fourteenth Chapter of the *Pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*.
The Fifteenth Chapter.

The accomplishment of the rites of pacification and so forth, whether mentioned or unmentioned, does not occur without the thorough knowledge of the illusion-like samādhi. Introducing the fifteenth chapter, [the text] says "atha" and so forth:

King Vajradhara, the Great Vajradhara, who is all space, whose nature consists of the four voids, the great imperishable, the indestructible, and the consecration of all—because he is the consecration even of consecration, and because he is the essence of all families, the Omniscient One, uttering the indestructible speech of the Vajra of Speech, proclaimed [this].
Not without a hidden meaning.

Demonstrating the practice free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcacaryā*), he says: one should cause a daughter of an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*)—who is twelve years of age and endowed with qualities such as faith—to become a "Great-Souled One" (*mahātman*); that is, one should have her well-trained in the *tantras* and *mantras*. One should train her constantly, at all times, for fear of the loss of mindfulness. One should train her in places completely devoid of the crowds of people; thus he speaks of the preparation of the site (*sthānaparikarma*).

Excrement, green cow-dung, and urine—these very things are the constituent parts of the practice (*sādhana*). That which is correctly reached is the *samaya*; that which has this as its first element is "that which begins with the *samaya* of excrement and urine.
By the word "first" (*ādya*), sandalwood and other such items are also included.
It is called "quadrangular" (*caturasra*) by way of indication (*upalakṣaṇa*), because it is endowed with four gates and so forth; thus, it is accepted.
The "procedure" (*vidhāna*) here refers to the procedure for the mandala; how [is it performed] by that procedure?

By means of the "meditations on the vajra-mandala"—the vajra-mandala being the mandala of Akṣobhya—those who meditate upon it, that is, manifest it, are the "meditators on the vajra-mandala. The intended meaning is that one should cause the mandala to be constructed as adorned with those forms of the deities belonging to the mandala (*māṇḍaleyadevatā*).

She who possesses all the auspicious marks from the feet to the hair at the crown, who is completely purified by those auspicious signs, radiant, with a beautiful face, looking toward the practitioner, most lovely, devoted to no other, and fully endowed with all ornaments and skill in the arts of love—the practitioner, having meditated on himself as the Great Image of Vairocana, the Vajra of Body, Speech, and Mind, situated in the center of the mandala, should practice for accomplishment by becoming Vairocana, possessing a splendor equal to a Buddha; for how could the mantras, such as Akṣobhya and the others, be meditated upon otherwise? Their application is according to the state of reality; thus, having become Vairocana, he should accomplish [the goal].

In the commentary on the six crores [of verses] for the fifteenth chapter, the phrase "having the form of a blue lotus petal" is to be connected with the phrase "completely purified of all characteristics and having a beautiful face. The remainder, beginning with "Akṣobhya’s washerman," is to be connected with the Vairocana-samādhi mentioned immediately above. One should practice and train a fair-complexioned washerwoman.
"By means of the practice of Vajrasattva" refers to the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Vajrasattva;
this very [absorption] is the ritual procedure for the yoga of Vajrasattva,
and this is the yoga.
Having made her [the consort] thus, one should commence the ritual action;
together with her, one may perform whatever action one desires.
"For this," and so forth.
The commitment (*samaya*) and the method of accomplishment for all mantras—namely Ratnasaṃbhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi, and so forth—is difficult to transgress and not to be violated.
That practitioner, at that very moment immediately following the meditation, becomes equal in radiance to Vajrasattva, equal to Ratnaketu;
endowed with that yoga, he becomes a king who upholds all phenomena, equal to Amitābha.
One who is engaged in that yoga and has attained success in both desire and liberation becomes equal to Amoghasiddhi; and one who is a yogin skilled in ritual action [becomes equal to him].
With the words "cāruvaktrām" (one with a beautiful face) and so forth, he shows the specific procedure for the yoga of Amitābha:

the practitioner should always cultivate a woman with a beautiful face, who is attentive to the practitioner, large-eyed, wise, very lovely, and reddish-fair, by means of the meditations on Vajradharma and the applications of Amitābha.

Proceeding in this manner, the practitioner— whose nature is Vajradharma and whose essence is Amitābha— becomes a master of the ten stages (*daśabhūmīśvara*), the vow of speech (*vāksamaya*), and the possessor of mastery over speech. Sustaining that state, he becomes the foremost of all, distinguished above all beings, the supreme lord, and a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) by virtue of his cultivated yoga.

Having thus demonstrated the classification of mudrās for those who practice through conceptualization (*kalpita-yogin*), he speaks of the mudrā for those established in the stage of completion (*niṣpanna-krama*) with the words beginning "Brahmā" and so forth:
having taken a maiden from among any of the four castes, one whose nature is Vajradharma— where "dharma" refers to that which is indivisible like a vajra— is one who possesses the yoga of completion.
Then, he who has realized that [nature]—
the secret Mahāvajradhara— should accomplish, that is, perform, the bringing about of that which brings about this secret;
and since that is to be accomplished through the sequence of manifest enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi*), he speaks in order to show the means for that:

"Set" (astaṃgata) and so forth: when the Vajra-sun has set—that is, when the sun has gone down, the time of twilight has passed, and it has vanished—one should propitiate the Guru with whatever requisites are available.

Then, by the Guru’s grace, having received initiation at midnight, one attains accomplishment through the supreme meditations—the instructions on the stages of awakening—at the moment of sunrise, when the portion of night has departed and before the sun rises; thus one becomes purified. This is the external stage of awakening.
Now he speaks of the internal:
"Vajra," and so forth:

when the Vajra-Sun—that is, the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*) characterized by meditative union—having arisen and subsequently set, having entered into the state of wisdom (*prajñā-bhāva*) and ceased; considering the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) to be preceded by luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), one should commence the practice of the achiever of luminosity, which is the attainment of light (*ālokopalabdha*). Dawn breaks: ignorance (*avidyā*). At the moment of its emergence, at the time of its passing away, the practitioner is accomplished through the causes and conditions of the supreme emptinesses—the empty, the exceedingly empty, and the great empty—by means of the direct realization of luminosity, whereby the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā-siddhi*) occurs.
Asking what she is like, he says "all" and so forth:

[one should visualize her] as complete with all ornaments, adorned with all the [major and minor] marks, and decorated with perfumes and flowers; endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses; and one shall quickly—that is, swiftly—attain the supreme accomplishment of the Vajrasattvas, the practitioners, which is the attainment of Mahāmudrā.

Thus, he is accomplished as the bestower of boons through the three bodies (*trikāya*), the granter of desired boons throughout the three worlds. He is characterized by and endowed with the marks of a Buddha—the well-known *lakṣaṇas*—and because the phrase "extending for a hundred *yojanas*" is intended as an illustration, he illuminates the entire world-system (*lokadhātu*) beginning with the trichiliocosm with his radiance. The application of the two organs refers to the production of the Great Vajradhara by means of the non-dualization of the two truths; this is the application of the two organs.
Therefore, one should undertake all yogic practices for pacification and so forth.
This aforementioned perfected samādhi is the producer of the samaya that is difficult to transcend or violate—the samaya of all mundane and supramundane accomplishments.
One should consume the samaya of feces and urine.

Excrement refers to objects such as form and so forth; urine refers to the sense faculties such as the eyes and so forth. Their "samaya" (union) is their meeting through the relationship of object and subject. One should "consume" that, meaning one should experience it through the process of sensory withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). If the "Vajrin"—the practitioner who possesses the vajra—should pray for "siddhi," that is, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, this indeed is the "samaya" of all accomplishments, a path difficult to transgress. This is what is meant by the "samaya of excrement and urine," and so forth.

By means of the practitioner who is preceded by the objects and sense faculties just described, through the application of the two organs and the non-dualization of the two truths, the unsurpassed reality—the state of the Buddha’s enlightenment, non-abiding nirvāṇa, the auspicious and excellent reality, the non-deceptive, unsurpassed, and most distinguished of all accomplishments—is perfected and attained. "Thus he said," and so forth, is the speech of the compiler: he who goes to (eti), that is, knows, having unified and made equal desire (saṃsāra) and liberation (nirvāṇa), is the Kāma-mokṣa-samayavajra, the Great Vajradhara.
Having thus explained the practice for the Great Vajradhara using intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*), he speaks again, introducing worldly accomplishments (*laukikasiddhi*),
beginning with "Now," and so forth.

The Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara, the Vajra known as the Great Samaya, at that time entered the meditative absorption (samādhi) bearing that name and emitted from his own body and so forth this wrathful deity in the form of a mantra, which causes terror to the bodies, speech, and minds—the vajras—of all the Tathāgatas who are to be accomplished. The mantra beginning with *Oṃ* is as follows: *Oṃ* indicates the display of the great mudrā of the mantra-deity; *Hrīḥ* is the invocation; and *Ṣṭrīḥ* describes his transformed physical appearance.

O you of deformed face and loathsome countenance, destroy all enemies and adversaries; paralyze them, and even those who flee, bring them back and cause them to meet their end! *Hūṃ Hūṃ*—this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) indicating this meaning. *Phaṭ*—this is the seed-syllable indicating slaughter. *Svāhā*—this is the consolation for the deity of the mantra.
Its piercing [is performed] with "dṛḍhavat," according to the commentary on the fifteenth chapter;
poison and so forth refers to the poisons of ritual diagrams (*karmayantra*) and the like.

Having combined all available artificial blood, salt, oil, and the well-known *rājikā* mustard seeds, one who is filled with wrath and possesses the application of any one of the wrathful deities such as Yamāntaka should offer them as a burnt oblation (*homa*) in a fire of thorns kindled by fuel from the thorns of the *madana* plant and the like. Reciting the mantra interspersed with the syllables of the intended name along with the words "of the girl" (*kanyānām*), and perfuming the offering with sesame oil and other substances, one should perform the oblation according to the sequence to be described.

At midday or at midnight, this rite of immobilization (*stambhana*) is effective in every respect, even against armies and the like. In a triangular or five-pointed sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should visualize the Great Samaya-Vajra-Krodha with his mouth wide open, terrifying with fangs, and with a lolling tongue; then, one should offer eight thousand oblations according to the ritual procedure. This refers to the specific procedures for immobilizing armies and so forth. This ritual should be performed for three days.

For the sake of attaining great enjoyment through a connection with maidens, the immobilization (*stambhana*) of a maiden occurs by means of an endless application directed toward someone other than the practitioner.
As for how long it lasts, he says:
"for three kalpas"—that is, having passed through childhood, youth, and middle age, it will remain until she reaches an incalculable and uncountable state of being worn out by old age.
The word "sadā" (always) indicates that even during the intermediate state,
the person lacks yoga;
[this refers to] the Buddha Vairocana-yogin.
Vajradharma is the yogin of Amitābha;
Vajrasattva is the yogin of Akṣobhya; Ratna is the yogin of Ratnasambhava; and Karma is the yogin of Amoghasiddhi.

"Or whoever, joined with some form of anger, should transgress"— meaning one who wishes to sever this *stambhana* (paralysis)— for that practitioner, "life ends there," meaning from the commencement of that rite until its conclusion, his life comes to an end. He states another application of this very mantra, beginning with "on the fourteenth day," and so forth.

On the eighth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight, one should take charcoal from a funeral pyre of a man killed by a weapon, place it in a skull-casket, and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight thousand times. Having done so, one should draw the form of the Great Samaya Wrathful Vajra in the likeness of Yamāntaka upon a hero’s rag (*vīrakarpaṭaka*), invoke him, and touch his heart with the hand while reciting the mantra mentioned immediately above. Following the syllable *phaṭ*, the mantra is: "Make this be given to such-and-such a person, *hrīḥ svāhā*. One should recite this one thousand and eight times at midnight or at noon.
That practitioner becomes a constant bestower of desired fruits upon sentient beings;
by means of this very mantra, he states another application,
beginning with "the line," and so forth.

Having recited [the mantra] as before, one should draw the effigy of any enemy whatsoever on a cloth from a cremation ground using charcoal. Having inscribed the name in the heart and having performed the *vidarbha* (interweaving) of the name, the yogi—remaining in a state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) with intense anger at the time of the *abhicāruka* rite on a black day—should say: "Oṃ hrīḥ ṣṭrīḥ! O you of distorted face, tear open the heart of so-and-so! Sādhaya! While reciting the remainder of the mantra, he should visualize that charcoal as taking the form of a weapon and, with the intention of splitting it in two starting from the head, he should draw a line through the middle. At the very moment the line is drawn, the victim dies with his heart split apart;
this is the "mallet" (*mudgara*) and so forth.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is stated that one who practices the yoga of Yamāntaka should fashion an image of the enemy out of clay, incorporating the dust from the victim's feet along with earth from both banks of a river; having internalized the consciousness [of the victim], being enraged, he should place it [in the ground], invoke it while uttering the syllable *phaṭ*, and strike it on the head.
When this is done, [the enemy] falls.
"Certainty" (dhruvam) means that the hammer falls directly upon the head of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through direct perception;
or else, one should bring about all calamities through meditation— this refers to the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth.

One who possesses the *nisumbha* yoga, having fashioned an image of the target according to the procedure just described, should meditate on a blazing, terrifying vajra held in his own hand, conjoined with the flames of the syllable *hūṃ*, and licked by black flames arising from a long *hūṃ*. He should visualize it falling upon the head of the target. When this is done, the practitioner becomes the destroyer and the caster-down of all evil beings.
To which yoga should one abide when performing this rite? He says:

"Recalled in the Vajrapāṇi family" means that the Vajrapāṇi family is the Vajra family; in that family, the wrathful deity Nisumbharāja, who possesses the yoga of Nisumbha, is "recalled" by Vajrapāṇi in this rite—that is to say, he is authorized.
All of this should be accomplished through meditation by one who is devoted to the inner [practice].
"Chalk," and so forth:

having drawn a man or a woman with any pigment whatsoever upon a cloth from a cemetery or similar surface, one established in the *samādhi* of Yamāri should visualize an axe produced from the transformation of a long *HŪṂ* syllable in one's own hand. Uttering the syllable *PHAṬ*, one should visualize their neck severed.

[The practitioner] is known as a Buddha because he is to be accomplished; he is the supreme among the three jewels of body, speech, and mind. He is the "Benefactor of All Beings"—that is, those who are inferior, superior, or middling—because he accomplishes their welfare even if not in its entirety. He is a "King" who dwells in extreme grace.
By this application, he is struck; he may be wounded or even die and go to the state of the five elements—of this there is no doubt.
This is known as the "Karma-vajra" and so forth.

The yogi, established in the *amṛtakuṇḍalī* samādhi, should visualize a blazing universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) of great radiance situated in the desired location; within that, he should visualize a terrifying vajra with upward-pointing flames, resembling the fire at the end of an aeon (*kalpāgni*), dense and agitated with sparks. He should then meditate on the masses of rain being scorched and consumed by the streams of its rays. This is the supreme and most excellent method for the "stopping of water" and the "stopping of rain.
[The passage continues with] "in the mandala," and so forth.
When the master is drawing the great maṇḍala of the Vajradhātu and so forth, "wind and so on" refers to a wind, a collection of winds,
and by the word "and so on," lightning strikes, rains of stones, the emergence of water and snakes beneath the maṇḍala, and other such phenomena are also included.

If, through negligence, obstacles such as wind-storms and the like arise—whether instigated by others or occurring as portents—one should then perform the *daṃṣṭrāmudrā*. Here, "fangs" (*daṃṣṭrā*) refers to serpents such as Vāsuki; the "mudrā of fangs" (*daṃṣṭrāmudrā*) is so called because it is a seal for the purpose of crushing them. Having formed that mudrā and taken possession [of the power], one should contemplate with the mind and meditate upon Hayagrīva, the enemy of those wicked obstructors, and duly repel the obstacles with the weapons held in one's own hands.

The Buddhas are those of one's own group, while the Bodhisattvas are those of other groups. Even by them, whatever host of obstacles might be produced or employed—such as the commentary on the fifteen chapters and sixty million verses—it is destroyed and vanishes merely upon being seen, that is, merely by the sight of the mudrā.
If it does not [vanish] when this is performed from the beginning, it shall meet with destruction; the task at hand will not be accomplished. "The Buddha," and so forth.

Whatever practitioners of our own or other schools there may be, as well as other wicked beings and ordinary creatures—those who have been terrified or threatened by this manifestation of mantra power will die; of this there is no doubt.
In that regard, concerning the fierce ritual (*raudrakarman*), this which is about to be described is the secret of all mantras and all Tathāgatas.
"The heart of so-and-so"—this is the life-force of cruel mantras.
What is it? *phaṭ* for killing.
Now, demonstrating the essential nature of the five secret great realities, he says "Jñānasattva," and so forth.
A *jñānasattva* is a being (*sattva*) accomplished through the sequence of gnosis (*jñāna*); its application is instantaneous visualization.
By that means, in the center of the four seats, one should visualize the central image, the image of Mahāvajradhara.

In the four locations—the positions of Locanā and the others—the knower of mantras, who knows the reality of the deities, should always, day and night, station four women who have not been trained in the mantra-tantras but are conceptually designated as Locanā and the rest.

Of what nature are they? Fully adorned with all ornaments, marked with all the [auspicious] characteristics, and endowed with the female characteristics as previously described. Then, having opened the lotus—so it is said.

Having opened and expanded the lotus of one's own heart and the lotus of the mouth, one should visualize—that is, know and resolve—that this fivefold wheel is the mantra *hūṃ*, meaning that it is to be determined as mind-only (*cittamātra*). Regarding the phrase "five rays" and so forth: the "Yogavajrin" is Mahāvajradhara, who exists in the form of the sense objects. The "five rays" are the eyes and the other [senses]; their "radiance" is the grasping of the three kinds of sense objects. One should visualize him as blazing—that is, vividly manifest—by means of that radiance; thus one should practice.

Practicing in this way, by causing the nature of the objects within one’s own body and so forth to descend and dissolve into the Vajra-holder, one shall attain—that is, reach—enlightenment, which is the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*).

Practicing thus, that yogi, in that very moment and without long delay, shall become equal in radiance to Vairocana, equal to Kāyavajra, Vajrasattva, Akṣobhya, Mahārāga, Ratnasaṃbhava, the Buddha Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi who holds the Vajra of the three bodies, and indeed equal to them all.

"All beings" refers to Vairocana and the others; the "vajra-gnosis" is that which produces their state. The meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which this occurs is named "The Vajra that Produces All Beings. Now, he speaks of practicing even with a single mudrā, beginning with the words "the woman," and so forth.
Having obtained or found a woman— a maiden born from any family other than that of the Brāhmaṇas and so forth— in accordance with the procedure described here,

one should begin the worship and meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in a secluded, solitary place that is pleasing to the mind; [the woman] being beautiful-faced, serene of countenance, and well-disposed toward the practitioner’s welfare.

Having grasped—that is, having ascertained—the three secrets of passion and so forth, one should consume them; that is, one should purify them by means of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*) and render them free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*). In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said: "The yogi who practices in this way becomes, at that very moment and without delay, equal in splendor to Mañjuśrī Mahāvajradhara, endowed with power equal to his. 'Invisibility' (*antardhāna*) means the abandonment of the ordinary physical body. Thereafter, he is a lord, a master, because he has attained accomplishment together with the *mudrā*. He is glorious, possessing a radiance like that of Jāmbūnada gold, and becomes like Ratnaketu through the *Gaganagañja* samādhi, by accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings."
Now, demonstrating the practitioner’s procedure for eating, he says:

having consecrated with mantras and prepared through the sequence of the *sādhana* and so forth, whatever food—whether common worldly items such as rice and the like, excrement such as cow dung, meat, or anything else obtained—the wise ones (who consider themselves learned) should consume it after purifying the heart and throat according to the prescribed rule (*vidhānataḥ*). This sequence is not seen nor known by those who are wretched.
And thus it says, "Mahāvajradhara," with reference to what is to be explained hereafter.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the ritual procedure for the consumption of that which has been entered": having taken [the substance] from the unclean ground, one should place and set it within a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*) or a pair of skull-cups (*kapāla*).

Then, having empowered it one hundred and eight times with the two-syllable mantra, one should form it into a pill, encase it in the three metals, and place it in the mouth; thus, one will not be seen even by the Buddhas, the Suns, or the accomplished Vidyādharas—this is the praise of the practice. Regarding "dogs" and so forth:

having taken the flesh of dogs, horses, or humans whose life-span has ended according to the ritual procedure—the method just mentioned—and having empowered it in the same way by means of a skull-cup casket (*kapāla-sampuṭa*), one should form it into a pill; while eating it or placing it in the mouth, one will not be seen by those Siddhas and others.

Having prepared a pill composed of the four nectars, joined with *viṣṭa*, encased in three metals, and wrapped in a fine cloth, one should, during a lunar eclipse, engage the two organs and insert it into the womb starting from the moment of contact; then, having performed union until the release, one should remove it and observe the sign. When it begins to smoke, one should know that success has been achieved and place it in the mouth;
then one will not be seen by any of the Buddhas.

In the same way, having prepared a pill combined with human flesh and the five nectars, encased in three metals, and accomplished it through the application of the two organs just described, one becomes invisible to all Buddhas by placing it in the mouth.

Following the instruction just mentioned—beginning with "with beef" and "with dog meat"—the practitioner who has completed his vow (*vrata*) should, together with beings that have gone outside defiled by living creatures, fashion a pill (*gulikā*) with *parāmṛta*. He should accomplish it as before through the application of the two organs. Having fashioned a pill with camphor, sandalwood, and red sandalwood along with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he should accomplish it as before.

Having fashioned a pill with *rocanā* and black agallochum (*kṛṣṇāguru*) and having accomplished it as before, he should place it in his mouth; while wandering about, he becomes possessed of great strength and unimpeded heroism.
"One should likewise prepare [the substance] combined with camphor and saffron, as well as the five nectars (pañcāmṛta)";
and he says the following now for the purpose of demonstrating the supernatural accomplishments (siddhi) that transcend the world.
"Having empowered," and so forth:

among the deities of the maṇḍala, having empowered the great mudrā—whether wrathful or peaceful—of Yamāntaka or any other [deity], and having accomplished the rites of pacification and so forth for the sake of attracting those to be trained by producing [the deity] according to the fifteenth chapter, that practitioner becomes exactly like that; not only this, but through the possession of the eight qualities of sovereignty, he is born as such, just like Mahāvajradhara himself.
The glorious one, possessing great strength and prowess due to his sovereignty over the three worlds,
would travel in a single moment to a height above the earth measuring a full ten million yojanas.
Even beneath the earth, his movement is as unimpeded as that of a diamond or a thunderbolt;

likewise, in an instant, he moves without obstruction throughout the thousandfold world-system in the cardinal and intermediate directions. Surrounded by a multitude of various mudrās, the glorious Buddha is endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and other such qualities.
The intention is that this too is similar to that because it is of such a nature;
thus, there is unobstructed movement because one moves according to one's desire, as in the case of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth.

The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is sixfold, consisting of the Cāturmahārājakāyikas, Trayastriṃśas, Yāmas, Tuṣitas, Nirmāṇaratis, and Paranirmitavaśavartins. Regarding the maiden residing therein—one who possesses divine enjoyments (*surabhogā*), meaning she has enjoyments like those of the gods—such as the daughters of universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) and others; having brought her from families such as those of the *nāgas* and *asuras*, he brings that radiance-bound maiden. He shows this as a hyperbolic statement (*atiśayokti*) to indicate that he does not merely desire one dwelling in the desire realm, but if there are women in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), he desires them as well.

The ordinary body, known as the *samayasattva*, is made to disappear by that being called the Great Vajra (*mahāvajra*); thus, he who is the Great Vajra of the disappearance of the pledge (*samaya*) is the Vajradhara, and it is he who speaks—so says the compiler.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Then" (*atha*) and so forth:

the Buddhas are jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) whose minds were previously bewildered by merely hearing [the teaching] because its meaning was so utterly marvelous; subsequently, however, their minds [became clear] because they had realized it through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The wise ones, having attained knowledge and thereafter being delighted in soul, with their eyes wide open by that very wonder through the grace of the Teacher, uttered these words about to be spoken—which indicate great joy—saying "Aho! and so forth.
That the accomplishment of many rites is achieved by means of a single mantra—that indeed is "Aho, a great wonder," an object of amazement.
That the secret syllable of the word "accomplishing worldly and supramundane attainments through play with women" is itself a marvel—
that attainment is achieved by means of pills made from the five nectars, lamps, and so forth— is because the nature of those phenomena is intrinsically pure.
This too is a marvel:

that by relying on any [form of] Mahāmudrā whatsoever, the ritual action is accomplished; and that the state of the Great Vajradhara which is attained is characterized by being unstained and perfectly pure—that too is a marvel.
This is in the *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language).
Now, introducing the consecration of one’s own tutelary deity according to the divisions of the families, he says "atha" and so forth.

Vajradhara is the Teacher because he subdues all the wicked; he is the Maker because he accomplishes mundane and supramundane siddhis; he is the Creator because he brings about the arising of Vairocana and the others. Furthermore, because his nature is the sixth [family], he is the Great Immutable (Mahākṣara). He is the Buddha Vairocana, the Vajra Akṣobhya, and the Great Dharma Amitābha. Being the essence of the three vajras, he produced—that is, uttered—the sound of the vajra.

*Sattvavajra* is Akṣobhya; by means of his application, there is the placing [of the crown] upon the head. By that, for those of noble family (*kulīna*), the satisfaction of *Sattvavajra-Akṣobhya* is the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) which is the awakening of a Buddha (*buddhabodhi*). *Vairocana* is [the Buddha]; his differentiation is the satisfying and inflaming (*uddīpana*) of those of excellent family who stand individually upon the heads of those "Buddha-Vajrins" belonging to the Vairocana family.
Regarding "Vajralocanā and so forth," it should be understood as Vajralocanā and the others;
the propitiation of the Uṣṇīṣa by means of forms such as Vimvādya and Avirocana is known as "making it a crest-jewel" (śekharīkaraṇa), which is to be understood.

For the wrathful deities (*krodha*) who are bound to those families as well, the Buddhas and Vajras—Vairocana and the others—are their manifestors; by means of them, there is illumination, which is the most excellent and desirable act of making [them] radiant while they abide upon the crown. *Vidyā* is Māmakī; her supreme king is Ratnasaṃbhava. Those for whom he is the sovereign of the foremost Dharma are the "Vidyārājāgradharmas. For those belonging to the Jewel family (*ratnakula*), the manifestation of Ratnaketu—the consecration of Ratnaketu upon the crown—must be performed.

The Vidyārājñī is Pāṇḍaravāsinī; because of the connection through that application and its relationship, those who possess it are "those whose application is the Vidyārājñī. For those belonging to the Lotus Family (Padmakula), the visualization of Amitāyus should be performed, and Amitābha should be established upon their crowns. All mantras of action belong to the Action Family (Karmakula); for them, the unfailing visualization of Jñāna should be performed upon their crowns. For all the lords of the families of mantras, such as Vairocana and the others, the visualization of Vajrasattva should be performed upon their crowns, and the visualization of Akṣobhya should be performed.

The *yakṣiṇīs* are those such as Vajravetālī and others; their *mantras* are the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth from which they arise. Those mudrā-forms by which these [mantras] are extended and accomplished are the *yakṣiṇī-mantra-tantras*. At the site of consecration for these *yakṣiṇī-mantra-tantras*, the visualization and installation of Yamāntaka himself must be performed.

Regarding all those [mantras] just mentioned, they are "yogas" because they are suitable for consecration; for those yoga-mantras situated above, the impelling [of them] together with their respective mudrās—the experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—is praised as the completion and nourishment.

"Oṃ," said the Blessed One, Mahāsamayavajra Vajradhara. By means of this extensive description of the consecration and meditative absorption just mentioned, the mantras are the deities; the *maṇḍala* of their propitiation consists of those who are the essence (*maṇḍa*)—the core—of the propitiation. That which takes up (*lāti*) or grasps them is the "Mantra Propitiation Maṇḍala. It is declared to be the "Mahāsamaya Sādhana," which brings benefit and bestows welfare upon practitioners who are striving. "Mahāsamaya" refers to the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*); it is the means for accomplishing—that is, bringing to completion—that [sādhana].
Now, introducing the procedure for donning the robes, he says "atha" and so forth.

Because he brings all obstacles to rest, he is the Teacher (*śāstṛ*). All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) refer to the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the rest; he is the leader (*nāyaka*) among them, the Lord of All Phenomena (*sarvadharmeśvara*), because he is the sovereign of the three realms (*traidhātuka*).

The Lord, whose nature is indivisible from the three vajras, is completely purified in body, speech, and mind; because he is non-different from the method of primordial wisdom—the vajra of wisdom that transcends past and so forth—he uttered and spoke [the teaching] beginning with "on the mountain peaks," while proclaiming that vajra of wisdom. *Pañcadaśapaṭala-ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* (The Sixfold Commentary on the Fifteenth Chapter).

Like mountains are the great palaces; at their frontages, on their upper floors, or in delightful yet secluded forests, gardens, and so forth—any one of these places that is agreeable to the mind—the practitioner, according to his ability, should perform the meditation-vajra (*dhyānavajra*) as a support for the two types of Great Mudrās (*mahāmudrā*) for the sake of concentration, through the application of mantra-recitation (*japa*). Recitation is "vajra-recitation" (*vajrajāpa*), while mantra is "speech-recitation" (*vāgjāpa*); the application of both constitutes the practice.
To the question, "Why is it done in this way? he says:

"Vajra," and so forth: Vajrasattva and the others, headed by Akṣobhya, being impelled by mantra and meditation—impelled and urged by their own respective mantras and by the focal point of their own respective mudrās—perform or accomplish various activities (*citrakarmāṇi*), that is, the paths of diverse actions. Amitābha is "one whose action is speech" (*vākkarma*), because his activity is bound to speech; he performs the two kinds of various actions according to his word.

The practitioner who has thus performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) himself becomes possessed of the yoga of Akṣobhya. Having meditated upon the vessel as the great image of Vajradharma, radiant with the luster of a ruby, according to the sequence of *tathatā*, the moon, the seed-syllable, and the emblem, and having placed the three syllables in the locations of the head, throat, and heart, he should internalize the three arrays (*vyūhatraya*) therein as the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
This is called the "conception of the family" (*kulakalpana*) in those three places.

Having thus performed the consecration of the vessel and carrying out all the procedures for the descent of power (*āveśana*) that will be described hereafter, he accomplishes them; he certainly succeeds and attains manifest realization.
Regarding "stobha-stambha" and so forth: *stobha* refers to leaping, trembling, and whirling;

*stambha* (stiffening) is the state of remaining motionless like a piece of wood due to a state of stillness, having first removed the ordinary ego-sense of the recipient through the possession by a deity (*devatāveśa*). This is called "stiffening" (*stambhana*).

The "great divine" (*mahādivya*) is that moment of possession (*āveśakṣaṇa*) in which the great, supramundane, and divine beings such as Vajrasattva enter and remain; it brings about the manifestation of objects of the past and so forth exactly as they are. This fourfold possession must indeed be performed by one who possesses the "vajra of accomplishment" (*siddhivajra*)—that is, one whose vow has been fulfilled—and by whom the nature of the vajra has been realized. When this is done, the eternal [state] is always accomplished and attains renown.
Pointing out the characteristics of one's own consort (*svās*), he says "twelve," and so forth:

having taken a girl of twelve years of age whose virginity is intact, and likewise a boy of twelve years who is ignorant of women and complete in all his primary and secondary marks— that is, possessing all limbs and appendages— one should consecrate them according to the previously described sequence and effect the fourfold or four-type possession (*āveśa*).

Having performed all the ritual procedures, such as the consecration of the drink and so forth, and having accomplished them as previously described in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, immediately thereafter the rite for accomplishing the descent [of the deity] must be performed;
otherwise, one becomes censured among the beings of the three realms— among those beings who are inferior, middling, or superior.

In that regard, concerning the procedure for the descent [of the deity], these syllables, words, and heart-mantras are "hearts" because they are born from the heart; they are "mantras" because of their secret nature;
they are "syllables" (*akṣara*) such as the four beginning with *haṃ*; and they are indeed "words" (*pada*) because they serve as the basis for the descent.

By means of this sequence, the practitioner causes the descent into the motionless corpse—which has become empty like the space-element (*khadhātu*) through the departure of consciousness—and by means of the ritual procedure for descent, he himself directly causes even Vajrasattva—who is free from all conceptual constructions and devoid of mental fabrication—to descend. Thus, the greatness of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is revealed.
He states the purpose of the four syllables, beginning with "the syllable *huṃ*": in the syllable *huṃ*, the Mind-Vajra, whose nature is Vajrasattva, resides.
In the syllable *haḥ* resides Kāyavajra;
in the syllable *āḥ* resides Amitābha, the King who upholds the Dharma.
This is the firm secret word, the firm word within the sphere of intense immersion.

It is taught that the *stobhana* (paralysis) arises through the *saiḥkāra*; the *paribhūmaṇa* (whirling), which is like the turning of a wheel, as well as the trembling and shaking, are likewise known to be brought about by the *saiḥkāra* alone. Indeed, this *saiḥkāra* is proclaimed and described as the secret and the very heart of all *stobhas*, including the triad beginning with *stambha*.
When possession occurs according to the aforementioned method, [the practitioners] rise from the ground into the air to the height of a cubit or more.
Impelled and inflamed by Vajrarāja through the Akṣobhya-samādhi and the mantra beginning with *hūṃ*, they arise trembling and agitated out of fear of transgressing the command of Vajrasattva;

"in that very manner," and so forth—this final seed syllable brings about the secret [union] and induces possession in such a way; likewise, the remaining three seed syllables, starting from the last one as before up to the first seed syllable, induce possession in exactly the same manner.
This is the synthesis here.

First, the practitioner—having performed the preliminary rites (*puraścaraṇa*) in a place such as a mountain that is favorable to the mind, possessing a steady mind, and desiring to effect the entry of the vessel (*pātrāveśa*)—should properly take recourse in the Akṣobhya-samādhi. Having consecrated (*adhivāsya*) a suitable vessel, having transformed it into Amitābha according to the rules, and having placed the three syllables on the head, throat, and heart regions, he should internalize the three arrays (*vyūhatraya*) therein. Meditating upon the vessel as being filled with channels from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, he should purify the body by means of masses of upward-pointing light rays issuing from the red syllable *rauḥ*, which are situated above a wind-mandala at the base; these rays enter through the center of the soles of the feet and reach up to the top of the head. Having thus purified the body, he should cause the *jñānasattva* to enter the state of clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

Then, for the sake of further transmutation, one should meditate on the syllable *hūṃ* above the lotus of the vessel at the heart; from that, one should meditate on Vajrasattva born of transformation.
