Likewise, having meditated on Kāyavajra born of the transformation of the syllable *haḥ* at the head, and again Amitābha born of the syllable *āḥ* at the throat-lotus—

Furthermore, having been exhorted by the rays of light from the author of the commentary on the sixty million verses of the fifteenth chapter, one should bring about the arising of the knowledge of means and cause [the disciple] to attain the great divine state.
Knowing that the vessel has become possessed, one should meditate while uttering the four seed-syllables along with the ringing of a bell for the purpose of causing *stobha* (paralysis) and so forth.

Having attained firmness in the possession of the vessel through whirling and other such methods, and for the sake of leading him to the state of reality as it is, one should meditate upon Vāgvajrin situated at the throat as being exhorted by a mass of rays emerging after passing through the region of the heart; then one should say, "Speak, O Vajra!"
Having spoken the truth in this way,

and having thus accomplished the purpose such as the scattering of flowers, one should utter *hūṃ haḥ āḥ muḥ*, place the vessel in its proper position, and protect it with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) and so forth.
Having thus determined one’s own task and the task of others through the descent of the vessel, he explains the means of accomplishment for one engaged in the subduing of the wicked:
"Then," and so forth:
"all Tathāgatas" refers to Locanā and the others;
their "lord" is the Trikāya (the three bodies) of body, speech, and mind; his "state" is the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*); purified by that, he spoke these words.

"Even by one whose mind is not one-pointed, even when engaged in agriculture, trade, festivals, and so forth, and even by those intent on firm vows or devoted to the subduing of enemies—it is not by another yoga.

This means that "another yoga" refers to the yoga of others than the Sovereign, such as those beginning with Vairocana and ending with Śumbha; therefore, this destruction of the wicked must be performed through the yoga of Akṣobhya. This is the sense.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy using charcoal from a cremation ground, poison, dhattūra, rājikā, salt, oil, and other such substances for malevolent rites; having inscribed the name of the person to be targeted on a cloth from a cremation ground with those very same malevolent materials and placed it within the heart of the image; and having performed the invocation, one should—facing south, naked, and with disheveled hair—recite any one of the wrathful mantras beginning with Yamāntaka. It is said as an exaggeration that "even the three worlds would be destroyed," and so forth regarding the enemy.

Having fashioned an image of the enemy with funeral ashes smeared with pungent oil, and having internalized the visualization of that [enemy], the yogi—remaining in the Akṣobhya-samādhi and reciting the wrathful mantra one thousand and eight hundred times—will certainly cause death.
Regarding "with beef" and so forth:

having drawn a triangular fire-mandala in a cremation ground using funeral ashes, kindled a fire therein with pungent fuel, and having fashioned an image of the enemy from beef and other such materials, he should perform the invocation as before and, while reciting the mantra, repeatedly cut the image and offer it into the fire.
Even a Buddha perishes—such is the greatness of karma.

Regarding "with great flesh" and so forth: the act of destruction performed with great flesh as previously described is remembered as being more cruel than all those acts performed with cow-flesh and the like, because it arises from the Vajra.
Therefore it is said:
"For this is remembered as the terrible destroyer of all enemies," beginning with the word *śatroḥ*.

And regarding those of the stage of supreme dharma (agradharmin), such as outcastes (caṇḍāla) and others, having fashioned an image of the enemy with feces and urine, and having first performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should recite the mantra while cutting [the image] in a triangular hearth (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*) over a fire of thorns; by throwing [it therein], even a Buddha perishes— so it is said in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*.

Regarding the passage beginning with "kā śatroḥ" and ending with "nadīsrotaḥ": having taken earth from both banks of a river that flows toward the western ocean, one should fashion an image of the enemy. Having filled it body by body with *śṛṅgī* poison and the like, or with *madana* thorns, or with the thorns of poisonous snakes such as the *saṃkoca*, using seeds of sesame as small as a grain to fill the interior, one should bury it while commanding: "Kill so-and-so! Phaṭ!"
"Even a Buddha would surely perish"—
thus he said,
"pha."
Regarding the passage beginning with "rājikā" and so forth:
having fashioned an image of the enemy from substances such as black mustard seeds (*rājikā*) and the like, one should likewise offer it into a fire of thorns.
This is the rite of killing (*māraṇakarma*), which is considered the most preeminent rite of killing among all the Buddhas who are to be accomplished.
In order to restrain those who harm the Three Jewels, this [method] was taught for those on the stage of the generation process (*utpattikrama*);

however, for those established in the completion process (*niṣpannakrama*), killing should be understood according to the method taught in the ninth chapter— thus [it begins with] "with charcoal," and so forth.

Having moistened and wrapped a *liṅga* fashioned from mustard seeds and other materials—which represents the enemy—in charcoal-water from a cremation ground, one who possesses the Akṣobhya-yoga, with a wrathful mind, should step upon it with his foot and recite the mantra of Sumbharāja accompanied by the injunctional words: "Cause such-and-such a person to be seized by the *rākṣasas*.
[The victim] is then seized by the *rākṣasas*.

"An image," and so forth: having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of powdered human bone mixed with poison and blood, one should step upon it according to the sequence just described and recite the mantra;
by doing so, he demonstrates the efficacy of the ritual application.

"Even Vajrasattva is seized by the rākṣasas"— this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*). Having made an image of the enemy with mustard seeds, excrement, and urine, and having likewise stepped upon it with the foot while reciting the mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalin, saying "Cause so-and-so to be seized by a great fever," one produces a burning fever in the victim.

Regarding the passage beginning with "In that" (*tatra*) and so forth: among all those fierce rites (*raudrakarman*) just mentioned, this which is being pointed out is the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) of Sarvatathāgata-mahāvajrakrodha Amṛtakuṇḍalin;
it is the most excellent garland-mantra (*mālāmantra*) for the purpose of killing. The mantra beginning with *namaḥ* has been explained previously.
"Fire offering (homa) and so forth":
the fire offering is of the manner previously described,
and meditation (dhyāna) is of the characteristics to be explained hereafter.

That *homa* or that meditation—which brings joy to the body, speech, and mind [of the practitioner] and destroys the body and so forth of the enemy—must be performed with no other thought and with focused mind; this is the supreme method of slaying. Regarding the commentary on the sixteenth verse of the fifteenth chapter, beginning with "Vajrasattva": one should first meditate upon the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) as being Vajrasattva, possessing great strength and prowess, terrifying and formidable with a frowning brow and the like, intent on violence, and holding an axe and a mallet in his hands. Having visualized the object of accomplishment in such a manner, one should then perform this present meditation.
In that ritual of slaying, one should visualize this Great Wrathful One Akṣobhya; his command, which must not be transgressed against the *samaya*, is as follows:
one should imagine the expanse of space (*khadhātu*), the hollow of the sky, completely filled with Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Samyaksambuddhas.
Then, having visualized the wicked victim struck by a mallet and cut apart by an axe, and devoured and slain, one may perform the rite for the past or the future.

When this is done, at that very moment, those established in the Buddha's teaching— bodhisattvas endowed with virtues such as ethical discipline and so forth, who are bound to that [practice] and possessed of the five precepts and the rest— die.
Having visualized that mortal world as completely filled [with enemies], and having contemplated that they have been slain by that wicked one, one should perform the rite;
"Vajradhara himself dies"— this is an exaggerated expression (atiśayokti)—
"one should contemplate them as slain," and so forth.
Having contemplated that the defilement acquired by the manner just described is terrified by remorse, and therefore agitated by fear and without refuge, one should perform the ritual action;
one dies hereof, there is no doubt. He states the slaying by means of meditation, beginning with "by rākṣasas," and so forth.

One should meditate upon the *sādhya* as being terrified by various cruel, violent, and fierce beings who consume flesh, fat, marrow, and so forth—beings whose nature is harmful, who are terrifying, and who are formidable with a fire of smoke-like wrath that is difficult to behold.
Through such meditation, even Vajradhara himself would die; this is an exaggeration (*atiśayokti*).
The passage beginning with "by owls" (*ulūkaiḥ*) and so forth is easy to understand.
[The text to be translated was not provided.]

Having drawn a black snake— black in color because it is infused with poison, extremely cruel, most terrifying, a source of fear even for fear itself, five-hooded, double-tongued, and possessing formidable fangs— one should meditate on the stationary and mobile poisons, which are the very essence of the tip of venom, as being drawn in by the black rays of the syllable *hoḥ* and deposited upon the forehead within the syllable *khaṃ* in its mouth;
thereafter, this form of the serpent becomes distinguished and spreads forth.
Then one should urge him, saying, "Eat such-and-such";
once he has been eaten by that snake, he will certainly perish;
this same procedure applies even to scorpions and other such creatures.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the ten directions" and so forth:

one should draw away from all sentient beings residing in the world-systems of the ten directions the fear caused by calamities—such as those known as serpents and flames—and the disturbances produced by the agitation of the elements; having visualized these in the form of black spirits (*bhūta*), one should perform their hurling, that is, their placement, upon the enemy, meaning within the continuum of the foe.
This incitement, this meditation, is the best for subduing the wicked; it is more powerful and superior compared to other acts of incitement.
Having thus placed the one whose defilements have been accumulated before him as the object of accomplishment, the practitioner should strike him in the chest with a mallet using the Yamāntaka yoga;
when this is done, the enemy is deprived of life.
This is the word of the Great Vajra-holder.

In the *Guhyasamāja-pradīpodyotana*, it is stated that the "striking" of that very object to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—the pounding with the aforementioned sling-bolt (*bhiṇḍipāla*) and so forth—is to be visualized by the practitioner (*vajrin*).

When this is done, Vajrasattva—the bestower of boons upon the three bodies, the giver of fruit to the three types of beings, firm in valor, and fierce—causes the object to be accomplished, whose defilements have been accumulated, to die.

For the sake of the health and nourishment of the one to be accomplished (*sādhya*), those who desire his welfare employ rituals such as recitation (*japa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*). His protection and so forth are also included; the mantra that is its cause, the mantras being recited by the practitioner—such as *mālā-mantras* and others—and the deities being propitiated by the practitioner, one should "pin" (*kīlayet*), "cut" (*chindayet*), and "paralyze" (*stambhayet*) them through the application of the ritual procedures for severing rival spells (*paravidyā*).
This sequence is the foremost among methods for the purpose of slaying; it is most distinguished, difficult to transgress, and an inviolable commitment (*samaya*), the ordinance of Vajrasattva.
Regarding this matter of slaying, he speaks of purification with the words beginning "skandha" and so forth:

by means of the *skandhavajra*— that is, by virtue of being composed of the five aggregates— one should contemplate, or know, that all sentient beings whatsoever who abide within this supreme triple world, such as those born from eggs and so on, have been slain through destruction and have become one's own self, having attained the state of Vajrasattva.

"They are satisfied thus" means that those beings who have been slain by the mantra-practitioner (mantrin) in this manner, having been accomplished [through it], become satisfied and delight in the realm of Akṣobhya;
otherwise, if they were destroyed by the injury of weapons and the like, they would not be so.
Revealing that very purity, he says "Buddha," and so forth:

"Buddha" is the Body-Vajra; "Vajradhara" is the Mind-Vajra; and "Vajradharma" is the Speech-Vajra. These three—the Body-Vajra and the others—are the Vajrin. They do not die through grasping at a composite whole (*piṇḍagrāha*) by means of duality, because they take suchness as their object.

Just as those existing in the mental continuum of another perish, so too do those existing in one's own mental continuum; thus, by the designation "killing," it is indicated that this has its objective support in ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
This is the procedure for killing for one who has entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*);
these are the words of the Great Vajradhara.

The Great Vajradhara, the pledge of great ferocity, having emerged from that [state] and attained a state of oneness, became Dveṣavajra, the Vajra-Wrath; thus says the compiler. Now, "atha" and so forth:

Vajradhara, the King Dveṣavajra, is radiant, the entirety of space, whose nature is universal emptiness; therefore he is the Great Sage. He is the consecration of all, the flux [of realization], and as such the Perfectly Awakened One has known him. Proclaiming the indestructible power of the Knowledge-Vajra, which resembles a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) and bestows desired fruits, he revealed it through the udāna verse to be spoken hereafter.
"Aho" expresses wonder.

The Vajrayāna is naturally pure because it is free from all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), and it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is the unsurpassed luminosity; by its power, there is the non-arising of the proliferation of activities such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth with respect to phenomena that are unarisen—being devoid of causes—and unborn, whether they be appropriated or non-appropriated elements. This reality (*tattva*) and so forth has been taught by the Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times, in the commentary on the fifteen chapters and the six points (*ṣaṭkoṭi*).

For one established in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), this which is about to be described is called a "rite of minor means" because it is accomplished with insignificant and small implements; nevertheless, because it is the very essence, it is a "vajra," and because it must be kept secret for that very reason, it is a "secret.
One should meditate upon it as being as unbearable as a blazing fire.

By the word "and" (ca), one should draw in any one of the serpents headed by Vāsuki with the goad consisting of the syllable *hrīḥ* from the *vijñāna* [of the victim], and having caused it to enter, one should visualize the serpent quivering;
there, in that serpent, the poison is certainly drawn out from all stationary and moving beings. What is its heart? [The answer follows: *kiṃ tat?* (What is that?)

One should visualize that everything—without exception—the various manifestations existing within the three realms, residing in inferior, middling, or superior vessels, consisting of both the stationary and the moving, is drawn in and attracted by that syllable *hrīḥ*. Then, one should contemplate the [syllable] entering and falling into the form of a serpent; this is what is to be remembered.
At that very moment, by mere meditation, it becomes as extremely terrible as an ocean of poison;
once this [being] impelled by the mantra has been touched, or merely upon being bitten or touched, the entire world dies from the emergence of the poison—
of this there is no doubt.
"Maṇḍūka," and so forth:
by the very method just described, specific beings such as tortoises and others are to be fashioned; by what means?
By the characteristics of the arising of yoga.
Yoga is poison;

the "instrument" (karaṇa) refers to the variegated frog and so forth. By means of the characteristics of skill therein, [the author] describes the transfer of the poison from one location to another with the words beginning with "tatra" and so on, and "dṛṣṭivajra" and so on.

Regarding the poison of those with venomous gaze, the poison of those with venomous fangs and so forth, and the poison of whatever other beings are fierce with venom—the practitioner should meditate on their vessel-like body as being black at the soles of the feet, quivering in form, and impelled by the white *praṇava* syllable situated above. Then, having drawn that which has entered the heart of the space-vajra mandala into the vessel [of the body] situated upon the syllable *khaṃ*, the mantra-practitioner causes it to enter by means of the wisdom-vajra, the hook (*aṅkuśa*) of the syllable *hrīḥ*. Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, the Great Vajra of Poisonous Illusion. Therein, beginning with the words "In this regard, this... and so forth, he begins the removal of poison; what is the Heart-mantra for the treatment of poison? It is as follows: [The mantra follows. Thus ends the section on the removal of poison. The Blessed One, the Great Vajra-holder, the Great Vajra of Poisonous Illusion, taught this supreme method for the extraction of all poisons. HŪṂ.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said: "In the heart, from the soles of the feet to the heart, one should visualize this syllable HŪṂ as white in color, a great vajra consisting of a mass of light rays, shining brilliantly like the moonbeams, by means of the application of the four locations."

Emerging through the hollow of the soles of the feet, the poison is cast upward by a mass of one's own rays; having reached the anus-lotus (*gudapadma*), it pierces it and exits from there. One should then visualize it as having gone to the navel-lotus (*nābhipadma*), and from there, having contemplated it as having reached the heart-lotus (*hṛtpadma*), one should meditate on it as having reached the throat-lotus (*kaṇṭhapadma*). Thus, by means of this process of withdrawal and release, the poison rises and moves upward.
Having meditated in this manner two or three times, one should visualize the poison in the form of black smoke enveloping the patient.
In this very sequence, starting from the head and proceeding as far as the soles of the feet, one should meditate on the poison as having emerged from that opening; thus say some.
And he says that even the *khadhātu*—the hollow of space—is instantly rendered free of poison by this practice, referring to what is being introduced.

In that regard, concerning the removal of poison, there are natural poisons such as *dhattūra* and *lāṅgalī*, as well as artificial poisons; what is the heart-essence for extracting all these poisons?
It is this: *āḥ*.
He shows that this remedy applies not only to *upaviṣa* but also to *gaṇḍa* and other such poisons by stating "gaṇḍa" and so forth; here,
*gaṇḍas* refers to *vyāla*, *gardabha*, and similar species.
Pustules such as *piṭaka* and *masūrikā*,

spider-bites, wounds, sores, and the like— their potency, as well as other diseases such as fever (*jvara*) and erysipelas (*vaisarpa*), fall away from the patient’s body and are removed by the mere act of meditation, namely, by the meditation that will be described hereafter.
This shows the words of Vajrapāṇi,
beginning with "Just as... eight," and so forth.

Having visualized a great white eight-petalled lotus in the palm of the left hand, one should meditate on the syllable *ĀḤ* filled with five-colored rays in its pericarp, and the syllable *Hrīḥ* upon the petals. While uttering the syllable *Hrīṃ*, one should crush [the affliction], draw forth the poison and so forth, and having caused it to enter via the syllable *ĀḤ*, one should cause it to go into the earth by means of the "fist-withdrawal" (*muṣṭisaṃhāra*).
Regarding that very seed-syllable *ĀḤ*, he speaks while distinguishing it through a specific meditation: "one should withdraw it as something resembling white"—this is how it should be applied;
for in the removal of poison, it should be visualized as white.

In the case of inciting or causing poison to arise, this aforementioned method of meditation— the secret seed-syllable of the meditative state— should be visualized as black in color; it is a secret that must be concealed from those who are unfortunate,
and therefore it is a "mystery," the mystery of the Buddha, stainless through knowledge because it has been purified by luminosity (*prabhāsvara*).
Having previously spoken by way of introduction while seated, he now says "Therein," etc., specifically introducing the treatment of diseases.

In that context of specific prescriptions, "external" refers to those caused by external factors such as weapons, sorcery (*abhicāra*), and the like; "internal" refers to those caused by the imbalance of the humors (*doṣa*), constituents (*dhātu*), waste products (*mala*), and food. The "treatment" (*cikitsā*) is the remedy for these external and internal diseases. For that purpose, there are the mantra-syllables and phrases which are the indestructible heart, like a diamond (*vajra*). Regarding the words "That which... and so forth, [this is] the commentary on the six-fold meaning of the fifteenth chapter of the *Jina-jig* (the *Guhyasamāja*).

Among these, whichever mantra-word is desired or intended—through devotion and practice—it becomes a bringer of qualities and a bearer of results; one should meditate upon such a corresponding image, the form of the deity. One should contemplate the "disease-vajra," which is an incurable disease, by means of its provocations and the resolute intentions that expel it.
How so?

One should visualize—that is, meditate upon—a disease in the form of a monkey, a disease in the form of a dog originating from a dog, or a disease of such a form, situated within the words of body, speech, and mind; by means of the stabilizations of body, speech, and mind, one should imagine it emerging and departing from the location of the person to be treated.

Then, having visualized that wheel or a terrifying vajra situated in the right hand at the "vajra-position," one should contemplate that by its release, the disease of the practitioner—which consists of the body, speech, and mind, and the body of the commitment (*samaya*)—is pulverized and reduced to ashes.

From that time forward, beginning from that moment, the perfectly awakened ones such as Akṣobhya and others, and the Bodhisattvas of great renown such as Maitreya and others, remaining within their own bodies, bestow and grant the state of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna-pada*) for the conquest of disease to that [practitioner], with joyful eyes and blazing gazes—thus says the compiler (*saṃgītikāraka*) with reference to what is to be said hereafter.
How so?

One should establish clouds of Buddhas in union with Locanā, arrays of Vairocana, and likewise great clouds of Vajrarāja, Akṣobhya-clouds, and Amitābha-clouds, as appropriate, within the body, speech, and mind of the afflicted person.
When this is done, there is liberation from disease.
This describes the subduing of disease for one established in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the ten directions" and so forth:

for all Buddhas whose nature consists of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the rest, for Bodhisattvas, for the eyes and other faculties of Bodhisattvas, and for the wise ones associated with consciousness—when these are enraged by the agitation of the humors (*doṣa*), one must effect their ultimate slaying, characterized by entry into the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*).

By means of this yoga of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-yoga*) and through the objective support of the Clear Light, whatever kind of disease has arisen—whether born of [past] karma or known to be born of karma—it will perish within seven days.

Alternatively, that Vajra-recitation (vajrajāpa) or mental recollection (anusmaraṇa) by which [the disease] is destroyed has been stated as "by the practice of one hundred and eight recitations. Having performed one hundred [recitations], there are eight hundred; thus, the recitation of nine hundred in the four mandalas is the "recitation of one hundred and eight" (śatāṣṭajapa). By means of that application, the disease is destroyed.

Alternatively, "one's own mantra-king" refers to one's own self-consecrated body; "vajra-meditation" is meditation that destroys diseases. Its "method" (vidhi) is its ritual procedure (vidhāna), which is said to be what should be remembered.
Indeed, this entire method has been taught as the "samaya"—the Vajrasattva designation—that is difficult to transcend and cannot be violated regarding all diseases, both external and internal.

Thus, having explained the expansion of activities (*karmaprasara*) in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, [the author] now says "atha" and so forth, in order to show the desired dreams for those who have entered the illusion-like meditative absorption (*māyopama-samādhi*) and are engaged in the practice of Mahāmudrā.

Vairocana and the others are the "elephant-goads" of gnosis; among them, the Lord of great splendor is Kāmamokṣa (the Bestower of Liberation through Desire) because he grants liberation by means of desire. He, the Great Vajra, surrounded by a great assembly, spoke these words:

"Regarding phenomena and entities that are like dreams, dream-visions, and whose intrinsic nature is unarisen due to the absence of a cause for arising—their intrinsic nature is luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*). That reality (*tattva*) which is pure and free from defilement is the form of the deity. Those [phenomena] in which this exists are 'pure by intrinsic nature' (*svabhāvaśuddha*); regarding them, the 'diamond of delusion' (*bhrāntivajra*) is proclaimed."

"Error" (*bhrānti*) means delusion; its "striking with the thunderbolt" (*vajropagamana*) refers to the thorough realization that all phenomena are like a dream, by means of the analogy of a dream. The intention is that the error of eternalism and nihilism is proclaimed [as such] and thereby abandoned.
This is what is meant by the words "they see," and so forth.

Practitioners (*sādhakas*) are of two kinds: those who constantly and perpetually practice, being intent on recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), and the awakened ones (*buddhas*) who are devoted to the inner self (*adhyātma*). Bodhisattvas are likewise of two kinds according to their distinction between having signs (*sanimitta*) and being signless (*animitta*), and they behold visions in dreams. Among these two types of practitioners, that which is being described is the "great dream" (*mahāsvapna*), which indicates great fruits; because it is non-deceptive, it is the *samaya* for the practitioner.

He sees himself entered into that luminous pinnacle of the wisdom of awakening; he sees himself as the Buddha of radiant light, the embodiment of gnosis. At times, that yogi quickly perceives himself as having attained the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Buddhas, and before long he directly realizes himself being worshipped by the great beings of the three realms, such as Śakra, Brahmā, and others of great power. That practitioner sees his own form, his own body, possessing a radiance equal to great gnosis, with a splendor like that of the Great Vajradhara, and sees himself being honored by those who are distinguished.

The practitioner perceives his own reflection—his own body—with a radiance equal to great gnosis, possessing a splendor like that of Mahāvajradhara, being worshipped by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with distinguished objects such as forms and so forth; he sees this constantly and exclusively, and thus, before long, he realizes the siddhi of Mahāmudrā.

That is to say, the practitioner perceives himself as his own reflection in the form of Vajrasattva, or in the form of Akṣobhya, or as the Great Image (mahābimba) in the form of Vairocana, or as Vajradharma in the form of Amitābha, or as the highly renowned Ratnaketu.

The great Buddhas, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas who possess equal wisdom, Vajradharas, and yogins engaged in practice likewise see that practitioner as having the form of Guhyavajra or Amoghasiddhi.

In this very way, the practitioner will before long behold in a dream such forms of Vajrasattva and others, which bestow upon others the accomplishments of body, speech, and mind, as well as the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā; such is the fruit of the dream.

In the commentary on the fifteenth chapter consisting of sixty million verses, it is said: he who sees a celestial maiden endowed with all ornaments, such as Urvaśī and other divine women, or else a human maiden, or a boy endowed with all auspicious marks, or even a young girl—at that very moment, he attains and achieves even mundane accomplishment (*laukikasiddhi*).

Whichever practitioner certainly and with certainty beholds all the Tathāgatas established in the ten directions and the Buddhas established in their own Buddha-fields, to him the Tathāgatas—with joyful minds—bestow the delightful and pleasing Dharma, the King of the True Dharma, contained within a book.

The fruit of vision is that the practitioner of the yoga-pledge (*yogasamaya*), established in meditation and abiding in the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*), beholds his own body—the physical form seated upon the Dharma-throne at the center of the wheel of Dharma—surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; he thereby accomplishes supramundane siddhi.

One who, established in yoga through the practice of meditation, beholds various delightful places such as groves, penance groves, gardens, and royal pleasure groves, adorned by celestial maidens, *nāga* maidens, and others—he, being empowered by all the Buddhas, attains the culmination of all the Tathāgatas;
therefore, he obtains the desired worldly happiness. This is the "maturation of dreams."

He who sees himself being consecrated by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in a dream sees himself being honored by the great kings of the Vidyādharas and the leaders of the Vidyādharas; such is the ripening of the dream, so it is said.

For the purpose of concluding the section on auspicious dreams, he says: "He sees various such dreams—both those not previously mentioned and those born of the Vajra, shown by the Tathāgatas, stainless and pure. By that, the unsurpassed reality born of the vajras of body, speech, and mind—the unsurpassed reality produced and perfected from the ordinary body, speech, and mind, which is the form of the completely pure deity—is accomplished and attained.
The passage beginning with "Caṇḍāla" shows the bad dream of one who has fallen from the *samaya*.

If the practitioner who holds the vajra— the wise one of firm vigor— should see contact with outcasts, dogs, and so forth (by the word "and so forth," monkeys, pretas, and other deformed beings are included), even though he has beheld the Being of Vajra, the body which is the abode of the mind of Vajrasattva will be perfected [in its purity]; [otherwise], sin accrues to him.

Having transgressed the commitments (*samaya*) and then having fully restored them, one who has engaged in mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*sādhana*) passes away without avoiding adverse circumstances; this is the meaning.

For the practitioner of reality (*tattvasādhaka*), this which is now introduced is the time for investigating dreams—the time for their examination—and therein [is] the "Heart," the essential word that cuts through doubt.

In the stabilization of the mind, in the investigation of the mind, and in the thorough knowledge of the intrinsic nature of the mind, all phenomena—appearing as external entities from the perspective of the mind at the time of seeing a dream—are established as being nothing other than one's own mind, according to the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*. As for where that mind resides, it is said: "It abides in the space-vajra mind."

The space-vajra is the clear light; the mind abiding therein is the "space-vajra-mind. These phenomena abide within that [mind]. If it is argued that in the waking state these phenomena exist as entities separate from the mind—unlike in the state of sleep—it is said: "not dharmas," meaning there is an absence of [independent] entities. If it is argued that the dharma-sphere (dharmadhātu) exists at some time [as a reality], it is said: "nor is there a dharma-nature" (na ca dharmatā).

In the same way, within this well-integrated duality of your cognitions regarding the elements, sense-bases, faculties, and so forth, one who is fast asleep while the state of "Greatness" (mahattva) is empty might indeed perceive a dream due to the influence of wind (vāta). Whether one is asleep or awake, there is no difference between them; yet, desiring the fruits of a dream, one might conceptualize a name for it. Indeed, all phenomena are like dreams; they are both false and not false, for even those two states are non-existent.
"Then," and so forth:

all the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, were struck with wonder (*āścarya-prāptāḥ*) regarding the vision of the dream and the attainment of its fruit; they were filled with amazement (*adbhuta-prāptāḥ*) concerning the "Samaya of All Tathāgatas," which is the Vajrasattva-samādhi.
They questioned Vajrasattva, the dispeller of doubts therein, asking: "What is this?"—this is the question.
The intention is that this is difficult to accomplish:

having attained the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) within those phenomena that indicate the fruit—which, though existing, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—the reality of the fruit is proclaimed.
Therefore, it is as if one were to perform the cultivation of space (*ākāśabhāvana*) upon space itself as its support.
Having manifested a wonder born of such marvels,
he spoke, revealing the very intention of the Tathāgatas:
Then, and so forth:
Mahāvajradhara addressed the Tathāgatas in this way; "O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas" is the address.
Space is not conjoined with any phenomenon such as a pot or a cloth, because their separateness is not perceived;
nor is it unconjoined, because all entities have that [space] as their very nature.
Its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) means its pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) even amidst existing entities, which is its presence within those entities without being attached to them.
He has no conceit that these two exist together;
this is what he means when he says: "It does not occur to space itself, 'I am all-pervading' or 'I am perceived everywhere.'"
Having thus stated the analogy, he says "in this very way" (*evameva*) while connecting it [to the subject]:
just as space is neither conjoined with any phenomenon nor unconjoined, so too should the conjunction and disjunction of dreams and their fruits be viewed.
Just as there is no conceptual differentiation regarding the omnipresence and universal manifestation of space, so it is with dreams and their results;
thus he says, "Dreams and those produced in dreams are to be understood [in this way]," and then,
demonstrating its very purity, he says:
"Namely," and so forth:
just as space is indefinable, so too is this intrinsic nature;
it is "non-demonstrable," meaning it is not made an object by the eyes and other sense faculties.

Just as that which is non-obstructive is not hindered by walls and the like, in the same way all phenomena—the aggregates and so forth—are to be fully understood; what need is there to mention dreams and the fruits of dreams? This is the intended meaning.
He spoke again, beginning with "tadyathā" and so forth:

"All phenomena— the vessel world, the body, speech, and mind, and the world of sentient beings— must be thoroughly understood as being pervaded everywhere by this vajra-word samaya, which is the self of all, extending throughout infinite and boundless world-systems, possessing a single nature and a single characteristic."

That is to say: how the nature of the mind, that which consists of mind, and the elements of body, speech, and mind—all phenomena and the element of space—are non-dual, indivisible, not two, and characterized by non-differentiation.
With the words "tadyathā" and so forth, he explains this very point:
all sentient beings, such as those born from eggs and others, abide within the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*);
and that space-element does not abide within the desire-realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the other realms.
In the same way, for that phenomenon which does not abide within the triple world, there is no arising.
That phenomenon which has no arising cannot be conceived by any phenomenon whatsoever, nor can it be established by any intrinsic nature whatsoever.
And that phenomenon does not transcend the absence of intrinsic nature; therefore, in this sense, all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and have luminosity as their intrinsic nature.
"Namely," and so forth.

"All Tathāgatas" refers to those existing in the three times; their "knowledge" is the body of knowledge (*jñānadeha*). For the production of that [body], it is precisely the *bodhicitta* which has the form of the vajra-word and the intrinsic nature of the vajra-word.

And that *bodhicitta* does not abide in the body, nor does it abide in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); it does not abide in speech, nor does it abide in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); it does not abide in the mind, nor even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, for that phenomenon which does not abide within the three realms, there is no arising.

This thorough knowledge of the characteristics of the three realms is the indestructible, non-deceptive cause for generating the wisdom of all Tathāgatas; it is the "vajra-word. Having thus ascertained the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of things through their similarity to dreams, he speaks again, casting further light upon the very certainty regarding dreams:
"And not," and so forth.
"I" [mean]: "In the three realms, I show the dream-state and the fruit by means of a dream for the three kinds of sentient beings."
In this way, there is no volitional construction regarding the dream;
nor is there a person's prayer, "May a dream be seen by me."

Moreover, the activities within the three realms—the auspicious and inauspicious actions of the various multitudes of sentient beings during the waking state—are like dreams; for they are dream-like, resembling a dream, and diverse like a dream. Just as these are produced by dreams and indicated by dreams, so too, in this very manner, all the Buddhas perfected in the world-systems of the ten directions, the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages beginning with the Joyous (Pramuditā), and all sentient beings—whether born from eggs, from wombs, from moisture, or spontaneously born—all of them must be understood through the principle of the selflessness of dreams; they are to be realized as being like illusions, just as in dreams, by one established in the Illusion-like Samādhi.

Having thus demonstrated the pervasiveness of the mind-made divine form, he speaks to reveal its essential nature, beginning with "tadyathā" (for example): "The wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇiratna*) is far superior to all worldly gems because it bestows whatever is desired; it is divine and human, endowed with human qualities, and sought after by sentient beings."

Just as gold and other such things that one brings forth merely by thinking of them or merely by desiring them do not emerge from the minds of sentient beings, nor do they come from a *cintāmaṇi* jewel, in the very same way, all phenomena have the characteristic of illusion. The Buddhas—the perfected ones and the multitudes of perfected beings—and their phenomena have the sixth [element] as their cause; therefore, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are to be authorized.
"Then," and so forth.

The Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, beginning with Akṣobhya, their eyes wide open with great joy because they were endowed with the five kinds of delight, and their eyes expanded as they beheld the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, spoke thus to the Great Vajradhara:

"O Blessed One, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! That within all phenomena—which are like space, pervasive as space, and non-abiding—the Buddha-qualities, the body of gnosis, reach and enter into a common convergence and a synthesis; this indeed is that which is marvelous."
Having thus encouraged them, he states what they did next with the words beginning with "atha" and so forth:
all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having prostrated by falling at the feet of Vajrapāṇi, the Great Vajradhara, spoke as follows.
By the Blessed One, you [were taught] the *Mantravajrasiddhisamuccaya*.
"Mantras" refers to the garlands of mantras and so forth;
"vajras" refers to the meditations (*dhyānas*).

The mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) produced by them—their collection or multitude—is that which has been spoken; the question is: "Where do all these spoken accomplishments of the compendium of mantras reside?
The response begins with "Now," and so forth:
Vajrapāṇi, Mahāvajrapāṇi, the Great Holder of the Vajra.
Having given them his approval, he spoke to them as follows:
"O Blessed Ones," and so forth.

As for the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of the collection of all mantra-vajras: "all mantras" refers to the practitioners; [the accomplishment] does not belong to their body, speech, or mind as long as [it has not been attained].
Therefore, they do not abide anywhere. For what reason? For what cause?
Because, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), there is an absence of the body and so forth, as well as the accomplishments (*siddhi*) of mantras and so forth.
He says that all means for accomplishing mantra-siddhis perish there in every way;
however, [he continues] with "But what... and so forth.

By way of conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisattva*), all siddhis—all the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhadharma*) such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*)—exist, having the nature of one's own vajra body, speech, and mind.
If that were so, then because the body and so forth exist, the supernatural attainments (*siddhis*) based upon them would be perceived.
Refuting that, he says:
"And that," and so on.
That body and so forth do not abide within the desire realm and so on.
Having set aside their abiding within the three realms, he says "the mind does not abide in the body," and so forth, while also refuting the relationship of mutual support and supported.
To begin with, the mind does not abide in the body,
nor does the body abide in the mind, because of the contradiction in the relationship of support and supported between the two.
Likewise, speech also does not abide in the mind.
It should be understood that the mind does not abide in speech, likewise speech does not abide in the body, and the body does not abide in speech.
Why is that? Because, being pure by nature like space, there is no relationship of mutual support and supported among these three.
"Then," and so forth. They spoke to Vajradhara;
"all the Tathāgatas" refers to Akṣobhya and the others.
"He wards them off"—this refers to all the dharmas of the Tathāgatas; this is the sixth [topic]. The question is: where does he abide, or from what is he produced?
Vajradhara replied: "He abides in one's own body, speech, and mind; he is produced from one's own body, speech, and mind."
The Tathāgatas have said: "They ask:
where does the mind abide?
Where does the vajra of the mind abide?"
Vajradhara spoke:
"It abides in space;
it abides in luminosity."
The Tathāgatas have asked: "Where is the luminous space situated?
The Blessed One replied: "It is situated nowhere.
That luminosity is not situated anywhere; it means that it is situated in itself alone."
The passage beginning with "Then," and so forth, is the speech of the compiler.

Those Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, having attained wonder through the causes and having attained marvel through the fruits, remained silent and entered a state of silence because they were free from doubt, as they meditated upon—that is, took as their object—the dwelling in the true nature (*dharmatā*) of their own minds and the play of their own minds.

The mind consists of both the stable and the moving; all minds have that as their essence. The *samaya* is the pledge of all minds, which is Mahāvajradhara. Its "essence" (*sāra*) refers to the mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhis*). These very accomplishments are "vajras" because they are unfailing. The collection of texts by which their "origination"—that is, their manifestation—is revealed is given that name.
This is in *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (twilight language).
