The Explanation of the Six Points in the Fifteenth Chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
[The text provided consists solely of vertical bars and does not contain content to translate.]
The sixteenth chapter.

Since all the accomplishments (*siddhis*) characterized as previously described are achieved only by one who has been consecrated in the mandala, [the author], introducing the sixteenth chapter which is useful for the procedure of the mandala in order to make the disciple a worthy vessel,
says "Now," and so forth.

Again and again, becoming single-minded, they entreated Mahāvajradhara with hymns established upon the vajra-words of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas—those vajras of body, speech, and mind of the Tathāgatas residing in infinite and boundless world-systems—and with such expressions as "the peace of all Tathāgatas. Having thus brought him face-to-face, they worshipped him with arrays of jewel-vajra offerings of all the Tathāgatas and with divine clouds of sensory objects;
the implication is that this was done with the intention of hearing the ritual procedure for the maṇḍala.

"All Vajras" refers to the Tathāgatas; their "maṇḍala" is the body-maṇḍala (*kāyamaṇḍala*). That itself is the "Lion" because it destroys the deer of the afflictions (*kleśa*); it is the "King of Samaya" (*samayarāja*). Having entered into that meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which a specific resolve has been formed and a manifested array—the retinue of the maṇḍala—is revealed, Vairocana, who possesses the vajra-body, emitted from his own body and so forth that maṇḍala presided over by him, which serves the purpose of all Buddhas and all practitioners.
The word "atha" (then) is used as a particle of introduction;
the word "ataḥ" (from this) indicates a reason.
Since there are those who are curious to hear about the maṇḍala, I shall explain it by unfolding it correctly from here and there.
The body-maṇḍala is the supreme Vairocana-maṇḍala, which bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
To the question "How is that so?", he says "The mind," and so forth.
That which resembles the Akṣobhya-maṇḍala, appearing like the Vajra of Mind, and possesses qualities such as being square—that is the supreme of all maṇḍalas.
Regarding the phrase "sixteen cubits":
with respect to the four sides, it should be understood that each side is four cubits; thus it is square, not circular.
The term "quadrangular" (*caturasra*) is used as an illustration; by this, the four gates and other features are included.
It should be very beautiful due to the application of colors and powders.
Of what kind is it?

The mandala of all Buddhas is praised by all Tathāgatas; it is adorned by Vairocana, the Body-Vajra, who is established therein as its presiding lord. Within that square mandala, there is a circular wheel, decorated with a garland of wheels.
To the question "How so?", he says: "According to the ritual procedure."
One should draw [the mandala] with that intellect in which the ritual procedure—the drawing of the mandala as taught in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other texts—is firmly established as the "Vajra.

Having thus drawn the mandala, one should place the station of Vairocana and the station of the Mudrā-vajra—the form of the deity conjoined with its own mudrā—in the center among the deities of the mantras; and one should draw Akṣobhya and the others situated in the east and the other directions.
One should establish only the commentary on the sixteen chapters and sixty million verses.

One should draw and install Locanā and the other goddesses— the foremost of the Vajra Body, Speech, and Mind— in all the corners, that is, in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneyī) as appropriate.

The knower of mantras, the preceptor, should place Krodha Yamāri at the beginning of those [deities]—namely Aparājita, Hayagrīva, Amṛtakuṇḍalin, and the others—at the four gates; he should place Mahābala and Parākrama, as well as Acala and the rest, in the corners; and he should place Rūpa and the others, along with Maitreya and the rest, in their respective positions. In the center of the maṇḍala, accompanied by his own mudrā, he should perform the worship consisting of the union of the lotus and vajra, empowered by the secret vajra.
This is the procedure for all mantras, the commitment (*samaya*) of practitioners, the established rule of the Yoga Tantra, which is difficult to transgress and must not be violated.
The five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), beginning with feces and urine, must specifically and exclusively be offered and consumed within this maṇḍala of the body.

This consumption of the five nectars is the *samaya*—which must not be transgressed—of all mantras and all practitioners who are devoted to the maṇḍala of the body of the Vajra-holders. This maṇḍala of the body is favored by all the Tathāgatas. Then, with the words beginning "atha," Mahāvajradhara [expounds] the procedure for the maṇḍala of speech; the *samayas* of all the Vajras of Speech are the deities of the retinue of Amitābha.

A "cloud" (*megha*) is a collection; its "array" (*vyūha*) is its arrangement according to its respective positions. Having entered the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that [collection], one should personally emanate from one's body and so forth this "mandala of speech-vajras"—that is, a collection of words for that purpose.
He demonstrates this with the passage beginning "Then, therefore" (*athātaḥ*), the meaning of which has been analyzed.
One should make it twenty cubits on each side.

One should mark out a five-cubit square with threads colored according to the five Tathāgatas through the visualization of the vajras. In the center of that square mandala, one who is intent on the ritual and skilled in the rules should draw a great, primary, circular wheel adorned with lotuses. Within that mandala, one should draw all the mudrās in their entirety.
How so?
One should place the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) of Amitāyus, conjoined with one's own seal, in the center of that.
One should likewise conceive and perform the vajra-position (vajrapada) of body and mind—the arrangement of the Tathāgatas—for all [the deities].

Having properly and clearly constructed the mandala according to the prescribed rite taught in the tantra, one should accomplish the secret worship, which is the worship of the Tathāgatas characterized by the union of the two organs.
When this is done, the Buddhas—the Vajradharas residing in the ten directions—are pleased and become gracious toward the practitioner.
By worshipping the disciples and oneself with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) consisting of feces, urine, and semen, the accomplishment of one's desired aim is attained.
The phrase "This indeed" has its meaning fully explained.
Regarding the mandala of Amitābha, which is most highly praised by all the Tathāgatas:

having thus described the triad of mandalas of the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, [the author], wishing to demonstrate the preeminence among the remaining two Tathāgatas and other members of the mandala, says "Then," and so forth.

Because they bring about the accomplishment of all purposes like clouds from various directions on every side, they are the Tathāgatas known as Samantamegha (Universal Clouds). Their *vyūha* is their assembly or multitude; the *vajra* is the distinct mandala within which [this] samādhi is taught. Having brought to mind this samādhi called Samantameghavyūhavajra—which consists of one-pointedness of mind—he brought forth from his own body and so forth this secret of the mandala, which resides in the intellect, is supremely secret, must be strictly concealed, and is not to be revealed.
Regarding the words "of whom," and so forth:

Among the foremost Vajradharas and the other mandala deities beginning with Vajradhara, the maṇḍala-circle of whichever particular deity’s image is established in the center of the maṇḍala shall belong to that specific deity.
It is born from the secrets of body, speech, and mind, and consists of the three secrets, since the Ratna and Karma families are included within those.

"All Tathāgatas" refers to Akṣobhya and the others. Their "vajra-words of body, speech, and mind" are the maṇḍalas of the body and so forth. The "knowledge" regarding them consists of the procedures such as the laying of the ritual lines (*sūtrapātana*). The "secret" of that knowledge is characterized by the transformation (*parāvṛtti*) of the maṇḍala; that which exists within this supreme secret and supreme instruction is thus described. Now, beginning with "Then," etc.:

The maṇḍala-circle of all [deities] beginning with Akṣobhya is the foundational maṇḍala from which they arise. Having entered into that samādhi—one-pointedness of mind—named after it, he proclaimed and revealed from his own vajra-body and so forth the secret nature of the body, speech, and mind of all those very maṇḍalas.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therein," etc.:

In that regard, these vajra-maṇḍalas and Tathāgata-cakras, which are being introduced here within the secrets of body and so forth, have as their nature the propitiation of the mind; they are *hṛdayas* (hearts) because they are deities, *sūtras* (threads) because they are the yoga for laying out the maṇḍala, and *akṣaras* (syllables) because they are indestructible.
They are *padās* (words/footsteps) because they serve as the foundation for all mantras.
As to what they are, he says:
Oṃ āḥ hūṃ.
"Throwing [the line]," and so forth.
The *vajras* are Akṣobhya and the others; the thread of their colors is the "vajra-thread.

The throwing of that [thread], which is the laying out of the maṇḍala lines, as well as the throwing—that is, the scattering—of the five-colored powder, should be performed with the mantras beginning with *oṃ*, etc.; this is the remainder [of the meaning].
"Should not be performed," and so forth.
By one who is devoted to the reality of mantra and endowed with the knowledge of non-duality, the drawing of the mandala in the manner described should not be performed.
If he were to perform it, his awakening—the state of Vajradhara—would be difficult to attain and remain far away.
The sense is that one should perform [the rite] according to the procedure taught in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other such texts.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*):

one who abides in the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), one who abides in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), and one who has fulfilled the vows of knowledge (*vidyāvrata*)—if such a person should perform the drawing of the mandala, the procedure for that consists of the commitments (*samaya*) and the mudrās taught according to the divisions of the families (*kula*). The commentary on these sixteen chapters consists of sixty million verses. The "procedure" refers to the arrangement according to the method taught in the *Samāja*; the "mantrin" is one who knows that.
"Having brought down," it is said.

The practitioner is the *mantra*; his deity is his own *mudrā*. Having brought her down and established her before him, one should meditate upon—that is, accomplish—the "foot" or location of the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is the transformation into the five families (*pañcakulīkaraṇa*). Then, one should perform the construction of the mandalas—the body-mandala and so forth—according to the sequence beginning with the casting of the lines (*sūtrapāta*).
Having thus stated the general procedure, he now states the ritual according to the distinctions of the families.

Therein, the mantra-practitioner desiring to draw the body-maṇḍala, himself possessing the yoga of Vairocana, should manifest his own mudrā Locanā as if she were the actual Locanā, and together with her perform the drawing of the maṇḍala lines and so forth. Regarding the merit of this practice: the body is Vairocana; the locus of that [body] is the maṇḍala, and the circle dependent upon it is "delightful" (*ramya*), meaning charming because it bestows slight fruit. Kāyavajra is the Vajra-body; its quality is the setting in motion of the teaching of the Dharma to sentient beings in various forms throughout infinite and boundless world-systems. This becomes the means for bringing that [quality] about for practitioners.
"Vajradharma," and so forth.
The mantra-practitioner, having visualized himself as the great king Vajradharma, and having visualized his own consort, the mudrā Pāṇḍaravāsinī, should cause [the deities] to descend.
He should draw the maṇḍala of speech.
This is the sequence:
the supreme, eternal secret and mystery of all mantras belonging to the Lotus Family, of the Tathāgatas who are beginningless.
"Vajrasattva," and so forth.
Having meditated upon oneself in the form of Akṣobhya and having empowered one’s own mudrā, Māmakī, one should cause [the deities] to descend and draw the mind-maṇḍala.
This is the supreme, most wonderful, and progressively higher secret of all mantras belonging to the Vajra family for practitioners.

By performing the ritual procedure of the maṇḍala in this manner, the wise Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, being well-pleased, approach and assemble; filled with joy and exceedingly satisfied, they draw and bring to completion the maṇḍala that is the supreme secret and the ultimate mystery.
This means that, having empowered the body, speech, and mind of the practitioner who is accompanied by the mudrā, they bring the maṇḍala into being through those two.
The phrase "thus he said" is the statement of the compiler.
"Should be performed," and so forth.

By the mantra-adept—the practitioner who has completed the mandala according to the procedure just described—the "Vajra-secret," the most wonderful and extraordinary secret of the Tathāgatas, must be enacted.
To the question "What is that? he says:
"Having drawn in," and so forth:

having drawn in all the Buddhas who have arisen through the assembly and are situated in the mandala of space by means of the Wrathful King Nisumbha, one should worship them after uniting them with their respective [consorts]. The "pledge-worship" (*samayapūjā*) is the worship performed with those [consorts], such as Rūpavajrī and the others, during the three times—that is, at the three junctions of the day—for the one possessing the stainless vajra of the three vajras; this must be performed for the deities of the mandala.
How so?

By means of the yoga of the three vajras—that is, by means of the yoga consisting of the unification with the Buddhas of the three times who are the "three vajras"—one should worship; such is the meaning. Regarding this procedure, [the author] asks what it accomplishes in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*:
Regarding "the setting in motion of mantra-accomplishment" (*mantrasiddhipravartanam*):

*mantras* are the Tathāgatas; from them comes *siddhi*, characterized as both mundane and supramundane. Its "setting in motion" means its accomplishment. This is what he says with the words beginning with "of all. One should offer—that is, bestow—the *bali*, which is a satiating oblation, to the mantras. They gather together.
It is most wonderful and exceedingly sublime.
This very thing is the internal offering (*adhyātmika bali*).
Demonstrating this, he says: the five objects, beginning with excrement (*viṭ*), are intended by the etymological explanation (*nirukti*).
Now, he asks "What then? regarding the case when the five objects of sense do not exist; [the answer is] "by means of *śukra*.

That which cuts through or destroys sorrow (*śuca*) like a saw is *śukra*, namely liquor (*madya*). By that, the gratification and satiation of all mantras and their practitioners is proclaimed—that is, it has been taught.
For this rule is a commitment (*samaya*) that must not be transgressed.
"Supreme" means being the foremost. "Buddhas" refers to the ministers; their "enlightenment" is their mind, and he is its "fulfiller," meaning its nourisher.
The intention is that the satisfaction of the mantra itself is the complete satisfaction of the Tathāgatas.
Having thus explained the procedure for drawing the mandala together with a well-trained mudrā, he states the procedure for one who is devoid of her, beginning with "of the thread," and so forth.

When one performs this laying out of the maṇḍala lines alone, being devoid of wisdom, then, having manifested oneself as Vairocana within the body-maṇḍala, one should manifest the disciple as Vajrasattva;

or else, one should conceive of the disciple as Vajramahādyuti or Amṛtakuṇḍalin. The ritual procedure for constructing the maṇḍala, which follows immediately thereafter, is praised and practiced by all the Buddhas.
Likewise, in the mind-maṇḍala, having meditated on oneself as Akṣobhya, one should conceive of the disciple as Vairocana or Amṛtakuṇḍalin.
In the same way, it should be understood that in the mandala of speech as well,

one should place and meditate upon the five great kings of the Buddhas, Akṣobhya and the others, who have entered into the threads in the form of the syllable *HŪṂ* and so forth, situated within the black and other colored threads according to their respective positions.
This is the procedure for laying the threads, the most wonderful, distinguished, and secret secret of all the Buddhas.
Regarding the passage beginning with "twenty ribs" and so forth:
since each individual *rajas* (strand) consists of five aspects, it is shown that one should effect the deposition of the aggregate of the five *rajas*s, which is divided into twenty-five types;
thus, within each *rajas*, one should meditate upon the five Tathāgatas in both primary and secondary forms.
He explains the procedure for pacifying obstacles at the time of drawing the mandala—the supreme secret of all mantras and all Tathāgatas, the distinguished tradition of awakening:
"All mantras" refers to those belonging to the mandala; for the sake of protecting them from external calamities, one should perform the meditation on Vajra-huṃkāra, who is Yamāntaka.
To explain how this is so, he says "body," and so forth.

One who possesses the yoga of Yamāri should meditate upon and manifest the divine, extraordinary commitment (*samaya*) of body and speech—the miraculous display (*vikurvita*) of body, speech, and mind—during calamities caused by the earth and other elements.

The commentary on the sixteen chapters, known as the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*, states: the crushing of obstacles through the *tattvālīḍha* posture and other means is the miraculous transformation of the body;
the recitation of mantras with a voice like the roar of the clouds at the time of universal dissolution is the miraculous transformation of speech;
and taking emptiness (*śūnyatā*) as the object amidst all obstacles is the miraculous transformation of the mind.
That [suffering] consists of disturbances caused by earth, such as wood, clods of earth, or spells;
disturbances caused by water, such as floods, rain, and so forth; and those caused by fire, which is unbearable. This is the suffering of the element of fire.
A wind-storm caused by Vāyu,
a disturbance of space caused by that which transcends the senses—
in these five instances, the meditation on the Vajra-hūṃkāra should be performed.

When this has been done, the hosts of obstructors (*vighnagaṇāḥ*)—who have arisen from that Great Vajra-holder (*Mahāvajradhara*), the indivisible vajra of the three vajras (*trivajrābhedyavajra*)—being terrified with fear and seized by the dread of their own destruction, are unable to perform the presence (*sānnidhya*), the approach (*upasarpaṇa*), or the attendance (*sannidhāna*) for the wise and knowing practitioner (*vajrasattva-sādhaka*) during the ritual of the mandala; they are incapable of performing the placement (*nyāsa*) of the vases and vajras.

Regarding the placement (*nyāsa*) of the sprinkling vessels, the victory flask (*vijayakalaśa*), and so forth—what is its specific nature? It is that which is "remembered" (*smṛta*) by the masters of the mantra-system (*mantratantrādhipāḥ*), those who apply themselves to the *Mantratantra* (the tantra that collects mantras) and protect it according to the prescribed rules, such as those proficient in the *Tattvasaṃgraha* and other works.

By means of the placements of locations, medicinal herbs, seeds, signs (*liṅga*), and so on, the flask is thus fashioned and prepared. The Maṇḍala Master, established in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of Vajrasattva, firm in intellect and with undistracted mindfulness, should fashion [the arrangement] and place [the flasks] in their respective positions.

Having thus completed the mandala, the practitioner who knows the mantras and desires the fruit of all accomplishments—seeking both mundane and supramundane siddhis—should then perform the fire offering (homa) and the invocation (havana), according to the procedures taught in both tantras; this is the implied meaning.

By means of the passage beginning with "feces and urine," he describes the internal fire offering (ādhyātmika-homa). Therein, one should present the oblation to the deities of the body-mandala as an offering, using such foods and drinks as feces, urine, semen, fish, solid foods, oil, and liquor.
Regarding the passage beginning with "pūrṇā" (the full oblation):

having partaken [of the offerings], the yogins who possess the wheel of the indivisible three vajras should offer the full vajra-oblation (*vajrāhuti*) into the fire—prepared with fuel according to whatever is available—with a particularly unified ritual action.

How so? Having meditated upon the form of one's own deity—the form of the deity distinguished by the various types of rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth—in the center of the hearth (*kuṇḍa*), one should offer the full oblation into the wheel, that is, into its mouth.

Thus, having completed the fire offering while situated within the circle of the assembly (*gaṇacakra*), one who remains engaged in the union of the two organs should offer or perform the oblation of leftover food and so forth—one hundred and eight times according to the specific ritual action—by means of attaining union with the deity.
The explanation of the passage beginning with "This indeed" (*eṣo hi*) and so forth is easy to understand;
by means of the words "Vairocana" and so forth, he demonstrates the procedure for entry preceded by possession (*āveśa*).

He who shines in various ways is Vairocana, the Great Vajradhara; the application (*prayoga*) is the transformation of him into the nature of hatred. In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, by means of that, one makes the disciple "born from the three vajras"—that is, born from the triad beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ). Having visualized the red-colored syllable *āḥ* emitting rays of light upon all the limbs of the body, speech, and mind, when the ritual of possession (*āveśa*) has been performed, he is seized—that is, taken possession of—by the "Vajra of Possession.
This very point is stated: Vajrasattva is Akṣobhya, and the Great King is Amitābha.
Vairocana, the one of great renown,
bestows the empowerment of the commitment (*samaya*) of body, speech, and mind— the domain of body and so forth.
Since this must be performed without exception therein, this is the vajra-word that constitutes its limb for the purpose of entering the great maṇḍala.
What is that? It is "Āḥ Khaṃ Vīra Hūṃ.

This is the heart-mantra of all commitments (*samaya*), consisting of body, speech, and mind; it is the "heart of body, speech, and mind" (*kāyavākcittahṛdaya*). This mantra-vajra consists of the syllables that illuminate that [heart].

In that ritual of the mandala, the Great Vajra is the disciple for the purpose of initiation; his initiation is the "Great Vajra Initiation" (mahāvajrābhiṣeka). That very thing, because it is to be kept secret, is the "Secret" (guhya), the mystery of gnosis.

One should visualize or meditate upon the element of space, the hollow of the sky, as being completely filled with all the Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, with great clouds of music and incense—that is, with the five qualities of sensual pleasure such as those that cover the directions. Having worshipped those residing therein, the Vajra-wisdom Preceptor should himself meditate; having visualized the Vajra as written by himself within the mandala, he should perform the union according to the sequence.
And thus he said:
"By the three vajras," and so forth:

the practitioner, that is, the master, should visualize the Tathāgatas with mustard seeds— which are drops of bodhicitta produced by the unification of one's own mudrā’s body, speech, and mind with the three vajra-samayas—
and he should strike or impel them for the purpose of bestowing initiation upon the disciples.
At that time, the Tathāgatas, being impelled, will themselves come and bestow empowerment and consecration;
or else, one should meditate upon the Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, through the samādhi of Vajrasattva.
Having meditated thus, one should visualize those vases as being held by Sulocanā and the other goddesses.
Then the teacher Budha, being firm-minded and one-pointed in intellect, said: "What then?"

Immediately thereafter, the knower of mantras should visualize the disciple as Vajravairocana. He should perform the proper placement (*nyāsa*) of the seed-syllables for the generation of the deity upon the body-mandala of the disciple, who possesses the vajras of body, speech, and mind.

When this placement has been performed, the consecration to be described hereafter is the "all-consecration" (*sarvābhiṣeka*) in every mandala. Regarding that, the "secret" is that which is to be concealed; it is the bestowing of consecration by all the masters in the mind-mandala and so forth. Their proclamation of the speech-vajra (*vāgvajra*) toward the disciple is the manifestation of the speech-vajra.
Regarding that which is the commentary on the six million [verses] of the sixteenth chapter,
he says "consecration" and so forth.

The consecration that establishes one in the sovereignty over the triple world, the great vajra that is impossible to relinquish, and which is honored by the triple world—all this, arising from and descending through the lineage of all Buddhas and all Tathāgatas, I, the Great Vajradhara, the Vajra of the Three Secrets, bestow upon you today. What shall you do in this regard? Thus is the consolation of the disciple.

When the Vajra Guru has spoken thus, all the disciples, established according to their respective *kula* divisions, [should perform] this which is about to be described: the request (*prārthanā*) or entreaty (*adhyeṣaṇā*) directed toward him, the Great Vajra (Mahāvajra), the Vajra Guru. The procedure (*vidhi*) or ritual method (*vidhāna*) therein is itself the secret.
What is it? "By the Bodhicitta-vajra," and so forth.

"Bodhivajra" is the Great Vajradhara. "The great festival" (*mahāmaha*) refers to the great consecration (*mahābhiṣeka*) bestowed upon the Buddhas, such as Akṣobhya and others, in whatever manner it was given for the sake of crossing over—that is, for my own crossing over the ocean of *saṃsāra*. "O you who are equal to the Great Vajradhara of Space, now, at this very moment, grant it to me who has gone for refuge to you"—this is the supplication.
Then, at that time, with a joyful mind and a heart well-pleased by the request, the Guru should bestow the consecration.

The deity’s image is the outer mandala; the yoga with it consists in its placement within the disciple’s body-mandala as far as possible. For that reason, one should place—that is, establish—the Lord, the sovereign of the mandala, in his very heart, in the heart-lotus.

To the wise disciple who has thus prepared himself and is endowed with wisdom, one should show the mandala according to the sequence in its true nature, beginning with the words "the pledge" (*samaya*) and so forth.

This commitment (*samaya*), which has been proclaimed and spoken by all the Buddhas—the perfected Tathāgatas—is not to be transgressed; it must be performed. One should cause the Vajra-disciple to hear and reveal it, such as [the command] "you must kill living beings," and so forth. This fourfold commitment is to be understood through the explanation of the intentional terminology (*sandhyābhāṣā*) as stated in the fifth chapter.
By means of this aforementioned Vajra-path, which is the indivisible meditative absorption (*abhedyasamādhi*), one should impel—that is, instruct—all sentient beings who are Vajra-disciples.
This path of all the Buddhas is difficult to transcend; what is the nature of this commitment to the samaya? It is supremely eternal, without beginning or end.
And so it is said:
"One should give the mantra," and so forth. Having received the pledges and vows (*samaya-saṃvara*), he should be touched by the Guru, who asks: "Which siddhi do you prefer?"
When he should say, "This pleases me," then one should give him the mantra for accomplishing that particular task.
How?
By means of those spoken as injunctions of the mantra.

The Guru has spoken the exhortations regarding the meaning of the mantra; having understood the disciple’s intention through those spoken exhortations of the mantra—the words of the disciple—he should grant [the initiation]. This is the application (*yoga*). Having bestowed the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the King of Mantras and the corresponding deity-yoga, he should commence—that is, perform—the secret initiation (*guhyābhiṣeka*) for the sake of the success (*siddhi*) under discussion. Showing this in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, he says "semen" (*śukram*), and so forth.

Because of his mastery, he takes the remaining three nectars. Having consecrated this pentad of nectars according to the rule with the two-syllable mantra, and having rendered them immortal through the ritual procedures of purification and so forth, the Vajra-lord—the Vajra-ācārya—should cause the Vajra-disciple to consume them; he should have him partake.
In this way, the desired accomplishment is not difficult to attain.
Thus, showing the secret [teaching] to one who has been consecrated by the external initiation, he says:
"These four," and so forth.
This is the secret, not to be disclosed, for all practitioners who have newly set out upon the vehicle.
Those which are earth and so forth— these are the four great secrets, the supreme mysteries. By means of the mantra-circle in the form of women,
they exist as those who have assumed the forms of women through the intrinsic nature of the Tathāgatas.
For what purpose?

For the sake of acting for the benefit of sentient beings—that is, for the purpose of acting to bring about their peace and so forth—the elements such as earth and the others take on the forms of Vairocana and the rest; furthermore, having concealed their status as being appropriated by a person (*puruṣaparigraha*), they attain the forms of the [deities] such as Locanā. This is the meaning. In that context, at the time of bestowing the *samaya*, the "Vajra-maṇḍala" is the Mind-maṇḍala; the "mantras" therein are the deities. The "secret" therein is the propitiation and subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) of all of them.
What is that? "Elephant meat," and so forth.
One should practice this visualization upon oneself.
One should offer [oblations] to the deities of the mantras in the form of *homa* and *bali*.
In this way, the leaders are satisfied; they attain satisfaction by the granting of desired objects.
"Every day," and so forth.

The Vajra Guru, who is like a Buddha, should demonstrate and instruct the disciple who has received initiation regarding the mandala and the procedure for the *gaṇacakra*, which is to be performed daily, monthly, or annually.
How?
By means of the practice involving feces, urine, and flesh.
In this context, by the mention of feces and urine, the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) are included; by the mention of meat, the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*) are included;
and by the mention of ritual actions (*kṛtya*), the inclusion of things that are not to be eaten or drunk is intended.
The meaning is that through these—feces and so forth, the secret vajra term, the union of the two organs, and dancing, singing, and so on—one should demonstrate everything that is pleasing.
He describes the manifestation of the sign at the time of consuming the food of the five nectars, beginning with "Oṃkāra":

having meditated upon the *praṇava*, which is the beginning of all mantras, upon the food that has been previously purified and awakened, the Blessed One—the Great Mantra-Vidyā-Puruṣa, the Great Vajradhara—immediately, at that very moment, blazes forth and causes [the food] to blaze; thus he spoke.
Thus, since there may occasionally be even that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) which transcends the world, I have said "the means" (*sādhana*), and so forth.
The means for all accomplishments—including the minor accomplishments such as pacification (*śānti*) and the rest—occurs by this very path.

The accomplishment of the Great Pledge (*mahāsamaya*), the accomplishment of the eightfold great accomplishments beginning with the pill (*gulikā*), and even the awakening of a Buddha—the state of Buddhahood characterized by the accomplishment of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*)—which in the system of the Perfections (*pāramitānaya*) is accomplished only with extreme effort, is accomplished by one's own self through this very method.
That is to say, not by any other means.
This very point is illuminated by the passage beginning with "disappearance," which is easy to understand.

The sixteenth chapter, the commentary on the *Ṣaṭkoṭi*: "Feces and urine," and so forth. Feces and urine are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*); "great flesh" (*mahāmāṃsa*) refers to the five lamps (*pañcapradīpa*). Having made these two equal parts, one should draw them out on the eighth or fourteenth day, form them into pills, purify them in the shade, place them in a covered vessel of lotus shape within a pair of shallow bowls (*śarāva*), and consume one pill every day.
To the question "What then? he says: "One shall dwell together with the Buddhas. The Buddhas are the Siddhas; one shall dwell together with them.
And so it is said:
"In that regard," and so forth.

In that context, regarding the discussion of accomplishment (*siddhi*), "all secret vajras" refers to the preeminent *yakṣas*; they themselves are "servants" (*kiṃkara*) because they seek [the practitioner's] command. This is the "basis for their accomplishment," meaning this is the method for accomplishing them.

One should contemplate and meditate upon the syllable *hrīḥ*, red in color, blazing with intense radiance, and pervaded by five rays of light, situated in the center of space within the middle of the vajra.

Having done this, one should visualize the realm of space (*khadhātu*), the hollow of the sky, pervading the ten directions and completely filled with all the Buddhas, beginning with Akṣobhya and ending with the wrathful deities.

One should then cause these three—the words of body, speech, and mind of those Buddhas, which are the seeds of the body and so forth, namely *āḥ*, *khaṃ*, and *vīḥ*—to descend into that mantra, the syllable *hrīḥ*.
Regarding this, the passage beginning with "In that regard" (*tatre dam*) and so forth:
therein, in the accomplishment of the *kiṅkara*, the "mantra-vajra"—which is the secret state—of body, speech, and mind is the "stage of empowerment" (*adhiṣṭhāna-pada*), the stage of accomplishment.
What is that?
"ĀḤ KHAṂ VĪḤ"—having thus accomplished the servant (*kiṃkara*) who consists of these three syllables, one should employ him in whatever task is desired.
Furthermore, showing a specific type of servant, [the text] says "Vajrapāṇi," and so forth.

Having meditated upon Vajrapāṇi Akṣobhya and his similar great image with a formidable body—namely Nisumbharāja—and likewise having contemplated Padmapāṇi Amitābha and his similar Hayagrīva of great splendor and great power; and having meditated upon the great image produced from that [Amitābha], known as Mahāprabha and Yamāntaka according to the distinction of families—Vairocana being "Unconquered" (Aparājita) because he is not to be recited due to his peerless array of radiance—one should place and establish the secret word, the holder of secrets, within them.
In that regard, while they are being thus generated, the Vajra-secrets are the wrathful deities; their "place" (pada) is the application of the command.
What is that?
It is the solar mandala, and so forth.

Because he is immovable and is an emanation of Vajradhara, Akṣobhya is Nisumbharāja; having placed him within a solar disc and having enjoined him to the secret vajra-word, one should fashion—that is, perform—the rite. Likewise, having placed Amitāyu’s great wheel, Hayagrīva, and the servant (kiṅkara) within a lotus-solar disc, one should enjoin the secret word to them.
Similarly, having placed the servant of Vairocana upon the moon and sun, one should bestow it.
"Codayed" and so forth:

one should impel all these vajra-attendants (*vajrakiṅkara*), who possess great splendor and great radiance, by means of "intense sufferings"—that is, by the intense sufferings of Akṣobhya and the others, who are themselves afflicted by the suffering of rescuing the world from intense suffering. One should urge them toward the granting of *siddhi*. In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, this is the seed-syllable for that impelling.
"All Vajras" refers to Vairocana and the others. "In their heart" means in their mind; "incitement" refers to the urging toward the delivery of the command of wrath.
"ĀṂ HŪṂ" is the utterance of the promise for the purpose of inciting the wrathful deities.

Having thus incited the wrathful deities (*krodha*) by means of their presiding lords, and desiring to have them likewise performed by their retinues as well, he says "with great spears," and so forth.

With those bearing great spears, those bearing spears; with those wearing great garments, those bearing the vajra; with those holding hooks, those bearing hooks; with various others bearing different weapons; with excellent, indivisible hosts of retinues—one should incite them according to the sequence prescribed by rule.
To the question, "What is accomplished when this is done? he says: "The awakening of the Buddha (*buddhabodhi*) is successfully achieved."
The Buddha is the practitioner; his awakening is the intended goal, which is accomplished and reaches its consummation.
Thus he spoke, and Mahāvajradhara also said this.
The passage beginning with "parvata" has its meaning already explained. Here, Buddhahood itself is the subject under discussion as the means (*sādhana*).
With the words beginning "of the thirty-six," he states the fruit of that means.

As many as there are atoms and dust particles in thirty-six single mountains, so many are the servants (kiṅkara) distinguished by various types such as the Ceṭas and others belonging to that Vajrasattva and the rest. All of them, who belong to the Bodhivajrin—the practitioner—become accomplished; they remain seeking his command in the form of a retinue.
The mention of "thirty-six" is stated to show that there are no fewer than this number.
Furthermore, he speaks of the benefits, beginning with "in the ten directions" and so forth:
one would traverse—that is, go to—all the buddha-fields of all the Buddhas in the ten directions, starting from the east, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
having gone there, one hears the Dharma—which serves as the cause for attaining the state of a great upholder of the Dharma—from the presence of the Tathāgatas.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And one shall attain the stage of a Buddha.
This is what is meant:

one established in the meditative absorption of the generation stage (utpattikrama), having attained the siddhi of the *kiṅkara* by means of the sequence just described, and having reached the meditative absorption of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) through the propitiation of the Tathāgatas, shall attain the state of Mahāvajradhara.
Thus spoke the Blessed One, Mahāsamayavajrahāsa, the Great Vajradhara: "This is yours," and so forth. All the *kiṅkara*s, both worldly and supramundane.
Because they are to be concealed, they are "secret" (*guhya*); for the purpose of addressing them, [the text says] "The Secret of Vajra.
The secret activity, which constitutes the instruction of Vajrasattva, is now introduced with the words "Vajrasattva," and so forth.
Vajrasattva is Akṣobhya; his great gnosis, whose nature is mind, is the syllable *HŪṂ*. Vāgvajra is Amitābha; he is called "Vāgvajradhara" because he holds or brings about its manifestation.

Vairocana is the Body-Vajra; his seed-syllable *Oṃ* is that which accomplishes the Great Deposition (*mahānyāsa*). With these syllables, one should impel the servant (*kiṅkara*) and consecrate him at all times, beginning from the moment of his accomplishment.

This is the commentary on the six crores [of verses] in the sixteenth chapter. Regarding the subject of the practice of the servant therein: "The Vajra-Wisdom Tathāgatas" refers to those [deities]; their "wheel" (*cakra*) is their assembly. The "mantras" are their utterances, and their "pledge-word" (*samayapada*) is the inviolable rule. And that [rule] is fourfold, distinguished by the impelling of the pledge and so forth.

"Samaya" refers to the exhortation, the request, and the instigation by the one known as Mahāvajradhara; it is the purpose and the task to be performed by that very same samaya; it is the goal to be accomplished, and the address therein is the application of a designation; "samaya" is the duty, and "bandha" is the forceful application thereto. To explain what those who have thus attained perfection do, he says "khadhātum" and so forth:
the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is vast, infinite, pure, unobstructed, devoid of all phenomena, and transcends seeing and the other [sensory faculties].
"Such a space-element as this, the servants (kiṅkara) impelled by the practitioner make into a solid mass, hard like a vajra;
what, then, could not be accomplished by them? This is a hyperbolic expression (atiśayokti).
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the sole son of all Buddhas—he whose single son is all the Buddhas—Mahāvajradhara.

Now, he describes the subjugation of kings and others, beginning with the words "or the Buddha. If one should desire to bring even a wise Buddha—one who belongs to the lineage of the masters—to subjection, that is, to establish him in one's own intention, one should contemplate, that is, meditate upon, this great secret which is being presented, which is of the nature of the three supreme vajras—the body and so forth—and which is the form of Mahāmañjuśrī.
To the question "How? he says "the space-vajra," and so forth.

One should instantly visualize oneself as Mañjuvajra, possessed of great power, the subduer of those difficult to subdue, situated in the center of the space-vajra, perfected through luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), by means of the application of the five arrows. Regarding the "five arrows": they are intoxication, delusion, infatuation, fainting, and paralyzing; these are the five shafts. If one should meditate, one should cause them to radiate forth from the tip of the crown upon the excellent object of practice through their application—that is, their impelling.

How so? The mantra-knower, the practitioner who knows the seed-syllables, should—with a firm resolve and by means of the fierce vajra—cause [the target] to fall upon the five locations: the head, the navel, the secret place, and the two feet;

or he should discharge the five arrows. The "one of childlike intellect" (*vālabuddhi*) refers to the practitioner whose mind and thoughts are fixed on Mañjughoṣa. With the arrows of passion and the like, which possess great fame and great power, he should contemplate—that is, visualize—the target as rendered unconscious, stupefied, and defenseless.
This meditation on subjugation,
through the secret exhortation, should be meditated upon for one fortnight— that is, half a month— by those devoted to the inner self.
This secret of all mantras and all Tathāgatas was sung and spoken by the Great Vajradhara, whose intellect realizes the meaning of the Vajra.
He states the application for the purpose of the Vinaya, beginning with "khavañe" and so forth:
having meditated upon the syllable *hūṃ* situated within the hollow of space, one should contemplate the supreme mandala of the Buddhas—the array of all Tathāgatas—through its transformation;
the Vajra-mantra is the syllable *oṃ*.

Then, by means of the five seed-syllables beginning with *ta*, one should visualize the malevolent beings who are the objects to be accomplished—such as those consisting of the three vajras—as described in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*. Having meditated on the syllable *Oṃ* located in their eyes—that is, within the eyeballs—in a throbbing form, one should demonstrate the procedure for the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) such that they perceive the maṇḍala of Buddhas residing in the hollow of space.
When this is done, the objects to be accomplished see the image of all mantras, the form of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), which is the form of all Tathāgatas. They behold it.
Overcome by hunger, thirst, burning sensations, and so forth, the practitioner should contemplate this yoga;
thus all sufferings— both physical and mental— are cast off and destroyed, just as [the state of] the Mind-Vajradhara is attained.
Demonstrating this very teaching of the Mahāvajradhara, he says "Vairocana," and so forth:

having meditated on the form of Vairocana as the perfection of all aims, one should place the syllable *vaṃ*, shaped like a full moon mandala and raining down drops of nectar, within the mouth; and one should place the white-colored syllable *oṃ* located in the middle of the palate, which causes the drops of nectar flowing from the syllable *vaṃ* to enter within.

Adorned with jewels, because it bestows the excellent happiness of youth and health, it is worthy of worship like a *cintāmaṇi* jewel; it removes all suffering, wards off all calamities such as poisons, venomous insects, and spirits, is peaceful, pacifies all afflictions, is impelled by the *jñānavajra*, and its meditation brings about the attainment of the state of a Mahāvajradhara—thus spoke the Blessed One, Cintāmaṇivajra, who is the very nature of Ratnaketu and the Great Vajradhara. Now, regarding the passage beginning with "atha" and so forth: "Mahāvajradhara," "Mahāvīravajra," and "Tathāgata" refer to a certain specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

The vajra-meditation is that which brings about its accomplishment; the supreme state manifested by one-pointedness of mind is a specific seed-syllable (*bīja*). One should emit that from the speech-vajras—namely, the syllable *Vīḥ*. That seed-syllable, situated in the center of the space-vajra, possesses the brilliant radiance of the Buddha-maṇḍala and is surrounded by the circle of Buddhas such as Akṣobhya and the rest. By means of the yoga of the three vajra-bodies—the unification of body, speech, and mind—one should bring it forth as a vajra and contemplate this:

Nourished by all ornaments because he is endowed with the marks of a Great Being (*mahāpuruṣa*), he is the yellow Vajra, Ratnasaṃbhava; one who possesses such a manifestation and play of that very [deity] is thus described. Having meditated upon him as peaceful, wearing a crown of matted hair, one should undertake and perform all rites for pacification and so forth.
This is the Hero-Vajra, the Great Vajra-Holder.
That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which there is a garland of waves— a garland of surging billows— is thus described.
"Then," and so forth:
Mahāvajradhara is the Great Heroic Vajra. "The Tathāgatas" refers to a particular distinction of meditative absorption (*samādhi-viśeṣa*).

"Vajra-cultivation" (*vajra-bhāvanā*) is the one-pointedness of mind that brings that [absorption] to completion; by means of this, the "supreme word" (*padāgra*), which is a specific seed-syllable (*bīja-viśeṣa*), is manifested.
One should cause that seed-syllable "Bhīḥ" to issue forth from the speech-thunderbolts;
such is the seed-syllable.
The commentary on the six million verses of the sixteenth chapter begins with "atha" and so forth.

That samādhi in which all Buddhas everywhere proclaim and praise a multitude of forms is named after that; having entered that stainless samādhi, which is one-pointedness of mind, and having consecrated it through mental cultivation, the Great Vajra is meditated upon—that is, brought to completion—thus it is the "Great Vajra Meditation Multitude. Its "pada," meaning the seed-syllable that brings it to completion, he should cause to issue forth from his own body, speech, and mind-vajras.

What is that? One should visualize the solar disc in the *cu~* syllable at the mouth, place therein the seed-syllable mentioned immediately before, and through the ritual procedure of the emanation and reabsorption of the Tathāgatas, one should meditate upon Cundāvatrī—she who causes the clouds of Buddhas, established within her own maṇḍala, to descend; she who is the three vajras empowered by the body-vajra and the others; she of great renown, having attained fame by removing all suffering; and she who effects the "falling" (*pātana*) of the wicked from their body, speech, and mind-vajras. One should thus bring her to manifestation.

Having meditated upon Vajrasattva, the Great Being, fully adorned with all ornaments, one should place the mantras and the Tathāgatas; that is to say, one should place their positions and their emblems, and place Vajrasattva and his emblem. "Vajra" refers to Akṣobhya; "samaya" means that which conforms by way of an emblem. "Vajrasamaya" is the form of Cundā. "Jñānaraśmi" is the light of gnosis within that samādhi.
"Atha" and so forth [follows].

Because it consumes—that is, protects—like a *vajra* that hope for all wealth and grain, it is called *Vajrasambhoga*. Entering into that [state], one should bring forth this wheel of meditative concentration (*samādhicakra*), which is a specific Jambhala-samādhi, by means of a seed-syllable; from that seed-syllable, one should emanate him from one's own body and so forth.

"Jaṃ" is the Buddha Jambhala situated in the center of the space-vajra (*khavajra*). Because he is the essence, he is the *maṇḍa*; because he takes (*lāti*) and brings that about, it is the "seed of the Buddha-maṇḍala."

Therein, by means of the ritual procedure and the yoga of summoning, one should cause all the Buddhas belonging to the Jewel Family to descend and enter [into oneself]; through the transformation of their seed-syllables, one should meditate upon oneself as Jambhala, the Great Yakṣa, golden in color, with a large belly, being a dwarf, having three faces and six arms. With his right hands, he holds a citron, a goad, and an arrow; with one left hand he embraces his own consort (vidyā), and with the other two he holds a noose and a bow of sugar-cane. Wearing a crown of matted hair, one should meditate upon oneself in this form as Jambhala, the means for accomplishing material wealth.

One should visualize the five Buddhas, Vairocana and the others, in their proper sequence according to the ritual procedure, located in the head, throat, heart, navel, and shanks, by means of the seed-syllables beginning with OṂ. Then, having emanated from one's own heart a Jambhala identical to oneself and having made him similar [to the deity] as before, one should meditate upon him with Mahāsukha—joined with his own consort—in his crown, showering him with a stream of bodhicitta arising from the syllable JAṂ. Meditating thus while reciting the mantra "OṂ JAMBHALAJALENDRĀYA SVĀHĀ," one should offer one [libation] of vajra-amṛta water upon his head.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, it is said: "One should visualize Vajrasattva upon his crown according to the ritual procedure.
When this is done, the Vajramudrā—the indestructible mudrā of Jambhala—becomes pleased and fulfills the practitioner's hopes.
Because that very [state] is worthy of adornment, it is the *samaya*;

by means of that, the "acquisition of wealth" (*dravyārādhana*)—that is, the production of wealth—is like a raised banner (*ketu*), and the prosperity (*śrī*) which is its capacity (*sāmarthya*) is present in that meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
With the words beginning with "atha," he describes the accomplishment of the *yakṣiṇī*.

Having entered the meditative absorption named *Śrīvilāsa*— in which there is the splendor (*śrī*) of enjoying objects such as those of desire and form— he emitted from his own body, speech, and mind this *vajrapada*, the seed-syllable that accomplishes the commitments (*samaya*) of all *yakṣiṇīs*, namely: *kṣiṃ*.
"In the *khadhātu*," and so forth:

having meditated upon a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) born from the syllable *kṣiṃ*, endowed with qualities such as being square, and filled with flowers and perfumes—having thus performed worship through both external and internal offerings—one should meditate on the *khadhātu*, the sky, as completely filled with all the *yakṣiṇīs*, the hosts of *yakṣiṇīs*. By means of the yoga of the three vajras, one should cause them to descend and enter into the interior of the peaked pavilion.
Immediately thereafter, one should visualize the entire retinue of yakṣiṇīs as a single yakṣiṇī form.
With the words "trivajra" and so forth—

meaning by means of the differentiation of the three vajras and the activities— one should contemplate the meditation on that yakṣiṇī form through the empowerment of desire and the rest, which constitutes its transformation into the five families.

The practitioner, established in the Mañjuvajra-samādhi, should visualize a wrathful deity—such as Yamāntaka or another—for the purpose of immobilization upon the crown of the Yakṣiṇī’s head. Having meditated on the syllable *kṣiṃ*, the mantra-word, within the heart-lotus at the center of the Yakṣiṇī’s heart, he should commence the vajra-yoga of meditative union.
The equality of all Yakṣiṇīs is their unification; that itself is the dwelling and the play, and its cultivation is the practice.
That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which that vajra-step, which is to be practiced again and again, is indivisible, is thus [described].
Showing the minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*),
he says "atha" and so forth.
The Vajra-mantras are the Tathāgatas,
and the Siddhis are the goddesses;
their manifestation is the activity of meditative absorption.

Having entered that samādhi, he emitted—that is, spoke—the means for attaining the siddhi of those inferior worldly ḍākinīs from the vajras of his own body, speech, and mind, by demonstrating the power of their very own body, speech, and mind.
How so? By the words "body, speech, and mind" and so forth;

they are called Vajra-ḍākinīs because they have attained the perfection of body through assuming various forms, the perfection of speech through various sounds, and the perfection of mind through the attainment of whatever objects are desired.

The goddesses known as *prabhā* shine pre-eminently, bearing forms similar to those [deities] they represent; they possess the radiance of Jāmbūnada gold, and by way of illustration, they may also possess the radiance of gold and other metals. They are based on the characteristics of inferior accomplishments (*hīnasiddhi*), such as the transformation of one’s own physical form.

In the sixteenth chapter, the commentary on the sixty million verses explains the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) and the distinction of the fruits for both the Vajraḍākinīs and the worldly ḍākinīs, stating "disappearance," and so forth.

"Antardhāna" means the rendering of something devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvīkaraṇa*); those [practices] beginning with that, such as *uccāṭana* (expulsion) and so forth, are "antardhānādayaḥ. Through the accomplishment—that is, the meditative union (*samāpatti*)—with these Vajra-Ḍākinīs, the practitioner becomes the Lord Vajradhara. The distinction is this: through union with the worldly Ḍākinīs in the realm of the Yakṣas, one who is devoted to the mantra becomes a lordly Vidyādhara.
Furthermore, the method for accomplishing them is shown by the passage beginning with "therein" (*tatra*) and so forth.

The Vajrasiddhis are goddesses, and they possess the perfection of animal forms; regarding that, as to what the forms of the mantra-siddhis— the mantra-words established by recitation— are like, he says:
"All" and so forth:
these beautiful forms, radiant and pleasing, nourish [the senses] by their mere sight;
they manifest them.

Regarding "Uṣṇīṣa" and so forth: Uṣṇīṣa refers to the practitioner of the Uṣṇīṣa-cakravartin mantra. In the accomplishment (*sādhana*) of all *siddhis* and all goddesses, he becomes a lord of the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) due to his swiftness of action; like a wish-fulfilling gem, he is the accomplisher of desired objects. One might ask: does he accomplish only this much? To this, he says: "Buddhabodha. The "awakenings of the Buddhas" (*buddhabodhi*) are the Vajra-ḍākinīs; he accomplishes them as well.
Not only does he do this, but he also effects the manifestation of the awakening of the Buddhas (*buddhabodhiprabhāvana*).
"It accomplishes both Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara," said the Blessed One, the Fulfilled of All Aspirations.
Having thus explained the means for attaining the mudrās for the yogin who has completed his task, he introduced the sequence for practicing together with them, saying:
"Then," and so forth:

"all Tathāgatas" refers to Kāyavajra and the others; their "vow" (*vrata*) is a specific mode of dress consisting of their body-vajras and so on. Regarding the undertaking of that vow, he "emitted"—that is, spoke—to the practitioner engaged in the training, by means of describing the very nature of those [deities'] bodies and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "kāya" and so forth:
the cultivation of the body, speech, and mind of the yogins of Vairocana and the others must be performed through their very own form and attire, not merely through mental visualization;
in this way, the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is attained.
With the words "therein" and so forth, he demonstrates the vow (*saṃvara*) of the three families.
One should have an image— the form of the deity— fashioned according to the rules from wood or other materials, adorned with a crown of matted hair, clad in white garments, and exceedingly beautiful.

"Mantra" refers to the Body-Vajra; its "vow" (saṃvara) is that which will be described hereafter. One should cause [the practitioner] to be endowed with that vow, together with a consort (mudrā) sixteen years of age, and practice the conduct of a Vairocana-yogin.
Regarding her attire, it is said: "by means of the enjoyments of the state of Locanā."
One should cause [the deity] to be made with the facial color and attributes such as weapons as before;

however, one should cause him to bear the vajra symbol—this refers to Vajrākṣobhya. The yogin of Akṣobhya, endowed with those symbols and his own facial color, arms, and weapons, should perform that [practice], together with the mudrā who bears the form of Māmakī.

Having obtained a consort who knows the rituals, understands gestures, is well-trained in the mantra-tantras, and is skilled in the expansion of ritual activities— a yogi who possesses the infinite vidyā-mantra according to the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*— he should observe the vow or cause her to do so; by such statements, he shows the female practitioner of the Dharma for the Amitābha-yogin.
The Tathāgata intended here is Amitābha;
his consort is Buddhabodhi,
and by the very mention of her seal (mudrā), his companion is also thereby indicated.

Thus, one who is restrained by the vows and commitments (*samaya-saṃvara*) of the three families and observes the *vidyā* vow should perform secret worship and meditative union (*samāpatti*) with them at the four junctions of the day. With the words beginning "the ritual action" (*karma*), etc., he describes the practitioner’s rule for food: having maintained the body with grains and edible foods, one should practice the conduct of the vow; thus he avoids a life of wretchedness. With the words beginning "thus," he demonstrates the benefits (*anuśaṃsā*).
Likewise, the restraint beginning with "the seizing of another's property" is explained in the ninth chapter by means of *saṃdhyābhāṣā* (intentional language);
similarly, here too, he distinguishes Māmakī with the words "Rāgavajrāṅkuśī" and so forth, and one should separate her from the Vāgvajra, Agrecitta, Amitābha, Vairocana, and Akṣobhya yogins.
This procedure is joined with and praised by the phrase "one's own mudrā" and so forth; it demonstrates the companionship with the *jñānamudrā*.

One should take one's own mudrā, Vajradhātvīśvarī who resides in the heart, from among the multitude of external women belonging to the yogins of Vairocana and the others, who are the three-syllable Vajrīs.
Therefore he says "thus" and so forth;
"in the forest" and so forth means that one should practice the seeking of alms in the forest, that is, in a great wilderness.
To that practitioner who possesses firm resolve and ardent vigor,
they present divine food— food not shared by ordinary humans, adorned with the divine, and brought forth by a divine retinue.
By the passage beginning with "one should transcend according to the literal meaning," he states the fruit of the practice:

the yogi whose nature is the three vajras should transcend—that is, overcome and destroy—the human state. Having transformed that perishable, ordinary body (*prākṛta-śarīra*), he shall become indestructible and imperishable, like a vajra.

The passage beginning with "asurīm" and so forth is easy to understand. The *trivajrajñāna* (three-vajra wisdom) is that which is practiced by the yogins; one should perform the *vidyāvrata* (wisdom-vow). This is the general rule. This aforementioned *caryāvrata* (conduct-vow) is the Mahāyāna for all mantras and all practitioners; it brings about the great purpose, is the secret reality (*guhyatattva*), and is the supreme mystery. It is born from the three vajras and, through the vajras of body and so forth, produces the vajra-body. It is the awakening of the Buddhas, the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), that which causes entry into and attainment of that [truth]. It is, in short, the purity of clear light (*prabhāsvara*) and the bringer of the wisdom-body (*jñānakāya*).
With these words, the compiler concludes the chapter:

the *maṇḍala* is the assembly (*vṛnda*) of all *siddhis*; within that is the *abhisaṃbodhi*, the arising of gnosis (*jñāna*), for the sake of which this textual composition—the sixteenth chapter—is written.
According to the literal meaning.

The commentary on the six points in the sixteenth chapter of the *Pradīpoddyotana-ṭīkā*.

The seventeenth chapter:

Even for one who has mastered the two stages, accomplishment remains distant without the practice of the worldly and supramundane commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*). Introducing the seventeenth chapter which establishes this, the compiler, demonstrating the supplication made by all the Tathāgatas, says "atha" and so forth; the meaning of these words has already been analyzed.

"O Akṣobhya," and so forth: his vajra-mind is unshakable and immovable by the arrays of all afflictions (*kleśa*); because he consists of the four voids, he is the Vajradhātu, who "holds" the vajras born of great gnosis, such as Akṣobhya and the others. Because of his thorough knowledge of the distinction between the two truths, he is the Great Sage (*mahābuddha*). Because he has the nature of the maṇḍala of ultimate reality, the body-maṇḍala, and the emanation-maṇḍala, he is the "Three Maṇḍalas.
Because he is the foremost among the vajras of body and so forth, they praise him through the gateway of Akṣobhya, saying: "O Supreme Vajra, speak! Reveal to us the reality of the secret samaya!"
Because he blazes with the fire of radiant light, he is Vairocana;
for that very reason, he is the Great Pure One (*mahāśuddha*). Because of the state of purity of those Vajra Tathāgatas, he is the sixth and thus tranquil (*śānta*).
Because his nature is supreme bliss, he is Mahārati (Great Delight).

He reveals the phenomena (*dharmas*) which are naturally luminous and pure by nature; addressing them as "Vajra," he speaks. He is Ratnarāja because he pleases—that is, illuminates—the *ratnas*, those belonging to the Jewel Family.
Because its nature is equanimity, it is profoundly deep;
for that very reason, it is as stainless as the sky-vajra of space;
and because it is pure from the beginning, it is pure by its very nature.

Because he is unmixed with all phenomena, he is unstained (*nirlepa*). He reveals the secret, O Vajrāmṛtas who belong to the Lotus family (*padmakulīna*); because he possesses sovereignty over them through the nature of the Great King’s discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā*), he is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).

Therefore, "Khavajrin" refers to one who has reached—that is, attained—that intellect which has gone to the "pāra," or the limit, of "rāga," characterized here by attachment to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Thus, he is "one who has attained the perfection of passion" (*rāgapāramitāprāpta*).

Because he bestows unfailing gnosis, he is "Amoghavajra. He is "perfectly awakened by those of the Amogha family" (*amoghakulīnasambuddha*), meaning he is honored by them. Because he fulfills the intentions of practitioners through rites such as pacification (*śānti*) and so forth, he is the "Fulfiller of All Hopes" (*sarvāśāparipūraka*).
"Of pure nature, luminous, because it arises from that [luminosity], born of the pure nature—O Vajrasattva who is thus, homage to you! This is the conclusion of the praise;
it is not in code (*nāsandhyam*).

Whoever should praise and worship Vajrasambhoga with these aforementioned verses of praise—which indicate the nature of the five Tathāgatas, are peaceful, pure by nature, impelled by all Tathāgatas, and spoken by Tathāgatas existing throughout the three times—that worshipper, being one who abides in the Buddha-samaya, shall become equal to Mahāvajradhara. This is the benefit of the praise according to the literal meaning.
Now, with the words beginning with "atha," [the text] demonstrates the favorability of Mahāvajradhara’s presence.

He is the Teacher because he pacifies all afflictions and secondary afflictions; he is compassionate because all Buddhas, who consist of the five aggregates, bring about the attainment of heaven and liberation for all sentient beings as appropriate;
and he is the Vajra Secret, which is the fourfold commitment (*samaya*).
Uttering the vajra-speech that is his foundation— pure and untroubled—
he proclaims the great syllable, which is the nature of the dharmadhātu of all Buddhas such as Akṣobhya and the rest, beginning with the words "Aho hi! and so forth.
Oh, how wonderful!
For it is naturally luminous, pure, stainless like the expanse of space, and not subject to the twilight.
Having thus accepted the praise and eulogy of the Tathāgata, he says "Now," and so forth, in order to demonstrate how he reveals it according to the occasion.

This marvelous pledge (*samaya*)—consisting of the four pledges beginning with the taking of life—which was spoken by the Buddhas, the practitioners of Vairocana, for the sake of the Body, Speech, and Mind Vajras of the Vairocana-yogins and others, is the eternal and constant pledge of all Buddhas and all yogins; it must be guarded and maintained in order to attain the state of the Great Vajradhara, the Holder of the Vajra.
This samaya is not only for the yogins of Vairocana, but is indeed the same for the yogins of Mahāvajradhara as well; showing this, he says "And whoever," and so forth, which is easy to understand.

Having thus explained the samaya for those who aspire to perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), he introduces the samaya for those who are inclined toward individual awakening (*pratyekabodhi*) by saying "Now," and so forth.
Teaching is the means for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings by generating faith in the Three Jewels; furthermore, that [teaching] consists primarily of speech and body.
Since Pratyekabuddhas lack instruction from others, such teaching does not exist for them;
nevertheless, the performance of beneficial activity for those to be trained occurs through the display of wonders such as the miracle of the twin-fold manifestation (*yamakaprātihārya*).
Therefore, the teaching is physical; for this very reason it is said to be "established in the body-vajra," because there is an absence of the activity of speech.

That restraint of the body which serves as the cause for leading sentient beings [to liberation] is also the teaching; this is the supreme, eternal, and beginningless *samaya*. Regarding the restraint of those who are counter-agents (*pratiyogin*) belonging to the lineage of the *pratyekabuddhas*, he says "Now," and so forth, showing the *samaya* of the *śrāvakas*:
those who attain the state of an Arhat by means of the realization of the selflessness of the person (*pudgala-nairātmya*) are the *śrāvakas*.

Application for the sake of attaining the state of a Śrāvaka is itself the training; that very training is the *samaya*. One should emanate it from one's own body and so forth as an instruction for those practitioners who are inclined toward the Śrāvaka vehicle.

These consist of the ten paths of virtuous action, characterized by the abstention from taking life and so forth. Devoid of [Mahāyāna] knowledge, turned away from non-abiding nirvāṇa, having inferior inclinations, and intent solely on their own individual liberation—for them, this is the most wonderful *samaya*.
The seventeenth chapter, the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*: demonstrating the discipline (*samaya*) of Brahmā for those who are intent upon becoming Brahman, he says "Now," and so forth.

Since liberation is understood as the state of being Brahman, delusion (*moha*) is its manifestation; its path is the practice (*pracāra*), by which there is action characterized by fasting and the like, which is terrifying and fearsome.

For those who desire happiness, [the Buddha]—who is intent upon the state of Brahmā—produces terror; for them, awakening is knowledge, and its proponent is the one who causes it to be attained. He should teach the commitment characterized by self-mortification to those who are not yet liberated from it;
therefore, he says, "one becomes the Body-Vajra."
Showing the convention for those to be trained by means of the form of Maheśvara, he says "atha" and so forth;
this is easy to understand.
Showing the convention of Viṣṇu, he says "atha" and so forth.
One should slay all sentient beings, such as those born from eggs and so forth, by means of the meditation-vajra through the process of emptying them;
one should likewise empty the space-vajra— the realm of space, the vessel-world, and oneself.
This is the *viṣṇu-samaya*.

Having thus explained the *samaya* for those who are devoted to Brahmā and the others, [the text] says "atha" and so forth in order to remove confusion regarding the *samaya* by means of its inclusion within the *kāyavajra* and the rest;
the "triple-vajra *samaya*" (*trivajrasamaya*) is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the *kāyavajra* and the others.
The passage beginning with "kāyavajra" and so forth is easy to understand.

Having thus explained the commitment (*samaya*) of the principal deity, he speaks the words beginning with "atha" and so forth, while alluding to the commitments of the minor deities such as the *yakṣiṇīs*.

The *yakṣiṇīs* consume food consisting of meat, wine, blood, and the like; they are devoted to sexual union, and these great vajra-beings are of a cruel nature. One should propitiate them through these commitments characterized by the offering of meat and so forth, which are difficult to approach.
Introducing the convention (*samaya*) of the serpent maidens (*bhujagakanyā*), he says "atha" and so forth.

The lords of serpents (*bhujagendra*) are Vāsuki and others; their queens are the wives of those kings. Their convention (*samaya*) is the intended purpose. Slander (*paiśunya*) refers to speech intended to cause enmity. One should accomplish—that is, bring under control—those nāginīs by means of these conventions (*samaya*), that is, by means of these practices (*anuṣṭhāna*). This implies that otherwise, they would not become subject to one's will.
If one should desire to practice with asurīs, [the author], showing the means for accomplishing that, says "atha" and so forth.
Those who are cruel (*krūra*) are of a violent nature; they are overcome solely by the burden of pride and are attached to the enjoyment of perfumes and other such things.
This is a portion of their *samaya*.

The detailed rule (*samaya*), however, is difficult to master and difficult to carry out; therefore, Vajrabhairava, speaking while introducing the *rākṣasī*-rule in the *Vajrapātālatantra*, says "Now," and so forth:
one should offer to them incense made of meat and the like, using the powder of skulls and bones along with oil and fat.

Thus, this very same commitment (*samaya*) is the means for pleasing those [goddesses] as well as all beings, including *piśācas* and others; it is pure and destroys obstacles. The "Vajras" are the practitioners (*sādhakas*); because it accomplishes abundant aims, it brings about their great purpose.
In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, for the sake of pleasing the Vajraḍākinīs, he states that commitment beginning with "Now," and so forth.
One should emit the commitment (*samaya*) of all the vajra-ḍākinīs, such as Gaurī and the others, from one’s own body and so forth;
that is, one should consume feces and the like, consecrated by mantra.

One should drink liquor such as *maireya* and offer it to them through the yoga of the Vajraḍākinīs, the yoga of Gaurī and the others, by means of the characteristics of the [lotus] petals; and one should kill the wicked through applications such as the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*) of blood from the dead.
This is the *samaya* of Vajraḍākinī.
Having thus explained the *samaya* from Brahmā down to Ḍākinī, he says "by their very nature" (*svabhāvena*) and so forth, showing the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) in that statement:

these [beings] beginning with Brahmā, by their very nature—that is, through their own sovereign power—have existed from time immemorial; they have arisen together with the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), possess great supernatural powers (*mahārddhika*), and while performing the favoring and subduing of sentient beings within the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*), they move about in various forms, appearances, and ornaments.

Therefore, the practitioner of the *sāmājika* should perform their entire, complete observance (*samaya*) which brings about all accomplishments, as indicated by the passage beginning with "sarva" and so forth. He concludes the section with this: those who exist within the three realms are "tridhātukāḥ"; "sarvatraidhātukāḥ" refers to specific beings such as Brahmā and others. Their "vajra-samaya" is that which is not to be transgressed and must be practiced; it is the command of the Vajradhara. That meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which there is a convergence or entry (*samavasaraṇa*) into that [command] is described as such.

And it has been said in this regard: "Even those who, while not certain of the doctrines of others, are established by means of various signs, should not be disregarded here; O Vajrasattva, one should act [accordingly].
Now, he speaks of the purification of the paths of action, beginning with the word "atha" (now).
The accomplishment of the body is bodily action;
that itself is the Samayavajra, which one should emanate from one's own body and so forth, as it is threefold in its bodily aspect.

One should cause all that characterized by the taking of life, taking what is not given, and violating the wives of others—which arises from the Vajra—to become luminous clarity (*prabhāsvara*). One should practice while disregarding the protection of dharma and adharma;

thus, within the realm of sentient beings in the triple world, one attains the indestructible vajra-body that produces the Buddha-body, because of the absence of any cause for going to happy or miserable destinies.

Likewise, the accomplishment of speech (*vāc-siddhi*) refers to vocal activity, the locus of vocal karma—characterized by the fourfold [unwholesome acts] of false speech, slander, harsh words, and frivolous chatter. The "stainless one of the three worlds" (*trailokyāmala*) is the Great Vajradhara; his *maṇḍala* is his abode. What is that? It is the *maṇḍala* of the stainlessness of the three worlds, which is the purity of luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). One should practice that path of vocal karma. To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "The accomplishment of speech," and so forth.

The state of perfection of speech is mastery over speech; delightful by that means, it is exceedingly captivating. This rule (samaya) is difficult to transgress, as is the purification of the mind and the activity of the mind.
"All is composed of mind-vajra" refers to the threefold karma characterized by covetousness, malice, and wrong view.
Among these, covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the longing for the property of others;
malice (*vyāpāda*) is the desire to separate sentient beings [from their happiness]; and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is [the belief] that there is no giving, and so forth.
One whose intellect is firm like a vajra and whose mind is bowed toward luminosity (prabhāsvara) should set this threefold mental action into motion while cultivating and discerning it;
with the words "For this indeed," etc., he concludes the section.

This threefold commitment (*samaya*) just mentioned—the practice that must not be transgressed—belongs to those who possess the indivisible vajra of the three vajras and who abide in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*); it does not belong to others. Thus spoke the Blessed One, Samantabhadra-vajra. Now, he describes the practice for the practitioner (*mantrin*) who has begun the sādhana, beginning with the words "Then," etc.: "One should emanate from one’s own body and so forth the commitment of those who are devoted to all mantras and vajra-mantras."
Regarding the phrase "to the Buddhas" and so forth,
"by means of the union of body, speech, and mind" means that one should prostrate by becoming unified with the body and the other [faculties].
If, for a specific purpose, one performs the prostration with only the body, or with speech, or with both body and speech, there is no fault.
One who bows with a mind not joined to the body or speech would suffer the loss of the attainment of desired goals.

Having explained the procedure for bowing to others for one who has ascended the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), he speaks beginning with "Now" (*atha*) and so forth for one who has realized the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*).

All Tathāgatas are all sentient beings; from his own body and so forth, he should emanate the mode of visualization (*ālambanaprakāra*) as the meditative commitment (*dhyānasamaya*) within their bodies, speech, and minds.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of Vajrasattva" and so forth:
