everywhere, the body, speech, and mind mandala of all sentient beings—the aggregate of the body and so on—is that of the Lord Vajrasattva and the others. By means of the yoga of the three vajras, which is the nature of the indivisibility of the three vajras, one should take meditative absorption as the object and practice meditation through the recitation of mantras by those devoted to vajra-recitation and dedicated to the internal [practice].
To explain how the homage to these is performed, he says "atha" (now) and so forth.

All the mantras and vajras abide in the stage of the yuganaddha (union) sequence; one should cause their *saṃvara* (vow/discipline) to issue forth from one’s own body and so forth. One should impel—meaning practice—the realms of sentient beings, who are both perfected and unperfected multitudes of beings, by means of the "sameness" in brief, that is, by means of the *dhyānavajra*, which is the three-vajra meditation just mentioned. The "salutation of the three vajras" (*trivajravandanā*) is the prostration of the body and so forth before the Tathāgatas and others. The "supreme of the supreme" (*agrāgram*) is the most distinguished *vajra*. It is called "origination" (*saṃbhava*) because the perfected yoga arises from this. It refers, in short, to the conduct that brings about the state of a Mahāvajradhara.

Regarding those engaged in the four yogas beginning with service (*sevā*) at the time of practice, he states the *saṃvara* (vow/observance) starting with "service," etc.; the meaning has already been explained.
One should visualize the *khadhātu*—the infinite space—as being completely filled and pervaded by the "vajra of feces and urine," which refers to the sense objects and sense faculties.
Then, one should give—that is, distribute—from the "vajras of the three times," which are the three bodies (*trikāya*).
One should meditate on the cavity of the three realms throughout the three times as being pervaded by wisdom and skillful means, which are the very nature of the objects and the sense faculties;
this is the eternal, beginningless commitment (*samaya*).
Having thus realized reality, [the text] says "Now," and so forth, demonstrating the method for abandoning the ordinary body and assuming an indestructible body.

"Every vajra disappearance commitment" (*sarvavajrāntardhānasamaya*) means that the common body, speech, and mind of all vajras undergoes disappearance, which is the entry into clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Because one comes together (*sameti*) through this into the vajra-body, it is called a "commitment" (*samaya*) in every respect.
One should emanate from one's own body and so forth this twofold commitment (*samaya*) of the Vajradhātu and Antardhāna;
daily, constantly, at the four junctions of the day, one should desire and meditate upon the fourfold emptiness—the supreme and unsurpassed.
Furthermore, one should take away and seize the substance and the body; the sense is that one should always, at all times, perform both entry for the sake of activity and emergence.
The Vajrapūraka is the commitment (*samaya*) that brings about the grace of the Tathāgatas.

Regarding the method for maintaining one’s own body—so that it may endure for a long time for the sake of sentient beings who have realized reality, being independent of external substances—the text says "atha" and so forth.

*Khavidyā* is suchness (*tathatā*); he who holds (*dhārayati*), that is, takes as his object (*ālambate*), that is the *khavidyādhara*, the yogin. Because nourishment of the body arises from this commitment (*samaya*), it is called *samaya*: the procedure for replenishment (*āpyāyana-vidhi*).
The practitioner should emanate that [deity] from his own body and so forth;
for the sake of the stability of his own body, speech, and mind-vajras, he should place and perform the meditation called "Nectar" upon the crown [of the head].
This is its benefit.
Regarding the passage beginning with "trivajra":

the *trivajra* is the body; because it follows (*samaya*) that [body] from its very inception, the humors such as wind (*vāta*) and so forth are called the *trivajrasamayas*. It is impossible for this body to be conquered—that is, overcome—by all of these when they are enraged or provoked.
As stated by the Blessed One in the *Prajñāsūtra*: "That which is eternally composed of the stream of nectar certainly rains down upon the head."
"Having drunk this, the lord of yogis destroys old age and death;
just as a man draws up water through the stalk of a lotus, so should the yogi of great power subsist upon it and live."
The Root Tantra also says: "Having placed the tongue against the palate, one should contemplate the tip of the nose;
through the touch of the bliss of the subtle vajra, the mind becomes concentrated."
Having thus explained the method for nourishing one who is devoted to the internal [practice], he speaks of the one devoted to mantra with the words "Now," and so forth.
"All Vajradharas" refers to beginners who recite the mantras of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas]. He should cause their *samaya* (pledge) to issue forth from his own body and so on.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Food," and so forth:
At the time of consuming food and so forth, one should perform the consecration of the Body-Vajradhara and the external Vajradhara;
that is to say, apart from the act of eating, one should perform the consecration of Vajradhara with respect to other objects.
"One should always perform [the rite] for Vajradharma" means that the consecration (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Vajradharma— that is, of Vāgvajra— should always be performed;
where?

The "substance" refers to the teaching and so forth; its "opening" is the recitation and the performance of rituals. The "performance of rituals" includes commands such as "come" or "go," as well as acts of subjugation. Furthermore, one should effect the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Amitābha during the recitation, chanting, and singing of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
Thus spoke the Blessed One, the Vajra of Natural Purity.

In order to demonstrate that which has been passed over and that which is yet to be spoken—the expansion of ritual activities (*karmaprasara*) and so forth—by joining them with purification through transformation (*vikurvita*), he entered a meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and said, "Now," and so forth, showing this. *(Note: This is a commentary on the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* of the seventeenth chapter.)*

All the Vajra-holders are perfected Tathāgatas, the vajras of body, speech, and mind; sentient beings are unperfected. Having reflected upon and meditated on the equality of their heart-vajras—their minds—as being solely grounded in luminosity (*prabhāsvara*), he became silent.
Then, the passage beginning with "atha khalu" and so forth is easy to understand;
[the passage] beginning with "bhagavantaḥ" and so forth...
The non-apprehension of the vajras of body, speech, and mind, which is the nature of luminosity (*prabhāsvaratā*), is the syllable-word (*akṣarapada*) by its very nature;

in reality, O sons of noble family, this syllable-word is an indestructible word. Having investigated, sought out, and realized this indestructible state—the syllable-word devoid of intrinsic nature and ineffable—this Great Vajradhara remains silent for the purpose of demonstrating it to us; the meaning is that he has entered into luminosity.
He elucidates this point with the words "of this" and so forth;
"the syllable of the body" (*kāyākṣara*) and so on means that the body itself is the syllable of the body, because it is unarisen due to its existence throughout the past and other times.
That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), consisting of color and shape; that which lacks this is "without characteristics" (*alakṣaṇa*).

This body and so forth are the conceptualization of the space-vajra, which is suchness (*tathatā*); having attained that reality, it is "the reality of the conceptualization of the space-vajra. If one asks: how can the triple world (*traidhātuka*) be the mandala of deities?
Regarding the phrase "the compendium of false gathering" (*mithyā-saṃgraha-saṃgraha*):

"false" (*mithyā*) means illusion (*māyā*); one who gathers or takes up that [illusion] is thus a "false gatherer" (*mithyā-saṃgraha*), referring to the teaching that resembles an illusion. That which is gathered by this is the "compendium" (*saṃgraha*).
And it has been said: "The Blessed One, Vajrasattva, the Tathāgata, is indeed the union of all."

The Tathāgatas urge the Bodhisattvas—who, as if not knowing the intended meaning of this *vajrapada*, [think] that "all its enjoyment, indeed, is the three realms without exception" is a false grasping—in order to reveal that meaning. To show this, he says, "Then Mañjuśrī," and so forth.

The *vajrapada* of speech is the teaching of the Dharma; it is "false" (*mithyā*) because it is deceptive (*mṛṣā*), and that which arises from this is "false origination" (*mithyāsamudaya*). Ignorance is the cause. Do not grasp this as being the cause!
How so? He says, "That," and so forth.

"All Tathāgatas" refers to those of the past; their "course and movement" (*caritā cīrṇā gatāgatiḥ*) within the Vajra-realm, the realm of Nirvāṇa, by way of intrinsic nature and primordial essence, is the manifestation of entering the Clear Light (*prabhāsvara*). He whose such course and movement is the intrinsic nature of the Vajra-realm of all Tathāgatas is the Lord of All Tathāgatas. Therefore, it should be applied that the state of the Speech-Vajra (*vāgvajrapada*) is "identical" (*samā*) and not falsely conceptualized. Regarding the question of what the purpose of seeing such profundity and vastness—according to the manner just described—is, he says: "Why is that? and so forth.

"Brahmā and others" refers to Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest. "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*) is the non-afflicted ignorance characterized by the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); those whose mind (*citta*) is directed toward that are "Great Bodhisattvas. They possess "great superknowledges" (*mahābhijñā*), such as the power of transformation and greatness, and have attained "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is worldly omniscience. Nevertheless, they do not know the characteristics and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena. "All phenomena" refers to form and so forth; their "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) is their illusory-like conventional reality (*saṃvṛtisatya*), and their "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) is luminosity (*prabhāsvaratva*). Not knowing these two through analytical distinction, they merely conceptualize and speculate.

Regarding the doubt as to why [the Buddha spoke thus]: "Is this teacher, whose nature is the Great Vajra, teaching the secret syllable—the mystery not shared with any sentient beings—without knowing or having realized the *vajra*, which is the reality (*tattva*) and the ultimate form of all phenomena, whether stable or moving; or is he teaching it after having realized it?"—in order to dispel the doubt of those who held such uncertainty and to demonstrate his own realization of the two truths, he manifested the entry into and emergence from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
This is the underlying intention (*abhisandhi*) of the passage beginning with "Then," and so forth.
All the Tathāgatas, Akṣobhya and the others, spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas headed by Mañjuśrī:
"Wait a moment, O Great Bodhisattvas! By this they were indicating Brahmā and the others as the secret syllables of the vajra of body, speech, and mind.

Although we have directly heard from the presence of the Great Vajradhara the imperishable syllable that illuminates the secrets of body, speech, and mind— the vajra-word— regarding what is called the "awakening of body, speech,
and mind," we do not yet personally realize the attainment of the fruit of awakening belonging to that Great Vajradhara, the possessor of body, speech, and mind.

Furthermore, Brahmā and the others—namely Akṣobhya and the rest—spoke. With the words "Why is that? and so forth, they demonstrate the reason for their own lack of realization: because they have emerged from the nature of all conceptual constructions, they are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For this very reason, [they are] the imperishable (*akṣara*), which is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*); from that, he was born or produced—the Unarisen Vajra, the Great Vajradhara. Even his perfect awakening (*saṃbodhi*) is the non-duality of cause and fruit.

Thus, having demonstrated the difficulty of attaining the perfect awakening of Vajradhara, they spoke the words beginning with "As many as... and so forth, demonstrating its ease of attainment by virtue of being common to all sentient beings.

"O sons of noble family" (kulaputrāḥ) is how they address the bodhisattvas; those who are gathered through the gathering of sentient beings—including all beings such as those born from eggs and so forth—are established in awakening (bodhi). Awakening is the realization of reality (tattva); if they are established in that and have practiced by way of the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditation, they are indeed perfectly awakened Vajras, the Tathāgatas themselves.
To explain the reason for this, he says "tat kasmāt" and so forth, with "vata" expressing certainty.

These sentient beings, included within the three realms, possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind; they are Mahāvajradhara. His gnosis is non-dual gnosis. Having attained that, and being established in the vessel [of its attainment], they are metaphorically designated as "the vajra of the three bodies" (*trikāyavajra*) by way of conventional usage. The "three bodies" (*trikāya*) refers to the triad of the Dharma-body and so forth; he who holds these is the "Holder of the Vajra of the Three Bodies. He is the sixth [Buddha]. His state is "the nature of the Holder of the Vajra of the Three Bodies. Taking that as the basis and making it the cause, one should apply the [conclusion]: "All sentient beings are Buddha-vajras."

Thus, showing that the Blessed One, being pleased by the mutual resonance between the Bodhisattvas and the Tathāgatas, illuminates that very same meaning with his own words, he says "Then," and so forth.

All stable and moving phenomena are pure by nature; their selflessness is luminosity, which is the *dharmadhātu* and the *bodhicittavajra*. Because it is the locus (*nilaya*) where there is no remainder (*niḥśeṣeṇa*), and because it is the place of origin, those [phenomena] are "born from the *vajra*," meaning they are born from the *vajra* of body, speech, and mind.
Conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is said to be the activity of the transformations of the intellect (*buddhi-vikurvaṇā*) and so forth, because it is seen like a rainbow;
yet it is not so said, because it cannot be found upon investigation.

Having thus ascertained the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of the Great Vajradhara, [the author] says "Now," and so forth, in order to demonstrate—by way of resolving objections—the cause for the accomplishment of Buddhahood for yogins who are practicing.
"All Tathāgatas! From where do their accomplishments of body and so forth converge, arise, abide, or dissolve?
To this question of the Tathāgatas, Vajradhara gave this response beginning with "one's own body":
the continuum of one's own body, speech, and mind is their arising through a succession of moments.
That very *vajra* is so called because it is the entrance into the non-luminous;
all mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) are established therein, and it should be understood that they arise from that very source.
In other words, the three bodies (*kāyatraya*) are the cause for the arising, abiding, and dissolution of all accomplishments.
The passage beginning with "all" and so forth provides the following resolution:

not only are mundane accomplishments (*siddhi*) produced from the triad of body and so forth, but all qualities such as the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), as well as the three realms (*traidhātuka*), are likewise produced from body, speech, and mind, and are established precisely within body, speech, and mind.
This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "all Tathāgatas" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the vajra-accomplishment of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas": the question of the Tathāgatas is as follows: what are the signs of mundane and supramundane accomplishments? What are body, speech, and mind? And where do their elements and the [elements] such as earth abide? The answer is: they are established in the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*), which is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
When it was further asked, "Where does the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) abide?", Vajradhara replied, "Nowhere.
He then spoke the manner of the marvel of all the Tathāgatas, beginning with the words "Then," and so forth.
They were struck with wonder at its purity; they were struck with amazement at its emergence;
they exclaimed "O Vajra! O Vajra! in their faith;
and they reiterated, "O, the teaching of the Vajra! regarding the rarity of such a teaching—this is the wonder.

The concealment (*saṃvṛtti*) of the vajra is the teaching of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Wherein—that is, in that [teaching]—by means of the ultimate truth, the body, speech, and mind are therein and thereupon visualized and accomplished as the form of the deity, whose nature is endowed with the excellence of all aspects; this is the cause of wonder.
Having thus determined the signless concentration (*animittasamādhi*), he says "Then," and so forth, showing how the form of the deity, which is the means for that [concentration], is accomplished.

All sentient beings are the three vajras; the foremost among them are Hari, Hara, and Hiraṇyagarbha; the foremost among them are the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas; the foremost among them is Mahāvajradhara, the Supreme Lord of the Three Vajras (*trivajraparamaiśvara*). He is called the Supreme Lord of the Three Vajras because he acts with supreme and absolute sovereignty over the three vajras—body, speech, and mind. As it has been said: "Sovereignty of body, sovereignty of speech, and likewise sovereignty of mind; supernatural power, omnipresence, sovereignty, will, and the creator as the eighth quality."

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, [the author] speaks—that is, explains—the cultivation, which is the process of accomplishment, of the "knowledge-person" (*vidyāpuruṣa*). This is a person consisting of knowledge who serves as the means for accomplishing all mundane and supramundane attainments.
Regarding the passage beginning with "in the space-vault" (*khavatre*) and so forth:

one should meditate upon the mass of sentient beings—both those already accomplished and those not yet accomplished within the Buddha-maṇḍala—as being situated in the center of the vajra of the space-element (*khadhātu*), having entered into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).
Then, having meditated on the lunar disk as the cause of the body-vajra for the entire mass of sentient beings, one should manifest the vajra upon the head; that is,
one should manifest a five-pronged vajra above the moon-maṇḍala on the head.

Through the transformation of that [state], one should contemplate the unshakeable one who has three faces, who is born from the three bodies (*trikāya*), whose nature is the three bodies, and who is radiating, endowed with the emission and reabsorption of five rays of light. He is the "Holder of the Wheel and Vajra" (*cakravajradhara*) because he maintains and emits the host of deities of the maṇḍala as his own retinue.
Having meditated upon such a form of the deity, the yogi shall attain awakening, which is the state of being unshakeable.

In this very sequence, the yogin of Vairocana and the others, through the transformation of the wheels (*cakra*) and so forth, should contemplate this secret—the mystery of assuming the forms of deities according to the distinctions of the families—of all those [deities] such as Vairocana. The Blessed One stated that for those [deities] such as Vairocana, a meditation in any other way or by another method is not the accomplishment (*siddhi*), nor the cause of accomplishment. Having thus brought himself to completion, he asks what one should do next, and says: "Having become the creator," and so forth.

One should contemplate and visualize the Great Queen, the Goddess Vajradhātvīśvarī, who resides within the body—the three realms—there gladdening [the practitioner] and generating the bliss of joy; one should see her as she delights the yogins who abide in the vajra-like samādhi. To the question of what these "bulls" (vṛṣabhāḥ) are like, he says: "characterized by the three vajra-bodies."

Those characterized by the three—the passionate, the dispassionate, and the moderately passionate—which are experienced through the two vajra-bodies, that is, the male and female organs, are thus "characterized by the three vajra-bodies.
He states the benefit [of this] with the words beginning with "And whoever... and so forth.

Whoever has seen the truth is a *bodhi*; one whose mind (*sattva*) is fixed upon that *jñānamudrā* is a *bodhisattva*. Because he has ascended through the sequence of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and attained the completion stage (*niṣpannakrama*), he is of great renown; being the Great Vajradhara of the three bodies, he attains his accomplishment as one of great splendor and refined vigor within seven days, or even sooner.
Showing that those with firm minds should experience the bliss of supreme joy through union with a *jñānamudrā*, or through union with an external woman, he says "atha" and so forth.

That in which there is a unification (*ekībhāva*) through the arising in the form of drops (*bindu*) of the vajras of body, speech, and mind melted by the fire of passion—that is the *kāyavākcittavajrasamuccaya*.
What is it?
The secret is the *dharmodaya*; its ritual procedure as a limb of the *sādhana* is the esoteric teaching. That [teaching] he should emit from his own body and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "body and so forth" in the seventeenth chapter, according to the six-fold commentary (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*):
the *samaya* of body, speech, and mind is the *mahāmudrā*, because it follows by uniting with the *sādhana* through body, speech, and mind.
The practitioner’s goal is bliss (*ānanda*);
because she brings that about and accomplishes it through embracing and other acts, she is the "conceptualization of the meaning of Mahāmudrā.

Furthermore, she is the "pledge of body, speech, and mind" as well as the "conceptualization of the meaning of Mahāmudrā. One who would attain the state of all Buddhas should cultivate and attend upon her—the consort who practices the Dharma together—as the means for thoroughly understanding her characteristics, by means of the characteristics of all passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion, preceded by the ritual procedures such as the consecration of the mudrā.
With the words "Then," and so forth, he explains the mode of conduct for yogins who are in meditative equipoise. "Then," and so forth:

all practitioners are imagined yogins; because it is not an object of their body, speech, or mind, it is a secret teaching, which one should emanate from one's own body and so forth, beginning with the phrase "the hand-seal," and so on.

"One should desire supreme enlightenment and the state of a Vajradhara through the mode of identity and should meditate upon it; one should not bind hand-mudrās that cause attachment to external deities.
For there is this statement: 'Vajrasattva himself is manifest—what else could one seek?'"
"Of all," and so forth:

those for whom the secret mantra accomplishes all aims are "all mantras"; this is the *samaya* (commitment) of those practitioners of the *samāja*. Even by the *Jinas*, the Tathāgatas, it was declared that one engaged in the *samāja* must bind the hand-mudrā; this *samaya* is not to be transgressed, as it cannot be disregarded.
Thus, he states the *samaya* for the practitioners of the *kalpiyoga* among the members of the *samāja*, beginning with "Now," and so forth.

All the Buddhas belong to the family of the Body-Vajra; he caused their pledge (*samaya*) to be performed, which he brought forth from his own body and so forth, beginning with *viḍ*. The mantra-practitioner should never harbor contempt or aversion toward *viḍ* and the other substances.
Therefore, one should constantly consume and partake of that nectar (*amṛta*) produced through the ritual application of embracing, kissing, and so forth.
Why is this so? He says: "This secret born of the three vajras" means that which brings about the stability of body, speech, and mind; that is to say, it is an elixir (*rasāyana*).
Having begun precisely for that purpose, he speaks of the commitment (*samaya*) of the Speech-Vajra, starting with "the triple world," and so forth.

However many women there may be—superior, inferior, or middling—their path is the delightful path of the three realms (*traidhātukapatha*). The beings of the three realms are those whose path or way is the "path of the three realms" (*vaidhātukapatha*), which is the path of progeny; it is the lotus. In that delightful [lotus], which brings joy to all people, one should, according to the rule—that is, accompanied by the ritual of passion and so forth—move, desire, and gladden all the channels (*nāḍī*) such as Madana, Ātapatra, Pūrṇacandra, and Kūrma, by means of the "vajras of speech," which are the activities of the tongue. One should not feel disgust until the end of emission; whatever arises from that activity, one should not abandon it, but rather should savor it. This is the meaning.

With the words beginning with "atha," he speaks of the *cittavajra-samaya*. Regarding the words beginning with "yāvanta," all the *samayas*—that is, women such as the *padminī* and others—are established in the three vajra-bodies; they possess the intrinsic nature of Vairocana and the other [Buddhas].
One should please and gladden them through the three vajra *samayas*, which are the activities of one's own body, speech, and mind.

"One should not loathe the mind-vajra"—the meaning of this, as explained in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, is that one should not cause the mind to become dispassionate, because the body is rooted in the mind and the bodhicitta is rooted in the body.
"The great, uncommon three vajra-samayas" refers to those taught through the samaya of body, speech, and mind. "That Mahāvajradhara spoke thus" is the statement of the compiler (saṃgītikāra).

In order to remove the attachment of yogins established in the three types of conduct toward external Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and in order to manifest his own status as the presiding deity (*adhidevatva*), he says "atha" and so forth.

"All Tathāgatas" refers to the Victors (*jina*) of the three times. That which was taught by them is the "Secret Vajra" (*guhyavajra*), because it must be concealed from those of inferior inclination. He revealed that in brief; having condensed the hundred families, the five Buddhas beginning with Vairocana are proclaimed.
These five are the five aggregates (*skandha*).
If it is argued that those [entities] are the aggregates of form and so forth, and not others distinct from them— meaning that there exist external Bodhisattvas such as Kṣitigarbha and others—
the author says "Vajra... and so forth in order to eliminate that view.
Because of its mastery in grasping objects, the sense-faculty (*indriya*) is like a thunderbolt (*vajra*); its bases (*āyatana*) or locations are the eyes and so forth;

its source (*yoni*) is the supreme maṇḍala of Bodhisattvas, the circle of the sons of the Victors such as Kṣitigarbha and others. That which consists of these very sense-faculties is nothing other than the assembly of Bodhisattvas.
Regarding the attachment to the deities of one’s own mantra-family, such as Locanā and others, [the author], implying the means for removing that [attachment], says "Then" (*atha*), and so forth.

That by which the three realms—the triple existence known as the sentient beings and their environment—are gathered together and produced is the "Gathering of the Three Realms," namely earth and the other elements. From its entry into the Clear Light until its emergence, he brought forth that vajra of stability:

earth and the others, which are conceptually designated as the goddesses Locanā and so forth. These four elements, whether appropriated or unappropriated, such as earth and the rest, are none other than Locanā and the other goddesses.

Regarding the passage beginning with "khavajra" and so forth: the "space-vajra-realm" (*khavajradhātu*) is that space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). It is called "samaya" because it comes together with and follows after all that is stationary and moving. He says that this very one is Vajradhara.

The "all Tathāgatas" are Vairocana and the others, whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). The "world" (*bhuvana*) refers to the five elements (*pañcadhātu*), earth and the rest, whose intrinsic nature consists of Locanā and the others. Their Lord (*īśvara*) is Mahāvajrasattva; thus he says.

Having thus explained that Vairocana and the others have the nature of the five aggregates and so forth, he says "Then," etc., showing that he remained in the assembly to provide an occasion for questions: "The Tathāgata, the Vajra of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, the Great Vajradhara, [attained] the state of equality of all Tathāgatas."

"All Tathāgatas" refers to Vairocana and the others, Kṣitigarbha and the others, and Locanā and the others; their "equality" is their non-duality with the five aggregates and so forth. Their "abiding" is the prophecy, and the meditative absorption (samādhi) bearing that name is the manifestation [of that equality] by means of a one-pointed mind. Having entered—that is, having performed—that absorption, and having spoken thus, he withdrew the entire mandala of the assembly of all Tathāgatas. Having observed Vairocana and the others, who are the very nature of the five aggregates and so forth, abiding in their respective places, he became silent;
that is to say, having created an opportunity for questions, he entered the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya).

The commentary on the sixty million verses of the seventeenth chapter: Having fully understood the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of Vairocana and the others, the Blessed One developed a doubt regarding the full comprehension of the intrinsic nature within the domain of the teacher.

Since it is impossible to pose questions to the Blessed One when he has become invisible, he spoke the words beginning with "atha" and so forth, demonstrating how he questioned the Tathāgatas present in the assembly.

All the Tathāgatas—both those who have attained perfection and those who have not—their secret of body, speech, and mind is the reality (*tattva*); the composition of the text that reveals this is the *Samāja*.
One who has been consecrated therein, authorized by all the Tathāgatas, and empowered is addressed as "Bhagavān.
He is the *Ācārya*, the sovereign, because he demonstrates both mundane and supramundane conduct.

"How and in what form are you all—the Tathāgatas, all the Bodhisattvas, and we ourselves—to be seen and known? Thus addressed by Maitreya, the Tathāgatas replied: "The one who is the teacher, beginning with 'the thought of awakening' (*bodhicitta*), is to be seen and known as the Vajra of the Thought of Awakening itself, the Great Vajradhara.
For what reason? Because..."
Bodhicitta, Mahāvajradhara, the Ācārya, and Akṣobhya— these are non-dual and indivisible, because cause and fruit are not distinct in their essential nature as separate fruit and cause;
the passage beginning with "yāvat" and ending with "kulaputra" is an address to Maitreya.
"In brief" means "in extreme brevity.

In the world-systems of the ten directions—namely, the countable world-systems situated in the cardinal directions such as the east—and likewise in the innumerable [world-systems], there are Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who *abide* because they do not move from their Dharmakāya; they *endure* because they are sustained by their Saṃbhogakāya in the Akaniṣṭha heaven through their teachings; and they *sustain themselves* through their Nirmāṇakāya by leading sentient beings to the attainment of heaven and liberation (apavarga).

Coming at the three times and during the three junctions of the day, they worship that master who teaches the *Guhyasamāja* with the offerings of all the Tathāgatas and with offerings of body, speech, and mind; then they depart for their own buddha-fields.
They utter and chant a collection of words beginning with "Thus he is our father," and so forth.
The passage beginning with "Just as if... is easy to understand.

Being afraid, he wondered about the cause of his terror: "How should the Teacher be viewed by all the Tathāgatas? This apprehension arises because doubt regarding one who occupies a venerable position carries great fault.
For this very reason, he remained silent.

Since Maitreya received no reply through his silence, [the text] says "Then," and so forth, showing how he addressed other Bodhisattvas for the sake of having that [teaching] recited, and how they again revealed the true nature of the Great Vajradhara.

"Taking as an object the pledges (*samaya*) for the accomplishment of all Vajradharas" refers to the sixth reality (*tattva*), which is to be indicated by the *vajramaṇi*. Because it is maintained through the nature of emission and entry, he is "Vajradhara," the Lord of the Mandala. His "accomplishment-pledges" (*siddhi-samaya*) are his emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*). "All those [who are] the accomplishment-pledges of Vajradhara" means all the Vajradharas who are accomplishment-pledges; "taking them as an object" means making them manifest. Having entered that indivisible meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that, he addressed those Bodhisattvas, Akṣobhya and the others, with the words beginning "May they listen! and so forth.
Having heard the words of the Tathāgata, [the author], showing what the Bodhisattvas ask again, says in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: "Then," and so forth.
"The siddhi of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas" refers to the question of the Bodhisattvas: "Where do the emanation-forms whose nature consists of all Tathāgatas abide?"

The secret of the three bodies (*trikāyaguhya*) refers to the body, speech, and mind of the Vajra Master abiding as the body, speech, and mind [of the Buddhas]; this is the response that they abide as the body, speech, and mind of Akṣobhya.
The question is: "Where does the garment of body, speech, and mind abide? The response is: "Nowhere."

Regarding the phrase "they abide in the vajra of the *bodhicitta*," although it should have been stated that they "abide in the vajra of body, speech, and mind," the expression "nowhere" (*na kutracit*) is used because it is impossible to state specifically where [they abide], as it is to be understood through the guru’s oral instruction.
Showing how the Bodhisattvas thus became free from doubt, he says "Then," and so forth.
They were "struck with wonder" (*āścaryaprāptāḥ*) toward the Teacher, and "struck by amazement" (*adbhutaprāptāḥ*) toward its cause.

Now, Maitreya, beginning from the words "Then indeed" up to the end of the passage "not abiding anywhere," this collection of texts demonstrates the following meaning: just as the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have attained perfection have honored and revered the Lord of the Maṇḍala, Akṣobhya, by praising him with sweet words such as "He is the teacher of the *Samāja*, he is our father, and so forth," and having worshipped him with external and internal offerings; likewise, whoever explains the *Śrī-samāja* by relying upon the supreme non-duality according to the method of the narrative known as the sevenfold ornament—him too, future Vajrapāṇis shall regard as the Great Vajradhara himself and worship him with respect. This is the point shown.
Illuminating this very point, the *Śrī-māyājāla-mahātantrarāja* states: "How should the teacher be viewed? The Guru is equal to all Buddhas;
he is the King who holds all vajras, the Tathāgata Ratnaketu."
One should always accept the virtues of the teacher and never his faults;
by accepting virtues, success will be attained, whereas by focusing on faults, one's success is lost.
Therefore, by all means, those who desire the fruit of Buddhahood should worship him with devotion; he is the bestower of inconceivable fruits to all.
Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the *Mahāmahāyānaratnarājasūtra*, the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, seated on Mount Oḍḍiyāna, addressed all those trained in the Vajrayāna:
"Listen, all you who are trained in the Vajrayāna! You shall no longer see the Tathāgata who has entered parinirvāṇa as the Teacher; rather, the Vajrācārya is the Vajra-Guru."
Thus, he is the Teacher.
Therefore he says: "Having relied upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) in the presence of the venerable Lākṣī-bhaṭṭārikā, [one attains] the enlightenment of a Buddha."
"Then," and so forth.

At the time of the Bodhisattva’s vibration, having become of the nature of clear light (*prabhāsvara*), immediately thereafter Vajrapāṇi—the Tathāgata Akṣobhya—and the Guhyavajra Tathāgatas dissolve; that is, they are absorbed into the Guhyavajra-samādhi, which is the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as explained in the sixteenth chapter. Having arisen from that, he again becomes Dveṣavajra as before, and after addressing the Tathāgatas and others with the words "Listen! and so forth, he taught the Samādhi-maṇḍala.
"All Tathāgatas" refers to the Great Yogin who has ascended to the stage of the completion process (*niṣpannakrama*).
His "bodhicitta" is that from which the maṇḍala originates—
that is, its source or place of birth— and he invited [the assembly] to hear that name, the indestructible samādhi-maṇḍala, the mental maṇḍala.
To show how the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, satisfied by the words of the Blessed One, entreated the Blessed One with their speech, he says, "Then, indeed," and so forth.

Having heard that, Mahāvajradhara said, "The sphere of space," and so forth. The "sphere of space" (*khadhātu*) is the element of ether (*ākāśadhātu*). "Situated in the center" refers to the mandala which is square; "square" means that in it there are four corners, and it is that square body-mandala (*kāyamaṇḍala*)—possessing Locanā and the others whose natures are earth and the other elements—which is most beautiful and non-ordinary, that one should contemplate, i.e., meditate upon.

"By means of the yoga of the Buddha-maṇḍala" means that this very body is the Buddha-maṇḍala, consisting of the five secret realities (*tattva*). Yoga is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose essence is that [maṇḍala]. "Meditation-vajra" (*dhyānavajra*): it is called "meditation" (*dhyāna*) because it is meditated upon—that is, contemplated—by yogins; it is "Akṣobhya" because he is joined with the sixth [consciousness]; and he is a "vajra" because he impels that [meditation].
The meaning is that one should emit [the seed-syllable] and cause it to enter [the body], making them one with oneself like milk and water.

The Vajra-maṇḍala is the Akṣobhya-maṇḍala; the sequence for the arrangement of deities therein is meditation (*dhyāna*). By means of that meditation on the Vajra-maṇḍala, the placement of the seats for all the wheel-holders (*cakrin*)—that is, the deities of the maṇḍala—must be performed.
Having thus visualized the common body-maṇḍala, he speaks of what is to be done, beginning with "the worship" (*pūjām*), and so forth.

By that very procedure—the procedure of the mind-maṇḍala—the wise one should always perform, that is, carry out, the worship characterized by meditative union (*samāpatti*) together with his own mudrā.
He states "the preceptor" and so forth, meaning that one should perform the initiation of the disciple precisely while the worship has been commenced.

One who causes those who practice their own conduct (*svacaryā*) to fall—that is, to attain—their own state is the Preceptor (*ācārya*), namely Mahāvajradhara. Having meditated upon him correctly within the heart, in the lotus of the heart (*hṛtpuṇḍarīka*), one should perform the mental initiation.
Regarding "the space-element" (*khadhātu*) and so forth:

Having visualized the space-element as the source of phenomena (dharmodaya), completely filled with all the Buddhas stationed like a mind-mandala, one should visualize and meditate upon the disciple being consecrated in its center.

Immediately thereafter, one should cause all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, beginning with Vairocana, to descend upon the head of the disciple by means of the three syllables, *oṃ* and so forth, which constitute the three stages of consecration and abide within the regulation of breath (*prāṇāyāma*), thereby causing them to attain the state of the *bodhicittavajra*. One should meditate on them as having descended once they have fallen.
Regarding the benefits of the consecration, he says "by this" and so forth.

By means of performing this consecration, the consecrated disciple becomes fit for the benefit of all sentient beings and attains the *nirvāṇa* established in enlightenment; for the sake of others, there is the attainment of prosperity, and in this very life, there is the great wonder of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).

The "accomplishments" (*siddhi*) are the qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers and so forth; by means of these, the body, speech, and mind attain a great wonder and excellence, and thus they are accomplished—that is, they reach perfection—constituting the fulfillment of one's own welfare.

All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, such as Vairocana and Kṣitigarbha, enter into union with the *samaya* exactly as it is through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). That which is produced by meditative concentration alone for the purpose of conferring empowerment upon awakened beings is the "indestructible mandala of meditative concentration."

Again, introducing the manner of the sin of suppressing the wicked, he says "Then," and so forth. Vajrapāṇi is the teacher. The phrase "again" indicates the connection with one who delights in the cruel rites described in the thirteenth and fourteenth chapters. "The Vajra of the Yoga of All Tathāgatas" refers to all virtuous persons; those who go to *tathatā* (suchness) or the five [skandhas] are the "All Tathāgatas. Those of cruel disposition—[the text describes] their "Yoga-Vajra," which is the means of suppression. That body, speech, and mind, the secret which produces the body and so forth, the three imperishables (*akṣara*), he should emit from his own body and so forth.
HŪṂ HRĪḤ KHAṂ
"Khadhātu," and so forth.

First, the practitioner, having perceived his own body as consisting of bone, flesh, and sinew, should contemplate it as situated within the space-element (*khadhātu*) and entered into the clear light (*prabhāsvara*). Then, for the sake of accomplishing Vajrasattva—the Vajraḍāka of great strength and prowess—he should meditate upon the threefold heart of body, speech, and mind; that is, the three syllables consisting of the seeds of body, speech, and mind, which were just mentioned. He should visualize these.

Then, one should meditate upon the fierce, deformed, and enraged [deity], intent on consuming impure blood, possessing a luster like that of a blue lotus, according to the four-armed arrangement to be described later by the method of the present context. Having thus visualized his own form as the Ḍāka, the mantra-practitioner (mantrī) asks what he should do next; to this, the text says "five rays" and so forth. The five rays are the five seed-syllables of wind, fire, and the other elements, namely *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *ha*. The practitioner (vratī) should visualize his own tongue—shining intensely, illuminated by those rays which are black and so forth—as having the form of a five-pronged vajra.
"By means of the application of the meditation-vajra" means that the tongue-vajra, visualized according to the sequence just described, is that meditation-vajra.
Its application is as follows.

Having uttered the five seed-syllables (*bījapañcaka*) and caused the five rays of light to enter the heart of the victim, one draws out the blood from all his limbs like an owl; seeing him reduced to mere skin and bone, one withdraws the rays and causes them to enter one’s own body, meditating that they have been poured into oneself—this is the supreme extraction of blood.
By means of this very vajra-yoga, through the description of the weapon held in the hand, he introduces another application, beginning with "the trident," and so forth.

On the right, in the first [hand] is a trident, and in the second is the "supreme dreadful" (*dāruṇottama*), meaning a dreadful *kīlaka* with a single-pointed face. In the first [hand], a skull-cup has already been mentioned. By means of the Vajrayoga—that is, by means of the yoga of Vajraḍāka—the practitioner pierces and afflicts even the Buddha-body, the body of a Tathāgata, with these weapons;
how much more so an ordinary body? This is the excellence of the application.
Now, beginning with "atha," etc.

"Furthermore" (*punarapi*) recalls the previously mentioned time for eating and the previously mentioned [deities]. "Vajras" refers to the practitioners; their "time for eating" (*āhāra-samaya*) is the body of food. One should perform therein the duty that he brought forth from his own body and so forth.

The practitioner, whether of any of the three types of observances (*vratin*), should eat food such as *śāli* rice or drink beverages such as milk; all of that, according to the rule, should be combined with feces, urine, and flesh. Having first purified the heart and throat, one should contemplate the essence of the consumed food and drink as it transforms into the nature of chyle, flesh, and so forth, and imagine the remainder as being of the nature of feces and urine.
This is the first, internal (*ādhyātmika*) fire sacrifice (*homa*).
"Then," and so forth:
all Tathāgatas, whose intrinsic nature is Vairocana and the others, are all sentient beings because of the statement "all-victorious" (*sarvajaya*), which refers to the essence of the five Buddhas.
One should cause to emerge from one's own body and so forth the supreme offering—the most excellent form of worship—consisting of the body, speech, and mind of those [beings].
The five offerings are the five sense objects; with the most excellent worship of these—namely, with pleasing sense objects—one should worship oneself and these others.
This is the rule for all Vajras, a commitment (*samaya*) that is difficult to transgress and not to be violated by any yogins.
Having thus explained the common worship, he introduces the special worship by saying "Now," and so forth.
All the Tathāgatas just mentioned should proclaim the secret and hidden essence of the worship of their body and so forth:

by means of the application of the two organs, through the union of the vajra and the lotus, and by taking up one's own semen and so forth, with the great passion of one's own mind, one should—through the process of the *kalala* and other stages—continuously produce sons, grandsons, and so on, and worship them by properly performing the rites of protection, nourishment, and so forth, thereby gathering them in.
By doing thus, one shall attain the awakening of a Buddha.
Having thus described the worship of oneself and others, and having introduced the worship of the entire realm of sentient beings without exception, he says "Then," and so forth:
"Just as they came at the time of birth, so too do they depart at the time of destruction"—thus, all sentient beings are the Tathāgatas;
[this refers to] the restraint of body, speech, and mind.
The protection and favor for those yogins was emitted by the Blessed One through his own body and so forth;
[he emitted] Locanā as the mother of the infinite realm of sentient beings, the multitude of beings such as those born from eggs.
Which one?

He says that the earth is of such a nature: it is the "holder of the *samaya*" (*samayadhāriṇī*), because it sustains the three states—arising, abiding, and destruction—which are the *samaya* of sentient beings. One should desire that earth, the holder of the *samaya*, together with the entire realm of sentient beings.
"By the three vajra-samayas" means by one's own auspicious activities of body, speech, and mind, which are endowed with benefit and happiness; one should desire, delight, and favor [others].
This is the "samaya of the assembly," which is most extraordinary because it involves the gathering of a great multitude of sentient beings. It is even more distinguished [than other samayas].
Having thus explained the modes of worship, he says "atha" and so forth to demonstrate their purification:

because they are the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhyupakaraṇa*), the methods of worship just described are all means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). Their "taking up" (*samādāna*) is the vow (*saṃvara*); its essence is the *vajra*. One should emit that [vajra].

The remainder [of the meaning] is: one should resolve (*adhimucyet*) that whatever activity of body and so forth occurs within the rituals of worship—that enjoyment of body, speech, and mind—is born from the *vajra* of the abode of the three secrets and arises from the clear light (*prabhāsvara*).

Having thus resolved, what should one do? He says: "I shall accomplish"—one should generate firm resolve, thinking, "I shall accomplish, that is, attain, the auspicious state of Buddhahood and the state of Vajradhara.

If one does not act in this way, then what happens? He says: "One would destroy," and so forth; one would render all the accumulations for enlightenment fruitless because of being characterized by objective apprehension (*sopalambha*).
Having thus demonstrated the practitioner’s engagement with the realm of sentient beings, he speaks again—beginning with "Then," etc.—to show the nourishment of his own body.

That which accomplishes everything such as all-buddhahood is the "all-accomplishing own body. Its "vajrasattva-vow" (*vajrasattvasaṃvara*) is the means for achieving Vajrasattva; that is the vajrasattva-vow. One should emit it, [visualizing it] at the distance of a span (*vitasti*), and so forth.

One should first perform the visualization and meditation (*bhāvanā*) of a moon disc arising from the transformation of the syllable *vaṃ* in the sky above one’s own head. Then, having meditated upon the syllable *oṃ*, which represents entry, situated in the center of that moon disc, the descent of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) should be performed.

They are called "nectars" (*amṛta*) because they do not die; thus, the five nectars are the Tathāgatas. Their descent should be performed as a consecration (*abhiṣeka*) from the crown of the head down to the soles of the feet, by way of the nature of the five rays of light.

By this aforementioned vajra-yoga, which has the Tathāgata as its focal point, one becomes radiant and possessed of a beautiful body; one attains stability of the body and so forth in an instant, without delay—this is the benefit.
Now, beginning with the word "atha" (then), he describes the activity of one who has attained the stage of completion (*niṣpannakrama*) and has entered the practice of Mahāmudrā.

That which contains all secret mantras is the *sarvamantra*, the *samāja*; he who upholds it is the *sarvamantradhara*, the practitioner of the *samāja* (*sāmājika*), the great yogin. One should cause the secret of his body, speech, and mind—the secret of the activity of the body and so forth—to issue forth from one's own body and so on.

One should not perform the ritual of a *caitya*—the act of worshipping stupas made of clay, sand, and so forth—because it is improper for one who is oneself the essence of all *Tathāgatas* to be attached to the worship of a *caitya*. Nor should one engage in the recitation of books, because for one who is constantly engaged in *vajrajāpa* without effort, it is not appropriate to be occupied with other activities such as study and the like.
Likewise, one should not construct an external mandala;
for, having explained the mandala of one's own body, there is no mention of an external mandala in reality within the *Daśapaṭala-ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā*.

The "foremost of the three vajras" are the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; one should not perform prostration—that is, the pacification—by means of their body and so forth, because that would contradict one's own nature as all the Tathāgatas.

All of this should be performed by resorting to worldly convention (*lokaprajñapti*); it is indeed not contradictory when done without attachment. Thus, introducing the remainder of the minor rites (*kṣudrakarma*) mentioned in the fifteenth chapter, he says "Now," and so forth.

One should expel all poison—whether stationary (*sthāvara*) or mobile (*jaṅgama*), and of light varieties—from the body and other parts by means of its removal and so forth. This is as follows: "situated in the center of a wheel," and so on. One who is overcome by poison is situated within the center of a wheel; he stands in the hub of an eight-spoked wheel arisen from the white *praṇava* (syllable *oṃ*), which is dense with the rays of the moon. His body is pervaded by yellow-colored poisonous energies, yet his head is covered by a white wheel itself. One should visualize that the yellow radiance is being gradually removed by the masses of its rays, and thus one should render him free of poison. This is the removal of poison. [The phrase] "yellowish" refers to this.
One should meditate on all this as yellow in color with the intention of immobilizing; this is the immobilization of poison (*viṣastambhana*).
Having meditated on all this as smoke-colored, whatever one restrains, that should be transferred elsewhere; thus the extraction of poison (*viṣāpakarṣaṇa*) is explained.

By means of the pledges of the rays of the three vajras—through the application of white, yellow, and smoke-colored rays—this seed-syllable *oṃ*, which arises from the secret [place], should be meditated upon as established in the reality of the removal of poison and so forth.
Thus, for the sake of protecting the practitioner who has employed [mantras] such as those for removing poison, he says "atha" and so forth.

For the purpose of protecting body, speech, and mind, one should emanate from the body and so on the *cakra* (wheel), its *mantravajra*—the essence of the mantra—which begins with the syllable *oṃ* and ends with *phaṭ*, known as the *nirantara*. Having drawn an eight-spoked wheel on birch bark or similar material, established upon a *karmavajra* and situated within the hub (*varaṭaka*) of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and having placed the syllable *phaṭ* in the center—that is, having written the syllable *phaṭ* located at the navel of the wheel—one should write the name of the person to be protected in its middle.

One should worship it by placing it at all times within a casket or similar container— having properly adorned it with the syllables and words of the mantra beginning with *oṃ* in their correct sequence, and beautified at the joints of the spokes—
with the [mantra]: *yoṃ* on the first spoke, and *hulu hulu* on the second.
Stay, stay! Bind, bind in the third! Kill, kill in the fourth! [Kill] in the fifth!
The arrangement of the mantra syllables is as follows: *daha daha* in the sixth, *amṛte* in the seventh, and *hūṃ phaṭ* in the eighth spoke.
Thus, the arrangement of the protection wheel is the secret of the body, speech, and mind for practitioners of all mantras; it is their abode, their compendium, and the collection of protections.
Now, demonstrating the application of vajra-gnosis at the conclusion of the ritual activity, he says "atha" and so forth.
Vajrāñjana, because it is unfailing in rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like, is itself the *pada*—the foundation—being the locus of all perfections; one should bring that forth.

This is the instruction for the well-known practitioner’s site, such as a crossroads, which is called the "place of the vajra collyrium" (*vajrāñjanapada*) and so forth: having prepared a wick made from the fiber of a lotus stalk infused with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should place it in the middle of a skull-hearth filled with fat; then, having placed a skull-bowl filled with wine upon that [skull], one should recite the previously mentioned wheel-mantra one hundred and eight times.

On a lunar day coinciding with a Tuesday (bhūtadina), at midnight, the practitioner, seated upon a skull-throne, shall perform protection according to the procedure taught for the *ājñā-cakra* and cause the collyrium (*kajjala*) to fall; this is the ritual procedure for the "Vajra-Collyrium" (*vajrāñjana*). Then, having taken that collyrium and placed it in a casket, one should recite that same mantra one hundred and eight times.
There are three kinds of accomplishment: superior, middling, and inferior.

Regarding that, the Blessed One Samantabhadra has said: "In this context, invisibility is the highest [attainment], seeing treasures buried in the earth is the middling, and subjugation is the lowest accomplishment."
Then the compiler, manifesting the majesty of the tantra, said:

"Then all the Blessed Tathāgatas spoke thus to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas: 'Blessed One, with how many secret syllables are those Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas endowed who will have faith in and cultivate this secret samaya of all the Tathāgatas? Thus they questioned the Blessed One."

Then Vajrapāṇi spoke thus to all those Tathāgatas: "O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, those Bodhisattvas who shall have faith in and cultivate this Vajra of the Awakening Conduct of all Tathāgatas"—this was the response.

All the Tathāgatas asked: "By which three? This was the further inquiry. Vajradhara replied: "By the Body-Vajra of all Tathāgatas, by the Speech-Vajra of all Tathāgatas, and by the Mind-Vajra of all Tathāgatas—by these three. This was the response.
Then all those Tathāgatas, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi, remained silent.

To show that even for the Tathāgatas whose doubts had thus been dispelled, the Tantra is difficult to obtain—thereby increasing their faith—the Tathāgatas spoke otherwise; demonstrating this, he said: "Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, addressed those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas."

In the past, O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable Buddha-fields, even until the passing of the Blessed Tathāgata Dīpaṅkara, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, and even after the Great Sage Kāśyapa had attained perfect awakening, this was not spoken. For what reason?

"Sentient beings, O Blessed Ones, were incapable [of understanding] this matter of the great secret; therefore, at that time and on that occasion, it was not spoken. Having thus introduced the past narrative with the words "In the past... and so forth, he demonstrated the non-occurrence [of its teaching] following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata Kāśyapa.
Then, with the words "For what reason? and so forth, he asks: for what purpose was it not spoken?

Regarding this, he states the reason: at that time, sentient beings were of inferior inclination (*hīnādhimukti*), to be trained by teachings on detachment such as generosity and ethical discipline, and they possessed the notion of fear toward the profound teaching;
therefore, the Blessed One did not reveal the meaning of the great secret at that time.

At this present time, having observed the inclinations of sentient beings who are characterized by passionate conduct (*rāgacarita*) and are agitated by the five corruptions (*pañcakaṣāya*), the Tathāgata has come and taught [this] exclusively.

However, some might have the apprehension that Buddhahood is attained by this [other means]; therefore, to dispel that, he says: "Moreover, O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas accomplish the awakening of a Buddha in this *Guhyasamāja* in a mere instant, a moment, or a brief duration (*kṣaṇa-lava-muhūrta*).

That awakening which Bodhisattvas do not attain even after striving and exerting themselves for many eons equal to the sands of the river Ganges—herein, in this very life, a Bodhisattva devoted to the *Guhyasamāja* comes to be reckoned as a 'Buddha' among all the Tathāgatas."

The meaning is this: that one accomplishes the awakening of a Buddha in a mere instant, a fraction of a moment, or a brief hour, by entering the ultimate truth through the process of internal realization, washing away all the impurities of the kalpa, and then, in just a moment, a fraction of a moment, or a blink of an eye, arising through the process of self-consecration (*svādhiṣṭhāna-krama*) and becoming connected with every form of excellence.

In this *Śrī Guhyasamāja*, having heard that those who have realized the reality attain Buddhahood in this very life, even in this present existence, the listeners such as Candana and others—despite having heard the tantra in its entirety from the text and despite not having abandoned their delusion regarding the meaning of the tantra through the analysis of the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭi*)—were not satisfied. Demonstrating this, [the text] says: "Then those Bodhisattvas, having heard these syllables of the speech-vajra, wept."

Seeing those of dull faculties thus distressed in mind and weeping, the jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*), who were confident in both [the conventional and ultimate], comforted them accordingly; to demonstrate this, it says: "Then all those Tathāgatas spoke thus to those Bodhisattvas: 'O Blessed Bodhisattvas, do not weep, and do not cultivate the three types of suffering. Having been thus consoled by the jewel-like persons, Candana and the others announced the cause of their own suffering; to demonstrate that, it says: "Then those Great Bodhisattvas spoke thus to all those Tathāgatas."
O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, why do we not weep?
Why do we not manifest the three types of suffering?
For what reason?

The Blessed Ones are of noble nature (*suabhavya*), having reached the end within the three secret syllables; that vision [is attained] even without hearing [them]. Regarding the "three sufferings," these are the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkha*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛtaduḥkha*).

Alternatively, they are the sufferings of body, speech, and mind. The "three secret syllables" refers to the body, speech, and mind as the three secrets; the meaning of the syllables is the three syllables, which are the three secrets. The complete assembly of limbs, swift, unobstructed, and tearful, is the triple secret (*triguhya*).
The embryo is the realization of wisdom and means; these three secrets are the *kolika* [ultimate] secret syllables.

Thus, illuminating this purity, he said: "O sons of good family, all the Tathāgatas have declared this common syllable. Just as it has not been known or heard by you, so too, O sons of good family, it has not been attained nor fully realized by us—all the Tathāgatas and all the Bodhisattvas—regarding that secret syllable. Why is that? Because of the purity of the three secret syllables."

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: "Then all those bodhisattvas became silent. This means that as for what was neither known nor heard by you—that which is common to us and all the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas—why have you not attained those secret syllables? Because there is no object to be grasped (*grāhya*), they were not fully awakened; because there is no subject who grasps (*grāhaka*), why is that?
For what reason?
Because it is purified by the secret syllable, the secret syllable is the clear light (*prabhāsvara*); because they have been purified by that, the *tathāgatas* have illuminated reality (*tattva*).

Thus, for those jewel-like persons (*ratnapudgala*) who possess instantaneous understanding (*udghaṭitajña*), their doubts were removed. Candana and the others, whose wisdom was previously stagnant, having realized reality, became tranquil. To show what specific state they attained, he says: "Then those bodhisattvas became silent."
It is not without a hidden meaning (*nāsandhyam*).

In order to demonstrate the fruit for those Bodhisattvas who have become free from doubt through the word of the Tathāgata, [the text] shows how the five Tathāgatas became sixfold in essence; demonstrating this, it says: "Then the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, dwelt within the wombs (*bhaga*) of the Vajra Ladies (*yoṣit*) of the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas"—the meaning of which has been analyzed.

Thus, showing how the four consorts—whose minds were longing due to separation from him and who desired a vision of Mahāvajradhara, whose nature is such luminosity—lamented piteously, it is said: "Then the consorts of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas praised the Blessed One, Mahāvajradhara, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, with affection. Here, "all Tathāgatas" refers to Vairocana.

His beloved, Locanā, who is dear to his body, speech, and mind, praised him with affection and, desiring union, exhorted him with the *āṣāḍha* and other notes in a voice that was plaintive, charming, and sweet; she addressed him with the words "You" (*tvam*), as if imagining him standing before her, and spoke thus: "O Vajracitta"—so called because he has attained mastery over the mind and has reached the sovereignty over the Dharma of the two realms; "Lord of the World" (*bhuvaneśvara*), because the realm of sentient beings consists of the essence of all beings; and "Rati," because it is play.

Therefore, because it is pleasing to the mind and generates delight, it is "pleasing to the mind" (*ratimanojña*); because it is of great significance, it is "supreme bliss" (*mahārtha-paramānanda*). Those who desire and bring this about are "those who desire the great significance" (*mahārthakāmāḥ*). With such [beings] who desire the great significance that is pleasing to the mind through embraces and so forth, protect me; take your pleasure with me, for you are the progenitor of all beings as the cause of their arising, and the supreme kinsman of sentient beings because you bring about their welfare and happiness. O Lord, my master, desire me—take your pleasure with me. Furthermore, in order to demonstrate his awakening, he says:
"Then," and so forth:

the mind of all Tathāgatas is Akṣobhya; his beloved consort is the noble Māmakī, who is the supreme offering of vajra-love-play, characterized by the engagement in extraordinary and distinguished sexual union.
He praised him with words and phrases indicative of that [nature]:

"Because your body is indestructible, you are the Vajra-body; because you turn the wheel of commands beloved by many beings, you are the one who acts for the benefit of many beings; and because you turn the wheel of commands, you are the one who perceives the welfare of others through the ultimate meaning of awakening for the sake of the Buddhas."

The Buddhas are the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); their object is conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), while awakening (*bodhi*) is ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). The embodiment of the great bliss born from the union of these two truths is the form of the Seventeenth Chapter and the Sixfold Commentary. Because he reveals this with the intention of benefiting sentient beings, he is the "Beholder of Benefit.

Through passion—in the form of the purification of passion—please desire me, who am the pledge of passion (*rāgasamaya*) and whose nature is fashioned by passion; please delight me. Now, etc.: Lokeśvara is Amitābha; his guide of body, speech, and mind is Pāṇḍaravāsinī. She urges the Great Vajradhara: "O Vajra-Speech! you [should act].

Because he has attained mastery over speech, he is compassionate toward the entire realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*), possessing a nature of supreme mercy; for this very reason, he is always and at all times correctly engaged in accomplishing the welfare of beings through the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
"Desire me, enjoy me with the practice of sexual union"—he is Samantabhadra because he brings about the auspiciousness and well-being of the entire realm of sentient beings.
Another [deity] is Vibhakta, Amoghasiddhi, who is the Vajra of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas;

his beloved wife is Tārā. Having restrained the Great Vajradhara—who possesses the activity of one hundred and sixty intrinsic natures—within the sleep of gnosis and seeing him entered into total emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*), she awakens him, saying, "O Vajrakāma!"
He speaks by means of the gate of Amoghasiddhi; through the union of the vajra and the lotus,

he is the Vajrakāma because he purifies the realm of sentient beings whose conduct is dominated by hatred and so forth by means of the deities of the maṇḍala who have been emitted, and because he is the lord of the Karma-kula.
The foremost of commitments (*samayāgra*), he bestows liberation through the means of purifying passion for those beings who are dominated by passion; thus, he is of great benefit.

Because he is the preeminent ornament (*tilaka*) among those born of the Śākya lineage, he is the "Ornament of the Lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones" (*saṃbuddhavaṃśatilaka*). Alternatively, because he accomplishes the welfare of the entire world through his nature as the gnosis of the performance of activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), he is the "Ornament of the Lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones."
Because he possesses compassion for sentient beings even while being free from the perception of the distinction between self and other, he is "one whose compassion is equal.
O you who are distinguished by such qualities, please accept me— me who am a treasury of virtues and a source of many jewels— and take me as your consort.
Because she produces the luminous gnosis (*prabhāsvara-jñāna*) characterized by passion, dispassion, and intermediate passion, she praises herself, saying: "If you desire life, O Mañjunātha.
The intended meaning is: "Be victorious through the bestowal of the life-force of Vajrasattva by means of the purification of passion, hatred, and delusion."

Thus, being exhorted by the goddesses whose nature is the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*), and arising from the yoga of emptiness through the power of the continuity of his former vows, he manifested the conduct of passion for the bliss of glorious sexual union. Through the acts of embracing, kissing, adorning, horripilation, striking, biting, scratching, rubbing, swinging, piercing, and vulgar acts, and through the enchantment [of the senses], the sounds of his moving pearl necklaces, bracelets, armlets, earrings, and anklets, and the union of the vajra and lotus—the meeting of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*)—from the intoxication of the vowels and consonants (*āli-kāli*), he tasted the bliss of supreme joy (*paramānanda*) via the path of passion and illusion (*ratimāyādhvani*) by stimulating the three channels (*nāḍī*) of the tortoise-neck and full moon with the movement of his fingers. Then, having caused all the Tathāgatas, whose nature consists of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), to melt from his head in the form of a continuous stream, he established them in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) in the form of the essence of enlightened mind (*bodhicitta*). From that, in order to purify beings who engage in conduct such as hatred, he emitted the mandala circle; then, re-entering the clear light (*prabhāsvara*), he attained the state of non-conceptuality.

In the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*, elucidating this very point, it says: "Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi, entered the meditative absorption named 'The Splendor of the Enjoyment of All Desires'; desiring that beloved of all Tathāgatas by means of the wheel of the pledge (*samayacakra*), he became silent."

All desires are the objects such as forms and so forth; their enjoyment consists in the unification [of the senses] with the eyes and other faculties through the thorough knowledge of their intrinsic nature. Having entered—that is, attained—the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named after that state of abiding in the bliss of glorious *samatānanda*, the Lord of the Tathāgatas, desiring and delighting in her who is the beloved of all Tathāgatas, whose nature is Locanā and the others, by means of the *samaya*-wheel which has the essence of Vairocana and the rest, became silent, meaning he was devoid of activities such as teaching, and remained in meditative union (*samāpatti*) together with the *jñānamudrā*. This is the sense.

Then, immediately following the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) with the Knowledge-Seal (*jñānamudrā*), this entire expanse of space (*ākāśadhātu*) became filled by the Samaya-Wheel of the Body, Speech, and Mind of all Tathāgatas, like a vessel of Vajra-water.

The meaning is that this cavity of the sky, consisting of the nature of the Vajra-holder, was filled by the assembly of Tathāgatas beginning with Vairocana joined with the three Vajras; being as dense as sesame seeds or *śimśapā* fruits, it remained motionless like a vessel of Vajra-water, like a flask of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*).

Thus, demonstrating what is to be done for the sake of sentient beings while the Blessed One was in meditative equipoise, he said: "Then, in this adamantine space-element (*vajrākāśadhātu*), those sentient beings who had arisen from the three bodies (*trikāya*), being touched by Vajraśrī, all became Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, possessing the three adamantine gnoses (*trivajrajñāna*).
This is the meaning of this [passage].

In the realm of the Vajra-Space, those beings within the three worlds who were born from the three bodies (*trikāya*) and possessed the nature of the three vajras—having been touched by and made objects of the Great Vajra-holder’s splendor and bliss—attained the state of all Tathāgatas. They experienced the gnoses of that Great Vajra-holder, the Three-Vajra One, such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth.

From that time forward—that is, beginning from the empowerment by light rays—they were consecrated by the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas; thus they became Samantabhadras, possessing the name "Samantabhadra" according to its true meaning.

Having thus consecrated all sentient beings with the empowerment of gnosis and demonstrated the equality of all beings, he spoke as follows to reveal what they desired: "Then the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi said this to all those Tathāgatas: 'O Blessed Ones, all Tathāgatas, have you seen the equality of all phenomena? Then all those Tathāgatas said this to Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign of all Tathāgatas: 'We have seen it, Blessed One; we have seen it, Sugata—the conduct of the vajra-gnosis of all Tathāgatas.'"

In this regard, for the Great Vajradhara who is all the Tathāgatas, the practice of vajra-gnosis consists precisely in the acceptance of the meditative absorption-bliss of all sentient beings through the experience of the bliss of his own meditative absorption.

Having thus experienced the practice of the Blessed One’s vajra-gnosis, and having again emerged from meditative absorption, the Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, spoke to the Blessed One Mahāvajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, with delighted minds, as follows, demonstrating what they said: "O Blessed One, it is marvelous! O Sugata, it is marvelous! For indeed, it is marvelous that the awakening of a Buddha is to be realized through the syllables and words of passion! [This concludes] the sixteenth chapter of the *Ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyā* [commentary]. The Blessed Ones, all the Tathāgatas, having emerged from the wombs (*bhaga*) of the women, addressed the Blessed One Mahāvajrapāṇi, the Sovereign of all Tathāgatas, saying: "It is wonderful, O Blessed One; it is wonderful, O Sugata, that the awakening of a Buddha is indeed to be followed through the syllables and words of passion."

For indeed, because by means of the syllables and words of passion—that is, by those whose conduct is characterized by passion—the awakening of all Buddhas, the state of the Great Vajradhara, is to be followed and attained; when they heard this word "marvel" (*āścarya*), which signifies a marvel, they were filled with doubt due to the demonstration of the purification of those very passions and so forth. To demonstrate that, he said: Then Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of all Tathāgatas, spoke thus to all those Tathāgatas: "O Blessed Ones, O all Tathāgatas, do not speak in such a way. For what reason?"

Because all phenomena are equal to the space-vajra commitment (*khavajrasamaya*), there is no aggregate of form, no aggregate of sensation, no element, no sense-field, no passion, no hatred, no delusion, no dharma, and no non-dharma.
The sixth Tathāgata is the Space-Vajra Commitment; because all phenomena are equal to that, do not speak thus—this is for the purpose of eliminating doubt.

The passage beginning with "not the aggregate of form" elaborates upon this very same meaning. Then, "those all Tathāgatas became silent" means that immediately upon the words spoken by the Tathāgata regarding the luminosity of all phenomena, they directly realized that very ineffable nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and remained absorbed in meditation upon it; such is the meaning of the vajra-word.

Having thus concluded the secret teaching, [the text] says the following to demonstrate how he entrusts those beings to be trained to the Tathāgatas: Then the Blessed One Vajrapāṇi addressed all those Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas:
"May the Blessed Ones proclaim this secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas in all world-systems. For what reason?"
"These bodhisattvas situated in the ten directions are worthy of this Dharma-discourse.
Let them announce and proclaim it—the secrets of the body, speech, and mind-vajra of all Tathāgatas.

The two-fold samādhi of the Great Vajradhara and the King of Tantras that reveals it are now worthy of this Dharma-discourse, because they are vessels for the attainment of the state of awakening born of passion.

Having thus demonstrated that beings attached to sense objects are suitable vessels for this tantra, [the Lord] spoke while entrusting the Dharma-tantra to Vajradharma for the sake of revealing it to future beings: "Then Vajrapāṇi, the sovereign of all Tathāgatas, addressed Vajradharma:
'Take up, O son of good family, this reality of the commitment (*samaya*) of all Tathāgatas.
For you have been consecrated by all the Tathāgatas as the Lord of all Dharmas.'"
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vajradharma, having said, "So be it," became silent.
This is its meaning:

This assembly, the reality of the samaya of all Tathāgatas, the samaya descended through the lineage of all Tathāgatas, the inviolable reality, the secret of body, speech, and mind—this I have now revealed; you must grasp it and keep it in your mind.
