For by all the Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana and the others, you have been consecrated, authorized, and empowered as the sovereign lord over their teachings, which consist of the collections of all dharmas, due to your infinite eloquence regarding those dharmas.
And this is because of the authority of Vāgvajra in this teaching.
Having accepted the word of the Blessed One, the Mahāsattva remained silent.

After the entrustment of the tantra, he asks what was done by all the Tathāgatas, who are as numerous as the atoms in ineffable Buddha-fields: "Then all those Tathāgatas caused the body, speech, and mind to enter into the syllables of the three Vajrasattvas.
This is what is meant.

All those belonging to the five families, appearing in emanated forms—the infinite and boundless Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, wrathful kings, and so forth—have attained the state of Vairocana, Amitābha, and Akṣobhya; this is the sense.
In that regard, the Tathāgata Vairocana is the nature of the Body-Vajra of the triple world; demonstrating this, he says: "Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Vairocana," and so forth.

In this abode of the three realms of existence, whatever body belongs to the masses of sentient beings—whether superior, middling, or inferior—such as those born from eggs and so forth, that is Vairocana. This meaning is demonstrated by the phrase "he dwelt within the vajra-bodies of all the triple world," because there is no distinction between the body and Vairocana in terms of container and contained.

Likewise, demonstrating the non-differentiation between the perfected and unperfected bodies, he said: "Having taken recourse to the equality of the bodies of all Tathāgatas, which is like an illusion, he remained silent."
Thus, the meaning is that whatever speech belongs to sentient beings within the three realms is Amitābha.
Alternatively, this is shown by the statement that the Tathāgata Vāgvajra dwells within all the vajras of speech in the three realms.
In exactly the same way, the meaning is that whatever mind belongs to all sentient beings is Akṣobhya.
Then the Tathāgata Vajrapāṇi dwelt within the vajra-minds of the entire triple world; this is shown by the following vajra-word.

Demonstrating that the mind of all Tathāgatas and the mind of all sentient beings are one and the same, he said, up to the conclusion: "Having relied upon the equality of the minds of all Tathāgatas and the unity of the two truths, he remained silent"—this was spoken through the grace of the Guru's feet.
Within the *tantra*, regarding the reality (*dharmatā*) of the method of meaning (*artha-naya*), there is no longer any doubt for me; yet, there is a certain remaining doubt.

Mantrins who are averse to the explanation of the six parameters (*ṣaṭkoṭivyākhyāna*) rely on the literal recitation of the teachings and practice the yoga of the imagined deity according to their own teacher’s tradition, by way of the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisaṃbodhi*), the moon-vajra sequence, or the generation stage (*utpattikrama*).

However, the yoga of the utterly pure deity transcends all conceptual construction; it is to be personally realized, is the domain of the Buddhas, resides within the jewel-casket of the aggregates (*skandha*), is free from the positions of existence and non-existence, is not the object of logicians who follow the literal letter, and is accessible solely through the oral instructions of the Guru.

When the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa and even the compilers such as Vajrapāṇi are no longer present, who is it that, in the final age, maintains the Buddha’s tradition without interruption within the mental continuum of those to be trained (*vineya*), and how does it proceed?

Regarding this, the commentary on the six-fold [tantric] system of the seventeenth chapter states: "The venerable Mañjuśrī also questioned the Tathāgata concerning this future matter in the *Laṅkāvatārasūtra*;
that is now introduced here."
"O Lord, when you have passed away, tell us who will uphold this wisdom that is to be realized within oneself and is beyond the reach of logicians?"

who shall shatter the positions of both existence and non-existence.

Having illuminated in the world the Great Vehicle, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna,
and having attained the stage of Pramuditā, he shall go to Sukhāvatī.

Therefore, by this sequence, even after the Tathāgata has passed into *parinirvāṇa*, as long as the True Dharma (*saddharma*) remains in the world, so long will the realization of the *niṣpannakrama* (completion stage) through the successive stages of *utpattikrama* (generation stage)— relying upon the Mahāyoga-tantra scriptures of the Vajrayāna— be transmitted from the mouth of the Guru through the lineage of Gurus like a treasure, beginning from the venerable master Śrī Nāgārjuna, into the mental continuum of those members of the assembly who are vessels for Buddhahood in this very life. Thus, the venerable master Śrī Nāgārjuna attained his own goal.

Having established in the world the samādhi of the Great Vajradhara—which is to be personally realized—and having transcended the happiness of gods and humans, as well as the bliss of the meditations, samādhis, and attainments of the non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas, he attains the body of a Tathāgata, which is free from arising and destruction, endowed with all excellent aspects, a form that is most pleasing to behold, and adorned with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and other Buddha-qualities; then, having gone to Sukhāvatī, he dwells there possessed of the eightfold sovereign powers.

Having thus removed the conceptualization of the defined and the undefined, and having determined that for one who knows the intrinsic nature there is neither beginning nor end, he now concludes the tantra with the words "Thus," and so forth. Having heard the entire tantra according to the method of the narrative of the sevenfold ornaments, and having realized the reality of the principles of meaning, he has fully revealed it to the listeners by first imparting the instruction on the two stages. Now, completing [the work] for the sake of its preservation and manifesting his own intention regarding the promise, the compiler says: "He said this."

The Great Vajradhara, the Great Bliss, spoke this system of the *Guhyasamāja-tantra*, having revealed it with reference to the secret of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas. This is the chapter titled "The King of the Vajra Empowerment of the Samaya-Vow of All Tathāgatas" within the *Guhyasamāja*, the king of tantras, which is a collection (*samāja*)—a gathering—of secrets.

"All Tathāgatas" refers to Vairocana and the others. Their "pledge" (*samaya*) is the meaning of what is to be practiced, namely the fivefold restraint consisting of protection and so forth; this is the "observance. The fivefold [family] beginning with the Tathāgata family is non-dual; because it is not to be transgressed, it is a "vajra," and its empowerment is the King, Mahāvajradhara. As stated in the *Guhyasamājapradīpodyotana*: he is the essence of all that is wholesome, without beginning or end, the Primordial Buddha (*Ādibuddha*), the embodiment of the Great Knowledge-Man (*Mahāvidyāpuruṣa*), the embodiment of Gnosis (*Jñānamūrti*), whose nature is intrinsic luminosity, the self of the three worlds, the self of the three vehicles, the self of the three vajras, the self of the two truths, and so forth—such are the infinite synonyms of the name of the Sixth Tathāgata.
The entire collection of texts that expounds this, like a chapter (paṭala) as before,
is indeed free from the six extremes (ṣaṭkoṭi-yukti) in the Yoga Tantra; it most excellently expresses the exceedingly subtle word of the Sugata.
For he who perceives only the syllable does not see the reality, just as one desiring to see the moon but looking instead at the finger [pointing to it].

By whatever merit I have acquired through long explaining this tantra— which has been composed by many preeminent men of the world according to the path of the six crores [of verses]— may this commentary, radiant as a lamp, endure for a long time; and by that, may the world, whose intellect is like the moon, attain the supreme state of true bliss.

Thus ends the explanation of the six points (ṣaṭkoṭi) in the seventeenth chapter of the *Pradīpodyotana-ṭīkā*.
And this commentary, the *Pradīpoddyotana*, is completed.
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
This is the religious gift of the novice monk Guṇākarapāla, a follower of the most excellent Mahāyāna.
Whatever merit is herein, may it, preceded by his teachers, preceptors, mother, and father, result in the attainment of the fruit of supreme knowledge for the entire mass of sentient beings.
May there be auspiciousness!
O Great King, supreme lord and supreme follower of the Sugata.
May there be well-being for all sentient beings.
Those which are its *avṛtavya* [verses], the last one is *atantra*.
